Sports.title: Can Hamilton and Verstappen fight back for F1 Brazilian GP victory?
Sports.content:
With Lewis Hamilton and Max Verstappen 20th and 21st on the grid of the Brazilian Grand Prix, Sunday’s Formula 1 race promises to be fascinating – regardless of weather conditions.

Hamilton and Verstappen happen to be two drivers who performed memorable recoveries at Autodromo Jose Carlos Pace, a track where overtaking has always been easier than most.

Back in 2021, the seven-time world champion was excluded from qualifying results due to a technical breach, meaning he started the sprint from last; he fought his way up to fifth. With a five-place grid drop for a new engine, Hamilton was 10th on the grid for the grand prix but battled to the front and came out on top in a titanic duel against Verstappen.

Three years later, the Dutchman was eliminated in Q2 on a wet Sunday morning and also took a five-place grid penalty for his sixth internal combustion engine, ending up 17th on the grid. The rain also impacted the race, but Verstappen rose to the occasion and comfortably overtook Esteban Ocon for victory.

But the DRS device had facilitated Hamilton’s exceptional drives, and the overtake mode that now features on F1’s new power units instead isn’t as decisive; the Interlagos layout might actually make it worse.

When asked how easy overtaking would be compared to 2021, the Ferrari driver replied: “Harder, because back then we had, obviously, a very long straight, and if you got close, you had the DRS, and maybe a car wouldn't have it – whereas now, everyone is just opening up their wings.

“I think overtaking will be very, very, very hard. I'm not sure you're going to see the same sort of races that you've seen in the past. But maybe the wet conditions will change that.”

Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari, Max Verstappen, Red Bull Racing Photo by: Sam Bloxham / LAT Images via Getty Images

“Now we don't have DRS anymore,” Verstappen concurred. “And the overtake mode is very limiting around here because of the long straight, everyone is draining the battery. So, your speed difference on the straight is going to be a lot less – a bit like Mexico, really. So, it will be quite a lot harder to pass than normal.”

So what will Hamilton’s strategy be? “I don't have one,” he responded. “Try to win, somehow.”

Verstappen, meanwhile, is banking on a number of incidents if he is to be a contender for victory. “Lots of safety cars, so they can't pull away, it keeps coming back to me,” the Red Bull racer said. “We'll see. I don't really think about it too much. I'll just go from lap one and see where I end up.”

He added: “I hope [with Lewis] we can clear the cars in front of us as quickly as we can.”

Across 19 grands prix so far in F1 2026, just two races have been won from outside the front row. Verstappen prevailed from fifth on the grid in Mexico, though he was virtually in the lead on lap one, and Antonelli remarkably triumphed from 19th in Italy. But if the expected rain impacts the race, then 2026’s dry-weather history will be meaningless.

Additional reporting by Isa Fernandes and Federico Faturos

Sports.title: The wet-weather challenges thrown up by Brazilian GP qualifying
Sports.content:
One hour, 23 minutes. You could've squeezed most of a football match into the rain delay during Formula 1 qualifying for the Sao Paulo Grand Prix, and it looked for all the world like the session wouldn't actually get going again.

A repeat of 2024, where qualifying was squeezed onto Sunday morning, looked likely. Yet, a saviour arrived when a break in the clouds emerged, and the circuit had dried just enough for safety car specialist Bernd Maylander to give his approval of the conditions. It scarcely stopped a handful of drivers from having a moan about the visibility, but they soon accepted that they needed to lock in and focus up on getting around the track.

This meant the use of the lesser-spotted full-wet tyre, or the "x-wet" per the F1 lexicon. Often derided as a tyre only fit for bumbling around on behind the safety car, the blue-walled Pirelli was actually holding up pretty well and proved perfect for the level of standing water around the circuit. Aquaplaning, where the tyre struggles to break the surface tension of the water on-track, was nonetheless prevalent - but water dispersal as the rain held off soon brought the track to a more driveable state.

The downside of using the extreme wet tyre lies in the greater water dispersal (according to Pirelli, around 85 litres of water per second) which drastically cuts visibility as the spray rooster-tails out the back of the car. Yet, the dispersal is a necessary evil: without it, the circuit would just remain wetter for longer.

Although the rain lights ensure that the driver behind has at least some level of visibility, selecting your braking zone remains tricky; poor visibility means the driver must find a reference point in their immediate circle of vision. Stopping distances are also considerably longer, so a driver needs a different marker to their usual point of pedal application in the dry.

Considering all these climatic challenges, it's small wonder why race control takes a more tentative approach to wet conditions. Hence, it was a welcome surprise to see the session reopened - even if the circuit was still sodden with the afternoon downpour. Carlos Sainz reckoned that it was a "punchy" call from the FIA - but it only took a couple of laps to ensure the cars were more stable.

"It felt a bit punchy when we left on the x-wet because we were aquaplaning in sixth and seventh gear down the straights. And if you lose the car at those speeds, it's always going to be a big one," Sainz concluded after the session.

Carlos Sainz, Williams Photo by: James Sutton / Formula 1 / Formula Motorsport Ltd via Getty Images

"Also, very little visibility when you were running close to a car, but we were not forced to run close to cars in quali, so you can create a bit of a buffer to see. But it was very sketchy for two laps.

"Then we managed to create that little bit of dry line and the tyres started working, the aquaplaning started to go away. Everyone managed to keep the car on track until the end of Q1, which was a bit of a surprise, to be honest."

Liam Lawson agreed with Sainz's view of the session, stating that "when we started, it was extremely sketchy - I think we were definitely pushing it. But I like the fact that we were out there and not in the garage; I think obviously it is risky, but there weren't that many incidents."

As expected, the wet conditions delivered chances to those usually not accustomed to fighting at the top; the free practice performance-chasing was effectively rendered obsolete and the power units had slightly more parity as the effects of top-end performance and acceleration were mitigated by the low-grip track conditions.

This put a bit more of a premium on low-speed downforce and, crucially, keeping the tyres warm across Q1 - although Fernando Alonso nonetheless noted that "the engine is very important in terms of drivability and the way it behaves in the corners, and we still have a little bit of an issue there".

The approach through Q1 was, initially, simply about trying to set clean laps and hope that the progression of the circuit and the tyres would yield a lap-on-lap improvement.

Of course, each driver was tested on their reaction times in the event aquaplaning occurred, and the 2026 power units and the control over the rear brakes added another hurdle to overcome. But each driver (largely) became increasingly dialled in, watched as the laptimes improved, and then started to push the braking zones a little bit more as the circuit dried up.

There was a transition point in Q2, however, as the intermediates soon became the tyre to be on. With less standing water, the full wet was starting to overheat and was giving up performance in the middle part of the lap, initially enough to perhaps offset the dampness through the first and final sectors, before all three became much more suitable for the intermediate overall.

George Russell, Mercedes Photo by: Alastair Staley / LAT Images via Getty Images

This meant that they could chase the track grip more, and it was evident that the times had begun to peak at the end of Q2 as the circuit approached its best conditions under the downpour. Getting the intermediate timing right, which Lawson reckoned he and his Racing Bulls team had nailed, was key to getting a couple of quicker laps in without risking the threat of falling off the circuit.

A few drivers struggled at this crossover, particularly with harvesting and braking into Turn 12 - Sainz and Ollie Bearman both had offs here, as newcomer Rafael Camara couldn't get the car to slow down enough before he careened into the barrier at the close of Q2.

With more rain impending during Q3, it was more about a mad dash to get a clean lap in, rather than watching the progression. That's perhaps when it felt most like 'normal' qualifying, as the tyres were effectively good enough for one lap with the expected downpour setting something of a timer.

It appeared that the majority of the drivers genuinely enjoyed the rare chance to tackle properly wet conditions, although some had a few qualms about the session restarting. George Russell surmised that "I love driving in the rain - but at some point, if that was a race, that was no way we should be driving in it - the chances of seeing a really, really horrific incident is very, very high."

Perhaps there's a bit of a split of opinion between the younger and older drivers; both Lewis Hamilton and Nico Hulkenberg expressed their enjoyment of wet conditions, while new champion Kimi Antonelli labelled them "the wettest conditions I've ever driven [in]. So it was not the nicest of experiences"; both he and Bearman said that the circuit was over the limit at the Q1 restart, although the latter conceded that the early running did at least contribute to the circuit improving.

Regardless, it was valuable data for each of the drivers ahead of Sunday's race - where inclement weather is expected to play a role once again. And so begins the overnight discussions: does anyone risk a pit-lane start for a set-up change?

Sports.title: Why Russell was so angry in Brazilian GP qualifying despite already having a grid penalty
Sports.content:
In keeping with the theme of the Brazilian Grand Prix's weather-hit qualifying, George Russell had a thunderous look on his face when he faced the Formula 1 media in the post-session press conference.

The title has gone and a five-place grid penalty for an engine swap meant Russell was never going to start on the front row on Sunday. But at the end of a challenging year, it was still mentally important to claim another pole - with or without grid penalty - if only to lay the foundations for a stronger 2027.

Interlagos' frantic wet-weather qualifying gave Russell that opportunity. As conditions started to worsen again in Q3, Russell led the first salvo of runs on intermediates, and took four tenths out of Lando Norris' initial benchmark.

Right after setting a lap which was good enough for provisional pole, his race engineer Marcus Dudley urged him to carry on for another lap before conditions worsened: "Push if you can, I think we'll get one more lap before this rain."

Russell then caught the back of Alex Albon's Williams in the second sector, willing his friend out of the way: "Move, Albono!"

But when Dudley suggested Russell would have the opportunity to start one more flyer, confusion set in and a quick call had to be made as he approached Turn 12, the tricky Juncao corner which saw numerous cars slide onto the wet grass.

George Russell, Mercedes, Alexander Albon, Williams Photo by: Manuel Eletto / Getty Images

"You need to tell me, mate, what I'm doing. Am I backing or going?" Russell said over the radio.

The reply came instantly: "We can back up now, back up now," with an unconvinced Russell asking for confirmation.

It was at that very moment that Norris crossed the line for a second timed lap, and took two tenths out of Russell's benchmark to snatch pole away. And with conditions worsening quickly, Russell realised the call to abandon his lap had been wrong, and a chance for a redeeming pole was gone.

After all he had been through already this year, it was not something he took well.

"Mate, you fucking told me to back off. What the hell!" Russell vented. "George, you're P2," was an unsatisfactory intervention from team principal Toto Wolff, with Russell replying: "I don't want to be P2, I want to be P1. That was a P1 lap. Fucking hell."

The short interval between parc ferme and the compulsory top-three press conference did little to dampen his disappointment.

"I think it was just a bit of miscommunication. I needed to speak with the team because we believed we'd get another lap before the rain came in," Russell explained. "I was on a really strong lap and I was asked to back off because I caught up with Albon and then obviously the rain came.

George Russell, Mercedes Photo by: Sam Bloxham / LAT Images via Getty Images

"It was very disappointing. We need to understand how it happened and why we got that wrong. But I felt very strong the whole session. I definitely felt the pole was there for the taking.

"As soon as it was made, I think we knew it was the wrong one because already they could actually feel the rain pouring harder."

Russell was keen to keep his race engineer out of the firing line, though, as such a split-second decision in mixed conditions is the product of an intricate web of teamwork in the garage.

"We can't point the finger at somebody. We need to understand why we made that decision and were our systems telling us what we needed to know because you're relying on the radar," he said.

"It's not my engineer's fault. He's ultimately the one who passes the message on, but he's got 12 people talking to him, giving him that information to relay. So we just need to understand why we made that decision."

Speaking to Sky Sports afterwards, Wolff wasn't convinced Russell could have hung on to pole given conditions were getting markedly worse in Turn 12 than they had been for Norris just moments prior.

"You know, if we were to have a crystal ball to know whether you should back off or not, then that would be helpful," he said. "A difficult one, it's a 50-50 call.

Toto Wolff, Mercedes Photo by: Artur Widak / NurPhoto via Getty Images

"He was running into Albon, was 18 milliseconds up on Norris at that stage, so I don't think it would have been enough for pole. But obviously he's driven perfectly all sessions and he merited to be on pole."

Russell remained combative and wants Sunday to be in similar conditions as he starts from seventh instead of second. Team-mate Kimi Antonelli will line up alongside Norris instead after qualifying third, having been unable to match Russell's pace.

Other frontrunners Max Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton are starting from the rear of the field and are unlikely to be a factor, while Charles Leclerc and Oscar Piastri are starting in the middle of the pack.

"I felt really confident in the rain. I think my pace along with Lando's was by far the best out there," Russell declared. "I hope it is wet tomorrow. I feel I've got a greater chance if it's wet."

Sports.title: Hamilton insists Ferrari tensions with Leclerc are over: "We've squashed it"
Sports.content:
Lewis Hamilton has revealed he and Charles Leclerc have cleared the air in Sao Paulo following their clash at the Formula 1 Mexico Grand Prix and the tensions have been “squashed”.

Moreover, the seven-time world champion insists it didn't require Fred Vasseur's involvement – as the drivers resolved their differences between themselves.

"I mean, Fred hasn't cleared the air in the sense of me and Charles," he said, speaking to Sky Sports after qualifying in Sao Paulo. "We sat and spoke and we squashed it and we're moving on. I think we still have a huge amount of respect for each other.

"And I'm glad we had a chat. Now we move on along just fine as normal. So sometimes in those scenarios it just takes having a conversation and there's been no demands from either side."

The tension arose following the race in Mexico, in which Hamilton felt he lost the chance to win because of his team-mate. Leclerc attacked the Briton on the opening lap, both left the track – and as a result, the victory went to Max Verstappen.

Vasseur didn't have a chance to meet with both drivers together in Mexico, and talks were postponed until they arrived in Sao Paulo – with Leclerc staying longer in Europe due to the birth of his child.

Charles Leclerc, Ferrari, Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari Photo by: Colin McMaster / LAT Images via Getty Images

Before that, during Thursday's press conference, Hamilton doubled down on his comments from Mexico, confirming he thinks Leclerc races him harder than any other driver. Now that the conversation between the two has taken place, Hamilton insists the pair can move on.

"It's just been both giving our points and areas that we can do better and support each other. So I'm hoping to have better races moving forward," he said.

"It's okay sometimes to disagree"

Leclerc also confirmed that the conflict is resolved and the drivers have no issues with each other.

"Yes, of course," he said, when asked whether his relationship with Hamilton was good again. "I really believe that when we speak things are much better straight away. Of course there is tension, of course we want to finish ahead of each other and sometimes we are not going to do things right.

"And it's okay sometimes to disagree on the way you see things. But at the same time discussing about those then helps a whole lot.

"From my perspective, I was very straightforward of course and I think it was good to speak. I think this is always needed after a moment like this.

Charles Leclerc, Ferrari, Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari Photo by: Alastair Staley / LAT Images via Getty Images

"I think it took proportions that are way too big, but it has been around also for way too long. At the same time, it was a very special week for me so I couldn't really have those discussions before.

"And it was important to have those discussions, but now I consider that a closed chapter and I think it will be important to look ahead."

Sports.title: F1 Brazilian GP: Norris splashes to pole from Russell
Sports.content:
McLaren's Lando Norris has claimed pole in a wet qualifying session at Formula 1's Brazilian Grand Prix, beating George Russell on a treacherous Interlagos circuit.

In a challenging session that was red-flagged by over an hour due to heavy rain and standing water, Norris topped the final Q3 shootout with a 1m27.470s lap on the intermediate tyres, pipping Mercedes' Russell by two tenths.

Russell was nursing a five-place grid penalty for a power unit change, but was still incensed by his Mercedes team asking him to abort his second flying lap in Q3.

Antonelli qualified third, six tenths behind Norris, with Charles Leclerc fourth in the Ferrari. As well as Russell's demotion, Leclerc's 10-place engine penalty elevated fifth-placed Racing Bulls driver Liam Lawson to third on Sunday's grid.

Lawson is under pressure to retain his seat as Racing Bulls considers promoting reserve driver Nikola Tsolov instead, but the New Zealander delivered a standout performance to give the squad food for thought.

Nico Hulkenberg also shone in sixth for Audi, followed by Red Bull's Isack Hadjar and Haas driver Oliver Bearman. Fernando Alonso and Alex Albon completed the top 10 on Saturday.

George Russell, Mercedes Photo by: Colin McMaster / LAT Images via Getty Images

In Q2 Alonso was the first driver to switch to intermediates as he aimed to lift his Aston Martin out of the belly of the pack. Other soon followed suit, and Russell secured P1 with a 1m26.745s lap on the green-walled compound, ahead of an impressive looking Lawson and Hadjar.

Newly-minted world champion Antonelli only just managed to advance in 10th, knocking out Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton, who is already due to start at the rear anyway with a power unit penalty.

Oscar Piastri also failed to advance, the McLaren driver a disappointing 12th. Haas rookie Rafael Camara had done well to progress to Q2 despite going off, but he then crashed at the end of the session by going straight into the wall at turn 12, bringing out a late red flag.

In the second Racing Bulls car, Arvid Lindblad was dumped out in 14th due to a power unit issue, followed by Carlos Sainz in the Williams. Red Bull's Max Verstappen, who joins Hamilton at the back of the grid with an engine penalty of his own, did not go out in Q2 and was classified 16th.

Following an earlier downpour and more rain on the horizon, Q1 started on time but with conditions worsening right before the session went green.

Several drivers immediately parked their cars to be pushed back and exchange their intermediates for full wet tyres. Those who did go out confirmed that was a good idea, with cars heading straight back in after reporting aquaplaning as race control red-flagged the session.

Nico Hulkenberg, Audi F1 Team Photo by: Sam Bloxham / LAT Images via Getty Images

After a delay of over an hour and 20 minutes, the session was green-lit again with 15 minutes of Q1 running on the clock and conditions still treacherous enough to warrant full wet tyres.

With conditions still poor but continuously improving, that meant it was a matter of fuelling up the car, circulating and building up a rhythm to peak at the end of the session. Norris ended up leading the segment with a 1m30.939s, 10 seconds quicker than lap times just 15 minutes prior, ahead of Russell and Verstappen.

At the rear of the field Haas debutant Camara somehow survived a spin and contact with the wall after Turn 3, which broke his front wing but spared his suspension, to advance in 13th to the delight of the Brazilian fans.

Alpine was the biggest loser of Q1 with both Franco Colapinto and Pierre Gasly eliminated in 16th and 17th, ruing a complete lack of grip. Lance Stroll was also out in 18th, followed by Cadillac duo Valtteri Bottas and Sergio Perez.

The other Brazilian crowd favourite, Audi's Gabriel Bortoleto, was less fortunate than Camara and damaged the left-rear of his car after an off at Turn 12, engaging in a bit of tractor pulling to wrangle his car out of a deep muddy puddle and return to the pits.

Sports.title: Hamilton set for new penalty, will start F1 Brazilian GP from back of grid
Sports.content:
Lewis Hamilton will have to start Formula 1’s Brazilian Grand Prix from the back of the grid, Ferrari has announced.

Hamilton was given his fifth internal combustion engine of the season on Saturday morning, landing a 10-place grid drop as he was exceeding his quota for the first time.

However, the seven-time world champion endured a troubled Free Practice 3 session. He reported “strange vibrations” coming from his new engine as well as more powerful engine braking than usual during the first half of the session, as he ended up just eighth-fastest in the medium-tyre pecking order.

Hamilton eventually had to pit definitively moments later, with smoke emanating from the car. He therefore did not get any soft-compound running.

Ferrari has now announced that Hamilton’s power unit has been removed for further checks with a brand-new powertrain to be installed on the SF-26 – meaning he will get further grid penalties equating to a back-of-the-grid start.

Hamilton had been keen to improve his winning record at Interlagos, a track where he took victories in 2016, 2018 and 2021 – just three times across 18 races.

Lewis Hamilton, Ferrari Photo by: Manuel Eletto / Getty Images

Asked about potentially equalling Michael Schumacher’s record of four wins at Autodromo Jose Carlos Pace, Hamilton clarified: “Well, I haven't won here that many times, so I'm not too happy about that.

“Three wins, I'm grateful for the three wins that I've had, but I've been coming here since 2007. That's a low record for me that I want to change. That's what I'm focused on.”

His odds of doing so are now remote, but the Sao Paulo race will still mark his 400th grand prix start – second only to Fernando Alonso’s current 444.

“It's kind of crazy. I never ever thought that I would be reaching numbers like that,” Hamilton said, having made his F1 debut at a time when the all-time record holder was Riccardo Patrese with 256 races.

“It's crazy because I still feel young, and regardless of the things that people say, you saw my pole last week, I still have the pace, I still have the speed and I still have the dedication, which is most important, and the focus.

“For me, that number is kind of irrelevant. It's beautiful to be able to have that here in Brazil. I've heard of some photographers who have been here for 500 races; at some stage that's probably where I'll be.”

Sports.title: F1 Brazilian GP: Verstappen edges out Antonelli to top FP3 as Hamilton hits mechanical trouble
Sports.content:
Max Verstappen set the fastest time in Free Practice 3 at Formula 1’s Brazilian Grand Prix, narrowly edging out Kimi Antonelli as Lewis Hamilton’s Ferrari suffered a mechanical issue.

The impending threat of rain meant all drivers rushed onto the track – especially Nico Hulkenberg, whose Audi suffered a terminal issue at the hands of rookie Freddie Slater in FP1, preventing him from partaking in the second session at all. These laps were therefore the German’s first this weekend.

Everyone focused on the medium tyre compound in the opening 40 minutes of the session, Kimi Antonelli fastest in 1m12.209s, leading Verstappen by 0.075s – despite the new world champion reporting a steering wheel problem, while the four-time title winner reported his steering was “heavy to the right”.

Charles Leclerc was third, 0.230s adrift, while George Russell, Liam Lawson and Oscar Piastri were half a second down on Antonelli. Lawson, who set the fastest time in sector three, was nearly 0.5s quicker than Racing Bulls team-mate Arvid Lindblad and almost one second faster than any other midfield driver.

Hamilton, who reported “strange vibrations” emanating from his new powertrain and “big engine braking”, was just eighth-fastest ahead of Hadjar, who described his RB22 as “close to undriveable”. The Ferrari man’s issue would later lead to “smoke in the cockpit” amid a worrying sound.

As the field switched to soft rubber, Verstappen narrowly edged out Antonelli to set the fastest time, with a 1m11.622s to the Mercedes driver’s 1m11.647s. Lando Norris hauled his McLaren up to third, 0.131s adrift, followed by Russell and Leclerc – meaning the four top teams lapped within 0.274s.

Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes Photo by: Alastair Staley / LAT Images via Getty Images

This time, Lindblad was one tenth quicker than Lawson, with the pair again roughly half a second faster than Audi’s Gabriel Bortoleto and Alpine’s Pierre Gasly in the midfield. Hadjar also ended up behind both Racing Bulls in the classification, with a 0.591s deficit to pacesetter Verstappen.

Hamilton’s issue meant he was confined to the garage and performed no soft-tyre run, ending up 12th in the final results.

Debutant Rafael Camara was 15th-fastest, 0.128s quicker than team-mate Oliver Bearman.

Lance Stroll propped up the order after encountering a suspected ERS issue 15 minutes into the session, which proved terminal.

Sports.title: Norris wins after Antonelli spins out of the lead at soggy Interlagos | 2026 Brazilian Grand Prix report
Sports.content:
Lando Norris claimed his third grand prix victory of 2026 ahead of the two Red Bull drivers.

The pole-winner lost the lead of the race to Andrea Kimi Antonelli immediately after the start. However he returned to the front of the field when Antonelli spun off under pressure from the McLaren on lap 20.

The race began on a track wet enough for all the drivers to choose the intermediate tyres. It dried out over the course of the 71 laps and Lewis Hamilton triggered the field’s switch to softs on lap 15.

For the second year in a row, Max Verstappen climbed from the penultimate place on the grid to finish second. He did not make as much progress on the first lap as Hamilton, who started one place ahead of him, but the Ferrari driver’s pace was not as strong.

Verstappen soon worked his way past Hamilton and went on to clear Oscar Piastri and Alexander Albon. After the field switched to slicks he got onto the tail of his team mate, whom Red Bull immediately instructed to get out of the way.

Although Verstappen’s pace was not quick enough for him to pull away, he gained ground after pitting early for a second set of tyres. The rain returned late in the race and Verstappen nearly pulled off a perfectly-timed switch to intermediates. He opted to wait a lap, however, by which time his rivals had started to come in.

The rain intensified over the final laps and Verstappen briefly cut a chunk out of Norris’s lead. The McLaren driver responded, however, and took the chequered flag 14 seconds ahead of his rival. Hadjar completed the podium.

Advert | Become a RaceFans supporter and go ad-free

Antonelli appeared to be heading for victory as he pulled clear of the field in the opening laps. But he struggled badly with his car’s handling after his first pit stop, leading to his spin in front of Norris.

The Red Bull drivers passed him over the following laps. Switching to intermediates at the end of the race brought George Russell onto his tail, and with Antonelli facing an investigation for an unsafe release in the pits, Mercedes opted to swap them.

Russell therefore took fourth place despite losing a huge amount of time when he spun in the pit lane exit after his first pit stop. Like Antonelli earlier in the race, Russell was mystified by his car’s strange handling after his last pit stop. But with neither Ferrari finishing inside the top six, Mercedes easily did enough to secure the constructors’ championship title.

Oscar Piastri never had his team mate’s pace and finished almost a minute behind in sixth place. Charles Leclerc passed Liam Lawson on the penultimate lap but made contact with the Racing Bulls at Juncao as he did, which the stewards will investigate.

Hamilton unlapped himself from Norris at one stage in the race but finished a lap down in ninth place. He initially tried to stay out when the rain returned, but spun on the high-speed approach to the pits, and resigned himself to the inevitable.

Nico Hulkenberg claimed the final point after serving a 10-second time penalty for gaining an advantage off the track at the first corner. He led home Arvid Lindblad and Fernando Alonso, the latter having been first to call the switch to intermediates at the end of the race.

Lance Stroll in the other Aston Martin retired again. Poor Valtteri Bottas didn’t even get to start the race after a wheel became stuck on his car on the grid.

Mercedes have clinched the Formula 1 world championship for the ninth time.

The team previously won the title for a record eight consecutive seasons from 2014 to 2021. Their ninth win means they now have as many victories as Williams. Only Ferrari and McLaren have more constructors’ championship wins, with 16 and 10 respectively.

Sports.title: ‘Very high chance of a horrific crash’ if F1 races in same conditions as qualifying | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Formula 1 drivers warned today’s Brazilian Grand Prix cannot go ahead in conditions as wet as yesterday’s qualifying session.

Saturday’s qualifying session was delayed by almost an hour and a half after heavy rain hit the Interlagos circuit during Q1. More rain fell as the session came to an end.

Pole-winner Lando Norris said the first phase of qualifying took place in “some of the wettest conditions I think I’ve ever driven in before.”

But although drivers considered the conditions acceptable for qualifying, when the field tends to spread out, they warned trying to race in the same circumstances would bring unacceptable risks. Isack Hadjar said “the Q1 conditions would not have been race-able.”

George Russell, who set the second-quickest time in qualifying, said the risk of a serious crash in the poor visibility conditions was high.

“Q1 was extremely challenging,” said Russell, who is a director of the Grand Prix Drivers Association. “The visibility was zero down the straight into turn four.

“I was wheel-spinning in fifth gear [at] over 200kph, aquaplaning. When you’re aquaplaning on the straight and you can’t see in front of you, I’m not even sure what the word is to describe it. It does seem a bit crazy, I guess that’s what we have to deal with.

“I love driving in the rain here, but at some point, if that was a race, there was no way we should be driving in that because the chances of seeing a really, really horrific incident are very, very high.”

However other drivers, including Russell’s fellow GPDA director Carlos Sainz Jnr, praised the FIA’s decision to delay qualifying and start it later. “The FIA handled today well and made the right call to pause Q1,” he said, “and they did well to make the most of the gap between showers.”

Liam Lawson, who will start today’s race from third place, enjoyed tackling the extreme conditions.

“I liked it, honestly,” he told Viaplay. “I think it was risky at times, especially at the start of the session, but honestly, I don’t think there were too many incidents today.

“I think that shows that as tough as it is to drive these cars in the wet, it’s cool to go out in conditions like this, even if it’s a bit risky.”

Sports.title: Tony Yoka’s Five-Win Rebuild Has Taken Him Nowhere
Sports.content:
Tony Yoka has put together five consecutive wins, yet his heavyweight rebuild is chewing through critical years without showing that he has resolved the flaws exposed in his three career defeats. Saturday’s 59-55 points win over Kostiantyn Dovbyshchenko in Manchester kept the streak alive, but against opposition well below the standard required of a serious contender.

Six rounds against a durable Ukrainian journeyman on the Buatsi–Hutchinson undercard told us nothing new about the 2016 Olympic gold medalist Yoka. Over the past three years, the former Olympic champion has merely padded out his record while keeping his true ceiling carefully hidden from view.

Yoka controlled the range behind his jab and timed the Ukrainian with rear-hand uppercuts on the way in. What he failed to do was capitalize on that control. His corner repeatedly called for more spite, but Yoka settled for single shots instead of putting together sustained flurries.

Dovbyshchenko has never been stopped, so a decision win is not an embarrassment on paper. The red flag was Yoka’s refusal to turn up the heat on a fighter offering minimal return fire. That hesitation points to an uncomfortable reality: this run has not restored his confidence, it has simply matched him with opposition he can outpoint without evolving.

Yoka still left the ring with a bloody nose and a cut above his eye. Those marks are not catastrophic, but they highlight the danger of letting an aggressive target march forward unpunished. Against punchers with real stopping power, landing early leads means nothing if he cannot survive the inside exchanges that follow.

Scrapped bouts with Lawrence Okolie and Murat Gassiev account for the layoff, and taking Saturday’s contest on a few hours’ notice showed professionalism. Neither factor alters the urgency of his situation.

At 34, padding the record with routine six-round assignments brings zero value. A sink-or-swim test against someone like Frazer Clarke would finally answer whether Yoka can stand firm when an opponent walks straight through his jab.

Queensberry can keep finding him rounds. Finding a win that restores his credibility is the real challenge, and after five tune-ups, that test is long overdue.

Sports.title: Denzel Bentley Riding Fast Track To The Exit Door At Zuffa
Sports.content:
Denzel Bentley is acting like he just hit the jackpot with Zuffa, but scraping past Shane Mosley Jr. should bring him right back down to earth. At 31, Bentley does not have a massive fan base to protect him when things go wrong. If he thinks a busy media schedule guarantees loyalty, he is in for a rude awakening.

Bentley bragged that he received more publicity in two weeks with Zuffa than during his entire run with Queensberry. That is basic promotional launch hype, not a lifetime commitment. Every promoter rolls out the red carpet for a fresh signing. The real test is what happens to that promotional push the minute you take an L.

“I just felt undervalued there. Over here, I feel really valued. I feel like they want to push me and move me forward,” Bentley said after the fight. “I’ve had more press in the last two weeks than I’ve had my whole career at Queensberry. And that’s not a dig at no one. They have their priorities, and that’s who they want to move, and I didn’t think I was a priority over there. So I went where I was appreciated, and I feel appreciated here.”

Most of that early noise came from the controversy of Bentley ditching his promoter and getting stripped of his WBO belt. It gave writers an easy angle before he even laced up gloves. Once that headline gets stale, hype will not carry him.

Frank Warren gave Bentley plenty of patience. Bentley took losses against Felix Cash, Janibek Alimkhanuly, and Nathan Heaney. Queensberry did not toss him in the trash. They kept finding him dates, kept him active, and rebuilt him.

After the Heaney loss, Bentley ran through Danny Dignum, Derrick Osaze, Brad Pauls, and Endry Saavedra. That was a tidy domestic recovery run that fixed his ranking without matching him against the division’s monsters. Bentley might have wanted more spotlight, but Warren kept his career alive.

The mandatory defense against Yoenli Hernandez was supposed to prove whether Bentley had actually improved. Instead of facing the dangerous Cuban, Bentley opted for Mosley, lost his belt, and threw away his best bargaining chip. Now he is calling out Carlos Adames and Aaron McKenna with empty hands. Without a belt, you do not dictate terms to anybody.

Saturday night hardly helped his stock. Bentley dropped Mosley in the second round, got greedy looking for a quick knockout, and let Mosley drag him into deep water. Bentley admitted he ignored his corner because he thought the stoppage was right there.

Bentley claimed he did not gas out, which actually makes it worse. It means once Mosley shook off the knockdown and turned up the heat, Bentley simply lacked the ring generalship to stay in control. That kind of tactical drift gets you knocked out against punchers like Adames or Janibek.

A cash cow can afford an ugly night because ticket sales keep promoters hooked. Bentley does not have that luxury.

Zuffa comes from the UFC mindset where rosters get trimmed fast. If Bentley loses, they are far more likely to cut him loose than spend two years quietly rebuilding him at small domestic venues. Warren gave Bentley second and third chances. Bentley has yet to find out whether Zuffa has any interest in picking up the pieces when he gets beat.

For academics, it is publish or perish; under the Zuffa banner, it is produce or hit the pavement.

Bentley is walking around grinning about media scrums and spotlight time, completely blind to the fact that every camera pointed at him right now is a record entry. Dana White and company do not run a charity. The UFC promotional machine operates on an aggressive ROI formula: you either deliver explosive highlight-reel finishes that generate viral clips, or you pack the house with rabid, ticket-buying fans.

Bentley brings neither to the table. He is not a powerful one-punch artist who guarantees fireworks, and he certainly does not move tickets in the United States.

When you fight under a traditional boxing boss like Frank Warren, you can afford an ugly night or a bad loss because the promotional structure includes patience, domestic dates, and long rebuilding cycles. In the Zuffa ecosystem, fighters are viewed as content inventory. The second an import with zero domestic drawing power fails to deliver explosive content or drops a decision, there’s little reason to keep them on board.

Bentley was brought in to provide fresh content, look slick, and give their brand a boost. Struggling to pull away from an ordinary fighter like Shane Mosley Jr. was the absolute worst way to introduce himself. He thinks he landed a promotion that genuinely values him as an athlete, but in reality, he signed up for a high-turnover business that will hand him his pink slip the very second he stops producing.

Sports.title: Hutchinson Targets Bivol-Smith Winner After Beating Buatsi
Sports.content:
Willy Hutchinson grabbed the vacant WBC light heavyweight title off Joshua Buatsi and went straight to calling out whoever wins between Dmitry Bivol and Callum Smith. Going for all the belts sounds great on the microphone, but the loose, free-wheeling style that worked against Buatsi will get him picked apart against either of those two.

Against Buatsi, Hutchinson relied on speed bursts, weird angles, and flipping between orthodox and southpaw to completely baffle a rigid, predictable opponent. Try that against Bivol, though, and it turns into a disaster. You cannot switch stances right in front of a technician like Bivol without squaring your feet up and losing balance. The second Hutchinson gives away his stance, Bivol will drill him down the middle with a straight right.

“We’ll go for undisputed, isn’t it? I want to beat the best, be the best, beat the best. And I’m one of the best now. Got one of the belts,” Hutchinson said after the fight.

Hutchinson likes the idea of the Bivol vs. Smith winner, but his biggest bad habit will be an open invitation for Bivol. Whenever Hutchinson throws his lead left hook, he leaves his chin in the air and pauses to admire his handiwork. Bivol thrives on that exact mistake. He takes a clean step back, makes the shot miss, and snaps back with a check-hook or a 1-2 before his opponent can even tuck their chin. Hutchinson cannot showboat his way out of trouble against a guy who controls the ring that well.

Smith presents a totally different kind of danger. Hutchinson loves throwing wide, flashy flurries, but Smith is deadliest when backed up to the ropes, waiting to uncork a short inside left hook. Trading hooks at mid-range with Smith is asking to get caught. To beat Smith, Hutchinson would have to abandon the circus act, use a stiff jab to keep range, target Smith’s tall body, and make Smith come forward so that counter hook stays locked away.

Then there is the Ben Whittaker option. Hutchinson shrugged and said he would take the fight, but it makes zero sense for his career right now.

Whittaker hates fighting on his back foot, and Hutchinson has the hand speed and awkward angles to give him nightmares. Still, both guys rely on athletic reflexes instead of solid defense. Taking on Whittaker is pure risk. If Hutchinson slips up, he blows his new WBC belt on a domestic scrap and waves goodbye to massive unification paydays in Saudi Arabia.

It ultimately comes down to boxing politics. If mandatory defenses or rematch clauses hold up the Bivol vs. Smith winner, Hutchinson will have to decide whether to stay busy with a simple defense or risk it all in a domestic clash.

Hutchinson finally has the belt he wanted. Keeping it means figuring out that the wild, erratic showmanship that worked on domestic rivals will get him dismantled against the elite at 175.

Sports.title: The Hold And Hit Trap That Wrecked Chris Billam-Smith
Sports.content:
Cheavon Clarke stopped Chris Billam Smith in the seventh round at London’s Copper Box Arena, crediting former heavyweight champion Wladimir Klitschko for the tactical blueprint that unraveled the former cruiserweight belt holder.

Asked about grabbing on to mess up Billam Smith’s timing, Clarke gave full credit to Klitschko’s old tactics.

“I learned that one from Klitschko. So, shout out Klitschko. That was a Klitschko special right there,” Clarke stated at the post-fight press conference.

The maneuver served as far more than basic stalling. Inside the ring, holding functions as an offensive exit strategy. A fighter stepping back after launching an attack enters counterpunching range. Smothering the reply by stepping forward eliminates that hazard, outsourcing the retreat to the referee.

That approach neutralized Billam Smith, who relies on sustained pocket combinations to do damage. Getting inside accomplished nothing when every entry resulted in wrapped arms. Each intervention by the referee forced Billam Smith to reset, handing Clarke another opportunity to score before initiating the next clinch.

Beyond killing the return fire, Clarke used his upper torso to press his full weight downward across Billam Smith’s neck. Forcing a fighter to carry dead weight round after round burns out their legs. By the middle rounds, Billam Smith was flat-footed, lacking the spring in his lower body required to absorb contact or dip away from incoming punches.

Clarke pushed the referee’s patience to the limit, later admitting he was warned about losing a point. A verbal warning means nothing to the fighter trapped in a headlock, though. Billam Smith needed to solve the problem himself instead of waiting on the official.

All that holding set the trap for the seventh round knockout. Clarke spent six rounds getting Billam Smith used to being grabbed after every punch. When Clarke stepped in during the seventh, Billam Smith dropped his hands to brace for another clinch. Clarke did not grab him this time. He ripped hard shots straight through the open guard, dropping Billam Smith twice before the referee stopped it at 1:24.

For the rematch, Billam Smith has to stop the clinch before Clarke gets both arms around him. He needs to fight for inside control, keeping one hand free to dig hard hooks into Clarke’s ribs. Timing an uppercut right when Clarke ducks forward would also make him think twice about diving in to grab. Once Clarke has both arms locked, trying to wrestle him off just burns energy without landing punches.

Billam Smith wants an immediate rematch, but running it back without fixing that flaw will lead to the exact same result. He has to hit Clarke on the way in before Clarke grabs him and forces the referee to step in.

Sports.title: Abraham Perez Drops Yankiel Rivera, Wins Unanimous Decision
Sports.content:
Abraham “Hammer” Perez scored a second-round knockdown and defeated Yankiel “El Doctorito” Rivera by unanimous decision over 12 rounds Saturday at Kiva Auditorium in Albuquerque, New Mexico.

Perez (16-0, 7 KOs) retained his IBF Intercontinental flyweight title by scores of 118-109, 118-109 and 120-107. Rivera (8-2-1, 4 KOs), a southpaw who represented Puerto Rico at the 2021 Olympics, had stretches of success, but the judges favored the hometown champion by wide margins.

A right hand to the nose dropped Rivera in the closing seconds of the second round. Referee Tony Weeks administered the count, and Rivera continued with blood coming from his nose.

Rivera fought his way back into the contest, opening a cut over Perez’s left eyebrow with a right hook in the final minute of the fourth. He then outlanded Perez in the fifth and sixth rounds before Perez rocked him with a right to the chin near the end of the seventh.

Perez landed a three-punch combination late in the ninth, while Rivera answered with a competitive tenth and outworked him in the eleventh. Both fighters had their moments during an active final round, although the scorecards showed Perez had built an insurmountable lead.

The DAZN card was promoted by Legacy Promotions, King’s Promotions and Salita Promotions.

IBF minimumweight champion Pedro Taduran (21-4-1, 14 KOs) retained his title with a unanimous decision over Brandon Moreno (16-1, 5 KOs). The judges returned widely differing scores of 120-106, 115-113 and 115-113 after 12 rounds.

In the light heavyweight co-feature, unbeaten southpaw Atif Oberlton (18-0, 14 KOs) defeated Dean Nicholson (23-2, 19 KOs) by split decision in a scrappy 10-round contest. Two judges scored it 98-92 for Oberlton, while the third favored Nicholson 96-94.

The taller Oberlton used his jab to establish an early advantage. Nicholson struggled to get inside and developed swelling around his left eye after catching an elbow in the seventh round.

Nicholson continued having difficulty closing the distance in the eighth and ninth, but found some success with looping right hands in the final round. Oberlton said afterward that he had injured his left arm.

Heavyweight Pryce Taylor (14-0, 8 KOs) claimed the NABF title with a split-decision victory over Tsotne Rogava (13-2, 8 KOs). Two judges scored the 10-round bout 96-94 for Taylor, while the third had Rogava ahead 97-93.

Rogava’s jab gave him the better of the opening three rounds before Taylor increased his work rate through the middle rounds. Both men slowed in the ninth, but Taylor produced a strong finish, staggering Rogava with a left hook midway through the tenth.

Albuquerque’s Jose Luis Sanchez (15-7-2, 4 KOs) defeated Josh Torres (31-8-2, 17 KOs) by unanimous decision over 10 rounds. Sanchez won by scores of 98-92, 99-91, and 99-91.

Unbeaten heavyweight southpaw Sardius Simmons (11-0, 6 KOs) earned an eight-round unanimous decision over Cesar Navarro (15-5, 13 KOs). The judges scored it 78-74, 77-75, and 77-75.

Navarro started aggressively, pinning Simmons in a corner during the opening round. Simmons worked his way into the fight and outlanded Navarro through much of the middle rounds. Navarro rallied in the seventh, but Simmons finished with a competitive eighth to secure the decision.

In a four-round super middleweight bout, debutant Parminder Pannu (1-0) defeated Peter Balderas Jr. (2-4, 2 KOs) on referee David Rios’ scorecard, 40-36.

Sports.title: Dana White’s Shakur Split Weakens His American Boxing Plan
Sports.content:
Dana White dismissed talk that Conor Benn’s reported purse triggered Zuffa Boxing’s sudden split with Shakur Stevenson. Yet the real damage is far more practical: Zuffa lost its premier American headliner before ever using him to anchor a broadcast or sell the rest of its roster to domestic fight fans.

During Saturday’s post-fight press conference in London, White revealed that he initiated the separation during a phone conversation with Stevenson’s team.

“We were on a call one day, and I said, ‘Maybe it’s better if we all just go our separate ways.’ And everybody agreed,” White said. “That just didn’t work out. You win some, you lose some.”

When asked if Stevenson pushed for parity after seeing Benn’s reported $15 million payday for the Regis Prograis bout, White shut it down immediately.

“That’s completely not true. Completely not true,” White said.

Asked what Stevenson actually demanded, White clamped down on specifics.

“That’s between us. That’s business behind the scenes. If you want to ask Shakur that question, ask him that. I’m not going to talk about it,” White said. “We all decided to go our own ways, and everybody’s happy with the decision.”

White’s comments shoot down the rumor mill while keeping the financial mechanics under wraps. Without figures on the table, it remains impossible to tell whether Stevenson overplayed his hand or if Zuffa attempted to impose an MMA-style pay structure that elite boxing champions routinely reject.

The structural fallout for Zuffa is unmistakable. In modern boxing promotion, an expensive main event star operates as an engine for the entire evening. Fans tune in for the proven name, creating a massive captive audience for developmental talent on the undercard. Without Stevenson delivering eyeballs, Zuffa cannot expose its lesser-known prospects to large-scale viewership. The company must now shoulder the expense of building interest in raw talent from scratch.

Stevenson also presented an awkward commercial equation for White’s promotional philosophy. White sells high-octane violence and ruthless aggression. Stevenson delivers surgical, defensive brilliance that purists appreciate but casual fans rarely rush to purchase. If Stevenson sought superstar guarantees without bringing explosive mass appeal, the balance sheet became an uphill battle.

Replacing that caliber of stateside talent presents an immediate hurdle. Reporters pressed White on established American draws like David Benavidez, Jaron Ennis, and Jesse Rodriguez, pointing out that nearly every top-tier domestic fighter is locked into commitments with rival outfits.

“We’re like eight or nine months into this thing. We’ll see how it all plays out,” White said.

Patience works in matchmaking, but broadcast partners look for immediate, dependable fixtures on the calendar. Television executives commit serious capital to showcase proven stars, not to finance protracted rebuilding phases. Walking away from Stevenson avoids an untenable contract, but it strips Zuffa of its flagship American asset before the company staged its first major domestic show.

Sports.title: Umar Dzambekov Punishes Zach Parker To Stay Unbeaten
Sports.content:
Umar Dzambekov brought Zach Parker’s comeback to a sudden halt, dropping the former British super middleweight champion with a ferocious left hook downstairs in round four at London’s Copper Box Arena. The undefeated southpaw spent the early minutes testing Parker up top before digging deep to close the show.

The fight ended at 1:47 of the fourth round during their scheduled ten-round light heavyweight clash on the Zuffa Boxing 12 undercard. Dzambekov (15-0, 11 KOs) drove a pinpoint shot right into Parker’s solar plexus. Parker collapsed, unable to beat referee Kieran McCann’s ten-count.

Parker (26-3, 18 KOs) stepped into the ring determined to rebound from a controversial majority-decision loss to Joshua Buatsi in November 2025. What he got instead was a brutal reminder of Dzambekov’s punch selection, suffering back-to-back defeats for the first time in his career.

Trouble surfaced just sixty seconds into round one. Dzambekov ripped a heavy left to the temple, visibly wobbling the 32-year-old Brit. Parker steadied himself, answering back with stiff straight rights to the ribs to keep the advancing puncher honest.

Still, landing punches never masked Parker’s defensive lapses. Dzambekov’s looping left kept sneaking past the guard, giving Parker fits as he tried to anticipate where the blows were coming from.

Momentum broke momentarily early in the fourth when Parker hit the canvas, but referee McCann correctly ruled it an accidental tangle of feet. Moments later, there was zero ambiguity. Dzambekov shifted levels, sinking that same lethal left hand square into the body. Parker went down in pure agony, completely out of time.

Changing levels proved to be the masterstroke. Dzambekov primed Parker to guard his jaw, only to explode into the midsection and end things instantly.

For the 28-year-old Russian, taking out a seasoned veteran in such quick fashion serves notice to the entire 175-pound division. Parker faces a tough road ahead after another crushing setback, while Dzambekov heads home with the most impressive scalp of his rising career.

At his age, Dzambekov does not have the luxury of spending another two years feasting on fringe operators and faded names. The clock is ticking, especially in a division as punishing as light heavyweight.

Putting away Parker in four rounds looks sharp on paper, but Parker was coming off a loss and never belonged among the elite at 175 anyway. If Dana White and Zuffa Boxing intend to run their own private ecosystem where house fighters pad records against in-house roster depth, Dzambekov will look like a wrecking ball forever without proving a thing.

The trouble comes if they harbor genuine ambitions of competing with the unified champions and top-tier sanctioning body contenders. You cannot groom a fighter on soft touches until he is 30 and then toss him into the deep end against world-class punchers expecting him to swim. The defensive habits Dzambekov gets away with against Parker—dropping hands, relying purely on head movement, leaving himself open when he loops that power hand—get exploited instantly against top-ten talent.

If Zuffa wants credit for building a legitimate world champion rather than just protecting an investment, they have to throw him into the fire right now. A genuine contender who fires back with venom would tell everyone immediately whether Dzambekov is the real deal or just another carefully managed project.

Sports.title: Elif Nur Turhan Defends Her IBF Title Against Alycia Baumgardner
Sports.content:
On Sunday night, November 8th, in the Most Valuable Promotions main event, the IBF lightweight world champion Elif Nur Turhan (14-0, 8 KOs) will defend her title against Alycia “The Bomb” Baumgardner (18-1, 7 KOs).

The champion is making a third title defense, while the challenger is making her debut at lightweight. The action is set to take place at College Park Center in Arlington, Texas, with the event airing live on ESPN.

Back in December 2025, it was a battle of unbeatens, as Beatriz Ferreira defended her title against Elif Turhan. The challenger Turhan instantly put her power on display as she dropped Ferreira twice in the opening round.

At the midway point of the 5th round, Turhan stopped Ferreira when she landed a flurry of power shots. With the victory, the Turkey, Istanbul native Elif Turhan became a first-time world champion.

Turhan would go on to have two successful title defenses. Now the undefeated IBF world champion Elif Turhan is on the verge of taking the biggest test of her career when she faces a boxer who has had an incredible five-year run.

In November 2021, Alycia Baumgardner traveled to England, stopped Terri Harper in the 4th round, and won her first world title. Within a two-year span, Baumgardner collected all the belts.

After earning the undisputed super-featherweight crown, Alycia Baumgardner went on to successfully defend her titles on multiple occasions. Now her immediate goal is to become a two-division world champion.

Elif Turhan is a pressure fighter who has knockout power in both hands. Alycia Baumgardner is a boxer-puncher who is athletic, has excellent footwork, she’s sharp, and she has good timing.

This 10-round, three-minute-per-round fight features Baumgardner’s boxing skills versus Turhan’s punching power. The contrast in styles is the recipe for an action-packed bout.

If Baumgardner wins, she adds to her legacy, and if Turhan wins, she will have officially placed the other elite female boxers on notice. Airing live Sunday night on ESPN, the Turhan vs. Baumgardner clash is a fight you don’t want to miss.

Ghana News.title: KNUST student dies after diving from 17.6-foot platform into swimming pool
Ghana News.content:
The deceased, David Osei Oppong.

A student of the Kwame Nkrumah University of Science and Technology (KNUST) in Kumasi has died after diving from a 17.6-foot-high platform into a swimming pool on campus.

The deceased, identified as David Osei Oppong, was said to have gone swimming with some friends when he attempted a dive from the highest platform at the university's swimming pool.

In a short video circulating on social media, the Level 300 chemical engineering student is seen jumping from the platform and plunging into the water.

However, a few seconds after entering the pool, David reportedly failed to resurface, prompting an emergency rescue effort by other swimmers and bystanders.

Pool attendants at the facility immediately rushed to his aid and pulled him out of the water.

Despite attempts to revive him through cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR), he could not be saved.

He was rushed to the university hospital for emergency medical care but couldn’t be saved.

The incident reportedly occurred around 5 pm on Saturday, November 7, 2026.

In a statement, the university mourned the loss of the student and said police have begun investigations into the circumstances leading to the student's death.

According to the university, Mr Agyapong was an experienced swimmer, a regular user of the swimming facility and a member of the university’s basketball team.

His body has since been deposited at the morgue of the School of Medical Sciences at the University for autopsy.

Ghana News.title: MMFL selects five teams for Fintech Lab finals
Ghana News.content:
MobileMoney Fintech LTD (MMFL) has selected five teams from the Accra Zonal Hackathon Pitch Competition of the 2026 MoMo Fintech Lab to advance to the National Mentorship Programme.

The selection is part of the company’s efforts to nurture commercially viable financial technology solutions in Ghana.

The Accra competition, held as part of the Southern Sector MMFL Fintech Lab Hackathon, brought together developers, entrepreneurs and startups to present technology-based solutions to everyday challenges.

Speaking at the event, the Chief Products and Services Officer of MMFL, Sylvia Otu Achempong, said the journey began a few weeks ago with the launch of a technology-based competition for developers, entrepreneurs, and startups, creating a platform to bring the ecosystem together, involving banks, fintech companies, the central bank, and other partners. ”Following the competitions, MMFL began the zonal competitions, giving participants the opportunity to present their ideas and demonstrate how technology could address everyday challenges.

The competition started in Tamale, where 12 participants presented their ideas, and five were selected to advance.

As the competition progressed across the zones, organisers continued to see promising ideas and considerable enthusiasm from participants.

During the Accra hackathon, Mrs Acheampong served as a judge and also delivered the keynote address on behalf of the leadership of MMFL.

We heard 10 presentations covering areas such as small business support, savings, spending, and waste management, with mobile money serving as a platform for these solutions,” she said.

Five outstanding teams emerged, each proposing a solution to a pressing problem. The winning solution addresses language barriers in digital financial services.

Mrs Achempong explained that not everyone can read or easily understand the text-based interfaces used in digital financial services. “The team developed a model that allows users to interact with services through voice in multiple languages, helping to make those services more accessible,” she said.

She commended the partners who have devoted their time and expertise to coaching the participants and helping them refine their ideas.

Throughout this journey, our partners have devoted their time and expertise to coaching the participants and helping them refine their ideas, she noted.

According to her, the next step is to help the ideas develop into viable businesses. “Our next step is to help these ideas develop into viable businesses.

We want this platform to produce startups and solutions that can grow and serve customers,” she said.

To achieve this, MMFL will continue to provide technical support and help participants strengthen their business skills.

Mrs Acheampong said participants would also be encouraged to test their solutions with customers, gather feedback and use those insights to improve their products. “We hope that all 15 contestants emerging from the zonal competitions will return with stronger, more developed solutions,” she said.

Bringing a competition of that scale together, she said, requires considerable effort, but the response has shown the value of continuing and expanding it.“We will challenge ourselves to do more, broaden participation and encourage more people to develop the confidence to put their ideas forward,” she said.

She disclosed that this year, MMFL received 1,791 applications for the competition — the highest number recorded since it began running competitions of that kind.

Ghana News.title: We are united and ready to fight for Africa’s interests at COP31 – AGN Chair
Ghana News.content:
Nearly 200 countries are converging on Antalya, Türkiye, from November 9 to 20 to advance the implementation of the Paris Agreement on climate change, amid mounting pressure on world leaders to ensure that climate finance reaches communities hardest hit by climate change.

The UN Climate Change Conference (COP31), dubbed the “implementation COP,” will focus on translating existing commitments and pledges into tangible climate action to unlock greater resilience, improve health outcomes and create economic opportunities for people.

The African Group of Negotiators on Climate Change (AGN) has spent the past week in Antalya coordinating and aligning the continent’s priorities ahead of the negotiations.

The preparations have included consultations with UN Climate Change Executive Secretary Simon Stiell and the Chairs of both UNFCCC Subsidiary Bodies, providing opportunities to engage on Africa’s priorities ahead of the conference.

The Group’s Chair, Nana Dr Antwi-Boasiako Amoah, has acknowledged that securing agreement on the agenda when the conference opens on Monday will not be easy. However, he says Africa is seeking cooperation to ensure that its proposed agenda items are considered and that the necessary finance is made available for implementation.

Africa is particularly pushing for a tripling of adaptation finance and the replenishment of the Green Climate Fund.

“The agenda items that we have proposed are very important for the survival of our people within the continent, and there is no way we’re going to compromise on them,” said the Chair.

Nana Amoah has emphasised the need for “one Africa, a united voice and a shared ambition for development” in the climate process, as the continent seeks to advance outcomes that respond to its development aspirations.

“We will firmly defend the agenda items we have proposed and work for outcomes that respond to our people’s needs, protect our development aspirations and deliver on climate commitments. Africa’s voice must count, and our priorities must shape the decisions,” Nana Dr Antwi-Boasiako Amoah stated.

The AGN is advocating climate action that supports resilient economies, improves livelihoods and promotes sustainable development, backed by the necessary finance, technology and capacity to deliver meaningful results.

Delegates from across the world are arriving in Antalya, representing national negotiating teams, youth groups, Indigenous Peoples, scientists, civil society organisations and the media.

Ghana News.title: Judicial Service staff extend indefinite strike as gov’t fails to respond to final demands
Ghana News.content:
The Judicial Service Staff Association of Ghana (JUSAG) and the Judicial Service Staff Association of Ghana's Union (SSAJUG) have announced that their indefinite strike will continue on Monday, November 9, following the failure of the government and the Judicial Service management to respond to their revised demands.

The two unions said they had engaged the government and the management of the Judicial Service over the past few days in an attempt to resolve the dispute and reach an agreement that would address workers' concerns while taking into account the government's financial constraints.

However, as of 4:00 p.m. on Sunday, November 8, the unions said they had not received any official response from either the government or the management of the Judicial Service.

In a statement issued on Sunday, November 8 and signed by JUSAG General Secretary Abdulai Yakubu and SSAJUG General Secretary George Taylor, the unions said they submitted their final demands to government on Thursday, November 5, describing the revised proposal as the best position they could offer to improve workers' living conditions and restore effective justice delivery.

"The unions communicated their final demand to the government on Thursday, 5th November, 2026, stating that the revised position is the best the unions can come through to improve the living conditions of staff and restore justice delivery," the statement said.

The unions consequently maintained that their members would remain on strike until their demands were met.

"As at 4:00 pm on Sunday, November 8, 2026, no official feedback was received from either the government or management of the Judicial Service," they stated.

The unions have also directed all Judicial Service staff, including those working at the Supreme Court, to stay away from work throughout the strike.

They said that the industrial action would remain in force until an agreement was reached and workers were satisfied with the outcome.

"Notice is further served that all staff, including members serving at the Supreme Court, shall stay away from work during the pendency of the strike," the statement said.

The unions acknowledged the inconvenience the continued industrial action would cause members of the public and institutions that depend on Judicial Service operations.

However, they said the working conditions of their members had made it difficult for them to continue providing services.

"While we empathise with the people of Ghana and the institutions who require our services, our present conditions make it impossible for us to render our services," they stated.

They added that their members would only return to work when their demands had been met, and staff were adequately satisfied and motivated.

"We shall return when our demands are met, and staff are highly satisfied and motivated," the statement added.

Ghana News.title: Minority alleges 300 Ghanaians travelled abroad on passports obtained through an illegal scheme
Ghana News.content:
The Minority in Parliament has alleged that approximately 300 Ghanaians have travelled to Europe and other destinations using diplomatic and service passports purportedly obtained through an arrangement involving officials of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Passport Office.

According to the Minority, the alleged arrangement involved a travel and tour business through which customers paid money to obtain the special passports, despite not qualifying under the law to hold them.

Addressing a press conference in Parliament on Sunday, November 8, the Ranking Member on Parliament’s Foreign Affairs Committee, Samuel Abu Jinapor, identified one Ibrahim Wallee as the person managing the travel and tour business in Ghana, with Bright Yeboah Owusu serving as his agent in Europe.

Mr Jinapor alleged that applicants were assigned official positions and designations they did not occupy, or which did not exist, to facilitate their passport applications.

He further claimed that some officials assisted beneficiaries at the airport to avoid or minimise scrutiny by immigration officers.

“As at now, our sources indicate that some 300 Ghanaians have travelled to Europe and other destinations using diplomatic and service passports allegedly issued through this arrangement,” he said.

The Minority is calling for a parliamentary investigation to establish the number of people involved, how the alleged operation was facilitated and whether public officials benefited financially.

The Minority's press conference, which was advertised earlier, came a few hours after the Foreign Affairs Ministry issued a statement to clarify the allegations.

In that statement, the Ministry said it had revoked 10 Service Passports allegedly obtained through an illegal arrangement involving a syndicate operating within the passport administration system.

The affected documents were issued between January 2023 and August 2026 to individuals who, according to preliminary investigations, did not meet the requirements for obtaining Service Passports.

It added that the beneficiaries were being pursued, including two individuals who allegedly travelled abroad using the illegally acquired documents in 2023.

Read Also: 10 illegally issued Service Passports cancelled as Foreign Affairs Ministry pursues beneficiaries

The Ministry’s investigations followed two petitions received on October 8, 2026, prompting the establishment of an investigative committee on October 13, on the instructions of Foreign Affairs Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa.

The Ministry's statement also announced that the Acting Director of Passports, Mahama Yahaya Amantana, and a junior Foreign Service Officer, Alhassan Sumani, have been interdicted and referred to the Ghana Police Service for further investigations and possible prosecution.

Ghana News.content:
Dreams FC were denied a much-needed victory after Kwadwo Obeng Junior scored in stoppage time to earn Debibi United a 1-1 draw in their Ghana Premier League match-week 10 encounter at the Tuba AstroTurf on Sunday.

Dreams appeared set to claim all three points after Bernard Kokonu converted a penalty in the 71st minute to give the home side the lead.

However, Debibi refused to surrender and found an equaliser in the first minute of added time, with Obeng Junior striking to rescue a point for the visitors.

The result leaves Dreams rooted to the bottom of the league table, with seven points from 10 matches.

Debibi United remain 15th with 11 points from 10 games.

Dreams will travel to face Heart of Lions in their next fixture, while Debibi United host Port City.

World.title: Trump pleads not guilty to 34 felony counts
World.content:
News outlets will not be allowed to broadcast former President Donald Trump’s arraignment on Tuesday in a New York state court, a judge said Monday night, but he will allow some photographers to take pictures in the courtroom before the proceedings formally begin.

Acting New York Supreme Court Judge Juan Merchan rejected the request by several media organizations, including CNN, for permission to broadcast the historic proceedings. Trump’s arraignment — like most arraignments in the Manhattan courthouse — is a public proceeding, but news cameras are not usually allowed to broadcast from inside the courtroom.

However, the judge is allowing five pool photographers to take still photos at the beginning of the proceedings “until such time as they are directed to vacate the jury box by court personnel.”

Earlier on Monday, Trump’s lawyers urged the judge to reject the media’s request for live cameras in the courtroom. The Manhattan District Attorney’s office told the judge they didn’t have a position.

The media outlets that tried to get cameras into the courtroom argued that “the gravity of this proceeding … and, consequently, the need for the broadest possible public access, cannot be overstated.”

Trump is now in Manhattan ahead of the arraignment. A grand jury indicted the former president last week.

The arraignment is also expected to bring the unsealing of the criminal charges against Trump, which have not yet been seen by his lawyers or the public.

The indictment stems from Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s investigation into hush-money payments, made during the 2016 presidential campaign, to women who claimed they had extramarital affairs with Trump, which he denies.

Trump denies all wrongdoing and his lawyers said last week that they’ll fight to get the charges dropped.

World.title: Russian authorities detain suspect over St. Petersburg cafe blast
World.content:
A Ukrainian tank is seen near the frontline area amid the Russia-Ukraine war, in Bakhmut, Ukraine, on April 02. (Muhammed Enes Yildirim/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images)

The Ukrainian military has reported little change to the front lines but heavy fire from Russian forces at various parts of the front line in the Donetsk region.

The General Staff said that more than 45 enemy attacks had been repelled over the past day, with the focus on Lyman, Bakhmut, Avdiivka and Mariinka.

It said there were 17 air strikes and more than 20 strikes by multiple launch rocket systems.

“In the Bakhmut direction, the enemy is trying to take full control over the city of Bakhmut and continues to storm it,” the General Staff said.

West of the city, Ukrainian defense forces repelled about 20 enemy attacks, according to the General Staff.

Oleksandr Syrskyi, commander of Ukrainian Land Forces, posted on Telegram that in Bakhmut he had met with “soldiers and commanders who destroyed the myth of invincibility of the Wagner fighters and Russian paratroopers.”

“The enemy is weakening and trying to cover up its failures with new fakes about the capture of Bakhmut,” Syrskyi said.

Syrskyi referenced the possibility of a future counter-offensive, saying that “the forward movement of our entire army depends on what every soldier is doing right now on their section of the front.”

Some of the most intense fighting is to the northwest and west of the city of Donetsk – as the Russians continue months-long efforts to dislodge Ukrainian defenses in Avdiivka and Mariinka. The General Staff said that some 20 assaults had been repelled.

“There are also some operational successes of our military in the Donetsk area. Our military have taken some positions. They have taken a more strategic and favourable position,” said Oleksii Dmytrashkivskyi, spokesperson for the military in that zone.

He also noted that Russian special forces had been introduced in the area.

“The enemy is trying to attack our positions between Avdiivka and Marinka. These attempts do not stop. It should be noted that the enemy has suffered quite significant losses,” Dmytrashkivskyi said.

He also claimed that the Russians “don’t have the same amount of equipment and, as they themselves say, they are on a ‘diet’ of ammunition for assaults.”

Social media video showed both sides engaged in heavy fire in the Avdiivka area, which the Russians have surrounded on three sides.

Denis Pushilin, the leader of the self-declared Donetsk People’s Republic, claimed that Russian forces were still advancing in the Avdiivka direction.

“It is still premature to speak of encirclement, but the situation is being created, if not critical, then extremely difficult for the enemy… After clearing Kamianka, our units are moving further. There are difficulties both with the terrain, which must also be overcome, and there are also similarities with weather conditions. But these difficulties are mutual — both for the enemy and for us,” Pushilin said.
