"There's a lot of lip service paid … to the cost to your mental health in this profession. But this is the only place I have ever worked that actually provided support," he says. "I would love to see it take hold in other areas."

If counseling keeps two or three people from leaving, it's a wise investment, Kellner argues: "The cost of training somebody new into our organization is about $100,000."

As both air and ground EMS become even more essential, the task is to recruit and keep more people like Merklin and Saucier.

Because, if hundreds more hospitals do close, highly trained EMS workers may be the only people standing between patients dying and getting the care they need.

Elaine Appleton Grant's reporting was supported by the National Institute for Health Care Management.

World.title: A desert stirs to life: Chile's Atacama erupts in its biggest floral display in decades
World.content:
A desert stirs to life: Chile's Atacama erupts in its biggest floral display in decades

toggle caption i Tamara Merino for NPR

COPIAPÓ, Chile — A vast swathe of Chile's Atacama Desert is now a patchwork of pinks, yellows, lilacs and purples stretching across the craggy desert floor as far as the eye can see.

This winter, heavy rains brought by the El Niño super cycle caused flash floods in the Atacama Desert, with some areas receiving the heaviest rainfall since records began in the 1950s.

Floodwaters in July and August destroyed or damaged dozens of homes, forcing hundreds of people to evacuate.

toggle caption i Tamara Merino for NPR

But the floral bloom that followed has been the largest and most colorful in 30 years — and perhaps ever.

Sponsor Message

The rainwater penetrated deeper into the parched ground than it has in decades, allowing millions of seeds, bulbs and tubers to sprout above the surface. Many had lain dormant for decades under the sand.

Hide caption A field of colorful wildflowers blankets the Atacama Desert in northern Chile, transforming the world's driest non-polar desert. Previous Next Tamara Merino for NPR

Hide caption The blooms last only a few weeks before the flowers dry out and release their seeds, which remain in the soil until the next rainfall brings the desert back to life. Previous Next Tamara Merino for NPR

Hide caption This extraordinary event occurs when unusually heavy rainfall awakens seeds that have remained dormant beneath the desert soil for years, sometimes decades. Previous Next Tamara Merino for NPR

Hide caption Within weeks, thousands of flowers emerge, covering vast stretches of the desert in shades of pink, purple, yellow, and white. Previous Next Tamara Merino for NPR

Hide caption A field of Malvilla flowers blooms across the Atacama Desert. Previous Next Tamara Merino for NPR

Hide caption A field of colorful wildflowers blankets the Atacama Desert in northern Chile. Previous Next Tamara Merino for NPR

Hide caption A field of Malvilla flowers blooms across the Atacama Desert during the rare flowering desert phenomenon, known locally as the Desierto Florido, in northern Chile. Previous Next Tamara Merino for NPR

Hide caption The wildflowers blanket the Atacama Desert in northern Chile. Previous Next Tamara Merino for NPR 1 of 8 i

More than 200 species are in flower. A month ago, the first plants to emerge created a pale-yellow haze. This was followed by a soft purple hue as other bulbs germinated. Now, almost every indentation and crevice in the desert is streaked with color.

Scientists studying the phenomenon say there are patches of desert in bloom where flowers have never previously been recorded, suggesting that bulbs have remained dormant there since before the phenomenon was first studied in detail in 1997.

toggle caption i Tamera Merino for NPR

"This is a natural seed bank, a dormant archive that becomes a living one with the rains," says Moisés Grimberg, the administrator of Llanos de Challe National Park.

"But it's a race against time — this brief biological window allows these species to complete their life cycle, which lasts roughly two to three months."

Llanos de Challe is a 113,000-acre national park along the arid coastline, where waves lap at pristine white sand beaches.

Hide caption A cluster of Añañuca Amarilla and Coronilla de Fraile flowers blooms at sunrise. Previous Next Tamara Merino for NPR

Hide caption Wildflowers emerge from cracks in the dry soil of the Atacama Desert in northern Chile. Some areas receive virtually no rainfall for years or even decades. Previous Next Tamara Merino for NPR

Hide caption Raindrops rest on a leaf of the Pata de Guanaco flower in the Atacama Desert of northern Chile, widely considered the driest non-polar desert in the world. Some areas receive virtually no rainfall for years or even decades. Previous Next Tamara Merino for NPR

Hide caption A Garra de León flower blooms is known for its vibrant red petals and is one of the region's rare and emblematic desert species. Previous Next Tamara Merino for NPR

Hide caption A cluster of Diego de la Noche flowers blooms at sunrise. Previous Next Tamara Merino for NPR

Hide caption A cluster of Pata de Guanaco flowers blooms. Previous Next Tamara Merino for NPR

Hide caption Pata de Guanaco and Añañuca Amarilla flowers bloom. Previous Next Tamara Merino for NPR

Hide caption Clusters of Coronilla de Fraile and Añañuca Amarilla flowers bloom at sunrise. Previous Next Tamara Merino for NPR

Hide caption A cluster of Cactúa flowers blooms. Previous Next Tamara Merino for NPR

Hide caption A cluster of Malvilla flowers blooms at sunset. Previous Next Tamara Merino for NPR 1 of 10 i

Grimberg says the park normally receives about 10,000 visitors a year. But with the desert in bloom, 15,000 tourists have visited over the last few weeks alone.

Across the desert, the roads are lined with tourists' cars. According to Chile's national tourism board, the region is expected to see around 300,000 overnight trips during the two months the desert is in bloom.

Among the star attractions are the nectar-filled, crimson flowers of the garra de león, with their long tails of flame-like green leaves. This endemic flower is coaxed out of dormancy by the rains and grows along just a few miles of this stretch of coastline in the Atacama Desert — nowhere else in the world.

toggle caption i Tamera Merino for NPR

This bloom occurs every few years in what is the driest nonpolar desert on Earth. But scientists say the phenomenon is becoming more frequent as changes in the climate bring unseasonal rains.

Sponsor Message

The phenomenon gives rise to a thriving, transient ecosystem, with insects hatching and attracting lizards and bats, as well as larger mammals such as the guanaco.

toggle caption i Tamara Merino for NPR

Biologists from INIA, Chile's national seed bank, are collecting specimens to analyze in their laboratory before the brief flowering season ends.

"It's very exciting," said Ana Sandoval as she delicately shook seeds free from their casings to take back to INIA's taxonomist at its base in northern Chile.

"It's as if the desert is awakening. Sometimes people think it's an empty, arid place, devoid of life, but actually our desert is just waiting for the right conditions, and any precipitation, to awaken it."

The seed bank wants to preserve the genetic material and unique adaptations each plant has developed to survive the extreme, arid conditions.

Hide caption Ana Carolina Sandoval, 50, is a researcher at the Seed Bank of Chile's Agricultural Research Institute (INIA), where she has worked for more than 20 years. Sandoval takes in the sweet fragrance of a large cluster of wildflowers on October 20, 2026. Previous Next Tamera Merino for NPR

Hide caption Sandoval collects seeds during the rare flowering desert phenomenon, known locally as the Desierto Florido, in the Atacama Desert of northern Chile. Previous Next Tamara Merino for NPR

Hide caption Researchers from Chile's Agricultural Research Institute (INIA) collect seeds during the rare flowering desert phenomenon, known locally as the Desierto Florido, in the Atacama Desert of northern Chile. The seeds will be preserved in a seed bank to help protect the region's native plant species and safeguard their genetic diversity for future generations. Previous Next Tamara Merino for NPR

Hide caption Researchers from Chile's Agricultural Research Institute (INIA) record the number and variety of flowers per square meter during the rare flowering desert event. Previous Next Tamara Merino for NPR

Hide caption By monitoring the number and diversity of flowers in specific areas, researchers can better understand how different plant species respond to rainfall and how the desert ecosystem changes during these rare blooming events. Previous Next Tamara Merino for NPR

Hide caption Researchers from Chile's Agricultural Research Institute (INIA) record the number and variety of flowers per square meter during the rare flowering desert phenomenon. Previous Next Tamara Merino for NPR

Hide caption Sandoval collects seeds from Cacho de Cabra flowers during the rare flowering desert phenomenon. Previous Next Tamara Merino for NPR

Hide caption Claudia Loreto Bavestrello Riquelme, 40, a researcher at Chile's Agricultural Research Institute (INIA) since 2023, collects seeds. Previous Next Tamara Merino for NPR 1 of 8 i

Sandoval points out different ways plants harvest water as she walks. Some leaves are covered in fine hairs; others have a thick waxy cuticle.

A national park dedicated to the desert bloom was created in June 2023 to protect a 141,000-acre area where flowers spring up every few years. Now local authorities want to go further.

toggle caption i Tamara Merino for NPR

Miguel Vargas, the governor of the Atacama region, is beginning the process of seeking UNESCO World Heritage recognition for the desert bloom phenomenon.

"This represents a tremendous opportunity to strengthen special interest tourism and diversify our regional economy, which is currently heavily reliant on mining," he said. "Receiving UNESCO recognition would put the Atacama region on the world stage."

toggle caption i Tamara Merino for NPR

Vargas hopes this will become Chile's eighth World Heritage site within a couple of years.

This year, the bloom is projected to last until mid-November.

As the flowers begin to fade, scientists will be left with two tantalising questions: was this the Atacama Desert's largest flowering event on record, and might closer examination reveal any previously unknown species among the millions of plants?

World.title: How Gen Z voters helped fuel a blue wave for Democrats
World.content:
How Gen Z voters helped fuel a blue wave for Democrats

toggle caption i Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images

Democrats have done well in recent elections when they win young voters by a margin of at least 20 points. On Tuesday, they carried Gen Z — those under 30 — by nearly 50 points, according to exit polling.

It's a stunning shift from 2024, when the party lost critical ground with young people. Long seen as a part of the Democratic base, voters under 30 shifted right towards Donald Trump, motivated by his pledge to better their economic prospects.

But this week, the youngest generation of voters issued a strong rebuke of Republicans, taking another chance on Democrats and their change-focused message at a moment when many of them feel as though the American Dream is out of reach.

Sponsor Message

How young voters powered Democrats to victory

Americans ages 18-29 have a history of turning out at lower rates than older voters, and this year was no exception. Gen Z made up 11% of the total vote on Tuesday.

However, where young Americans may have made the greatest difference, is on the margins in House and Senate races where Democrats flipped seats.

The Texas Senate race is a key example. Democrat James Talarico won the state by 12 percentage points, however, when looking at just Gen Z, he won it by 60 points.

Loading...

Explaining the massive shift from 2024

When assessing gains more broadly, Democrats argue the party's strong slate of candidates helped drum up increased enthusiasm.

But another motivating factor remains strong opposition to Trump. Throughout his second term, Gen Z increasingly soured on the president, with some arguing he failed to make good on a number of core campaign promises — from pledging to lower prices and repeatedly vowing "no new wars," to calling for a crackdown on federal corruption and the release of the Epstein files.

Loading...

Much of that disappointment was reflected in exit polling. Economic issues were the top concern for a plurality of 18-29 year olds, at 43%, and these voters expressed broad frustrations with Trump's handling of the issue. More than eight in 10 said that Trump's policies have worsened economic conditions, with similar shares opposing his tariff strategy and the decision to go to war with Iran.

The young voters Trump lost

Early analysis from CIRCLE indicates that 15% of young people who backed Trump in 2024 voted for a Democratic House candidate in this year's midterms.

Democrats made gains with some young voters that backed Trump two years ago, including white men and Latino men, two blocs that narrowly voted Republican in 2024 and then voted blue on Tuesday by double digits. Democratic candidates also narrowed the margins with young rural voters and people without college degrees.

Some of those gains may have been helped by young Trump voters who chose to sit this election out, but it's unclear how many of them there were.

How the election results broke down by age

Loading...

The midterm results underscore how neither of the two major parties owns Gen Z, according to John Della Volpe, a left-leaning pollster who's extensively studied the politics of young Americans.

"The cohort of younger people in this cycle had a different set of experiences than the cohort of people two years ago, or four years before that," he said. "Every candidate, every party has to earn their votes."

Della Volpe, who runs the Harvard Youth Poll, notes that in the latest survey, released in October, there was a sizable enthusiasm gap between young Democrat and young Republican respondents. While half of Democrats said they definitely planned to vote, just a third of Republicans and less than a quarter of Independents said the same.

"I also think we shouldn't over read what's happened," he added. "Clearly a significant historic rebuke on the party in office — that's obvious — however, I think we need to more fully, kind of understand, the contour of the electorate, who showed up and who didn't show up."

By 2028, Gen Z and millennial voters will make up more than half of the electorate, a demographic shift with huge implications for Democrats and the GOP.

"Young adults can make a difference," said Elizabeth Matto, who serves as the director of the Center for Youth Political Participation at Rutgers University.

Sponsor Message

"They do care about politics. They can sway the outcome of elections. And they're a voting bloc worth paying attention to."

World.title: UFC's Dana White says he will meet with Trump Monday over offer to be White House press secretary
World.content:
UFC's Dana White says he will meet with Trump Monday over offer to be White House press secretary

toggle caption i Mark Schiefelbein/AP

WEST PALM BEACH, Fla. — President Donald Trump said Saturday that he has offered the job of White House press secretary to his friend and UFC boss Dana White, an announcement unconventional even for the norm-busting president. White said Saturday that he plans to meet with Trump on Monday at the White House.

Trump, while he was at his golf club in Florida, posted on social media that he made the offer to "the Great Dana White, a violent Fighter and Warrior" to become the Republican president's chief spokesperson.

Sponsor Message

White, who was in London on Saturday for a boxing event, was asked at a news conference about Trump's post and responded by saying that he planned to fly to Washington right after and meet with Trump on Monday.

When asked how he would balance the job with the current positions he has in the fighting world, White seemed confused by the question and then said, "Yeah, I got a lot of jobs already."

He declined to say what conversations he'd had with Trump but said, "I'm sure I'll have more to talk about after that."

Before the news conference, the UFC head shared an image of Trump's post on Instagram, along with an image of himself standing behind the podium in the White House press briefing room with the words "On to the next chapter."

The White House and a spokesperson for the UFC did not respond Saturday to messages inquiring about the Truth Social post.

Trump said in his post that he requested that White bring along several UFC fighters as "assistants," adding, "We need these people to defend us against the Lunatic Left. Dana will be a Press Secretary like none other. Dana, please take the job!"

Sponsor Message

While White didn't make it clear if he was seriously considering the position of becoming the primary spokesperson for the president of the United States, he did elsewhere in his news conference describe his ambitions to expand the Zuffa Boxing organization he also runs with Saudi Arabian backers and hold more of its events around the world.

Trump's post came as his White House is in a period of major transition and struggling with his party's deep losses in Tuesday's midterm elections. The historic wins by Democratic candidates, including in areas that Republicans had held for decades, led to the GOP losing control of both chambers of Congress.

Trump on Friday announced he was replacing his longtime adviser Susie Wiles, who was seen as something of a tempering force on the president's impulses, with aide Stephen Miller to serve as the next chief of staff. Miller is known as the architect of the administration's hard-line immigration policies and is among the most determined of Trump's inner circle.

The shake-up at the heart of his administration follows the brief but tumultuous week when Trump tried out a new press secretary in Katie Zacharia, who seemed uncomfortable in her sole appearance before reporters before leaving the job after five days.

The post had been vacant since Karoline Leavitt left at the end of August. Trump remains without a chief spokesperson.

Trump is close friends with White and has attended several UFC events with him since returning to the White House in January 2025.

He brought White and the sport to the White House's South Lawn in June for the celebration of America's 250th year of its independence and the president's own 80th birthday. A wire-mesh Octagon was constructed near the executive mansion under " The Claw," a spaceship-like metal arch fitted with lights, sound equipment and large screens.

Sponsor Message

"It was an amazing experience, this was a one-of-one," said White afterward.

White also spoke at the Republican National Conventions in 2016, 2020 and 2024.

World.title: Republicans took big hits in the U.S. midterms. Does that mean Trump's political era is over?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

As the dust settles on a stunning midterm election that saw Republicans take heavy losses in the U.S. Congress, former Canadian and American officials are unsure if the drubbing signals the end of U.S. President Donald Trump's political era and MAGA movement.

"It all remains to be seen as to how the next two years go," former Arkansas governor Asa Hutchinson said in an interview on Rosemary Barton Live. "I would expect the chaos to continue, and so that's not good for the Trump legacy."

Democrats made massive gains on Tuesday, flipping at least 40 seats in the U.S. House of Representatives and seven seats in the U.S. Senate, including a historic win in ruby red Texas. The party may also gain two more Senate seats in Mississippi and Alaska , depending on final results.

The underlying polls paint an even more concerning picture for the Republicans, suggesting the party lost significant ground across all demographics — including white men — just two years after they picked up support from Hispanic and Black voters.

WATCH | How Trump lost control of U.S. Congress: Midterms ‘bluenami’: The exact moment Trump lost control of Congress | About That | Duration closed caption 10:49 Democrats made historic gains in the U.S. midterm elections, winning majority control of both the House and Senate by flipping deep-red seats in several states including Texas, South Carolina and Kansas. Andrew Chang breaks down shifts across key battlegrounds to explain how the 'bluenami' unfolded as traditional Republican strongholds fell. (Photo credits: The Canadian Press, Reuters, Adobe Stock and Getty Images)

Democrats faced their own soul-searching questions after losing the 2024 election, in part due to eroded support from their key voting groups, only to make large enough strides this year that could propel them back to the White House in 2028 if they hold.

Hutchinson, a longtime Republican who ran against Trump in the 2024 presidential primary, acknowledged that Trump will not be a typical lame duck president and will likely continue to make controversy and try to command the attention of his party.

But he does see the drubbing as a chance for Republicans to realign themselves with "traditional values," including supporting likeminded allies and advocating for small government as well as free trade.

"The fact that president Trump was to receive this rebuke by the American voters is going to open it much more widely as to who will be contesting that and running in 2028," Hutchinson said.

Former Arkansas Gov. Asa Hutchinson in Clive, Iowa, on Jan. 15, 2024. (Andrew Harnik/The Associated Press)

Jaime Harrison, a former chair of the Democratic National Committee, said American voters are "fed up with the corruption that they see in this administration" and sent Trump a rebuke to his his trade policies and the war in Iran that drove up prices.

"It's a destruction-level type of event. I mean, [the Republicans] got wiped out," he said.

Harrison also said that the late Republican senator Lindsay Graham, whose sister Darline lost her election to Democrat Annie Andrews in South Carolina, warned the party in 2016 that Trump would lead to the downfall of the Republican Party.

Bruce Heyman, former U.S. ambassador to Canada, told CBC's The House that Trumpism and MAGA are "much diminished today," but will still have some flicker because of the deep loyalty that exists in parts of Trump's base.

"It wasn't really as much a Democratic win as it was a Republican loss," Heyman said.

"You needed to get the independents and the Republicans to come over…. It's going to be up to Democrats to see whether they can keep them on board or do they go back to a more stable Republican Party going forward."

Trump, centre right, attends a meeting in the Cabinet Room, at the White House, on Wednesday, May 27, 2026, in Washington. (Jacquelyn Martin/The Associated Press)

Frank McKenna, former Canadian ambassador to the U.S., expects to see an erosion of support from Trump's MAGA base "because nobody wants to go down with the ship when you're in politics."

But he pointed out Trump's recent promotion of immigration hardliner Stephen Miller to chief of staff signals the president isn't backing away from some of his key policies, like a mass deportation campaign.

"He's still going to want to be the centre of attention and he's still going to make life difficult for other people. The only difference now is that he has less power than he had a week ago," McKenna said.

What's Canada's next play?

The Republican wipeout presents a trade deal opportunity for the Canadian government, if Trump takes the loss as a sign to soften his approach to Canada.

Just a few days before the midterms, Prime Minister Mark Carney said he had a " good conversation " with Trump on the future of Canada-U.S. trade and that teams will work in the coming weeks on the outlines of a possible deal.

Heyman said it's hard to predict what will happen next, but there may be "jarring days ahead" for Democrats and Canadians alike, since Trump is now untethered to political concerns as he closes out his presidency.

But Carney should pursue multiple paths, Heyman said, including continuing negotiations with the White House, diversifying Canada's economy and building up relationships with the new U.S. Congress.

"Hopefully, we'll get us to a point where tariffs can be reduced or eliminated [and] building long-term agreements that we'll put in place that you'll need Congress for," he said.

WATCH | Michigan Democratic senator-elect on Canadian tariffs: El-Sayed willing to work with Trump to end 'stupid tariffs' on Canada | Duration 0:26 Michigan's Democratic senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed said he's willing to work with the Trump administration to end the trade war with Canada during an interview with MS NOW's Morning Joe program on Thursday. El-Sayed will be sworn into office in January 2027.

McKenna said one ticking time bomb remains for Canada: Trump's threat to increase tariffs on Canadian autos, car parts and steel to 50 per cent on January 1, 2027.

"It would effectively end cross-border auto traffic within Canada and North America," McKenna said, adding that Canada is the biggest single-buyer of U.S.-produced automobiles.

But, he said he feels good about the pressure that Trump will face to lift the tariffs and lead the two countries toward a deal.

"In a way, it might be a release valve for him. So I'm feeling pretty optimistic, actually, that we can get to a deal."

World.title: Weather challenges search for Vancouver Island man who failed to return from canoe trip
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

A community-led search is underway off northern Vancouver Island for 34-year-old James "Dakota" Smith, who failed to return from a solo canoe trip amid stormy weather Friday.

Smith, a member of the Ma’amtagila Nation, was last seen around 12 p.m. PCT at Adam River, about 85 kilometres northwest of Campbell River, according to family member and search co-ordinator Matthew Ambers.

Smith had planned to return bones from an earlier hunt to nature by dropping them into the ocean, according to his cousin Seneca Ambers.

Returning bones to nature, Seneca said, is a traditional practice among Ma’amtagila First Nations people.

"We just want him home," she said.

Authorities were called to search for Smith after he was a few hours late to return home to his partner and two young children, Seneca said.

According to Matthew’s post, search and rescue crews located Smith’s canoe about seven-and-a-half hours after the search began — six nautical miles west of Adam River.

His posts also called on the community to assist with the search.

"As soon as the sun came up [Saturday], [Matthew] wanted to make sure that people were out searching for Dakota," said Seneca.

Community search

She said most of those searching Saturday were family and community members, including "a lot of friends" who drove to the Adam River area from various locations across Vancouver Island.

Seneca said Smith and his family are considered "guardians of our territory" and he is experienced in the wilderness.

James "Dakota" Smith is a member of the Ma'amtaglia Nation. (Ma'amtagila Tribe Society/Facebook)

"We don’t know what’s happened," she said.

In a post to on social media, shortly after Smith was last seen, the province issued a high streamflow advisory for parts of B.C., including eastern Vancouver Island.

That stormy weather continued to challenge search efforts Saturday, Seneca said, as rough conditions on the water forced Matthew to retreat from the water and aid in the land search instead.

"We want to think as positive as possible right now. That he’s just found a place to hunker down," she said. "But obviously there’s a lot of fear and worry."

In an email, Victoria’s Joint Rescue Coordination Centre said it received the call on Nov. 6, and two Canadian Coast Guard vessels and two aircraft were tasked with searching for Smith.

The canoe was recovered, however there were no signs of Smith.

The centre said that based on survivability models, a search reduction was ordered at roughly 7:30 p.m. PCT.

"The RCMP has the lead now," read the email.

The RCMP says it received the report about Smith at approximately 4:20 p.m. PCT, as the search continued in the Johnstone Strait.

World.title: University libraries are being swarmed by AI bots, putting public access at risk
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Academic libraries are fighting off swarms of data-scraping bots — that are slowing or crashing sites meant for students, researchers and the public — as AI companies continue hunting for content to feed their large language models.

University libraries say entire collections are being knocked offline by persistent streams of unruly bots trying to access their archives, which include academic, historical and government documents.

"They're just out there on the internet, just bombarding us with trying to grab up as much material as possible," Jill Strykowski, cataloguing and government documents lead at San Jose State University, told CBC News.

The bots are used by both AI and third-party companies to scour websites and retrieve data, often to feed LLMs like Claude, Gemini and ChatGPT.

Libraries, museums and other cultural heritage institutions are prime targets because they have quality, vetted information that is generally not hidden behind paywalls or logins.

The bots are "causing an incredible amount of work and headache for every institution that does digitization work and every institution that is trying to make information openly available," Strykowski says.

Researchers found such reports started appearing in late 2024 across North America, Europe and Oceania and experts tell CBC News the problem continues to get worse.

LISTEN | Even smarter, with even fewer guardrails: The Sunday Magazine 23:41 Inside the global race toward an AI that might kill us all

And new challenges keep arising, says Dean Seeman, director of collections and digital infrastructure at University of Victoria Libraries.

"Sometimes the bot traffic gets so bad that it causes the sites to go down completely for a little while," he said.

Seeman says this creates a "real problem" for public access.

Regular people using library websites are now, effectively, in competition with infinite traffic from bot farms, says Peter Lewis, Canada Research Chair in Trustworthy Artificial Intelligence at Ontario Tech University.

"This is another instance of large, private companies making use of common-good public interest institutions in a way that's very extractive and just assumes that that stuff is available and is free — and then using it to be able to produce highly commercial models that then they can go and sell back to people," he said.

Workers enter data from an old document belonging to the McMillan Memorial Library during a digitization exercise at the Eastland Library in Nairobi on March 24, 2022. Libraries and other cultural heritage institutions are prime targets for AI bots. (Patrick Meinhardt/AFP/Getty Images)

Good bots and bad bots

Eric Hellman, executive director of Project Gutenberg — a U.S.-based volunteer organization that digitizes and archives cultural works and distributes eBooks — wrote in a blog last year that these bots, which he characterizes as poorly programmed "monstrosities," are "destroying open access" on the internet.

He tells CBC News that "everything's gotten worse" since he wrote that.

Hellman says the problem comes down to good bots and bad bots.

He explains that search engines like Google, and archiving sites like Internet Archive, use bots that follow robots.txt — voluntary sets of instructions on websites that tell them what they can and can't do, so they don't disrupt the site's functioning while gathering information.

AI scraping bots, on the other hand, sometimes ignore these rules and overwhelm websites — in some cases requesting thousands of documents a second and downloading them in every available format.

WATCH | Young AI researchers in Ontario: This is what young people studying artificial intelligence are thinking — as the future of AI grabs headlines | Duration closed caption 2:16 Developments in AI, and companies and developers warning about the future of the technology, are grabbing headlines again. But there are young people in Windsor studying the technology. The CBC's Jacob Barker caught up with them to hear their perspective.

As an example, the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill reported last year that it received more than 11,000 searches for Finnish music from thousands of different internet addresses on the same day. The university said its library catalogue was periodically shutting out students, faculty and staff due to bot traffic.

And because one company or bot farm can work from thousands of IP addresses, Hellman says the old fix of blocking problematic IPs is no longer useful.

Michael Weinberg, co-director of GLAM-E, a collaborative effort focused on open-access policies for cultural institutions, is working to protect public access to information. (Submitted by Michael Weinberg)

He says Project Gutenberg is happy for its materials to be used as AI training data and even offers a one-click download of its entire library of books, "but the bots are too stupid to use it."

"Our material is almost all public domain material. It's exactly the sort of material that they should be training on," he said. "We just wish they would do it in a respectful way that doesn't take down websites."

Open access a 'huge benefit'

Some libraries have set up CAPTCHA challenges or other verification systems to weed out bots.

The problem is, those measures can also weed out the good bots, says Michael Weinberg, co-director of GLAM-E, a collaborative academic initiative at NYU Law School and the University of Warwick focused on open-access policies for cultural institutions.

Some libraries have also begun to require login credentials, a controversial move that those who spoke to CBC News say they want to avoid because it puts barriers on human access to things they believe should be easily accessible.

And as the scraping bots get more advanced, experts say they could also learn to work around these strategies.

The Anthropic logo is displayed at during the Dreamforce technology summit in San Francisco, on Sept. 17. AI firms have broadly argued that scraping publicly available data is permissible under fair use and in the public's best interest. (Carlos Barria/Reuters)

Major AI firms have argued that scraping publicly available data to train their models is permissible under fair use and in the public's best interest.

But faced with widespread criticism and copyright lawsuits, Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and Microsoft expressed support last week for honouring a single, standardized opt-out signal in a website's robots.txt file that could block their web crawlers from harvesting data.

Compliance would be voluntary, however, and the agreement leaves out problematic bots from third-party companies and smaller AI startups.

Weinberg says the digitization of valuable information has been a "fantastic" development for humanity — giving researchers, teachers and curious citizens easy access to resources that, 20 years ago, "would have required driving for flying or a special permission to get access."

Organizations like GLAM-E are trying to figure out long-term solutions to preserve that access for humans and helpful bots alike.

Right now, the bots create "a disincentive for libraries and other institutions to make parts of their collection available online," Weinberg said. "I think it's been a huge benefit to society that libraries and museums and other cultural institutions have put a huge amount of work into making their collections available."

World.title: As Europe prepares for the worst, Britons get schooled in preparedness
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The last time any British government launched a national public preparedness campaign was at the peak of the Cold War in 1980.

The “Protect and Survive” message was delivered in short, eerie-looking public information broadcasts and booklets, meant to advise people on how to prepare for a nuclear attack. The campaign — whose guidance included hiding under a heavy table or tips about how to store a dead body in the house for five days — backfired and was ridiculed. Brits realized little would protect them from a thermonuclear strike, leaving them feeling that preparation was pointless as survival would be futile.

Nearly 50 years on, the head of the British Army, Gen. Sir Roland Walker, addressed some 700 soldiers last month at Britain's biggest garrison in northern England. The "business of soldiering" had returned to the national psyche, he told members of the light, high-readiness global response force, adding that anyone following world affairs will realize there is “extreme jeopardy."

“The political leaders of this country,” he said, “will start to have a frank conversation with the citizens of this country about just what is going on, and where the risk lies, and what the nation ... must need to be prepared to do.”

Exactly one week later, Britain’s “Be Ready” campaign was unveiled, a guide on preparing for 72 hours of self-sufficiency in the event of an emergency, be it a climate crisis, cyber disruptions or threats by hostile states.

WATCH | A look at Protect and Survive from the 1980s:

“It’s something that emergency planners have been wanting for a very long time,” said Lucy Easthope, a global disaster recovery specialist. Easthope has advised in emergencies from the Novichok poisonings in Salisbury, England, to the 2004 Indian Ocean Tsunami and 9/11.

Easthope says what the public wants is reassurance — not negative and depressing messaging.

“Ancient DNA, by that I mean 30 years ago, is being reawoken,” she told CBC News. “This is reawakening the idea that it's perfectly survivable.

“I’m really pleased in the U.K. we haven’t resorted to fear messaging.”

Other European nations have also recently introduced or updated their emergency guidance, including France, Ireland, Sweden, Norway, Germany and Poland.

Ottawa, too, has reiterated its longstanding advice . But unlike Canada with its emergency preparedness week — an annual event since 1996 — Britain faces a cultural hurdle, with the word "preparedness" not even being in most Brits' vocabulary. The U.K. has largely relied on community resilience to short-term disruptions, rather than self sufficiency. Now, it faces the challenge of convincing people that they must be prepared for the worst — without sending them into a panic.

Widespread warnings

In Hertfordshire, north of London, family physician Nyari Matebwe says her first reaction was to roll her eyes and ignore it.

“I feel like it’s scaremonger-y, or the skeptic in me thinks maybe they’re hiding something from us … another distraction from the real issues,” she said.

The recent suspected hacking attacks on supermarket freezers in multiple European countries and attempts to raise temperatures in French medical fridges containing critical blood donation stocks have made her question her own skepticism.

“After the recent airplane bomb hoaxes, I did start to think about it a bit more,” said Matebwe, whose teenage daughter is pushing her to take the prepping message seriously.

Sweden is advising seven days , Germany up to 10 , but the U.K., like Canada, has settled on three days' survival off-grid.

WATCH | Recent bomb threats in Europe: Europe's wave of bomb threats spreads from airports to newsrooms | Duration closed caption 2:12 The wave of bomb threats targeting European airports has now spread to newsrooms, including broadcasters in Ireland and Bulgaria. It's unclear who's behind these threats or the cyberattacks on grocery store freezers earlier this week.

School parents’ WhatsApp groups are lighting up with conversations

“I want to stockpile but I’m in a state of inertia,” one parent wrote. “My husband is totally unbothered.”

Another asked, “How will we cook if there’s no gas or electricity?” while one raised concern about rising crime rates and the risk of keeping cash at home.

Warnings have been widespread recently.

Richard Horne, the head of the U.K.’s National Cyber Security Centre (NCSC), which is part of the government’s signals agency GCHQ and the Five Eyes intelligence sharing group that includes Canada, told CBC News: “This is a moment of urgency.”

The NCSC says AI-powered malicious software is “highly likely” to be used in hacking attacks against the power stations, airports and hospitals in the U.K. within two years.

In Horne’s annual state of the cyber nation address, he said “military networks are subjected to sustained and persistent, widespread attempts to penetrate our systems."

That included Russian hybrid warfare campaigns, he said.

“All countries need to be taking this moment seriously," he told CBC News. “There are loads of vulnerabilities that do not need to be there,” which he said the country's adversaries are exploiting.

'Hard times have been forgotten'

Outside the need for companies to keep their technology safe, Horne said at home it is a case of keeping devices up to date and using passkeys.

“You do need to be thinking about, 'do I need to be having the levels of connectivity of devices across my house, apartment' … not unnecessarily introducing potential vulnerabilities.”

There are some who see the “Be Ready” messaging as another example of the "nanny state," or the government telling them how to live.

Others think cultural attitudes play a part.

WATCH | How to prepare for an emergency: Getting prepped to deal with emergencies | Duration closed caption 4:11 Emergency Preparedness Week aims to educate people about how to ready themselves for the unexpected, whether it’s a house fire, severe weather or a power outage. Thunder Bay Fire Rescue encourages residents to take a few simple steps now that could make all the difference later.

Luis Martinez Arnal, an IT professional from Spain now based in London, says his Mexican wife automatically prepares for emergencies, having grown up in a country prone to earthquakes.

“But in the U.K.,” Arnal said, “hard times have been forgotten.”

The accessibility of everything, he added, “psychologically is making us feel more comfortable.”

The recent cyberattacks have created a heightened sense of anxiety across Europe, and as people grow more reliant on the internet, questions are being asked how anyone can prepare to stay connected if it went down. Those haven't been easily answered — especially as Britain has long planned to switch all copper-wire landline phones to internet use-only from the end of January 2027.

“Call me crazy, but following the new guidelines, I do feel a bit nervous,” said one London mother, Amee Doshi, pointing to talk about the potential for a world war.

A Tesco grocery delivery vehicle is seen stopped at a police roadblock on Sept. 27, in Fairford, U.K. Police declared a major incident after evacuating residents from their homes in Whelford, a village about 1.6 kilometres from RAF Fairford, a military base that hosts U.S. Air Force bombers involved in the Iran conflict. (David Bown/Getty Images)

Others appear to be taking to it like true preppers.

“We bulk-buy,” said Preyal Shah, a working mother from Harrow in northwest London.

“I even now have 10 kilograms of rice, five kilograms of pasta … multiple cases of tinned food, each type being 12 tins.”

Preyal said she is also stockpiling newspapers to light a coal-burning stove: “Back to basics.”

Competing crises

In October, British Defence Secretary Wes Streeting warned that the country needs to be “ready for war in 1,000 days," flagging the potential of Russian aggression.

“To prevent the worst, we have to prepare for it,” he said.

“We’ve just got so many competing crises at the moment … and war in Europe,” said Reena Patel, a lawyer from north London, referring to Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

“It’s not necessarily that I’m thinking war is coming but…” she said, listing off all she wants to buy, from a wind-up radio to water purification filters.

“The only thing I have in my control is to try to be a little bit prepared.”

World.title: Regina councillor shared great replacement conspiracy theory with colleagues during mosque broadcast debate
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

As Regina debated a mosque's decision to broadcast a call to prayer , Ward 1 Coun. Dan Rashovich forwarded an email to his colleagues that contained what experts say is the "great replacement" conspiracy theory, which falsely suggests immigrants are attempting to replace a country's white population.

The email, obtained by CBC News through a freedom of information request, says the Islamic call to prayer or adhan is a "strategic tactic" to expand Islam in Canada through changing demographics.

"Thank You for your email. You nailed it!" Rashovich wrote in an email CC'd to every member of Regina city council, as well as Regina police Chief Lorilee Davies, Saskatchewan Premier Scott Moe and provincial Justice Minister Tim McLeod.

Rashovich declined multiple requests for an on-camera interview. Instead, in a series of emailed statements, Rashovich said he did not see the email's entire contents before sharing it.

The city councillor said his "You nailed it!" response was referring to a different email from the same sender — an email that doesn't refer to the great replacement conspiracy theory. That email was redacted when provided to CBC.

But one of Rashovich's colleagues did not interpret Rashovich's comment as reacting to a different email.

Ward 6 Coun. Victoria Flores pushed back on the email containing the Islamophobic screed, saying the City of Regina needed to call the email "exactly what it is."

"This unnamed person is explicitly calling for violence and the destruction of places of worship in our city," Flores wrote.

Rashovich told CBC he could not comment on the "accuracy of religious interpretations," and that he did not respond or agree with the email that contains the passage with the conspiracy theory in it.

Amin Asfari, a professor and researcher at the University of Regina, says the email promotes fears that Europeans or Canadians with European heritage are being replaced through a so-called "white genocide."

WATCH | Regina mosque halts prayer broadcast: Regina mosque halts broadcasting call to prayer after backlash | Duration closed caption 0:56 Regina City Jamia Masjid has decided to temporarily halt broadcasting the Muslim call to prayer from its rooftop speakers after a wave of online threats and pushback.

Jasmin Zine, a professor of sociology and religion at Wilfrid Laurier University who has studied Islamophobia , says the conspiracy theory is prominent among white supremacists, nationalists and neo-nazis.

This example, which hinges on Islamophobia, preys on fears of replacement.

"It assumes there's kind of a nefarious intention by people who are immigrants," Asfari said.

'A glaring hypocrisy': professor

Rashovich made his own views on the broadcast of the adhan clear in an email dated July 6, 2026.

The email shows Rashovich responding to an email that is entirely redacted. Rashovich's response is CC'd to the rest of council.

"I agree this should not be happening," Rashovich said, saying he believes in freedom of worship but not at the "expense of publicly expressing this on everybody."

Rashovich says the country was founded on "Judeo Christian values" and that "Religion and Politics should not mix."

"Every religion has the right to worship who and how they want and this should be done within their church besides some outdoor events or marches that happen," Rashovich said.

He goes on to say that the city's noise bylaw allows the broadcast of the adhan "when it should not be allowed."

"We do not need others religious messages being broadcasted. That is for every Religion," Rashovich wrote.

When asked whether he stands by this email, Rashovich said that it must be read in context.

Asfari said the email is an example of hypocrisy from Rashovich.

The University of Regina professor said the email shows Rashovich acknowledging that religious freedom is a central concept to the Canadian identity, while also stating that certain aspects of faith should be relegated away from the general public.

Asfari said religions often use a call to prayer. In Christianity there is the ringing of church bells, in Judaism the shofar horn is used and Islam uses the adhan.

"There's a glaring hypocrisy, and it comes across rather consistently, when people like this speak about what they believe to be the kind of supreme or dominant narrative that must be there, and then the other, which is foreign, must be tucked away," Asfari said.

The email

Rashovich's email that CC's the Islamophic conspiracy theory was sent on the evening of July 14, 2026. CBC obtained it through a freedom of information request filed with the City of Regina.

At that time, the Regina City Jamia Masjid mosque had recently paused its plans to broadcast the adhan over the noon hour on Fridays.

The mosque had obtained a permit from the Regina Police Service allowing it to broadcast the three-minute call over rooftop speakers once a week, under the city's noise bylaw.

M. Anisur Rahaman, director of the Regina City Jamia Masjid, told media that he later decided to pause broadcasts because the mosque had received threats after the first broadcast .

M. Anisur Rahaman, director of the Regina City Jamia Masjid mosque in downtown Regina, poses for a photo outside of the centre on July 17. (Randi LaRocque/CBC)

The email containing the Islamophic message — including who sent it — is redacted in the emails disclosed by the city, but it is partially quoted by Flores in a later email.

The message says the adhan directs adherents to spread the religion in "non-Muslim lands" through "public assertion" and "demographic presence," according to Flores' quotation.

Zine said the message references the great replacement conspiracy theory and the civilizational jihad conspiracy theory, which falsely claims that Muslims immigrants are attempting to establish social, cultural and political strongholds in nations that they are "infiltrating."

The tying of two different conspiracy theories together in one message paints a picture of a grand Islamophobic plan, he said.

"The idea is that Muslims are a Trojan horse that will unleash these invaders who will infiltrate Western societies. They will install themselves politically as a fifth column and then start installing Sharia law," Zine said.

Asfari said Islamophobic conspiracy theories can be precursor to violence, saying it "does tend to plant seeds in more nefarious circles where the propensity for violence is greater."

Zine and Asfari point to the 2017 Quebec City mosque shooting and the 2021 London truck attack as examples of rhetoric becoming action in Canada.

WATCH | Londoners honour the Afzaal family on the anniversary of their tragic deaths: Londoners honour the Afzaal family on the anniversary of their tragic deaths | Duration closed caption 2:12 Hundreds of Londoners gathered at the site where four members of the Afzaal family were tragically killed five years ago on June 6. The local Muslim community held a vigil at the intersection of South Carriage and Hyde Park Roads, then walked to Oakridge Secondary School. The event honoured the Muslim family known as Our London Family, and also aimed to raise awareness about combating hate and Islamophobia.

Asfari and Zine said it's particularly concerning that a municipal politician — rather than a random person online — is sharing the conspiracy theory.

Zine said municipal leaders and politicians are looked to as trusted sources of information. When they share conspiracy theories that are otherwise circulating in white nationalist echo chambers, it helps to legitimize beliefs that are otherwise clearly false and harmful.

"It does give average people more licence to share those stories. And maybe they believe that those are bona fide," Zine said.

A person within an institution, or an institution itself, sharing a conspiracy theory can help give it more weight, Asfari said.

"When we talk about institutionalized Islamophobia, this is precisely the kind of thing that we're talking about," Asfari said.

Asfari commended other councillors for pushing back against the rhetoric in the email.

In one example, Flores directly confronts Rashovich for sharing it.

"...Differentiate between a noise bylaw concern and someone who is using this opportunity to spread misinformation and hate," Flores wrote.

World.title: York University warns of personal data theft in cybersecurity breach
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

York University says it discovered last month it was subject to a cybersecurity incident that resulted in the theft of personal information, including personal contact details and student identification numbers.

"An unauthorized actor" gained access to online forms used by the university's departments ranging from 2007 to October this year, the Toronto institution said in a news release on its website. The forms were used in a "wide variety of university business," including residence applications and general surveys, it said.

York University said it acted quickly to contain the information after the incident was discovered on Oct. 25, but some personal information was stolen. The university did not disclose when the incident first took place nor how long after they discovered the theft.

The school is now warning people who may be affected to watch out for suspicious emails, texts or phone calls. It urged people to monitor their financial accounts for unusual activity and to use strong passwords and multi-factor authentication when possible.

"We recognize that this incident may be concerning to you. We take that seriously and regret these circumstances," York University said. "The University is committed to learning from this incident and will continue to strengthen its cybersecurity posture, incident readiness, and safeguards for personal information."

The impacted forms were not tied to the university's primary systems, such as applications, human resources or student systems, said York's deputy spokesperson Yanni Dagonas.

WATCH | Tips on how to protect yourself if you think you've been hacked: How to know if you've been hacked — and what you can do to protect yourself | Duration 1:26 Data breaches, hacks and ransomware attacks seem to be in the news more often. But cybersecurity experts say there are helpful steps you can take to protect yourself in the wake of a data breach, and to prepare for the next time it happens.

The university contacted some of the people impacted , including t hose whose "financial account and government identification information" was exposed.

Dagonas did not say how many people's financial account and government identification information was stolen, other than to say it was a small number.

"The university takes its responsibility to protect the privacy and security of its community seriously," he said, adding "responsive security improvements" have been added to the web forms for departments.

The stolen data included academic histories, citizenship, disability and accommodation statuses, email addresses, family contacts, financial information and phone numbers. A variety of department's were affected, including the centre for refugee studies, department of psychology and faculty of graduate studies.

A full list of affected departments and the kinds of data stolen is listed on the York University website.

People who had government identification and financial account information exposed were offered two years of complimentary TransUnion credit monitoring and identity theft protection, Dagonas said.

School provides credit, identity theft protection to some

After discovering the incident, York University began an investigation with help from outside experts to understand the scope of the issue and to regain impacted systems.

That investigation did not find evidence that other information or systems were affected by the incident.

The university has reported the incident to police and to the Information and Privacy Commissioner of Ontario, who is expected to open an investigation. York said people affected by the stolen information can also file a complaint with the commissioner.

" Most of the stolen information is not the type of information associated with an elevated risk of such fraud," the university said. "Identify fraud is regrettably a risk we all bear every day."

It said any suspicious activity should be reported immediately to relevant financial institutions or service providers. People also can report any issues to the Canadian Anti-Fraud Centre and to the university.

World.title: Driver dead after tree hits car in Surrey as 2nd windstorm batters B.C.
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

One person has died after a tree fell in Surrey during powerful windstorms across British Columbia overnight.

The Surrey Police Service said the tree fell across Highway 10 between 182 and 184 streets around 8 p.m. PT on Saturday, trapping two vehicles. One driver was pronounced dead at the scene.

The driver of the second vehicle suffered minor injuries. The road was closed overnight, but has since reopened to a single lane in each direction.

It came as powerful gusts battered much of the province, leaving thousands of people without power.

Environment Canada recorded gusts of up to 90 km/h over Vancouver Island, up to 80 km/h in Prince George and up to 70 km/h in the Lower Mainland.

Power out for thousands

As of 7 a.m. PT Sunday morning, more than 63,000 B.C. Hydro customers were without electricity, more than half of them in the Lower Mainland and Sunshine Coast — down from about 135,000 customers across the province at the peak of the storm around 1 a.m. PT.

B.C. Hydro said the hardest hit areas include Surrey, Duncan, Port Hardy and Prince George.

"Many times if a storm particularly hits Vancouver Island or the Lower Mainland or Prince George area, we're able to send crews from other areas to support them," B.C. Hydro Spokesperson Whitney Deane said.

"For these particular storms on Friday and Saturday so far, we've really had to have crews in place in their areas, bring in contractors. All hands are on deck, but we're responding in all regions of the province."

Deane said B.C. Hydro aimed to have power back up for most people in the Lower Mainland on Sunday morning, and everyone else by the end of the day.

After multiple sailing cancellations across several routes on Saturday, B.C. Ferries said Sunday that weather conditions had improved and that it was returning to its scheduled service.

Wind winding down

Wind warnings remain in effect for Metro Vancouver, the Fraser Valley, the Sunshine Coast and all of Vancouver Island south of Sayward.

Environment and Climate Change Canada (ECCC) has also issued wind warnings for the central Interior, including the Prince George, Stuart-Nechako and Lakes district areas.

The agency says gusts of up to 90 km/h are possible, but forecasts the wind to subside by midday.

"We have seen the worst," ECCC meteorologist Catherine Aubrey said.

Aubrey said B.C. will get "a little break" from the rough weather on Monday, with just showers in the forecast.

But she said a new system is forecast to roll in on Tuesday bringing more wind and up to 50 millimetres of rain to parts of the South Coast, including Vancouver Island, Howe Sound and the North Shore.

World.title: Hidden cameras reveal accessibility barriers at leading restaurants
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Malfunctioning power door operators, inaccessible self-service kiosks and the inability to get a braille menu were among the issues people with disabilities faced while eating out as part of a Marketplace investigation into accessibility at fast-food and full-service restaurants in Ontario.

Marketplace put 10 popular restaurants to the test: five fast-food chains and five full-service restaurants.

The findings raise questions about the effectiveness of Ontario's decades-old accessibility legislation, the Accessibility for Ontarians with Disabilities Act (AODA), and the province's overall approach to fulfilling the act's purpose: achieving accessibility for Ontarians with disabilities.

"There's so much more that can be done," said accessibility strategist Lorene Casiez, who manages Human Space, the accessible design practice of architectural firm BDP Quadrangle.

"There are a lot of better practices, a lot of lived experience … easy-to-do things to make the environment as usable as possible for everyone."

Robert Hampson, who is blind, visited five fast-food chains as part of a Marketplace investigation into restaurant accessibility. (Submitted by Robert Hampson)

Robert Hampson lost his vision at the age of four after undergoing surgery for a brain tumor.

"I remember as a very young kid bumping into things, walking over curbs, hitting my head, but I decided I could do anything I wanted," the Toronto resident said. "I just had to keep going and have no fear."

Watch the full investigation, "The Dining Divide," from Marketplace on YouTube, CBC-TV, or CBC Gem on Friday at 8 p.m.

Hampson said his confidence began to wane at a certain point, but it was restored when he decided to take on a mission.

"I need to educate people along the way," he said. "Every time I walk out the front door and step outside, I'm an advocate for people who are blind and people with disabilities."

Testing fast-food restaurants

Hampson, accompanied by a Marketplace producer, visited one Greater Toronto Area location for A&W, McDonald's, Thai Express, Tim Hortons and Wendy's to document his experience as a customer with a disability.

He started each trip with a simple question: Do you have a braille menu?

None of the locations he visited could provide one.

"I would have liked to have at least found one that had a braille menu," he said. "It's something that needs to be improved upon."

Two companies responded directly to the findings regarding braille menus. Tim Hortons said it doesn't offer them because of how frequently its menu changes. Wendy's told Marketplace braille menus are available across the country, but did not explain why Hampson wasn't offered one when he asked.

Accessibility strategist Lorene Casiez says Ontario’s accessibility laws fall short of what's needed for persons with disabilities. (Submitted by Lorene Casiez)

The AODA does not specifically require braille menus, but Casiez said having them on hand sends a positive signal to customers.

"If someone can't visually read, an alternate format might be braille. An alternative format might be an audible component," Casiez said.

"Thinking about different ways that people can understand the information is certainly a requirement in the AODA."

Beyond braille

Marketplace's fast-food restaurant test also included self-service kiosks, layout and washroom accessibility.

Hidden cameras documented Hampson's attempts to use self-service kiosks at McDonald's and Wendy's. Both had touchscreens and some accessibility features, but neither had a way for him to hear options.

At times, Hampson had difficulty navigating. He accidentally went through an emergency exit at Tim Hortons and was heading toward the drive-thru lane when a concerned motorist shouted toward him: "You're in the drive-thru."

WATCH | Testing self-service kiosk accessibility: Customer who is blind struggles with self-service kiosks | Duration closed caption 1:18 A Marketplace investigation found that self-service kiosks at McDonald’s and Wendy’s locations it visited were unusable for Robert Hampson, a blind customer.

He also got confused on the way to the washrooms at McDonald's and A&W. In the case of A&W, a producer intervened to help him.

On the bathroom door, there was no braille or tactile markings.

"I had no way of knowing, is that the women's? Is that the men's?" he said.

Casiez said a requirement for tactile signage on washroom doors has been in the Ontario Building Code for a long time.

"Not very expensive either, potentially."

Whether the A&W Hampson visited would have been required by the Ontario Building Code to have the signage is unclear.

When it comes to navigating restaurants independently, Hampson wants to see more consistency in how they're laid out. He's also in favour of markings on the ground he can feel with his white cane that can help him determine his location and direction.

In a statement, McDonald's Canada told Marketplace it's sorry to hear about the challenges Hampson experienced.

"This restaurant is independently owned and operated, and we have shared the observations provided to us with the franchisee for its review," the company said.

A Wendy's statement said the company is looking into what was documented during the visit and is working with the franchisee to "identify any opportunities to further support the customer experience."

"When this restaurant was built, it was built in accordance with all applicable standards at the time," said a statement from Tim Hortons. "We are working to identify design changes that could in the future better allow all guests to navigate the space independently."

A&W declined to comment on the investigation.

Taylor Lindsay-Noel and a Marketplace producer documented malfunctioning power door operators at chain restaurants in Toronto. (CBC)

Taking on full-service restaurants

Marketplace also visited one location in Toronto for full-service restaurants Boston Pizza, Earls, Milestones, Swiss Chalet and The Keg. At those locations, hidden cameras documented the experiences of two women who use wheelchairs.

Taylor Lindsay-Noel was one of the customers who, along with a Marketplace producer, dined at three of those establishments. She is a social media content creator who does accessibility-focused restaurant reviews.

"I want to show people that we live very full lives, but it also makes it hard for us to live our lives if places aren't accessible," she said.

The checklist included entrances, an area where Lindsay-Noel encountered challenges at Swiss Chalet and Boston Pizza. At Swiss Chalet, the power door operators malfunctioned on the way in and when she left.

The same was true of Boston Pizza, but on the way out there was a plant and a sign placed in front of the power door button.

"Even if it was working, I wouldn't have been able to hit it," she said.

Marketplace also documented that there were no power doors at the entrance to The Keg, which is required by the current building code. It's unclear which version of the building code applies to The Keg that Marketplace visited.

The full-service customers also asked employees if they were aware of the AODA, which is supposed to be covered in mandatory accessibility training. Of the five restaurants, only one frontline employee at The Keg said she was "a little bit" familiar with the legislation.

"It's part of who you're serving as your client base. So having an awareness of it is really important," said Casiez.

Government response

Marketplace shared the findings of its investigation with the office of Ontario's minister for seniors and accessibility, Raymond Cho, and requested an interview, but the request was declined.

Instead, his office sent a statement that said: "Individual businesses and organizations are responsible for ensuring they are in compliance with the AODA. The Ontario Building Code also sets out accessibility requirements for new construction and existing buildings undergoing extensive renovations."

A spokesperson for Cho said the ministry focuses its "compliance and enforcement efforts" on areas where it can have the greatest impact and added, "complaint trends are reviewed regularly to help determine which sectors should be prioritized for audits and inspections."

Under the AODA, businesses and non-profit organizations are required to file accessibility compliance reports every three years. The next deadline is Dec. 31.

Full-service restaurants make changes

Marketplace requested interviews with the full-service restaurant chains we documented in our investigation. None agreed to an on-camera interview.

Foodtastic, the parent company of Milestones, said in a statement that Milestones is committed to accessibility and added: "We have taken the opportunity to reiterate to our personnel the importance of being familiar with AODA rules, reminding all employees to ensure their training is up to date."

The company also confirmed it added braille and tactile washroom signs to the location in our test.

A statement from Earls said the location we visited "adheres to all municipal building codes and accessibility requirements." The response also affirmed the company's commitment to "a safe, inclusive and comfortable environment."

Boston Pizza, The Keg and Swiss Chalet provided no response to multiple requests for comment. But since sharing our findings with Swiss Chalet, new power door operators have been installed in the washrooms of the location Marketplace visited.

Swiss Chalet did not respond to Marketplace’s investigation, but has since installed power doors for the washrooms at the test location. (CBC)

Accessibility law 'pathetically weak,' advocate says

The AODA went into force in 2005. The regulations include standards for information and communications, customer service and design of public spaces.

"They're pathetically weak," said Toronto-based disability rights advocate David Lepofsky.

Lepofsky, who is blind, was at the forefront of efforts to create the AODA, but said it hasn't lived up to its potential.

"They deal with the public spaces in the built environment, but virtually nothing about the barriers inside buildings."

Lepofsky is pointing to the fact that many of the requirements for interior spaces are found in the Ontario Building Code, not the AODA. This includes details regarding doors, washrooms and signage.

But, according to Lepofsky, the Ontario Building Code has a crucial flaw: it only applies to new buildings or older buildings that have been extensively renovated.

"For the vast majority of our built environment, the building code's inadequate provisions won't even touch them."

WATCH | Power door problems at popular restaurants: Power doors absent or malfunctioning at popular restaurants | Duration closed caption 1:58 Diners Taylor Lindsay-Noel and Ruth Wallace encounter barriers at the entrances of leading restaurant chains.

Lepofsky said he wants standards that cover both old and new buildings "comprehensively."

He also wants to see better enforcement of the AODA.

"It's like a voluntary law because people who break the law, even though it has strong financial penalties built into it, sadly don't have to really worry about that at all."

That sentiment was echoed in the 2023 legislative review of the Accessibility for Ontarians with Disabilities Act, 2005, which said "enforcement is non-existent under the AODA."

The review cited a "lack of resources" and "the size of the private sector that falls under the jurisdiction of this legislation."

Restaurants are also subject to Ontario's Human Rights Code, which says every person has the right to equal treatment "with respect to services, goods and facilities."

Disability rights advocate David Lepofsky says Ontario’s accessibility regulations are ‘pathetically weak.’ (Submitted by David Lepofsky)

For Hampson, the restaurant visits were sobering, but he hasn't lost hope.

"It's definitely disappointing and frustrating," he said.

"But I think change comes slowly and it has to be people like myself, other people who are blind, visually impaired and other people with disabilities just continuing to push and say if we're going to continue spending money here and coming to your businesses we need to see more things made accessible."

World.title: Colombia’s war crimes tribunal JEP announces steep measures after being forced to cut $53M from its budget
World.content:
The president of the JEP announced radical cuts in the war crimes tribunal’s spending, which was forced to cut $53 million (COP170 billion) from its annual budget by Colombia’s Congress.

In a press statement, JEP president Danilo Rojas said that the court would abandon its 15,000m² main office in Bogota and move to a much smaller building in March of next year.

The court president additionally announced that it would eliminate 85% of its temporary employees and force staff to absorb administrative, technical defense, and psychosocial tasks previously handled by external contractors.

Many of the remaining workers will largely be working from home to facilitate the aforementioned move.

The court will also abandon personal security details for magistrates and the court directors and ask the National Protection Unit to take on the protection of victims, witnesses and defendants.

Last but not least, the court announced partnerships with universities, the Inspector General’s Office and local governments to secure regional presence, which is necessary to investigate war crimes.

The radical austerity measures became a necessity after Congress agreed with President Abelardo de la Espriella and hi far-right National Salvation party to slash the JEP’s budget.

The war crimes tribunal seeks justice for millions of victims of the military and the now-defunct guerrilla group FARC, which agreed to demobilize and disarm in 2016.

The JEP has long been the target of criticism of the far-right, which has historically downplayed the war crimes committed by the State and regional elites that used the armed conflict to accumulate wealth.

World.title: Colombia’s labor unions and social organizations call national strike on November 19
World.content:
Colombia’s main labor unions and a collection of civil society organizations called a national strike “against the fascist government of Abelardo de la Espriella and his tax reform” bill.

In a press statement, the organizations accused De la Espriella of, among other things, dismantling the “social, environmental, trade union, and labor rights achieved during the government of Gustavo Petro,” and surrendering sovereignty and kneeling before the imperialist government of the United States.”

The government of Abelardo, like that of Duque and Carrasquilla, intends to reach into the pockets of the people and privilege the ultra-rich with its “economic rescue” bill, which imposes a 19% VAT on food and other basic goods in the family basket, higher taxes on earned income, raises health contributions up to 8%, and conversely reduces the corporate capital income tax from 35% to 31%, eliminates the wealth tax in 2031, and reduces the capital gains tax to 20% for investments in 2027 and 2028. Civil society organizations

The organizations additionally accused the government of seeking special powers to facilitate the privatization of state-controlled companies like oil firm Ecopetrol.

The organizations said they united with the main opposition party, the Historic Pact, “with the purpose of opposing this fascist government and decisively participating in the National Strike.”

The National Strike on November 19 constitutes a new stage in the organization and expression of growing popular discontent, which was also manifested in the successful national mobilization day of October 14. It is about strengthening a collective action process capable of confronting the Government’s regressive measures, demanding respect for hard-won rights, and opposing the deepening of its neoliberal and authoritarian project. Civil society organizations

The last time a national strike was organized was in 2021 when the labor unions and their allies from civil society shut down parts of the country for months.

At the time, a tax reform propose by former President Ivan Duque triggered the initiative.

World.title: Colombia’s government presents “Economic Rescue Bill”
World.content:
Colombia’s Vice-President Jose Manuel Restrepo on Thursday presented an Economic Rescue Bill that seeks to reduce government spending and increase its revenue.

The bill grants extraordinary powers to President Abelardo de la Espriella to slash government spending by decree and includes a tax reform that includes higher sales tax rates on gasoline, coffee, cigarettes and vegetables.

The bill also includes tax breaks for corporations in an attempt to increase investment.

Abelardo’s extraordinary powers

While on campaign, De la Espriella powers vowed a 40% reduction of the State, which the bill falls short of doing.

Article 7 of the bill does grant the president extraordinary powers to “abolish, merge, and split ministries and administrative departments, as well as to determine or modify their names, objectives, and organizational structure,” and allows De la Espriella to “abolish, merge, split, and change the legal status” of other State bodies like the superintendencies, agencies, special administrative units, and public institutions.

Article 96 allows the government to change the personnel hiring of tax agency DIAN, which “would allow for the elimination of annual competitive exams for entry into the DIAN and a return to the practice of appointing thousands of officials,” according to former DIAN director Luis Carlos Reyes.

Last but not least, the bill mandates a 20% reduction in salaries of State employees, excluding the security forces, and cut half of the costs in temporary contracts.

VAT reforms and squeezing the middle class

The bill seeks to remove popular products like cocoa, coffee, sugar and fruits from a VAT exemption list and introduce a 19% sales tac on them.

An increase in taxes on gasoline will inflate its price.

The bill additionally seeks to charge VAT on vice products like liquor and cigarettes, which would make them up to 53% more expensive.
