The bulk of these tax increases wouldn’t take fore until after the November 2027 local and regional elections in an apparent compromise to Congress and Colombia’s political forces.

In an attempt to not impoverish the poor, the bill seeks a mechanism that would refund up to 100% of IVA payments to some 19 million of the country’s poorest citizens.

The increased pressure on the middle class has already resulted in opposition from within De la Espriella’s congressional coalition.

Tax benefits for the capitalists

The government seeks to gradually lower the corporate income tax from 35% to 31% and offer a reduced tax rate for large companies that decide to invest in new enterprises.

According to the Inter-American Development Bank, a similar scheme introduced by former President Alvaro Uribe “was ineffective in promoting investment.”

World.title: Accusations over De la Espriella’s narco ties “lack conclusive or solid evidence,” says Colombia’s justice minister
World.content:
Colombia’s Justice Minister, Ivan Cancino, downplayed the evidence of ties between President Abelardo de la Espriella and drug traffickers that was displayed in Congress by opposition Senator Ivan Cepeda.

In a video, Cancino said that “political oversight is a fundamental tool of our democracy. However, it cannot become an arena for launching accusations without proving and substantiating them.”

The justice minister admitted that the pieces of evidence provided to Congress “may seem serious,” but “lack conclusive or solid evidence, as well as any support that could jeopardize the innocence and the presumption of innocence of our president.”

It is not just about displaying organizational charts, deeds from over a decade ago, and business transactions to construct a narrative that supports neither judicial decisions nor the documentary, testimonial, circumstantial, or expert backing required for these types of accusations. Ivan Cancino

Cancino accused the opposition of remaining “silent regarding the grave scandals involving corruption, drug trafficking, and even alleged sexual abuse, as well as fiscal irresponsibility and possible links to criminal organizations that surrounded the previous government. ”

The justice minister was forced to come out after Cepeda showed Congress evidence of De la Espriella’s business ties with multiple convicted drug traffickers and announced criminal complaints against the president.

De la Espriella’s law firm rose to prominence during the demobilization of paramilitary organization AUC with whom he created a foundation that sought to justify the paramilitary violence that terrorized much of Colombia in the 1990’s and 2000s.

Once the ties between the AUC and elected politicians became known, the president ended up defending many of the “parapoliticians” in court.

According to Cepeda, De la Espriella plays a key role in a “revolving door” system that could end up benefiting the very drug traffickers and corrupt politicians that have paid the president for his legal defense in the past.

World.title: Colombia’s opposition announces criminal charges against De la Espriella over ties to drug traffickers
World.content:
Colombia’s opposition leader, senator Ian Cepeda, accused President Abelardo de la Espriella of leading an agrarian counter-reform designed to benefit land-owning clans and convicted drug traffickers.

During a congressional debate, Cepeda claimed that De la Espriella put allies of drug traffickers and paramilitaries in charge of key state institutions responsible for land distribution and asset forfeiture.

The president and his appointees are part of a revolving door system of people who, before being appointed to government positions, defended the interests of drug traffickers and paramilitaries associated with De la Espriella and his businesses, according to the opposition leader.

For example, the president put Diana Patrica Bravo, a former prosecutor and partner at his law firm De la Espriella Lawyers, in charge of The Society of Special Assets (SAE), which controls assets that were seized from drug traffickers.

The leader of the leftist Historic Pact party showed financial statements of one of De la Espriella’s companies, Dominio De la Espriella, that would prove that in between 38% and 40% of its capital deposits came from the family and corporate network of Hugues Rodríguez, a.k.a. Comandante Barbie, a former paramilitary financier who was charged with drug trafficking in the US.

The SAE would control more than 130 properties of Comandante Barbie.

De la Espriella family construction firm, Cosenza S.A.S., made property purchases in the city of Monteria directly with individuals under investigation for money laundering and illicit enrichment, according to Cepeda.

The president’s ex-wife, Yoly Beatriz Illidge, was appointed Superintendent of Notaries, making her “directly responsible for inspecting and monitoring all land entries and records issued by restitution judges throughout the country,” according to Cepeda.

De la Espriella is an associate of drug traffickers, owns assets purchased from drug traffickers, and defends drug traffickers from within the national government. Senator Ivan Cepeda

Last but not least, Agriculture Minister Indalecio Dangond “arrived at this post to execute an agrarian counter-reform at the service of paramilitary land-grabbers, foreign capital, and agro-industrial partners” while blocking investments for small farmers and displacement victims, the opposition leader stated.

Cepeda vowed that he would give the dossier to the United States Department of Justcie and to “Congressmen of the Democratic Party, given that mister De la Espriella is a US citizen.”

The opposition leader additionally promised to file criminal charges against the president and his agriculture minister in Colombia.

World.title: Colombia’s government claims Petro exploited 48 women as president
World.content:
The administration chief of Colombia’s President Abelardo De la Espriella told Congress that former President Gustavo Petro hired at least 48 women who were “trapped and exploited” for presidential parties.

During a hearing, DAPRE director Carlos Andres Rios claimed that Petro had 48 women “working in the Presidency, who were unfortunately exploited through temporary work contracts.”

We’re going to prove this to the Colombian people: how, unfortunately, the Casa de Nariño was set up, organized, and designed not for governing, but for partying there every day, bringing women there and engaging in behavior we should not be engaging in—behavior that sets a bad example. DAPRE director Carlos Andres Rios

“Forty-eight women are already speaking with us about how, through a contract and an OPS, they were trapped and exploited in order to be with President Petro,” said Rios.

Former DAPRE director Angie Rodriguez, who was sacked by Petro in July, doubled down on her successor’s allegations and asked the former president to prove that the president managed a network of women, including child transvestites.

Were there transvestite children there? Answer me, Mr. President. Were there transvestite children there? I am asking you a question, and I have every right to ask it. Were there? And if there weren’t, uh… prove that what I am saying is a lie. Angie Rodriguez

Last but not least, far-right magazine Semana published an interview with a woman identified as Deicy Jimenez, who claimed she as hired by Petro after meeting him on an adult website.

Jimenez even told Semana’s former presidential candidate Vicky Davila she trafficked drugs for the former president when he was senator.

VD: What happened on the day you say you transported drugs for Petro? DJ: Yes, I was traveling, and he asked me as a favor to bring him some drugs. VD: Were you outside of Bogotá? DJ: Yes. VD: How do you recall that favor Petro asked of you? DJ: He asked me as the favor to bring him some drugs. VD: Did you buy them? DJ: Yes, I bought them somewhere. He gave me money. VD: Did he give it to you in cash or deposit it for you? DJ: In cash. VD: How much money? DJ: Three million pesos. VD: What kind of drugs did you buy? DJ: Cocaine. VD: Where did you buy it? DJ: I bought it from some people. I can’t say (publicly) their names or the location. VD: Is it a gang? DJ: Yes. VD: Did he know you were going to buy the drugs from that gang? DJ: Yes. VD: At that time, was he a senator or the president? DJ: A senator. VD: How did you bring that drug in? DJ: I brought it through the airport. VD: You mean, on a plane? DJ: Yeah. VD: Did you get on a plane with Petro’s drugs? DJ: Yes. VD: How were the drugs packaged? DJ: In bags. VD: Like individual doses? DJ: Yes. VD: And where did you hide the drugs? DJ: In my suitcase.

In a response, Petro denied having hired women for sex and claimed that the far-right attack were the result of authorities’ failure to sustain corruption allegations.

World.title: “Brazil and Colombia need each other,” says De la Espriella
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella recognized the election victory of his Brazilian counterpart Luiz Ignacio Lula, who defeated far-right candidate Flavio Bolsonaro on Sunday.

In a post on social media platform X, the Colombian President said that “in the Colombian presidential campaign, President Lula openly supported Ivan Cepeda, and I won. In the Brazilian campaign, I supported Bolsonaro, and Lula won.”

“Neither does Lula decide for Colombians, nor do I decide for Brazilians. THE PEOPLE DECIDE! And when the people speak at the polls, their will is respected because it is sacred,” the president added.

Lula and I have major and profound political and ideological differences, but we agree on one fundamental point: Brazil and Colombia need each other. No other consideration can take precedence over the interests of our nations. Colombia and Brazil are sister nations, facing enormous shared challenges and opportunities.

President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella stressed that “we have much to do and much work to carry out for the benefit of our peoples” an ought to “fight against narco-terrorism and illegal mining, the protection of the Amazon, and the well-being of our citizens.”

Lula was the first leftist candidate and critic of US President Donald Trump to win an election, triggering celebrations among leftists throughout the continent.

De la Espriella, a US citizen, has been among the most fanatic among Trump supporter in trying to align his domestic policies to US foreign policy.

World.title: Controversy Over Aid to Cuba’s Political Prisoners
World.content:
In their September report Prisoners Defenders documents 1,351 political prisoners in Cuba.

By Francisco Acevedo

HAVANA TIMES – This week, the confrontation between influencers Yusmani Companioni Vila and Eliecer Avila over assistance to Cuba’s political prisoners went viral.

It is a thorny issue, and personally, I believe that those who call for insubordination in Cuba do far less than they should. It is very easy, sitting comfortably in a chair in Miami, to ask those of us who live in this country to take to the streets and risk spending several years in prison.

Obviously, the income anyone legitimately earns in the United States or any other country is not meant to solve Cuba’s problems. But just as no one demands anything from them, I don’t understand why they demand personal sacrifices from others. If you ask others to give, you must be willing to give yourself. None of them has thought of creating a fund to help the families of political prisoners.

According to the nongovernmental organization Prisoners Defenders, Cuba had 1,339 political prisoners at the end of August 2026, including 155 women (a record number) and 38 people who were detained when they were minors.

The cases include people imprisoned for protesting shortages of water and electricity, filming government agents, or denouncing abuses, actions that lead to imprisonment, threats, and punishments affecting entire families.

According to the organization’s records, 463 of those still imprisoned suffer from serious medical conditions, while 54 have severe mental health disorders resulting from beatings, forced labor, involuntary psychiatric confinement, and lack of medical care.

This is an extremely high number considering the reasons these people are serving sentences, but economically speaking, it would not be so complicated to ensure that they receive the assistance they deserve for their sacrifices. Mind you, everything they have done has been without asking for anything in return, so this is not about payment, but rather an expression of gratitude and, more importantly, a message to those who are afraid to take to the streets: if they do, they will not be left without support.

I know of people who were imprisoned following July 11, 2021, and spent three years behind bars without their families receiving a single dollar from abroad. That does not seem right to me when it comes to those who continue calling for sacrifices. Those who make so much noise from the comfort of their armchairs should be the first to reach into their pockets to help those who had the courage to express their opposition to the island’s regime.

Instead, many were left to fend for themselves, and only the best-known prisoners have received any kind of assistance, and even that has been sporadic because it depends on individual efforts.

We are not naive. We know that providing assistance also involves many complications, because anyone who approaches these people, considered “untouchables” by the regime, can face consequences such as losing the right to travel to Cuba. But there are many ways to help their families. For example, a bank account can receive money without revealing where it came from.

For years, dissidents living abroad have used these difficulties as an excuse to abandon those who need help the most, including people who have no stable source of employment because the dictatorship denies them that opportunity.

It is legitimate for them to argue that those who should first bear these costs are the Castro regime’s ruling clique, owners of hotels, luxury residences, yachts, and countless other assets, as US representative Mike Waltz denounced last week at the United Nations itself.

We are fully aware that those primarily responsible for alleviating the misery they themselves have created are the dictatorship’s chosen leaders. But then don’t ask others to make sacrifices if you are unwilling to help those who will subsequently face the wrath of the Cuban government. And not just the famous ones, but anyone.

Now Companioni says he wants to create a foundation to serve the Cuban people, according to his announcement, although not specifically to help the families of political prisoners.

The confrontation ended with Companioni asking Ávila to donate $200 to a child with health problems in the central province of Sancti Spíritus. Avila countered by proposing that two children of political prisoners also receive assistance, with all those involved identified by their full names.

The political implications here are considerable, but according to Companioni, he can reach everyone. We will see whether he can actually do so and, above all, whether he is allowed to.

Helping a political prisoner does not always mean performing some grand gesture. Often, it consists of delivering a letter, obtaining medication, accompanying a family to court, keeping a copy of a document, or repeating someone’s name so that it is not erased.

It is also necessary to stand by those left outside, because prison does not confine just one person: its bars extend into the home, to the dinner table, to the bed where someone lies waiting.

Families can lose income, housing, access to medication, or educational opportunities. Sometimes they need money, food, transportation, or simply someone’s presence to remind them that they have not been abandoned. Sitting beside a mother in a waiting room, helping care for her children, listening without demanding that she be strong: these gestures carry a quiet dignity.

But helping also requires thinking about safety, because for years the dictatorship has taken advantage of the recklessness of those who want to do good too quickly.

From outside the country, people can send letters to the authorities, support amnesty campaigns, contact international organizations, share reports from the independent press, and demand that governments, universities, labor unions, and associations keep public attention focused on those behind bars.

But putting food on the table is essential, and providing transportation so that relatives can visit prisoners is indispensable, because international pressure cannot replace the struggle of those who resist from within.

No one can sustain a cause if they are silently breaking down. Dictatorships want terror to isolate us, to make each person believe they are alone, because sometimes simply knowing that they have not been abandoned is enough to make it through the night.

Lee más desde Cuba aquí en Havana Times.

World.title: Brazilian Companies Test the 5 x 2 Work Schedule Before It Takes Effect
World.content:
Brazilian supermarkets have been characterized by intense work and little rest.

By Osmel Almaguer

HAVANA TIMES – Brazil’s Congress has put an end to the “6 x 1” work schedule, guaranteeing by law two days of paid rest per week. The new law will take effect on December 16, two months after its enactment.

However, some companies have already ventured into testing the new arrangement to become familiar with it and adapt. One of them is the supermarket chain where I work.

The first challenge was finding a way to distribute days off without favoring or disadvantaging anyone. The company’s internal rule prohibiting days off on certain strategic days, such as Saturdays, had to be eliminated. Sundays also had to begin being treated like any other day, since previously each employee was entitled to one Sunday off per month.

The number of employees on each shift had to be adjusted, with less priority given to the closing shift, which is the supermarket’s busiest period.

Even so, the challenge remained of deciding when each employee would take their days off, along with uncertainty about whether additional workers would need to be hired or whether we would have to close one day a week.

All these questions were crucial because their answers would determine the company’s future.

Closing one day a week would cause enormous losses, which could eventually lead to layoffs. On the other hand, if the company decided to hire more employees, it would inevitably have to pass the financial burden on to customers through higher product prices, ultimately affecting sales.

The solution, although ingenious, was to place the burden on the workers.

The owner devised a rotating system of days off, creating four teams whose members would take their days off together. Each team would include employees from both the morning and afternoon shifts, with representatives from every department. For example, the meat department would have at least one butcher and one salesperson working each shift every day.

Each team would be identified by a color because fixed weekly days off would disappear. Instead, days off would rotate. For example, the yellow team, which rested on Monday and Thursday this week, would rest on Tuesday and Friday the following week, then Wednesday and Saturday the week after that, and finally Monday and Sunday during the last week of the cycle.

When the schedule connects with the first week of the next cycle, which begins with Monday off, the team gets two consecutive days off. This applies to all four colors. With this ingenious but complicated structure, the company ensured fairness in the distribution of days off, maintained constant staffing, and avoided having to hire additional workers.

Since each of the four teams receives two days off, there was one remaining day on which an additional team could rest. They ultimately assigned it to Monday, the day with the lowest sales. On Mondays, two teams will have the day off.

The hardest part is that, because this is still a trial, we continue working 44 hours a week, meaning an additional hour and 18 minutes has been added to each workday. Starting in December, the workweek will be reduced to 42 hours, so the increase in daily working time compared with the previous schedule will be 40 minutes.

One year after the law takes effect, it requires the weekly workload to be reduced to 40 hours, leaving an increase of just 20 minutes per workday.

The difficulty with this system arises on public holidays because, when the supermarket remains open, the law requires employees who work on those holidays to receive an additional day off as compensation. This comes at a time when staffing is already stretched thin. Some employees will have three days off during those weeks.

The measure seems designed to provide relief, and to some extent it does. But we must not forget the owners’ bottom line, and that is where things get complicated. On the one hand, we will have two days at home to rest, go out, take care of personal matters, or even earn a little extra money. On the other hand, our daily working hours and responsibilities within the company will increase.

There will also be consequences for society as a whole, but we will have to wait a little longer to measure that impact.

World.title: It Doesn’t Take Much to be Put on the Cuban Gov. Blacklist
World.content:
Imprisoned Cuban independent journalist Henry Constantin, File photo: Facebook / Henry Constantín Ferreiro

By Lien Estrada

HAVANA TIMES – During a visit to a librarian friend in Camagüey, I learned that a meeting had been held at his workplace. At the meeting, employees were informed that everyone who contributed to the independent publication La Hora de Cuba was on the government’s blacklist (a way of saying that you are on the country’s political police watchlist). I remember bursting out laughing. Me, blacklisted by a government that calls itself Communist, just for sharing my opinions in a friend’s independent project? I found the whole thing laughable.

If I were threatening society or causing it harm in some way, whether material or spiritual, it might be understandable. But putting my observations and opinions about what I experience into writing… Is that really so dangerous that I should be blacklisted? At the time, 80% of the contributors were women.

On February 15, 2020, I was prevented from traveling to Bogotá, Colombia. I was pulled out of the line and told to wait. Then I was taken into an office, where I was informed that I was under a travel restriction. In other words, I was unable to make my planned trip, even though I had my ticket and all my documents were in order. That is what it means to be blacklisted in Cuba. Even if you complete all the required procedures, or are theoretically entitled to do so, the Communist government claims the authority to prevent you from taking certain actions or carrying out any process whenever it sees fit.

Right now, independent journalist Henry Constantin Ferreiro has been released from a punishment cell, but he has not yet been freed. He remains at a detention facility in Camagüey known as Kilo 7. He is the director of La Hora de Cuba, founded in 2013. That, too, is an example of what can happen when you are blacklisted.

Another example is when police officers show up at your home with a summons from State Security and order you to meet with them. Failing to appear can be very dangerous: you could be charged with disobedience. Under the guise of a conversation, they try to conceal the reality: it is an interrogation intended to intimidate you into stopping whatever they consider wrong (illegal), even though, from your perspective, you are simply expressing your opinions.

I imagine that, as Cuba continues to fall apart, the number of people placed on these blacklists grows by the day. The exodus becomes ever more intense. Possible solutions to the country’s economic and social chaos remain nowhere in sight. And it is painful to witness the strategies used by State Security to silence an entire people while trying, at all costs, to portray the country as peaceful and full of hope.

For my part, despite all the exhaustion, losses, and fears I have endured, I take pride in being blacklisted in my own country for these reasons. I am grateful to life for the reward I already feel in knowing that I am not among those who repress others for expressing their feelings, but rather among those who, at some point, asked themselves: Why shouldn’t I share my ideas, experiences, and aspirations…? And I did.

I trust, and my intentions and work are devoted to making it happen, that sooner rather than later I will be able to live in a free, democratic country. A country where no one is punished for creating an independent project. Where speaking one’s mind does not come at such a high price.

Read more from Lien Estrada’s diary here on Havana Times.

World.title: Why the Embargo Does Not Explain Repression in Cuba
World.content:
Berta Soler (left), photo: AP / Desmond Boylan. Camila Acosta and Yoani Sánchez, photos: taken from Facebook.

By Eloy Viera Cañive (El Toque)

HAVANA TIMES – When the Cuban government arrests a journalist or puts citizens on trial for organizing independently, a familiar explanation tends to resurface: Cuba faces exceptional circumstances because of the United States embargo, and those circumstances justify restricting rights. That argument can be challenged using legal and theoretical reasoning.

The starting point does not deny that sanctions have consequences. Recognizing that a foreign policy can harm a country is one thing; accepting that this conflict requires its rulers to persecute journalists, prevent independent associations, or prosecute people who organize on their own is quite another.

What Is the Argument for Exceptional Circumstances?

The argument works in three steps: Cuba is under threat, Cuba is subject to an embargo, and therefore those in power can do whatever is necessary to defend themselves. The practical consequence is that Cubans who disagree with government policies are expected to wait until the embargo ends before demanding their rights.

This idea is an old one, and at its core it has a concrete effect: if everything that happens on the island is the fault of the embargo and the exceptional circumstances it creates, then no one bears individual responsibility for what they do in the name of those circumstances. Defending exceptional circumstances as a justification for restricting rights amounts to defending impunity for those who carry out repression.

What Lies Between a Sanction and an Arrest?

Between a US sanction and the arrest of a journalist in Havana lies a series of decisions. Those decisions are made by people and are political in nature: officials issue orders, police officers carry them out, and authorities make choices. For that reason, the embargo cannot erase the individual responsibility of each link in that chain.

An ongoing case illustrates the point. Four men, members of the Freemasons, faced trial on November 5, 2026. The formal charge was an illegal dollar exchange transaction. The amount involved: US $300, which was used to purchase powdered milk for elderly residents of a nursing home. This is a political operation presented as a currency-related crime, and the connection between this case and any US sanction once again runs through a decision made inside Cuba.

The second example involves the independent press. Journalists Camila Acosta and Yoani Sánchez were detained on the street, prevented from moving freely, and had their equipment confiscated. Anyone who justifies these actions by invoking the embargo is siding with those who carry them out.

What Does Hannah Arendt Explain About Terror?

Hannah Arendt, the political thinker who developed the concept of totalitarianism, helps answer the fundamental question: Is violence by a totalitarian state a response to an external enemy? According to Arendt, it is not. Terror under totalitarianism does not arise solely as a reaction to adversaries who threaten the government. Rather, it is part of a system of domination that seeks to destroy pluralism and the individual’s capacity to act independently.

This leads to a conclusion applicable to Cuba: if the objective is to dominate through fear, rather than merely defeat the opposition, repression will continue even after organized opposition has been defeated. Cuba has lacked an organized opposition for years, yet repression continues.

A farm analogy helps explain it: repression functions like herbicide sprayed over an already plowed field to prevent anything from growing except what the owner wants. This interpretation is not new. It has been described since the 1940s by authors who understood totalitarianism as a model for organizing power, rather than a phenomenon tied to any particular country.

Why does a One-Party System clash with any form of autonomy?

A system that claims the right of a single party to direct society has a problem with any space for autonomy. Two examples illustrate this. The independent press is troublesome because it decides for itself what to investigate. Freemasonry is troublesome because its members chose their own leaders regardless of what the Ministry of Justice might say.

Neither case has anything to do with the embargo. With or without a blockade, with or without an embargo, any citizen who decides to organize without asking and receiving permission will run into trouble.

All states have policing functions and use force to maintain order, but that order must be enforced within legal and legitimate frameworks. Political repression in Cuba is not legitimate and often is not even legal under the island’s own laws. Regimes of this kind repress because they need to preserve their existing power structure intact. Allowing citizens to organize, obtain information, and compete politically would mean accepting the possibility of losing control.

Havel and the Independent Life of Society

To conclude, it is worth returning to The Power of the Powerless, the essay by Václav Havel, the first president of post-communist Czechoslovakia. Havel spoke of what he called the “independent life of society”: the lives of those who write, teach, create, practice their religion, or organize according to their convictions. Havel showed that, for regimes such as Czechoslovakia’s at the time or Cuba’s today, that autonomy, that independence of ordinary people, could come into conflict with the system even before it developed into explicit political opposition.

That is the conclusion tying together the arguments presented here. If conflict with those in power begins the moment someone acts independently, as with the Freemasons who buy milk for a nursing home or the journalists who go out to report, the embargo may worsen the country’s difficulties, but it does not explain why people are arrested, prosecuted, or have their belongings confiscated. Those are decisions made by people who bear responsibility for them.

First published in Spanish by El Toque and translated and posted in English by Havana Times.

World.title: “Neurotics Anonymous” – a Film Honoring the Role of Movies in Our Lives
World.content:
The Cuban film Neurotica Anonima at the La Rampa Theather in Havana.

By Irina Pino

HAVANA TIMES – Last Saturday, I watched the Cuban film Neurótica Anónima [“Anonymous Female Neurotic”] at Havana’s “La Rampa” movie theater. The film is directed by Jorge Preugorría, who is also an actor, and stars Mirtha Ibarra, the former muse and wife of film director Tomas Gutierrez Alea. The production is an adaptation of a play written by Ibarra and produced in Spain, where it enjoyed great success.

The plot centers on an usher at the [fictitious] Cine Cuba movie theater and is clearly an allegory of the country’s destruction. Together with the other movie theater employees, Mirtha Ibarra’s character is informed in a meeting of the theater’s imminent closure, due to the danger of the entire building collapsing. The employees are told they’ll be reassigned to other venues to continue their jobs.

The first of the group to react is Iluminada, the character Mirtha Ibarra interprets. She protests vehemently, since she loves this site where she has worked for many years. The other employees join her. Then, the projectionist has the idea of making a documentary to save the locale.

They fan out to the street to collect opinions. Most of those they interview agree that movie theaters are dying: people don’t go, due to the lack of transportation and a preference for the ease of watching at home.

That’s actually a reality here. Only two movie theaters are still functioning in Havana – La Rampa and Yara, each offering two shows on Fridays, Saturdays and Sundays. Those that are left from “Project 23” (which included several other theaters on 23rd Street in Havana) are subject to blackouts, making attendance at these theaters very risky.

The neighborhood movie theaters no longer exist, buried by disinterest and destruction. None of the government organizations has been interested in preserving them. This has contributed to people losing the habit of enjoying the cinematic arts in a darkened hall.

But back to the plot of Neurótica Anónima. It’s a bit fantastical, with elements borrowed from “Moscow Doesn’t Believe in Tears”, “Thelma & Louise”, “Throne of Blood”, and “The Passion of Joan of Arc”, as well as “Strawberry and Chocolate” and “To a Certain Extent”—both of the latter starring Cuban actress Mirna Ibarra.

These cinematic winks have their own beauty and are welcomed by the film buffs who detect them, for their artistic value and the feelings they evoke. This technique isn’t new – right now I’m recalling “Stardust Memory”, one of my favorite Woody Allen films, which echoes scenes from Federico Fellini’s “8 ½”.

But in this film, something very peculiar is happening: the protagonist is suffering from a neurosis that causes her to imagine herself playing the heroines from all these films. Her experience is vivid.

The sub-plot involves her real life as a couple. Her husband is an alcoholic who spent three years in prison for a crime at the foreign company where he worked. He now earns money renting out their patio for religious rites where animals are sacrificed, something Iluminada finds intolerable, along with his addiction.

I want to highlight one amusing scene, where she goes to a Research Center for Control of Neurosis. The Center has a series of different treatment rooms for different disorders. It makes me think that Cuba has us suffering from so many kinds of disorders that it would be very difficult to enumerate all of them.

In general, the film features a cast of outstanding actors and actresses, some of them now passed. Mirna Ibarra gives freshness and credibility to her character.

This feature film comes short of being memorable, nor is it as critical as other Cuban films. However, it still represents an interesting option for admirers of cinema from our island.

Read more from the diary of Irina Pino here on Havana Times.

World.title: Paraguay’s prosecutors charge Santiago Peña and seek his pre-trial detention over the Ueno Bank collapse
World.content:
Paraguay’s prosecutors charge Santiago Peña and seek his pre-trial detention over the Ueno Bank collapse

8th Sunday, November 2026 - 01:53 UTC Full article

Peña, who testified before prosecutors on Saturday, is accused of alleged breach of trust, as instigator, and self-serving administration, as perpetrator

Paraguayan prosecutors on Saturday charged former President Santiago Peña, removed from office by the Senate on Friday, and requested his pre-trial detention in the case over the collapse of Ueno Bank, which froze the savings of nearly three million customers. A judge must rule on the request. Prosecutors also charged former Central Bank president Carlos Carvallo, who is in custody.

Peña, who testified before prosecutors on Saturday, is accused of alleged breach of trust, as instigator, and self-serving administration, as perpetrator. Carvallo, who had been Ueno’s chief executive before Peña appointed him to head the Central Bank, is charged with breach of trust, producing false public documents and self-serving administration. According to prosecutors, between 2023 and 2026 the bank received large deposits from public bodies and the pension system while granting allegedly irregular loans to companies linked to its owners, the Vázquez Group. Peña denies any wrongdoing.

The former president, who had been placed under house arrest after his removal, was moved overnight to the barracks of the Presidential Escort Regiment, responsible for presidential security, after protesters threw stones at police and tore down fences near his residence in Asunción. Police dispersed the protest. Dictator Alfredo Stroessner took refuge in the same barracks in 1989 during the military coup that toppled him.

The new president, Pedro Alliana, began his term with cabinet changes. He appointed Ariel Martínez as interior minister, a post he held under former President Horacio Cartes (2013-2018), and Juan Carlos Baruja, also close to Cartes, head of the ruling Colorado Party, as public works minister. Alliana said he would suspend foreign travel to focus on the crisis and promised that all those affected would recover their savings.

Customers with balances of up to about US$1,500 have begun recovering their money, and payouts will later be extended to an initial maximum of 40 minimum wages, about 121 million guaraníes or US$19,300. Banks will open exceptionally on Sunday so that those affected can open accounts and complete the necessary procedures.

Tension remains high. Protesters and the opposition accuse Alliana of failing to act in time to prevent the bank’s collapse and are also demanding his removal and early elections in early 2027.

Princess Anne to arrive in the Falklands on the eve of the Hamburg hearing

7th Saturday, November 2026 - 02:55 UTC Full article

The visit, which runs until November 20, is in her role as Patron of the South Georgia Heritage Trust, an organisation working to protect South Georgia’s heritage and environment

Princess Anne, the sister of King Charles III, will visit the Falklands and South Georgia from Monday, November 9, the day before the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea holds hearings in Hamburg on Argentina’s case against the Sea Lion oil project, Buckingham Palace has announced.

The visit, which runs until November 20, is in her role as Patron of the South Georgia Heritage Trust, an organisation working to protect South Georgia’s heritage and environment. The Princess, who will travel with her husband, Vice Admiral Sir Tim Laurence, will begin with a series of engagements in the Falklands: she will meet members of the community, visit Cape Pembroke Lighthouse, Tussac House and the newly completed Falkland Islands National Sports Complex, and attend a reception at Government House in Stanley.

In South Georgia, a territory with no permanent civilian population, she will see the Trust’s work, meet British Antarctic Survey staff and members of the territory’s government, and commemorate the explorer Sir Ernest Shackleton (1874-1922), who sailed some 1,500 kilometres in a lifeboat to the island to seek help for his crew, trapped by ice in Antarctica.

The palace presents the trip as a heritage and commemorative visit. Its timing, however, coincides with a key week in the dispute over the islands: the Hamburg tribunal will hear Argentina and the United Kingdom on November 10 and 11, and Argentina’s Chamber of Deputies plans to debate the sovereignty defence bill on November 12, which toughens sanctions on companies linked to resource exploitation in the archipelago. Argentina claims sovereignty over the Falklands, South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands.

World.title: “They all must go”: Peña’s removal fails to calm anger on Paraguay’s streets
World.content:
“They all must go”: Peña’s removal fails to calm anger on Paraguay’s streets

7th Saturday, November 2026 - 02:50 UTC Full article

Many protesters, mostly young people, turned their anger on the entire Colorado Party government and kept vigil in the city centre with flags, placards and drums

Thousands of Paraguayans celebrated in Asunción on Friday as the Senate removed President Santiago Peña from office, but the joy turned almost immediately to anger among those who wanted a complete change of government. “Out with them all,” hundreds of protesters chanted outside Congress as Vice President Pedro Alliana was sworn in as the new head of state.

Celebrations erupted at the news that Peña, 47, was leaving office without immunity and, hours later, was placed under house arrest accused of breach of trust over the collapse of Ueno Bank, which had more than 2.9 million customers in a country of 6.1 million people. But many protesters, mostly young people, turned their anger on the entire Colorado Party government and kept vigil in the city centre with flags, placards and drums. “If the same people stay, there is no change”, “We want jail” and “Where is the money?” read the signs.

“The people are staying here until they all go,” Celicia Lugo told the EFE news agency, adding that Peña and Alliana “are the same”. “The incoming government is more of the same, because only Peña will be gone, the rest will stay,” said Milda Cuevas, who celebrated the removal and demanded that the former president “be tried” and “go to prison”. For Andrea Gutiérrez, Ueno “was just one example” of what she sees as the ongoing plundering of citizens.

The crisis erupted on Tuesday, when the Central Bank took over Ueno Bank, which had received large amounts of public funds during Peña’s term, and froze its deposits. Those affected include some 32,000 pensioners of the Social Security Institute, according to EFE.

In an attempt to contain the anger, Alliana announced after being sworn in that those affected by the bank’s closure “will be fully compensated”, without saying how. The legal deposit guarantee covers up to 75 minimum wages, about 228 million guaraníes per depositor.

World.title: Leo XIV begins his tour in Uruguay, praising Mercosur and peace and questioning abortion and euthanasia
World.content:
Leo XIV begins his tour in Uruguay, praising Mercosur and peace and questioning abortion and euthanasia

7th Saturday, November 2026 - 02:30 UTC Full article

Photo: AFP

Pope Leo XIV arrived in Montevideo on Friday, the first stop on his South American tour, and in a speech to Uruguayan authorities praised Mercosur, peaceful coexistence and care for the environment, but also defended life “even that which is still growing in the mother’s womb” and questioned euthanasia, in a country where both are legal and which is considered the most secular in the region.

The pontiff’s plane landed at 4.19 p.m. at Carrasco airport, where he was met by President Yamandú Orsi and the Cardinal Archbishop of Montevideo, Daniel Sturla. Leo XIV travelled in the popemobile along the waterfront promenade to Plaza Independencia, accompanied by some 3,000 volunteers, received the key to the city and visited the Cabildo and the Cathedral. Orsi welcomed him to a region “where there are no wars between countries”, called him “dear friend” and noted that in Uruguay former presidents sit together “in peace and joy”. Former presidents Julio María Sanguinetti, Luis Alberto Lacalle Herrera and Luis Lacalle Pou attended the ceremony, along with Lucía Topolansky, widow of former president José Mujica.

In his speech, the Pope took up Francis’s ideas on the common good and care for natural resources, and praised the transformation of Uruguay’s energy mix. He stressed the importance of peace and dialogue in resolving differences and praised the role of Mercosur, the bloc Uruguay forms with Argentina, Brazil and Paraguay. “Coexistence between people of different origins and traditions is also part of Uruguay’s history,” he said.

Leo XIV also addressed the most sensitive issues for the country. He defended life from conception, a reference to abortion, legal in Uruguay since 2012, and to euthanasia, approved in 2025. “Everyone deserves to receive [care] until the natural end of life,” he said. He also referred to the high suicide rate: “No one should feel like a stranger among their own or think that their absence matters more than their presence.” And he said secularism does not mean religion must be confined to private life.

Uruguay separated Church and State in its 1919 Constitution. Only 36% of Uruguayans describe themselves as Catholic, according to Latinobarómetro, and one in ten of those consider themselves practising. A survey by Usina de Percepción Ciudadana found that 37% of Uruguayans attach importance to the visit and 63% little or none.

On Saturday the Pope will celebrate Mass in Paysandú, visit the Montevideo neighbourhood of Casavalle and the Catholic University of Uruguay, and lead a vigil at the Centenario Stadium. On Sunday he will celebrate Mass in Florida, before the shrine of the Virgin of the Thirty-Three, the country’s patron saint, and travel to Buenos Aires. After Argentina and Peru, he will return to Rome on November 16.

World.title: Paraguay’s Senate removes Santiago Peña, who is placed under arrest, and Pedro Alliana takes office
World.content:
Paraguay’s Senate removes Santiago Peña, who is placed under arrest, and Pedro Alliana takes office

7th Saturday, November 2026 - 02:17 UTC Full article

The removal was approved at 6.55 p.m. local time by all 44 senators present out of 45, including those of the ruling Colorado Party, after a trial lasting some ten hours

Paraguay’s Senate on Friday removed President Santiago Peña from office in an impeachment trial for “poor performance of his duties” over the collapse of Ueno Bank, and hours later prosecutors ordered him placed under house arrest over alleged economic crimes. Vice President Pedro Alliana was sworn in before Congress that night as the new head of state and will serve out the term until August 15, 2028.

The removal was approved at 6.55 p.m. local time by all 44 senators present out of 45, including those of the ruling Colorado Party, after a trial lasting some ten hours. With it, Peña loses the lifetime Senate seat and parliamentary immunity he would have obtained had Congress accepted the resignation he tendered on Thursday, which was never considered. Thousands of savers gathered outside Congress celebrated the decision.

Prosecutor Christian Benítez said Peña will remain detained at home until he is placed at the disposal of the Specialised Unit for Economic Crimes and Anti-Corruption. According to La Nación, prosecutors are investigating him for alleged breach of trust, influence peddling and self-serving administration. The order also covers former Central Bank president Carlos Carvallo, according to the Associated Press. Peña denies any wrongdoing.

The Senate rejected the 72-hour extension the president had requested to prepare his defence. Peña, who had said on Thursday that he would appear, ultimately did not attend and sent his lawyers, Adolfo Ferreiro — who in 2012 defended President Fernando Lugo, also removed through impeachment — and Ricardo Preda. Both argued they had not had enough time to prepare a defence and that the trial was moot after the resignation, arguments the Senate rejected.

“I submitted my resignation to avoid further harm to the country and help restore calm to Paraguay. I do not want my presence to be a cause of further division or instability,” Peña wrote in a farewell message. “I say goodbye with gratitude, without ignoring the anguish of those who are waiting for answers today.”

Alliana, 52, born in Pilar, a former governor of Ñeembucú department and former president of the Colorado Party, was sworn in minutes after the removal. Antonio Barrios took over as vice president, according to ABC Color. The opposition accepted the succession, albeit with reservations. “We accept this situation to ensure institutional continuity for the country,” said opposition senator Rafael Filizzola, who called Alliana “complicit” in what happened. Alliana had publicly distanced himself from Peña on the eve of the bank takeover and is expected to make changes to the government and the Central Bank.

The fall of Peña, a 47-year-old economist who took office in August 2023 with a modernising message, unfolded in just four days. On Tuesday, the Central Bank took over Ueno Bank over insolvency and irregular loans to companies owned by its owners, freezing the deposits of nearly three million customers, about 60% of the adult population, as well as hundreds of millions of dollars in public and pension funds. Carvallo had been the bank’s chief executive before Peña appointed him to head the Central Bank, and Peña himself was a shareholder in the bank’s holding company until April 2025. On Thursday, the Colorado Party withdrew its support, led by its president, former President Horacio Cartes, who backed the impeachment.

World.title: Peña says he will face his impeachment trial as Argentina denies he has entered the country
World.content:
Peña says he will face his impeachment trial as Argentina denies he has entered the country

6th Friday, November 2026 - 01:56 UTC Full article

“We have no record of him being in Argentina.” Javier Milei’s government, a political ally of Peña, has not commented on the Paraguayan crisis.

Paraguayan President Santiago Peña announced on Thursday night that he will appear before the Senate to defend himself in the impeachment trial against him, after Congress failed for lack of a quorum to consider the resignation he had tendered hours earlier, leaving him formally in office. Argentina’s government, meanwhile, denied any record of Peña entering Argentina, following reports that he might have left Paraguay.

“Given the continuation of the impeachment trial, I will appear and exercise my right to a defence,” Peña said in a message released after the joint session of Congress called to accept or reject his resignation was suspended. The session lost its quorum when deputies of the ruling Colorado Party walked out. The Senate called an extraordinary session on Thursday night to set the impeachment trial in motion, on grounds of “poor performance of his duties”, and another on Friday morning to begin proceedings in the president’s presence, according to the Paraguayan press. The Chamber of Deputies had approved the charges by 78 votes to none. A two-thirds Senate majority is needed to remove him.

Uncertainty over Peña’s whereabouts persisted through the afternoon. Presidential spokesman Guillermo Grance acknowledged he did not know where the president was, according to ABC Color, and the speaker of the Chamber of Deputies, Colorado Party member Raúl Latorre, also admitted not knowing. “While we debate, the media are saying that President Santiago Peña has already set foot on Argentine soil,” opposition deputy Johana Ortega said during the session. In Buenos Aires, official sources quoted by La Nación ruled it out: “We have no record of him being in Argentina.” Javier Milei’s government, a political ally of Peña, has not commented on the Paraguayan crisis.

The reports recalled the departure of former Brazilian presidential candidate Flávio Bolsonaro, who on October 27 crossed into the Argentine city of Puerto Iguazú and flew from there to Miami after refusing to accept his defeat by Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.

The dispute between resignation and impeachment has legal consequences. If Congress accepts the resignation, Peña would take a lifetime Senate seat with parliamentary immunity; if the Senate removes him, he would lose that protection. The opposition and much of the ruling party, including Colorado Party leader and former President Horacio Cartes, back the impeachment. According to the press, prosecutors have announced they are opening proceedings against Peña, although no formal charges have yet been brought.

The crisis erupted on Tuesday with the takeover of Ueno Bank, which froze the deposits of nearly three million customers and hundreds of millions of dollars of public funds. If Peña leaves office, Vice President Pedro Alliana will take over the presidency until August 15, 2028.

World.title: Lula sees his win as “a lesson for the world” after setbacks for Netanyahu and Trump
World.content:
Lula sees his win as “a lesson for the world” after setbacks for Netanyahu and Trump

6th Friday, November 2026 - 01:42 UTC Full article

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva described his October 25 re-election as “a lesson for the world” and linked it to the electoral setbacks suffered in recent days by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and US President Donald Trump. “In the same week, Netanyahu lost in Israel and I think my friend Trump is losing in the United States,” he said on Thursday in a live broadcast on YouTube.

Lula, 81, spent an hour and a half on a livestream with congressman André Janones, the architect of the digital strategy that helped his electoral comeback, watched by some 600,000 viewers. “I am more afraid than in my first term,” he admitted. “My obsession is back: I cannot fail, I cannot betray them. I have to do better.” The president defended some of his priorities, such as ending online betting, the sovereign exploitation of critical minerals and the importance of the university entrance exam, and promised to find ways for people to take part in government decisions.

Lula said he would speak more often through social media. “I will speak more directly to the people through social media. I will no longer allow the press to interpret what I think,” he said. He also invited Janones to accompany him next week on his first official trip since re-election: the UN climate summit, COP31, in Turkey, and a summit with Southeast Asian countries in Manila.

In Israel’s October 27 election, Netanyahu’s bloc lost its parliamentary majority, winning 53 of the 120 seats, although his Likud party came first; Netanyahu has alleged fraud. In the United States, Democrats regained control of both chambers of Congress on Tuesday. Lula will begin his fourth term on January 5.

World.title: Watchdog publishes a list of 77 clergy accused of abuse in Peru ahead of the Pope’s visit
World.content:
Watchdog publishes a list of 77 clergy accused of abuse in Peru ahead of the Pope’s visit

6th Friday, November 2026 - 01:38 UTC Full article

US-based organisation Bishop Accountability on Thursday presented in Lima a list of 77 members of Peru’s Catholic clergy publicly accused of sexually abusing minors, days before Pope Leo XIV, who lived in the country for more than two decades, begins his tour of South America. Victims and the organisation called on the pontiff to take concrete steps, including setting up a truth commission.

The list, published on the website of the organisation, which documents sexual abuse cases in the Catholic Church, includes priests, brothers, seminarians and consecrated laypeople who have worked in Peruvian parishes and schools, as well as Church officials accused of allegedly covering up complaints. It is based mainly on the book Den of abusers or safe Church?, published this year by Reinaldo Nann, a former bishop of Caravelí in southern Peru who has left the priesthood. Those on the list have been publicly accused; not all have been tried or convicted.

“The Peruvian Church is stubbornly putting children at risk by covering up for abusers,” said Bishop Accountability co-director Anne Barrett Doyle. José Enrique Escardó, president of the Peruvian Survivors’ Network and one of the first to denounce the Sodalitium Christianae Vitae, the Catholic movement Pope Francis suppressed in early 2025 after abuse allegations, said “victims need comprehensive reparation” and that “the most important thing is prevention”.

The organisations made three requests to the Pope: that bishops and religious superiors in Peru publish the names of clergy accused of abusing minors; that a Truth Commission be set up to investigate the cases; and that a universal zero-tolerance rule be enshrined in canon law.

Leo XIV, who holds Peruvian nationality, was bishop of Chiclayo and chaired the Peruvian Bishops’ Conference Commission for the Protection of Minors, where he worked alongside Nann. According to the former bishop, the current Pope was then “more open to listening to victims than the rest of the bishops”, although he considers him “too cautious a man” who is not driving change fast enough. According to El País, the Vatican has announced that the Pope will meet victims during his visit, although the meeting is not yet on the official schedule. There has been no response from the Peruvian Bishops’ Conference to the list.

The Pope will visit Uruguay and Argentina before arriving in Peru, where he will stay from November 11 to 17.

World.title: An early flu outbreak is hitting the US West Coast. Here’s what it means for Mexico
World.content:
This time of year, travel from the U.S. changes from family vacationers to snowbirds heading south to Mexico for warmer weather and tourists wanting to experience Día de Muertos. But this year, travelers from the West Coast may bring an unwanted illness along for the ride.

The flu season started prematurely in the U.S., unexpectedly hitting the states bordering the Pacific Ocean sooner than usual. The early arrival is driven by a mutated influenza A strain. Over the summer, Mexico saw a surge of off-season flu that was mostly influenza B, and as of early October, Mexico’s Health Ministry had not detected this new mutation. As travelers decide whether to mask up for their flights, they should also consider extra precautions before crossing the border this year.

What’s different this year

In the U.S., flu season typically starts in the south in places like Florida, where the virus arrives from the Southern Hemisphere. The flu then spreads throughout the rest of the country during the fall and winter months. But this year, Western states along the Pacific Ocean, including Hawaii, are seeing flu levels that are normally seen in December or January. For example, Hawaii’s most recent positive flu test rate is 27.1%, significantly higher than the 5.6% rate for the same time last year. Both California and Washington have positivity rates above 11%.

The flu strain affecting these states appears to come from Asia and is a mutated version of the H1N1 virus. H1N1 is a subtype of influenza A, and the current G155E mutation can evade a person’s existing immunity. Japan first detected this H1N1 mutation in May and is now seeing surges spreading rapidly among children, leading to school closures. The H1N1 virus first emerged in 2009 in La Gloria, Mexico, and created a pandemic that mostly affected children. At this time, no G155E mutation has been identified in Mexico.

Who’s most at risk

Teens and young adults appear to have a weaker antibody response to the G155E mutation. This means the virus may spread more easily past their body’s existing immunity. So far, there is no evidence that the mutation causes a more severe illness.

Those most at risk for severe illness are the same as with prior flu seasons and have priority for free flu shots in Mexico. This includes:

Children 6 to 59 months of age

Adults age 60 and older

Pregnant people

People ages 5 to 59 who have chronic health conditions, such as diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease, lung disease, kidney disease, cancer or HIV

Healthcare workers

Other groups considered at higher risk, but not a priority for free flu shots, include:

People with disabilities

Individuals living in long-term care facilities

People with weakened immune systems

The cross-border risk

The U.S. accounts for 67.1% of international travel into Mexico, with 19 million visitors expected this year. Border crossings begin to increase in late October, driven by cultural tourism around Día de Muertos. Travel levels remain high through January because of holidays, family vacations and snowbirds escaping the cooler winter weather in the north. This travel peak coincides with the same timeframe for higher flu levels.

Health officials in both Mexico and the U.S. are urging everyone to vaccinate early. This is because it takes about two weeks for the body to develop immunity after vaccination. For the best protection for yourself and those around you, now is the time to get your shot and build immunity before holiday travel and celebrations.

Protecting yourself in Mexico

Mexico administers 30 million flu vaccines annually to prevent influenza and related complications. The Health Ministry launched the National Vaccination Campaign for the 2026-2027 fall and winter season on Oct. 12, and it runs until March 31, 2027. This year’s goal is to reduce and prevent respiratory illness complications during the cold and flu season by administering more than 50 million doses of vaccines against COVID-19, influenza and pneumonia.

Additionally, for the first time, the respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) vaccine is available to pregnant women between 32 and 36 weeks’ gestation. This intervention aims to protect the unborn child from the virus during the first few months of life. RSV is a common virus that typically causes mild, cold-like symptoms. However, infants and older adults with certain risk factors are more likely to develop severe illnesses or need hospitalization.

Free vaccination clinics are available across Mexico in local health clinics and gathering places. The Secretaría de Salud has an interactive map to help locate a clinic near you at dondemevacuno.salud.gob.mx, or you can call the toll-free number 079 for information about available sites. If you are not in a priority group for a free vaccine, you can purchase vaccines at private pharmacies and hospitals.

Leanna Coy is a contributor to Mexico News Daily.

World.title: Mexican caves: What you need to know before you step into one
World.content:
If you hike in Mexico long enough, sooner or later you’re likely to find yourself standing in front of a cave entrance, wondering if you should venture inside.

Whether invited by locals or entirely on your own, here are a few thoughts from someone who has spent many hours underground in Mexico.

Bags of golden coins

All over the world, people find caves enticing, but even more so in Mexico, which has a long history of colorful bandidos who, we are told, could think of no better place to hide their stolen coins and bars of bullion than a cave.

This stubbornly held belief has given rise to treasure-in-cave stories that I have heard again and again.

“This cueva has a small entrance, but after you crawl a while, it opens up into a huge room as big as a cathedral and then there’s a long tunnel that goes all the way through the mountain to the other side … además,” the storyteller often says, adding, “I was told that a guy went inside this very cave years ago and came upon bags filled with doubloons, but just when he was going to carry one away, a voice boomed out: ‘Todo o nada,’ meaning either you take all of it at once or you get nothing.”

Inevitably, these stories say that the beguiled explorer never made it out — but that has not discouraged countless treasure hunters from digging countless holes in just about every cave in the country.

Crystals 14 meters long

A more aesthetic sort of treasure does actually lie much deeper inside many caves: beautiful, delicate stalactites, stalagmites, aragonite crystals, and bizarre formations called helictites, which look like stalactites that have decided to defy gravity, pointing every which way.

But the most stupendous cave formations of all are the famed selenite crystals of Mexico’s Naica Cave: up to 14 meters (about 46 feet) long and 4 meters (about 13 feet) thick.

North America’s deepest cave

Equally exciting is the unbelievable size of Mexico’s cave systems.

In 1965, students in Austin, Texas, asked their geology teacher where they could find the deepest cave in North America.

The answer turned out to be Oaxaca, Mexico, and led to the discovery of Sistema Huautla. At 103.4 kilometers (64.2 miles) long and 1,560 meters (5,118 feet) deep, it’s currently recognized as the deepest cave in the Western Hemisphere.

At the same time, exploration of Mexico’s cenotes has led to the discovery and mapping of 2,096.4 kilometers (1,302.6 miles) of wet and dry caves on the Yucatán Peninsula. If these huge systems are eventually linked up, Mammoth Cave in Kentucky will have to cede the title of “Longest Cave in the World” — 686 kilometers or 426 miles — to Mexico.

No wonder speleologists widely consider Mexico the new frontier in underground exploration, where one can experience the exhilaration of being the first person to step into a passage.

Which, when standing before the entrance to a Mexican cave, prompts the question: Should you go inside?

‘Thank God for my helmet!’

Consideration No. 1: Unless we are talking about a commercial cave, you need to have the proper equipment for going underground. Experienced cavers always carry a minimum of three sources of light, for example, a headlamp and two flashlights, each with spare batteries. Serious cavers also use helmets. They not only protect you from collisions with stalactites or low ceilings, but also make all the difference should you trip and fall. “Thank God for my helmet!” is one of the most often spoken phrases (in every language) beneath the surface of the Earth.

Consideration No. 2: Many caves flood during the rainy season. To appreciate the consequences, see “The Rescue,” National Geographic’s 2021 documentary on what happened to 13 boys when a cave flooded in Thailand.

So, if it’s the dry season, you’ve got the right equipment, and you are accompanied by experienced espeleólogos. But are you clear to crawl into a Mexican cave?

Invisible spores

Hold on. There are still a few more considerations. The most serious is Histoplasma capsulatum. This is a fungus that grows on bat guano and continuously produces tiny spores, invisible to the eye. Once you breathe them in, they lodge in your lungs, and your body fights them, subjecting you to nonstop coughing, fever and chest pains — if you are lucky.

Some years ago, 17 people went to visit a small, dusty cave in Jalisco, all of them wearing face masks. After the typical histo incubation period of 11 days, all of these individuals were feeling bad, and ended up at the IMSS medical center in Guadalajara. After hours of studies, they were told to report back the following morning.

“But what about the medicine? What do we take?”

“There is no medicine. Just relax at home for two weeks and you’ll be okay.”

“But why do we have to come back tomorrow?”

“Oh, it’s because we’ve never had 17 people with histo all here at the same time. This is very exciting for us!”

Bad air

Another complication you could run into in a wild cave is “bad air.”

At low spots, carbon dioxide — which is invisible and odorless — can accumulate. If this lake of CO2 is deep enough and you step into it, you will first find yourself panting heavily as if you were running a marathon. Should you find yourself in this situation, you have about two minutes to get yourself out of there.

On top of all that, we have slight inconveniences such as low, tight crawl-ways half-filled with mud, guano and bat urine … and then there are the frequent encounters with rabies-carrying vampire bats (usually harmless unless you try to sleep in the cave). Perhaps you can see why some people in this country consider cueveros “locos.”

So, finally, should you or should you not crawl into that enticing Mexican cave?

We’ve given you (just about) everything you need to know. But the decision is ultimately yours.

John Pint has lived near Guadalajara, Jalisco, for more than 30 years and is the author of “A Guide to West Mexico’s Guachimontones and Surrounding Area” and co-author of “Outdoors in Western Mexico.” More of his writing can be found on his website.

World.title: Mexico’s week in review: INE crisis deepens, economy gains momentum and Latino voters reshape US midterms
World.content:
Plan Michoacán progress report

Wednesday’s mañanera was devoted to progress on Plan Michoacán, the federal response to Uruapan Mayor Carlos Manzo’s killing in November 2025. Sheinbaum said the plan is 67% complete, with 1,680 of more than 2,500 “actions” finished. Planned investment through 2030 has more than doubled from the original 57 billion pesos to 118 billion pesos (US $6.3 billion), and 72.43 billion pesos has been spent.

Cabinet members each highlighted a piece of the plan. Interior Minister Rosa Icela Rodríguez said 115 “Well-being Fairs” across all 113 municipalities helped residents complete more than 1.1 million administrative procedures, and that 673 firearms were exchanged for cash. The government, together with the private sector, is investing more than 41 billion pesos in six highway projects covering 411 kilometers, and work on the 9.3-billion-peso Bajío Industrial Park in Zinapécuaro starts this month. Other officials cited scholarships for 795,000 students, 177,000 people aided by the Sembrando Vida reforestation program, electricity coverage reaching 99.99% of homes and a new addiction-treatment hospital in Apatzingán. Tourism is up 10.1% through August. Mexico News Daily noted that not all the investment cited is directly tied to Plan Michoacán funding.

Security was left for a separate update next Tuesday. Homicides in the state fell 40.3% in the first nine months of 2026. At the Uruapan march, Quiroz demanded an “exhaustive” and “independent” investigation into Manzo’s killing, noting that more than 30 people have been arrested, including seven of his bodyguards. She hasn’t decided whether to run for governor.

Banxico surprises with rate cut

The central bank lowered its benchmark rate 25 basis points to 6.25% in a split vote, though 30 of 36 institutions surveyed by Citi expected no change. Banxico raised its fourth-quarter headline inflation forecast from 3.5% to 3.7% and signaled it would hold the rate “for an extended period.” The dollar hit 18.96 pesos before closing at 18.75.

Mexican judge faces extradition

Luis Benítez Alcántara, a Mexico City district judge, was arrested in Colombia on Nov. 1. U.S. officials accuse him of accepting a US $2 million bribe to help free Andrew Clark, second-in-command to ex-Olympic snowboarder Ryan James Wedding’s trafficking organization. Benítez is the first Mexican federal judge indicted by the United States, and he faces nine counts, each carrying up to 15 years. Separately, Édgar Aarón Vázquez, leader of the New Empire Cartel and accused of protecting Wedding, was killed Thursday in a confrontation with police in the State of Mexico.

Phone-free schools

Starting Tuesday, cell phones and tablets are restricted during classes and recess at public and private primary and secondary schools nationwide. High schools will set their own rules with their school communities. The Education Ministry’s slogan was “Turn off the screen and turn your imagination on!”

The rules follow a Sept. 18 decision by the National Council of Educational Authorities, in which officials from all 32 states agreed to the measures. Education Minister Mario Delgado said the goal is to boost focus, encourage socializing in schoolyards and hallways, and promote responsible technology use. The guidelines grew out of expert presentations on the addictive nature of certain algorithms and forums with parents and educators. According to Delgado, 81% of 565,000 educators surveyed backed guidelines for safe device use.

Papal visit confusion

A comment by the Vatican’s new communications chief about the pope visiting “Our Lady of Guadalupe” set off reports of a 2027 Mexico trip. Televisa’s Vatican correspondent Valentina Alazraki reported that a Vatican spokesperson clarified the comment referred to a parish in Casavalle, Uruguay. Mexico City Mayor Clara Brugada said she had no confirmation, and Alazraki reported that Leo XIV wants to come but “there is only the intention.”

Mexican-American María Montserrat Alvarado took office as the Vatican’s communications chief on Sunday. The 39-year-old Mexico City native, raised in Miami, is the first laywoman to lead a ministry-level Vatican department.

Mexico’s economy gains momentum

The MND Economy Index™ hit a record 74.5 out of 100 for August, half a point shy of “strong.” Mexico-Canada trade rose 18.3% in the first eight months to 34.42 billion Canadian dollars, while Mexico’s trade surplus with the U.S. jumped 26.1% through September to a record US $184 billion, driven largely by AI-related equipment purchases.

2026 annual growth forecasts improved in both Banxico (1.5%) and Citi (1.8%) surveys.

Mexico City weighs tougher penalties for animal poisoning

After four dogs died from poisoned meat in Condesa’s Parque España, lawmakers proposed tougher penalties. Labor Party lawmaker Diana Barragán’s bill would allow three to nine years when poisoning kills an animal, and other proposals would bar convicted abusers from acquiring animals. A 58-year-old suspect is jailed pending trial.

Travel headlines

Looking ahead

Banxico and Citi both predict Mexico’s economy will grow about 1.8% to 1.9% in 2027, with year-end 2026 inflation near 3.9%. Banxico has signaled it plans to hold its rate steady for an extended period.

One sector that will shape that outlook is data centers. Economy Minister Marcelo Ebrard said last week that companies have announced more than US $8 billion in data center projects, led by Querétaro, with Guanajuato and Nuevo León also drawing investment. Sheinbaum has said Mexico needs data centers to advance in artificial intelligence, but not necessarily to become a hub for the rest of the world, given their energy and water demands.

Data centers were also a hot topic in the U.S. midterms. The Associated Press reported that a campaign season filled with outrage against them ushered in a wave of Democrats pledging to clamp down on the facilities. Gina Hinojosa, who won the Texas governorship, campaigned on a moratorium on new data center construction. Whether the issue crosses the border is an open question as Mexico heads to its own midterms on June 6, 2027.
