World.title: From the archive: Is the beach the real Mexico?
World.content:
The goal of our “From the archive” series is to revisit popular stories that capture the unique history and culture of life in Mexico. This Sarah DeVries article — originally published in February 2025 — explores whether living in a beachfront community really qualifies as an authentically Mexican experience.

About 15 years ago, when I had my first online job, one of my supervisors lived in Los Cabos. She very much enjoyed telling people “what it was like in Mexico,” and was proud of her knowledge.

“Well, in my experience here, that’s not a problem at all!” she’d say when one of the many other Mexican residents would casually bring up an issue. “Things are pretty easy in Mexico, you know. All you have to do is …”

A friend of mine who worked with me and lived in Mexico City would privately express her annoyance to me. “That’s easy to say if you live in a gringo paradise with low population density. I’d love to see this ‘Mexico genius’ get by in my own barrio.”

Even in Xalapa, where spotting a foreigner is like stumbling upon Waldo, I’ve been on the receiving end of this kind of annoyance. “You live in a bubble in Xalapa; that’s not the real Mexico!” a friend of mine once insisted. She herself had lived for years in a tiny town outside of a fairly dinky and unglamorous city. I rolled my eyes and let it go; it wasn’t something I cared to debate.

Besides, if that was “the real Mexico,” I’d happily leave it all for her.

Where is the real Mexico, and how do I get there?

Chances are that you clicked on this article primed for a debate. It’s a sensitive topic, especially among those of us who consider Mexico home and ourselves to be fully integrated. Whether we foreigners live in beach towns or tiny towns, everyone’s surely got an opinion!

So what is the measuring stick that people use to define the “real” … any place, actually? Because this tendency isn’t at all unique to Mexico.

Think of every Hallmark rom-com you’ve ever seen: a high-powered and glamorous businesswoman travels from her sleek New York City apartment back to her home for the holidays. It’s always a small town in the U.S. Midwest. Everyone knows each other, and her high school sweetheart is there, handsome and single, or perhaps widowed.

That small town? That’s the “real” America, the movie says. Not like New York City, which was actually established first. Similarly, people in Mexico — especially foreigners — often have some strict ideas about what counts as “authentically Mexican.”

I suspect, actually, that Mexicans do not have conversations about this, which is telling: they have nothing to prove. They’re Mexican, and wherever they live in the country is “really” Mexico, period.

Not all beaches are developed equally

Still, beach communities receive special scrutiny. Not all beach communities are alike, though. Living in Cancún or Los Cabos, for example, is very different than living in Chachalacas, Veracruz.

Cancún and Los Cabos are full of fancy beach resorts and the kind of development that could attract royalty. Everyone who works there has to speak at least some English.

Chachalacas is a tiny town that only recently got paved roads. Its fanciest hotels are fancy simply because they have in-room air conditioning and a pool. English can most certainly not be counted on, and beach parking is on the sand … or you can take a bus from a small, unfancy town nearby. Bathrooms are bare toilet seats in the middle of small wooden shacks; 1 star for sure. To flush the toilet, there’s a large tub of water outside and a bucket. But boy, is the seafood good!

So here’s the question: Is Chachalacas more real than Cancún? It’s hard to argue that they share much in common besides the beach. Or perhaps it’s the presence, or not, of foreigners in a place, be it the beach or somewhere else. Does the fact that one might look around and see a sea of one’s paisanos make it less authentic? For some, I think it absolutely does.

We were in the real Mexico all along

And of course, the question might not even be a consequential one. People live where they want to live. Does it matter if they’re adapting or not? Do people even care if where they’re living is authentic in a stranger’s view? But no matter where you are, if you live on or near the beach, expect to get side-eyed when you talk about your knowledge of Mexico.

The word “beach” is practically synonymous with “vacation,” which explains a lot. You hear it in our language: “Time to leave the beach and get back to the real world.” This is a sad phrase to me, since it separates the real world from the kind of world that you’d actually like to live in. So perhaps the rest of us are just jealous?

My daughter has an educational book about sex. It spends some time talking about the differences between boys and girls. It does a good job of emphasizing that things like haircuts and clothing are pretty much never exclusive to one sex. “There are all kinds of different ways to be a boy,” it says, and “there are all kinds of different ways to be a girl.”

This, I believe, is the correct attitude to have with most things. Like everywhere else, Mexico is a very diverse place. There are as many different ways to “be Mexico” as there are different ways to be Mexican.

So wherever you are, maybe don’t worry about it too much. If someone wants to challenge you on it, like my friend above, shrug your shoulders and suggest a Tex-Mex style margarita, or maybe a caguama … you know, depending on where you are.

Sarah DeVries is a writer and translator based in Xalapa, Veracruz. She can be reached through her website, sarahedevries.substack.com.

World.title: Carlota de Limón: The Mexican cocktail that transported me to my mother’s kitchen
World.content:
“You have to try one of these; it’s like a refreshing key lime pie,” a hotel guest at the bar said. I walked over to the friendly group, all with the same drink in hand. The cocktail in front of them resembled a blended piña colada that was pale yellow and frothy on top, garnished with a thin lime wedge on the rim.

My friend and I were staying at the Dreams Estrella del Mar in Mazatlán, Sinaloa, for a few days to check out the hotel and all its amenities. After the nightly show, we stopped by the bar for a drink and tasted what would ultimately be the most memorable part of the trip.

The cocktail was tangy from the lemon, sweet from the sugar, and instantly took me to something very familiar. The creamy texture and the balance of tart and sweet also felt familiar, as if I had tasted this combination many times before.

Then it hit me: It was a dessert my mom used to make growing up, and one I’ve always requested when I’m home. It was a favorite of mine that she called “lemon dessert,” which I know now as a Carlota de Limón.

Back in my mother’s kitchen

Carlota de Limón is a Mexican icebox cake made with lemon juice, Galletas María (sweet, thin vanilla cookies), and a creamy mixture of evaporated and condensed milk. Layered and chilled until set, it has the perfect balance between sweet and tangy.

It was one of my favorite desserts growing up. I remember eating it by the spoonful, freshly made and the day after, as well as the feeling of disappointment when it was gone. It wasn’t reserved for special occasions, and my mom made it regularly whether we were having dessert at home or sharing a meal with guests. It was a dish that was made on a whim, ingredients almost always on hand, and one that didn’t last long.

In other words, it was always a hit.

My mother’s kitchen was where our family came together and where some of our deepest conversations happened. While water boiled for pasta or soup simmered in spices, we would all gather around the island, almost like magnets pulling us closer, filling the space with conversation, laughter and connectedness. That feeling is still there today when I visit my parents, especially around the holidays or special occasions.

An unexpected connection

At the hotel, I pulled up a bar stool and watched the bartender make another drink. Curious about its inspiration, I struck up a conversation with him. He was 23 and working his first hotel bartending job, where he had been experimenting with flavors and creating cocktails, something he found to be a fun, creative outlet.

When I described the dessert the cocktail reminded me of, he recognized the Carlota de Limón, a favorite of his, too. He had been experimenting with ingredients to create the drink, combining Licor 43, the vanilla and spice notes echoing the María cookies, and the fresh lemon juice, sugar and heavy cream to match the creamy layer. He would then shake it vigorously with ice until the mixture turned frothy and cold, adding a simple lime wedge as the finishing touch.

What began as an experiment in flavors had unexpectedly recreated something familiar to me. The bartender didn’t know my personal backstory of the dessert, but his experimentation with a new cocktail and my memories of my mother’s kitchen had led us to the same place.

Why flavors stay with us

Research from the National Library of Medicine has a name for the way a familiar smell or taste can bring back a personal memory: the Proust effect, named after the French writer Marcel Proust. The theory is that taste and smell can trigger autobiographical memories, leading to powerful emotions. Research on the brain’s olfactory pathways also shows direct connections between smell processing and the regions involved in emotion and memory, which makes sense given my strong and positive response to the citrus cocktail.

To me, Carlota de Limón was more than just a dessert; it was something my mother made regularly, in a kitchen where conversations and laughter occurred. The flavor was familiar, but so was everything I associated with it.

When I returned home, I found myself thinking less about the resort’s beautiful pools, manicured grounds or nightly shows, and more about that cocktail. A drink I’d encountered on vacation that had brought back a dessert so familiar that I hadn’t thought much about what it meant to me until that moment.

On the drive home from the airport, my husband asked how the trip went. My answer was simple: “Do we have any lemons? I have a drink in mind.”

Sandra Lee is a contributor to Mexico News Daily.

World.title: My family always travels during Día de Muertos. Here’s what we’ve enjoyed most
World.content:
There are certain magical aspects of living in Mexico that simply cannot be replicated elsewhere — its foods, traditions and seasons. And because of Mexico’s vast geography and cultural topography, many of those elements can be heightened by being in the right place at the right time.

In that regard, nothing compares to Día de Muertos: A time of year in which colors are blooming, communities are celebrating and honoring loved ones, and regional gastronomy, customs and superstitions are on display for everyone to be collectively immersed in.

Beyond the obvious, increasing importance of the Mesoamerican holiday in Mexico for so many native families and local households, Día de Muertos means something especially personal for me and my family since it marks our anniversary of having moved to Mexico from California. The holiday always reminds me of arriving in Mexico after having gained dual citizenship and being received by festive parades, open-armed friends and relatives, and getting a dose of Mexico’s fullest, most complex flavors that have come to define what we most enjoy about living on this side of the border.

Building our own annual tradition

My wife’s and my own appreciation for Día de Muertos extends further back, years before we had fully relocated to Mexico. In 2019, we visited my mom, who is Mexican-born and was living on my abuelo’s ranch in Oaxaca at the time. We spent a month traveling the state of Oaxaca with her. The highlight? A full week of Día de Muertos in Oaxaca City.

I’ll never forget when we arrived, hopped off the bus, dropped our things off and went into the loud, colorful streets as Oaxaqueños had already kicked off their days-long celebration in the middle of the afternoon. A man wearing a Spider-Man mask saw us standing among the crowd, and as we soon found out would be a common occurrence and part of the local hospitality, he offered to pour out a shot of mezcal from the bottle in his hand.

As an outsider, there is no warmer welcome on the planet than someone picking you out of the masses on the street and pouring you mezcal. It’s a spirit and energy that would come to embody every Día de Muertos holiday we’ve experienced — the sense of connection and togetherness.

Since then, we’ve turned it into our own tradition to celebrate the holiday in different parts of Mexico as often as we can.

The regional nuances of Día de Muertos

My wife recently shared a visual map with me that outlines the different kinds of pan de muerto that are prepared throughout Mexico, based on each state’s history and gastronomic influences. Her point, besides nudging me to pick up another round of pan de muerto for our house, was that Mexico offers more to try than we know, especially whenever Día de Muertos rolls around.

It’s true. Everywhere we’ve been during this season has always presented a new way through which to experience and understand the multidimensionality of how the holiday is celebrated and revered.

Nearby, in the town of Naolinco, Veracruz, and its surrounding mountain communities, the festival is largely centered on the cempasúchil. This year, the community of San Pablo Coapan welcomed thousands of visitors for its fifth annual Festival del Cempasúchil, in which the local cempasúchil farms open to the public with a festival-like array of activities, food and Instagrammable photo ops.

The flower fields are decorated with playful calaveras that are decorated in Veracruzano style, ranging from a 25-foot-tall Jarocho skeleton to a human-sized fútbolero in the afterlife wearing a Tiburones Rojos soccer uniform from the 1990s (a team that no longer exists but certainly evokes memories for anyone who recalls the historic Veracruz team and grew up watching Liga MX).

In the pueblo of Naolinco proper, just a few miles up the mountain, Día de Muertos is celebrated with “La Cantada” (or a townwide serenade), where locals go around singing from the cemeteries to the streets throughout the night.

Major cities and regional rituals

Of course, there are the more globally popular and large-scale interpretations of Día de Muertos that can be seen in Oaxaca or Mexico City. In both cases, the holiday draws countless international and domestic visitors who join in on the fun and traditions as local families honor their deceased relatives with a mix of humility and bombast.

In both Oaxaca and Mexico City, expect massive gatherings of happy-go-lucky tourists and locals, as you’ll have to shuffle your way around the crowds and generally pay higher prices. The celebrations are bigger, louder and, to a degree, more capably geared toward tourism than other locales. I’d say for starters, both Oaxaca’s capital and Mexico City are a comfortable entry point into Mexico’s sprawling multiverse of Día de Muertos, as they provide broadly appealing and easy-to-navigate celebrations, both of which my family has enjoyed and experienced ourselves multiple times.

Of course, we still have a bunch of places to visit on our wishlist that I’ve been told about by my Mexican family members and other travelers. In the Huasteca jungles, “Xantolo” brings the holiday to life with “La Viejada,” a regional masked dance in which townspeople dress up as elders (similar to Veracruz’s “El Viejo del Año Nuevo” custom at the end of every year) to remember their relatives.

1 of 17

Indigenous customs from Huasteca to Campeche

In parts of Michoacán, there is a lake procession where the Purépecha fishermen use torches to light their path across the water and celebrate with all-night vigils.

Choo Ba’ak, a bone-washing ritual that happens every year in the Campeche pueblo of Pomuch, is part of Hanal Pixán (the Maya Day of the Dead) and offers an idiosyncratic version of the holiday unlike the contemporary mainstream version that is usually portrayed.

National Geographic described the ceremony as such: “…families wash the tombs and clean the bones of their deceased. After the cleaning they keep the ossuaries, or the box where the bones are deposited, open so the skulls and bones receive sun and air, as dictated by tradition. Relatives also arrange, paint and adorn the ossuaries and cover them with an embroidered white tablecloth bearing the name of the deceased.”

In Huaquechula, Puebla, unique altars — three to four stories tall, resembling a pyramid — are on display inside homes, with each layer of the altar representing a different aspect of life and death (the earth, the heavens and a celestial summit). The elaborate designs are typically defined by white cloth and marigolds.

As a taxi driver in Oaxaca once told me, you’d need more than a few lifetimes to truly experience all that Mexico has to offer regionally for Día de Muertos.

Our highlights from this year in the mountains of Puebla

The Pueblo Mágico of Cuetzalan del Progreso is tucked away in the northernmost edge of the state of Puebla, high up in the Sierra Norte mountains.

Unlike the majority of Puebla, which is commonly known for its arid plateaus and Talavera pottery in its state capital and surrounding areas, northern Puebla offers a microclimate and culture of its own that more closely resembles the humid, tropical and high-altitude Indigenous communities of Papantla in northern Veracruz, which is located just a few miles away on the other side of the mountain.

It’s not what one might think of when thinking of Puebla. And yet, it’s where regional customs for Día de Muertos are flourishing. We drove roughly four hours north of Xalapa (or about five hours northeast from Mexico City) to experience it for ourselves this year.

We weren’t disappointed, to say the least.

The town’s architecture alone is worth the winding mountain curves that one must navigate to reach the small, ages-old village that is — because of its elevated location in the mountains — famously drenched in drizzly mist and rainfall. The narrow alleys and steep, cobblestone paths (which all lead to the gorgeous Parroquia de San Francisco de Asís and its Totonac voladores, who perform their flying ritual on a sky-high wooden pole at the center of the plaza) resemble a miniature version of Guanajuato’s capital city, without the overcrowded tourism and with a hyper-local texture.

Flying globos de Cantoya into the night

I was told by a couple of young locals that families don’t commonly celebrate Día de Muertos by visiting the graveyards overnight (which is the tradition elsewhere). Instead, they light “globos de Cantoya” (miniature hot-air balloons made from paper and other materials) and send them off into the night.

From groups of high schoolers to older professionals who’ve mastered the craft, the town gathers on Día de Muertos weekend, as everyone takes turns setting up and sending off hundreds of their custom, artisanal balloons. The balloons — and their makers — vary in style, decoration and success (often, the small balloons will self-combust in flames and come burning back to earth, which can sometimes cause fires in the area). But generally, it’s a safe and spectacular tradition to witness in person.

The tradition, as it was explained to me in the pueblo, is meant to represent a path back to the heavens for the souls who are visiting their altars to enjoy the ofrendas laid out. Each globe, as it ascends brightly and colorfully into the night sky, is meant to guide family members back to the spiritual realm.

In recent years, Cuetzalan has turned the tradition into a legitimate state-funded festival, known locally as “El Vuelo del Quetzal” (The Flight of the Quetzal), and officially as Festival Internacional de Globos Artísticos de Papel. Surprisingly, the festival is only in its second year of formal operation, which helps it retain a charmingly niche, DIY feeling.

Local flavors and looking ahead

During the day, it is all preceded by local dances, voladores, Catrina costume contests and the general ambiance of a Pueblo Mágico worth its salt: excellent food, tianguis and a dense number of historic stairways and nooks to explore.

Among the standouts in town, you cannot skip TAOL, which is led by Chef Adriana Márquez and offers elevated, accessible takes on local dishes, including tlayoyos, chilpozontle, itacate, pipián, coffee and more. It’s the kind of chic eatery that would draw lines out the door in Mexico City, but since it’s hidden behind an unassuming stone exterior in Cuetzalan, it is able to offer ample space and friendly prices for what I would consider among the best cuisine I’ve tasted this year.

Paired with Día de Muertos activities and the hordes of costumed kids making their rounds on Halloween night to ask for their calaverita at local shops, which my son participated in, a few nights in Cuetzalan is a slept-on destination for late October and early November.

Though we elected to stay home last year to dedicate our time and resources to building and decorating an altar inside our home — with the help of my mom, who supplied many photos of our relatives — we’ve enjoyed going on the road to see how others embrace the spirit of the tradition.

I’m already thinking about where we might end up next year and what it will impart.

World.title: Moving to Ethiopia in 2026, A Practical Guide
World.content:
Moving to Ethiopia means settling in Addis Ababa, the capital at high altitude, and it suits people who arrive with a job, a spouse or a business. It is hard for anyone without a plan, because the Immigration and Citizenship Service (ICS), the national immigration agency, and the banks work differently from those in the United States.

For a reader in the United States, the stakes are practical, since the State Department, the US foreign ministry, rates the country Level 3 on its four-level scale, Reconsider Travel. Ethiopia also hosts the African Union, the continent’s political body, which makes Addis Ababa a diplomatic centre, so the rules below are worth knowing before any commitment.

Your first month after that is US$1. Start my free brief Yes, email me my free daily brief — I can unsubscribe any time. Entry. Tourists apply online for an eVisa, an electronic visa, and the fee shows at checkout.

Residence. The immigration service (ICS) offers marriage, student, business and employer-backed five-year permits.

Money. Banks set their own rates, about 161 birr (Ethiopia’s currency) per US$; plan to pay in birr.

Health. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) advises malaria prevention even in Addis Ababa.

Safety. The US government rates Ethiopia Level 3 of 4, Reconsider Travel, with some areas at Level 4, Do Not Travel.

Foreign residents can enter Ethiopia through several documented routes, but the practical limits sit in banking, health and safety rather than in the visa alone.

Visas and Residence

Tourists apply for an eVisa online at the official government portal, and the fee is shown at checkout. Third-party websites list conflicting amounts, so check the portal before paying.

The ICS site lists business and student visas, temporary residence through marriage, renewals and a five-year renewable Permanent Residence ID. Most applications take about 5 to 10 business days, and some take longer.

Residence Routes at a Glance Conversions use 161 birr per US$ throughout this guide. Business visa. Passport valid six months, form, two photos, invitation letter from a partner in Ethiopia, proof of business activities.

Passport valid six months, form, two photos, invitation letter from a partner in Ethiopia, proof of business activities. Student visa. Passport valid six months, acceptance letter from an accredited Ethiopian institution, proof of tuition payment or scholarship, proof of financial means.

Passport valid six months, acceptance letter from an accredited Ethiopian institution, proof of tuition payment or scholarship, proof of financial means. Marriage permit. Marriage certificate (authenticated by the foreign ministry if issued abroad), a copy of the entry visa, the spouse’s kebele ID (a local residence ID) or Ethiopian passport, and a bank statement of 500,000 birr (about US$3,100) or more, a house title or a vehicle licence.

Marriage certificate (authenticated by the foreign ministry if issued abroad), a copy of the entry visa, the spouse’s kebele ID (a local residence ID) or Ethiopian passport, and a bank statement of 500,000 birr (about US$3,100) or more, a house title or a vehicle licence. Permanent Residence ID. Employer’s letter to ICS, the company’s valid trade certificate, a passport copy and a valid working or tourist visa.

Renewals must be filed before the current permit expires, with proof of continuous residence such as a rental agreement or utility bills. Our guide to the Ethiopia Golden Visa covers a 10-year permit for foreign investors that was launched in March 2026, reported, not confirmed by us at a primary source.

Several legal guides report, but we have not confirmed, that the employer applies and the Ministry of Labour and Social Affairs issues the work permit. They also report that working without one breaks the law, and they warn against entering on a tourist eVisa while planning to switch later.

A section of the Addis Ababa light rail line, pictured in December 2015. Photo: Ludger Heide / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 2.0)

This also signs you up to our weekday newsletter, Africa Intelligence. Nothing arrives until you click the confirmation link, and you can stop either with one click. Privacy policy

Addis Ababa Neighbourhoods

Bole, near Bole International Airport, is the most common choice of foreigners, with many apartments, restaurants and hotels. Kazanchis is central, with offices and hotels.

Old Airport and Sarbet are residential districts popular with families. Piassa, also called Arada, is the historic old centre, and it is busy with older buildings and less housing aimed at foreigners.

Megenagna is a busy transport junction in the north-east of the city. Ask people who live there which district suits your daily route.

The right district depends on where you work, where your children study and how long a commute you accept. Visit at least two areas before you sign a lease.

What Life Costs in Birr

Estimates reported by listing platforms, not official statistics, put a furnished one-bedroom in Bole, Kazanchis or Old Airport at about 113,000 to 193,000 birr (about US$700 to US$1,200) a month. A furnished two-bedroom is put at about 161,000 to 242,000 birr (about US$1,000 to US$1,500).

Flats in less central, local neighbourhoods are put at about 24,000 to 64,000 birr (about US$150 to US$400) a month. Landlords often ask for several months upfront, reported, not confirmed.

In Plain English ICS. Immigration and Citizenship Service, the national immigration agency.

Immigration and Citizenship Service, the national immigration agency. NBE. National Bank of Ethiopia, the central bank.

National Bank of Ethiopia, the central bank. Birr. Ethiopia’s currency.

Ethiopia’s currency. eVisa. An electronic visa applied for online.

An electronic visa applied for online. Kebele ID. A local residence ID issued in a person’s neighbourhood.

Annual inflation has run near 15% since July 2026, at 15.3% in July and 14.9% in September. Prices in birr therefore rise quickly, and cash held in birr loses value against the dollar over time.

Food, transport and utility prices vary widely and are not covered here. Treat every rent figure above as a starting point and check it on the ground.

Banking and Foreign Currency Rules

Since July 2024 banks and authorised dealers set their own exchange rates under a National Bank of Ethiopia (NBE) directive, FXD/01/2024. The NBE publishes an indicative daily rate, a weighted average of the previous business day’s bank transactions, only as a reference.

The NBE sets the rules on which businesses may accept foreign currency inside Ethiopia. Plan to pay in birr for daily costs.

Rules on cash limits, foreign-currency accounts and traveller allowances have been amended several times since 2024. Confirm every figure with the NBE and your bank before you travel or move money.

It is not clear whether resident foreigners who are not of Ethiopian origin can hold a foreign-currency account, so ask your bank early. Ask what documents it needs before you transfer money.

Healthcare and Vaccines

The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) recommends prescription malaria prevention for all areas below 2,500 m, including Addis Ababa. Options include atovaquone-proguanil, doxycycline, mefloquine and tafenoquine, and you should speak to a doctor.

The CDC recommends yellow fever vaccination for all travellers aged nine months and over, though generally not for travel limited to the Afar or Somali regions, two regions of eastern Ethiopia. It is not required for direct travel from the United States, yet it is required on arrival from yellow fever risk countries, including after layovers of more than 12 hours.

The CDC also recommends hepatitis A, hepatitis B and typhoid vaccines for most travellers. It advises a polio booster, because poliovirus was found in Ethiopia in the past year, and a meningococcal vaccine for the dry season from December to June in meningitis-belt areas, a band of African countries with frequent outbreaks.

Cholera transmission is widespread but rare in travellers, and infected dogs are common, so rabies is a risk. The CDC advises medical evacuation insurance and lists a Level 2 travel health notice for global polio, dated 23 September 2026.

Safety and Travel Advisories

The US State Department rates Ethiopia Level 3, Reconsider Travel, citing unrest, crime, kidnapping, terrorism, landmines, communications disruptions and exit bans. The rating covers the whole country, and some areas carry a higher one.

The advisory also lists some areas at Level 4, Do Not Travel, including the Amhara Region in northern Ethiopia. The list covers other areas too, so read it in full.

The list changes, so read the current advisory before every trip. Our guide to the Level 3 travel alert for Americans explains what the rating means in practice.

Before You Fly Checklist Read the current State Department advisory.

Keep offline copies of your passport and permits.

Carry a backup SIM card.

Plan malaria prevention and yellow fever vaccination with a doctor.

Buy medical evacuation insurance.

Confirm current cash limits with your bank.

Communications disruptions, meaning internet or phone cuts, are a named risk. Exit bans, which stop a person leaving the country, are named too.

Altitude and Climate

Addis Ababa lies at about 2,350 m (7,700 ft) above sea level, which makes it one of the highest capitals in the world. New arrivals can feel breathless or tired for the first days.

Plan a slow first week, and ask a doctor about altitude before you fly. Rainy seasons and temperatures are not covered here.

Americans should also read our guide to the Ethiopia health declaration form before they fly. The form is a separate step from the vaccines and prevention described above.

Ask your insurer whether altitude problems and medical evacuation are covered by your policy. Settle that before you leave, not after you arrive.

Schools for Children

Families have three named options in Addis Ababa. The International Community School of Addis Ababa is an International Baccalaureate (IB) school, which offers a worldwide diploma programme.

Lycée Guébré-Mariam is the French school, and Sandford School, a private school, is the third option. Tuition is set by each school and not all schools publish it, so ask admissions.

Fees are not quoted here. Ask each school about tuition and the documents it needs before you commit to a lease.

Our guide to Ethiopian holidays and events helps you plan around public dates. Check each school’s own calendar as well.

Internet and Phones

Ethio Telecom is the long-established national operator. Safaricom Ethiopia, the Ethiopian unit of the Kenyan operator, launched mobile service in 2022 after its consortium won a US$850 million licence bid.

Safaricom Ethiopia reached 10 million active customers in July 2025. Check coverage at your street address before you sign a lease.

The State Department lists communications disruptions as a risk, so do not rely on a single connection. Connection speeds are not quoted here.

Keep offline copies of key documents and a backup SIM card. Save embassy and insurer numbers on paper as well.

What It Means for You

For an American, moving to Ethiopia is a documentation project more than a leap of faith. The visa route, the cash rules and the health plan each need settling before you land.

The strongest cases are tied to an employer, a spouse, a school or a business, because those routes have written requirements on the ICS site. Open-ended arrivals on a tourist eVisa are the weakest, and legal guides warn against planning to switch later.

Money needs the most thought, since inflation is near 15% and the rules on foreign currency are tight and change often. Check the cash limits and ask your bank early about a foreign-currency account.

Getting there is part of the plan, and our guide to Ethiopian Airlines flights from Atlanta to Addis Ababa covers one route from the United States. Read it alongside the safety advisory before you book.

Government policy drives many of these rules, so it helps to know who sets it. Our report on the new cabinet Ethiopia approved for Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed in October names the team behind them.

Ethiopia’s rules have changed in recent years, from the exchange rate system in 2024 to the Golden Visa in 2026. Check each rule at the official source before you act.

A calm approach works best, with a short first visit, documents in order and a plan that still works if the internet goes down. That preparation costs little and protects the larger decision.

What Is Not Known

We could not confirm the current eVisa fee, so check the portal at checkout. We also could not confirm whether resident foreigners can open foreign-currency accounts, so ask your bank.

Exact work-permit fees and processing times are not confirmed, and the work-permit process described by legal guides is reported, not confirmed. School fees are not confirmed either.

The rent figures above are estimates reported by listing platforms, not official statistics. Safety advisories and Level 4 areas change, so read the current advisory each time.

We have not forecast the birr, and we have not quoted the Golden Visa investment amount. Nothing here is legal, medical or financial advice.

Frequently Asked Questions

How do I get a tourist visa for Ethiopia?

Apply online at the official eVisa portal, where the fee is shown at checkout. Third-party websites list conflicting amounts, so check the portal before paying.

Do Ethiopia’s currency rules change often?

Yes. The National Bank of Ethiopia has amended its foreign-exchange rules several times since 2024, so confirm cash limits and account rules with your bank before you travel.

Can I pay in US dollars in Ethiopia?

Plan to pay in birr for daily costs. The National Bank of Ethiopia sets rules on foreign-currency payments and has amended them since 2024, so ask your bank what is allowed.

Do I need vaccines to live in Addis Ababa?

The US CDC recommends malaria prevention and yellow fever vaccination, plus hepatitis A, hepatitis B and typhoid vaccines for most travellers. Speak to a doctor before you go.

Is Ethiopia safe for Americans?

The State Department rates Ethiopia Level 3, Reconsider Travel, with some areas at Level 4, Do Not Travel. Read the current advisory before every trip.

World.title: Cost of Living in Nigeria in 2026
World.content:
The international terminal of Murtala Muhammed International Airport in Lagos, photographed in March 2019. No patient or suspected case is shown. Photo: Sm105 / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

On Sunday 8 November 2026, rent, power and petrol cost an expat roughly US$800 to US$1,250 a month in our Lekki Phase 1 and Ikoyi examples, before food, school and health cover. It matters for US citizens, remote workers, diaspora families and travellers weighing a move or a long stay.

The naira is firmer than at the end of 2025, so each naira price now converts to more dollars, and data for Port Harcourt, the oil hub in Rivers State, is too thin for a budget. Our Lagos cost of living detail goes deeper on the largest city.

Key Facts Free daily brief — no card needed Get every Africa story in one morning email We build you a personalized brief around the topics you follow — free for 7 days. Love it? Your first month after that is US$1. Start my free brief Yes, email me my free daily brief — I can unsubscribe any time. Rent. Reported Lagos two-bedroom rents run from about US$6,300 to US$12,800 a year, paid in advance.

Power. Band A, the tier for homes with 20-plus daily hours of supply, was last reported at US$0.16 per kilowatt hour.

Fuel. Petrol is about US$1.01 a litre in Lagos at NNPC, the state oil company, stations.

Prices. Yearly inflation was 14.63% in September, and the naira is firmer than at end-2025.

Date. As of 8 November 2026.

File photo. Victoria Island and the lagoon in Lagos, Nigeria’s commercial capital. Photo: Ayorinde Ogundele, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.

In Plain English •Rent is paid yearly. Rent is commonly paid a year ahead, so the cash needed on day one is far larger than the monthly figure. •Band A is the electricity tariff tier for homes on feeders (district power lines) with at least 20 hours of supply a day. •Official versus parallel market. The naira trades at an official rate and on a street market; every figure here uses the official rate. •Generators. Power cuts are common enough that many homes keep a petrol or diesel generator, or a battery inverter, as backup.

How the Exchange Rate Changed Costs

All dollar figures here use about N1,347 per dollar, the official market level in the first week of November, where N is the symbol for the naira and m means million. The naira traded at about N1,535 per dollar at the end of 2024 and about N1,429 at the end of 2025, based on year-end official market rates reported at the time.

The official market traded at about N1,347 in the first week of November. One dollar now buys about 12% fewer naira than at the end of 2024 and about 6% fewer than at the end of 2025.

For someone paid in dollars, a stronger naira makes every local bill more expensive in US$. A rent of N10m (about US$7,400) would have cost about US$6,500 at the end-2024 rate.

Africa Intelligence One email, every weekday morning. African markets, politics and business — filed from our newsroom in Rio. Yesterday’s subject line: “Zuma's party disputes Durban's vote” Get the brief Free. We send a confirmation link first — nothing arrives until you click it. Unsubscribe with one click in any edition. If you stop opening us for 30 days we stop sending by ourselves, as we assume the interest is no longer there. See our privacy policy. We never share your email.

Anyone paid in naira gains buying power on imported goods, while dollar earners lose some of their edge. We used the official market rate throughout and did not check the parallel market rate, which can differ.

Rent in Lagos

Rent in Nigeria is commonly paid per year in advance, which is the biggest cash hurdle for newcomers. A 2026 market report by the real-estate firm Lagos Realty, covered on 9 August 2026, gave average annual rents for a two-bedroom flat in several Lagos districts.

Ikoyi, a wealthy district on Lagos Island, came to N17.25m (about US$12,800) a year, or about N1.44m (about US$1,070) a month. Other Lagos districts in the same survey were cheaper, as the list below shows.

Lagos two-bedroom flat, average annual rent •Ikoyi: N17.25m (about US$12,800) •Victoria Island: N15m (about US$11,100) •Lekki Phase 1: N10m (about US$7,400) •Ikate: N8.5m (about US$6,300)

The report gives no method for its averages, and other listing guides show lower or wider ranges for Lekki. Treat every figure as indicative.

We found no confirmed rent for one-bedroom or three-bedroom homes in Lagos, so we give no number. The surveys behind these averages are not confirmed by the landlords or agents themselves.

Rent in Abuja and Port Harcourt

In Abuja, one property-market site, whose page carries a 30 December date and is probably from 2025, listed annual rents for three-bedroom apartments, and none of these figures is independently confirmed. Maitama, a district of Abuja, Nigeria’s capital, averaged N22m (about US$16,300), within a range of N15m to N40m (about US$11,100 to US$29,700).

Abuja three-bedroom apartment, annual rent (reported) •Wuse II: N15m (about US$11,100) •Jabi: N14m (about US$10,400) •Gwarinpa: N7m (about US$5,200)

Wuse II, Jabi and Gwarinpa are also districts of Abuja, and the listing site did not state how it gathered its averages. Our Abuja city explainer describes the districts in more detail.

Port Harcourt data is thin and weak. A property listings site showed an average of about N2.5m (about US$1,860) a year for two-bedroom flats in August 2026, with premium listings near N7m (about US$5,200).

Electricity and the Generator Question

The Nigerian Electricity Regulatory Commission (NERC), the national power regulator, last reported a Band A tariff of N209.50 (about US$0.16) per kilowatt hour, applied from 1 July 2024. We could not confirm the current rate on the regulator’s own site.

Band A covers feeders that supply at least 20 hours a day. At the last reported price, 500 kilowatt hours in a month would cost N104,750 (about US$78).

Supply was uneven in early 2026. In June 2026 NERC issued Directive 2026/002, ordering compensation for Band A customers on feeders that supplied under 18 hours a day in February and March.

Many households run a generator or an inverter as backup. We found no verified generator running cost, so we give no number.

Petrol, Diesel and Cooking Gas

On 4 November 2026, petrol at NNPC stations cost N1,355 (about US$1.01) a litre in Lagos and N1,325 (about US$0.98) in Abuja. Abuja prices were N1,370 to N1,405 (about US$1.02 to US$1.04) before.

We found no confirmed pump price for Port Harcourt. Prices differ between filling stations, so these NNPC figures are a guide rather than a rule.

The Dangote oil refinery near Lagos, Africa’s largest, raised its wholesale price from N1,265 (about US$0.94) to N1,350 (about US$1.00) in mid-September. Our report on Dangote’s petrol pricing follows later moves.

We found no reliable current diesel price and no confirmed cooking gas price. Generator owners and households that cook with gas should check local prices before budgeting.

Inflation and Food Prices

Headline inflation, the yearly rise in consumer prices, was 14.63% in September 2026, down from 15.39% in August, the National Bureau of Statistics (NBS), Nigeria’s official statistics office, said on 15 October. Food inflation was 19.59% year on year, although food prices fell 1.55% from August to September.

Food inflation in Lagos was reported at 34.4% year on year, the highest among the states. The national minimum wage is N70,000 (about US$52) a month, and the federal government has told labour the next review is due in June 2027.

The NBS price watch for March 2026 put a 50 kg bag of local rice at N112,000 (about US$83), up 20.5% from N92,946 (about US$69) in February. A crate of 30 eggs cost roughly N6,100 (about US$4.50).

A market check around the same time found local rice nearer N60,000 (about US$45), so official and street prices differ. We found no confirmed prices for a grocery basket, chicken or restaurant meals.

Getting Around and Staying Safe

The Lagos State government raised fares on its bus rapid transit (BRT) and Bus Reform Initiative buses by 13% from 2 March 2026, after an 18% rise in February 2025. We could not confirm prices for ride-hailing, Abuja taxis or mobile data bundles.

The US State Department’s advisory for Nigeria is reported at Level 3, which means reconsider travel. In April 2026 it widened its Do Not Travel list (Level 4, the highest warning) to include Plateau, Jigawa, Kwara, Niger and Taraba states, and reports put the total at 23, so check the current advisory.

Security can add cost, from guards to estate service charges. We found no confirmed prices for either, so no figure appears in the budgets below.

Schools and Health Cover

International school fees can be a large extra line for families. Fees vary widely by school and by grade.

Charterhouse Lagos, a private British-curriculum school, lists N23m to N35m (about US$17,100 to US$26,000) a year for 2026/27, from Primary 1 to its final year, SS3. American International School Lagos, a private school with a US curriculum, lists tuition of about US$17,600 to US$32,200 a year for 2025/26 on its own fee page, plus other fees, and the school says tuition can be paid in dollars or naira.

We found no confirmed fees for international schools in Abuja or Port Harcourt. We also found no verified premium for expat health insurance, so we give no number.

Sample Monthly Budgets

The lines below are our own arithmetic, an illustration and not a survey. They assume 500 kilowatt hours of power at the last reported tariff and 100 litres of petrol a month, and they leave out food, school, health and security, with the Lagos petrol price for Lagos lines and the Abuja price for Abuja lines.

Illustrative monthly lines, rent plus power plus petrol •Lagos, Lekki Phase 1 two-bedroom: N1,073,583 (about US$797) •Lagos, Ikoyi two-bedroom: N1,677,750 (about US$1,245) •Abuja, Wuse II three-bedroom: N1,487,250 (about US$1,104) •Abuja, Gwarinpa three-bedroom: N820,583 (about US$609)

Schools add the next big block. Charterhouse works out at about N1.92m to N2.92m (about US$1,420 to US$2,170) a month, and American International School Lagos at about US$1,470 to US$2,680.

Port Harcourt has no budget line because verified data is missing. Its thin rent listings and its unknown pump price leave too many blanks to build one honestly.

Single Person, Couple or Family

A single person can lean on the lower lines, such as Gwarinpa in Abuja at about US$609 a month or Lekki Phase 1 in Lagos at about US$797, before food and health cover. Rent is paid yearly, so the cash needed upfront is far larger than the monthly figure suggests.

A couple shares one home, so rent and power stay nearly the same, while food and fuel costs rise with each extra person. We have no confirmed grocery prices to size that.

A family faces school fees first, and every option here is a large extra line. Charterhouse or the American school would add US$1,420 to US$2,680 a month per child to any of these lines.

What It Means for You

For US citizens on dollar contracts, the stronger naira means each naira bill converts to more dollars than at the end of 2024. Remote workers paid in US$ should budget a full year of rent upfront and a backup for power.

Diaspora families sending money home now get about 12% fewer naira per dollar than at the end of 2024, and our Nigeria history explainer gives the wider background. Travellers heading to Lagos for Detty December, the city’s festive season of events, can read our guide to Lagos events and costs for event costs, and should read the current State Department advisory before booking.

What We Could Not Confirm

Several costs that matter to a household have no reliable figure yet. We list them here so that no gap is filled with a guess.

Not confirmed, so no number is given •Rents for one-bedroom and three-bedroom homes in Lagos. •Generator running costs, a current diesel pump price and cooking gas prices. •A pump price for petrol in Port Harcourt, and international school fees in Abuja and Port Harcourt. •Grocery baskets, chicken and restaurant meals. •Ride-hailing, Abuja taxi and data bundle prices. •Guard costs and estate service charges. •Premiums for expat health insurance, including plans from the National Health Insurance Authority (NHIA), the federal health insurance agency, and hospital consultation fees. •The parallel market exchange rate, and any provider confirmation of the rent, school and insurance figures.

The next NBS inflation release, for October, will show whether price growth keeps slowing. A steadier naira and a lower inflation rate would make budgets easier to plan, but the cost of power backup and school fees will stay the main variables.

Frequently Asked Questions

How much does it cost to live in Nigeria as an expat?

Rent, power and petrol alone run about US$797 to US$1,245 a month in our Lagos examples, and reported Abuja examples come to about US$609 to US$1,104. Food, school, health cover and security come on top.

Is Lagos or Abuja cheaper for an expat?

Our data cannot rank the two cities, because the Lagos lines use two-bedroom flats and the Abuja lines three-bedroom ones. Gwarinpa in Abuja comes to about US$609 a month, Lekki Phase 1 in Lagos to about US$797 and Ikoyi in Lagos to about US$1,245.

How much is petrol in Nigeria in 2026?

At NNPC, the state oil company, stations on 4 November, petrol cost N1,355 (about US$1.01) a litre in Lagos and N1,325 (about US$0.98) in Abuja. A Port Harcourt pump price is not confirmed.

Is Nigeria safe for foreigners to live in?

The US State Department’s advisory is reported at Level 3, reconsider travel, and it widened its Do Not Travel list in April 2026. Check the current advisory before you plan a move.

Sources National Bureau of Statistics (nigerianstat.gov.ng) · Central Bank of Nigeria (exchange rates) · Nigerian Electricity Regulatory Commission (nerc.gov.ng) · Lagos State government · US State Department (travel.state.gov) · NNPC Figures from these institutions were read in published reports; rent and school figures come from reported listings and reports, not confirmed by the providers.

World.title: South Africa’s Role in Africa Explained
World.content:
Apartment blocks and the Hillbrow telecom tower in Johannesburg, in a March 2020 photo. Photo: Bertrand van der Berg / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0)

Africa Explained: South Africa

South Africa is the economic and diplomatic hub of southern Africa, yet in 2026 it is also a country under strain. It runs a coalition government, faces a 30% US tariff on most goods and was kept out of this year’s Group of 20 (G20) talks.

Key Facts Free daily brief — no card needed Get every Africa story in one morning email We build you a personalized brief around the topics you follow — free for 7 days. Love it? Your first month after that is US$1. Start my free brief Yes, email me my free daily brief — I can unsubscribe any time. Who: President Cyril Ramaphosa was named interim chair of the Southern African Development Community (SADC) in November 2025.

Economy: Official unemployment reached 33.6% in the second quarter of 2026, up from 32.7%.

Money: The South African Reserve Bank, the central bank, raised its benchmark repo rate to 7.25% on 23 September 2026.

Trade: US duty-free trade programme AGOA (African Growth and Opportunity Act) is renewed, but its end date is unsettled.

Next: Third-quarter unemployment data, October inflation and a Reserve Bank rate decision are due in the coming weeks.

A plain guide to what South Africa does for Africa, what holds it back, and what US readers and investors should watch next.

Why South Africa Matters to Africa and to US Readers

South Africa is one of the continent’s largest economies, with deep mining, car-making, banking and shipping sectors. Its ports, power grid and banks also serve neighbouring countries.

That role comes with duties and risks. When South Africa’s power grid, ports or politics wobble, neighbours that depend on its rail lines, ports and electricity feel it too.

Cancel anytime. Start for US$1 Email address Get the PDF Free. We send a confirmation link first, and the same address then receives The Rio Times Brief, our daily briefing. Unsubscribe with one click at any time; see our privacy policy. Your checklist is ready. Download the PDF checklist

Industry, Mining and the Continental Hub

The country’s industrial base stretches from platinum and gold mining to vehicle plants and food processing, and its financial sector in Johannesburg handles banking and listed investment. That sector also includes crypto firms, as in our report on a South African bitcoin firm that lost four of its six directors.

We do not rank it against Nigeria or Egypt here, because the ranking changes with the exchange rate and the year. What is clear is that few African countries combine heavy industry, deep capital markets and large ports in one place.

The G20, BRICS and the Rift With Washington

South Africa held the G20 presidency in 2025 and hosted the summit in Johannesburg, the first on African soil. The United States then took over the presidency and said South Africa would not be invited to its 2026 meetings.

Finance Minister Enoch Godongwana has said Washington did not accredit South Africa for G20 finance talks. The South African government in Pretoria calls this a temporary setback and expects to return when the United Kingdom takes over the presidency.

South Africa is a member of BRICS, a group of emerging economies that began with Brazil, Russia, India and China and has since grown. It uses that platform to argue for a bigger voice for developing countries in global institutions.

For US readers, the two roles pull in different directions. Washington is a key market and investor, while BRICS gives Pretoria options beyond the West.

SADC and African Union Leadership

The Southern African Development Community (SADC) is a 16-member regional bloc that covers trade, power and security. On 7 November 2025 its leaders met in an extraordinary virtual summit after Madagascar gave up the chair following political upheaval there.

President Ramaphosa was elected interim chair, a role the summit said should run until August 2026. We could not confirm who chairs the bloc today, so this article does not name a current chair.

South Africa also sits at the centre of African Union (AU) diplomacy, the continental body based in Addis Ababa. Pretoria has long taken part in AU peace efforts, though its record on each crisis is debated.

The Government of National Unity

After the May 2024 election, the African National Congress (ANC), which has governed since 1994, lost its outright majority. On 14 June 2024 it formed a Government of National Unity (GNU) with the Democratic Alliance (DA), until then the main opposition, plus the Inkatha Freedom Party and the Patriotic Alliance, both smaller parties.

The coalition has survived into its third year, with Ramaphosa still president. Critics inside and outside it, including the smaller party ActionSA, say it has delivered too little.

Local government elections were held on Wednesday 4 November 2026. We have not confirmed the final results of these local elections, so we do not publish vote shares here.

The Rand and the Reserve Bank

The South African Reserve Bank (SARB), the central bank, sets the repo rate, the benchmark borrowing cost for banks, which also steers the rand, the national currency. On 23 September 2026 it raised the rate by 25 basis points (0.25 percentage points) to 7.25%, and the prime lending rate, which banks charge customers, rose to 10.75%.

The bank now expects growth of 1.2% in 2026. Inflation was 5% in June and 4.4% in August, according to the Reserve Bank’s September statement.

Investors also watch credit ratings from agencies such as Fitch, S&P Global and Moody’s, where Fitch upgraded South Africa to BB (below investment grade) in June 2026 with a stable outlook. S&P did the same in November 2025 with a positive outlook, and Moody’s is reported to have a positive outlook too.

Upgrades matter because they lower the government’s borrowing costs. Further upgrades depend on debt, growth and the performance of state companies.

Power Cuts, Ports and Rail

Load-shedding, the planned nationwide blackouts, has eased sharply. Eskom, the state power company, said in April 2026 that it expected none through the winter.

The risk has not gone away, because new generation and grid expansion are still needed. Reform of electricity markets and pricing is also still under way.

Transnet, the state rail and port company, is the other bottleneck. National Treasury, the finance ministry, says in its 2026 budget document that Transnet continued to fall short of its operational and financial targets.

Slow trains and ports raise costs for miners and farmers. They also hold up goods bound for landlocked neighbours across the region.

File photo. Traffic at a central Johannesburg intersection, South Africa. Photo: Gsalamander, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.

Trade With the United States and AGOA

The African Growth and Opportunity Act (AGOA) gives eligible African countries duty-free access to the US market on hundreds of product lines. It lapsed on 30 September 2025 and was later renewed with retroactive effect.

Several law-firm and trade-press reports say the renewal runs to 31 December 2026, and South Africa remains eligible for now. Some reports say a later funding law moved the end date to December 2028, but we have not seen the statute, so treat the end date as open.

Eligibility is reviewed every year by the US administration, and the result of this year’s review is the next thing to watch. Separately, South Africa has faced a 30% US tariff on most goods since August 2025.

Exporters selling into the US feel that gap most. The two governments have also clashed over the G20.

What Investors Are Watching

Data is due in the coming weeks. It starts with third-quarter unemployment from Statistics South Africa, the national statistics agency, where the previous reading was 33.6%.

October consumer price inflation follows. The Reserve Bank then holds its next rate decision, from a starting point of 7.25%.

Rating reviews and the AGOA eligibility decision are also pending. Longer term, investors track whether the coalition holds together, whether Transnet recovers and whether growth moves above the 1.2% the Reserve Bank expects for 2026.

What It Means for You

If you invest in South Africa through US-listed funds or the Johannesburg exchange, rates, ratings and trade rules matter more than the daily headlines. A higher repo rate supports the rand but squeezes households and companies that borrow locally.

If you travel or do business there, including for the Cape Town Sevens rugby weekend on 5 and 6 December, the power cuts that dominated recent years have eased, but ports and rail still slow freight. Our South Africa history explainer explains how today’s political system took shape.

What Is Not Known

We could not confirm the final results of the 4 November local elections, the current SADC chair, or whether AGOA now runs to 2026 or 2028. We also could not confirm the dates of the next rating reviews.

We do not know how Washington will treat South Africa’s AGOA eligibility. Nor do we know whether the 30% tariff will change.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is South Africa’s role in Africa?

South Africa is a major economic hub, with large mining, manufacturing and financial sectors, and a leading voice in the African Union and the Southern African Development Community. Its power, port and rail problems also affect neighbouring economies.

Is South Africa still in the G20?

Yes, it remains a member. The United States, which holds the 2026 presidency, has not invited it to the 2026 meetings, and the South African government expects to return when the United Kingdom takes over.

Does South Africa still have duty-free access to the US under AGOA?

For now, yes. The programme was renewed after it lapsed in September 2025, but the end date and the annual eligibility review are not settled.

What is South Africa’s interest rate?

The Reserve Bank’s repo rate is 7.25% after a 25 basis point rise on 23 September 2026. The next decision is due in the coming weeks.

Who governs South Africa?

A Government of National Unity formed on 14 June 2024, led by President Cyril Ramaphosa of the African National Congress. It includes the Democratic Alliance and other parties.

Sources South African Reserve Bank monetary policy statements (resbank.co.za); Statistics South Africa labour force survey, Q2 2026 (statssa.gov.za); National Treasury 2026 Budget Review (treasury.gov.za); SADC communique of the extraordinary summit, 7 November 2025 (sadc.int); Independent Electoral Commission election timetable (elections.org.za); US Trade Representative AGOA page (ustr.gov); BRICS and G20 member statements. Read on 8 November 2026.

World.title: Ghana’s Role in Africa Explained
World.content:
GHANA · EXPLAINER

Ghana is one of Africa’s most closely watched economies in November 2026, and it matters far beyond West Africa for gold, cocoa, oil and a stable democracy. This guide explains Ghana’s role in Africa in plain English, with the latest figures, for readers in the United States and elsewhere.

Key Facts Free daily brief — no card needed Get every Africa story in one morning email We build you a personalized brief around the topics you follow — free for 7 days. Love it? Your first month after that is US$1. Start my free brief Yes, email me my free daily brief — I can unsubscribe any time. Economy Ghana’s economy grew 6.0% in 2025, and inflation was 5.5% in October 2026.

Gold Ghana mined 5.94 million ounces in 2025, and small-scale miners out-produced large mines for the first time.

Debt The IMF, a global lender, completed its final review of Ghana’s programme on 27 July 2026.

Trade The secretariat of the African Continental Free Trade Area sits in Accra, and 50 countries have ratified it.

Next Finance Minister Cassiel Ato Forson is due to present the 2027 Budget on Thursday 12 November.

In Plain English Cedi: Ghana’s national currency.

Ghana’s national currency. IMF: the International Monetary Fund, which lends to countries in financial trouble.

the International Monetary Fund, which lends to countries in financial trouble. ECOWAS: the Economic Community of West African States, a regional bloc.

the Economic Community of West African States, a regional bloc. AfCFTA: the African Continental Free Trade Area, a single-market plan for the continent.

the African Continental Free Trade Area, a single-market plan for the continent. Galamsey: the local word for illegal small-scale gold mining.

Why Ghana Matters Beyond Its Borders

Ghana is a Gulf of Guinea country of gold, cocoa and oil, and it has become a reference point for how an African state can climb out of a debt crisis. Its capital, Accra, also hosts the secretariat of the African Continental Free Trade Area, the continent’s single-market project.

Readers in the United States feel the link through remittances, visas, trade rules and a large diaspora. For the long background, see our Ghana history guide, which traces the country from its origins to 2026.

Golden Jubilee House, also called Flagstaff House, the office of Ghana’s president, seen from a road in Accra. Photo: jbdodane / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0)

Gold, Cocoa and Oil Pay the Bills

Ghana mined 5.94 million ounces of gold in 2025, up 23.41% from 4.82 million ounces in 2024, according to the Ghana Chamber of Mines, the mining industry body. Small-scale miners produced 3.11 million ounces, or 52.4%, and for the first time out-produced the large mines.

GoldBod, the state gold-export regulator, is to buy 30% of large miners’ output under a deal in force since 1 July 2026. The governor of Ghana’s central bank, the Bank of Ghana, said on Thursday 24 September that gold exports had become irregular in August rather than stopping, and that a significant amount shipped the week before.

If you stop opening us for 30 days we stop sending by ourselves, as we assume the interest is no longer there. See our privacy policy. We never share your email.

Cocobod, the state cocoa marketing board, opened the 2026/27 season on Friday 25 September with a farmgate price, what farmers are paid, of GH¢42,400 (Ghana cedis) per tonne (about US$3,646 at about 11.63 cedis to the dollar). That is up from GH¢41,392 and equals 71.18% of the realised export value.

Ghana pumped 37.3 million barrels of crude in 2025, the sixth straight annual fall from 71.44 million barrels in 2019, according to PIAC, the Public Interest and Accountability Committee that watches oil income. In the first half of 2026 petroleum revenue rose 52% to US$561.41 million.

How Ghana Left the IMF Programme

The International Monetary Fund approved a US$3 billion, 39-month loan programme for Ghana in May 2023, the Extended Credit Facility for low-income countries. Its board completed the sixth and final review on Monday 27 July 2026, releasing a last payment of about US$371 million.

The board also approved a Policy Coordination Instrument, a programme that carries no IMF money but keeps reform targets under review. By the IMF’s count, Ghana’s economy grew 6.0% in 2025 and gross reserves nearly doubled to US$11.9 billion by the end of 2025, about four months of imports.

The IMF now rates Ghana’s risk of debt distress as moderate. Credit rating agencies have followed, with rating agency Fitch lifting Ghana from B- to B on Friday 8 May 2026 and rating agency Moody’s raising it from Caa1 to B3 on Friday 9 October 2026.

Prices, Rates and the Cedi

Annual inflation was 5.5% in October 2026, up from 5.2% in September and a third straight monthly rise, the Ghana Statistical Service said on 4 November. In October 2025 it was 8%.

The Bank of Ghana, the central bank, held its policy rate at 14% in September, the third hold of the year. Finance Minister Cassiel Ato Forson is due to present the 2027 Budget on Thursday 12 November.

The cedi lost 7.9% against the dollar by the end of June 2026, according to the Bank of Ghana. Reserves stood at US$12.05 billion on 22 September, against a peak of about US$14.5 billion earlier in 2026, according to the governor.

The Home of a Continental Market

The African Continental Free Trade Area, known as AfCFTA, aims to join Africa’s markets into one trading bloc. Its permanent secretariat is in Accra, and 50 countries have ratified the agreement, according to the secretariat.

ECOWAS, the West African regional bloc, elected Senegal’s President Bassirou Diomaye Faye as its chair on Sunday 19 July 2026 at a summit in Lungi, Sierra Leone. Ghana does not chair the bloc, but President John Mahama named former security chief Larry Gbevlo-Lartey as special envoy to the Alliance of Sahel States in January 2025, the group formed by Mali, Burkina Faso and Niger after they left ECOWAS.

A Democracy With a Peaceful Record

Freedom House, a US-based democracy watchdog, rates Ghana 80 out of 100 and “Free” in its 2026 report. It notes that competitive elections since 1992 have brought peaceful transfers of power between the two big parties, Mahama’s National Democratic Congress and its rival, the New Patriotic Party.

In December 2024 Ghana’s election authority, the Electoral Commission, initially declared Mahama, of the National Democratic Congress, the winner with 56.55% of the vote. Mahamudu Bawumia, the New Patriotic Party candidate and then vice-president, took 41.61%.

Diaspora and US Ties

Ghana received about US$7.8 billion in remittances in 2025, up from about US$4.6 billion in 2024, Bank of Ghana Governor Johnson Asiama has said. He added that the United States is the largest source of those transfers.

In September 2025 Ghana agreed to accept West Africans deported from the United States, a deal Mahama says carries no quid pro quo. In the weeks that followed, Washington restored five-year multiple-entry visas for Ghanaians after earlier curbs.

The ties reach individual US cities too, as our report on Ghana’s agreement to send nurses to Columbus, Ohio shows. Ghana’s own cost of living is covered in our guide for foreigners.

Galamsey and the Fight Over Illegal Mining

Galamsey is the local word for illegal small-scale gold mining, and it is the most visible threat to Ghana’s rivers. The state water company has shut treatment plants in the past when mining muddied the raw water.

The tension is built into the economy, because small-scale gold now supplies more than half of national output. Our explainer on Ghana’s illegal gold mining sets out the history and the law.

What It Means for You

For US investors, Ghana offers gold exposure, cocoa supply and a government recovering from default, with Moody’s and Fitch both now rating it in the single-B range of credit ratings. The risks are a weaker cedi, oil output that fell for six straight years to 2025 despite a rise in the first half of 2026, and pressure on gold exports.

Travellers heading to Accra this winter can plan around our Detty December guide to Lagos and Accra events, which covers Ghana’s year-end festival season. Prices and entry rules change, so check them before booking.

What Is Not Known

We could not confirm whether gold exports are back to normal, because the central bank has described them as both paused and merely irregular. We also could not confirm an official size for the 2026/27 cocoa crop.

The current US tariff rate on Ghanaian goods is unclear, and so is whether the Sahel states will rejoin ECOWAS. One report says the government revoked a regulation that allowed mining in forest reserves in July 2026, but that is reported, not confirmed.

What to Watch

The 2027 Budget on Thursday 12 November will show how the government plans to hold its gains after the IMF exit. The central bank’s next rate decision will show whether it reads rising inflation as a threat.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Ghana’s role in Africa?

Ghana is a major gold, cocoa and oil producer and the home of the AfCFTA secretariat. It is also one of the continent’s steadier democracies.

What does Ghana export?

Gold, cocoa and crude oil are its main exports. Small-scale miners produced 52.4% of its 5.94 million ounces of gold in 2025.

Is Ghana still under an IMF programme?

No, the IMF board completed the final review of the US$3 billion programme on 27 July 2026. Ghana now has a Policy Coordination Instrument, which carries no IMF money.

Where is the AfCFTA secretariat?

In Accra, Ghana. Fifty countries have ratified the free-trade agreement.

Is Ghana a stable democracy?

Freedom House rates it 80 out of 100 and “Free”. Power has passed peacefully between its two main parties since 1992.

Sources: Ghana Chamber of Mines; Cocobod; Public Interest and Accountability Committee (PIAC); International Monetary Fund, Executive Board release of 27 July 2026; Bank of Ghana, policy rate page; Ghana Statistical Service, inflation release of 4 November 2026; AfCFTA Secretariat; ECOWAS Commission; Freedom House, Freedom in the World 2026; Electoral Commission of Ghana.

World.title: Ecuador’s Role in Latin America Explained
World.content:
PILLAR · ECUADOR

Ecuador is a small country with a big job on the map: it runs on the US dollar, feeds the world’s breakfast tables and sits on the front line of the cocaine trade. For a reader in the United States, it matters as a supplier of shrimp and bananas, a source of migrants and remittances, and a test case for how to fight organised crime.

This guide explains how Ecuador fits into Latin America in plain English, from its money to its gangs to its friends and rivals. It is current as of Sunday, 8 November 2026.

Key Facts The country Ecuador is a Pacific nation of about 18 million people that uses the US dollar, led by President Daniel Noboa.

The money Shrimp passed oil as the top export in 2025, and migrants sent home US$7.7 billion.

The danger 2025 was Ecuador’s deadliest year on record, though killings fell about 8% in the first nine months of 2026.

The partners The US signed a trade deal on 13 March 2026, and a tariff fight with Colombia began in January.

What is next Ecuador votes for more than 220 mayors and 23 provincial governors on 29 November 2026.

Power Index Ecuador ranks 8th of 14 in Ecuador ranks 8th of 14 in The Rio Times Latin America Power Index , with 37.2 points (November 2026 edition).

Pedestrians on the Malecón 2000 riverfront promenade in Guayaquil, February 2024. Photo: Freddy eduardo / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY-SA 4.0).

In Plain English Dollarised means Ecuador uses the US dollar as its money and cannot print its own. Prefect is the elected head of a province, the level between the national government and the mayors. Remittances are the money migrants send home to their families. Organised crime here means drug-trafficking gangs that fight over ports, prisons and smuggling routes.
