World.title: Week in Review: Between Hope and Apathy
World.content:
Bulgaria has a newly elected president – government-backed candidate Iliana Iotova. In the November 1 run-off for the presidency, she won 57.6 per cent of the votes cast to her challenger Andrey Gyurov’s 39.5 per cent.

Yet unlike their neighbours in Serbia, who voted in record numbers in recent elections, Bulgarians voted in record low numbers. Only 29.1 per cent of eligible voters cast ballots in the run-off, slightly more than in the first round. Our analysis looks at why many Bulgarians are tuning out of politics altogether.

World.title: With Change of Power, Serbia Can Reinvigorate EU Accession Bid
World.content:
“Catastrophic” - that’s how Dragana Djurica describes the current state of Serbia’s European Union accession process.

On Wednesday, the bloc’s executive arm, the European Commission, delivered its annual assessment of the progress made - or not - by countries bidding for membership. One of the main takeaways was the substantial progress made by Montenegro; another was the dramatic backsliding by Serbia.

“This is not a progress report, as it is officially called, but a report on backsliding,” said Djurica, head of the European Movement in Serbia, an NGO that advocates for Serbia’s EU integration.

“It is one of the most critical, and I would even say the worst, reports Serbia has received from the European Commission since the start of accession negotiations.”

World.title: Turkey Arrests Former Minister Over Stock Market Fraud Scandal
World.content:
A court in Istanbul on Friday ordered the arrest of Fatma Betul Sayan Kaya, a former minister and deputy chair of Turkey’s ruling Justice and Development Party, AKP, over her alleged role in a major stock market financial fraud.

The Istanbul Prosecutor’s Office accused Kaya of “being a member of an organised crime group and violating stock market law”.

Her husband, Ilyas Kaya, and a former chair of the Capital Markets Board, Ibrahim Omer Gonul, were given a travel ban but not arrested.

Fatma Betul Sayan Kaya, who was family and social policies minister from 2016 to 2018, resigned in September as a deputy chair of President Recep Tayyip Erdogan’s ruling AKP after allegations emerged about share transactions by her and her husband.

She is accused of illegally profiting through share-price manipulation after she received 2.17 billion Turkish lira (about 38.4 million euros) after reportedly investing 163 million lira (about 2.7 million euros) in an investment fund.

The couple deny wrongdoing. They have transferred some of the profits to an account designated by the banking regulators.

The AKP and the government welcomed the arrest order as proof of their good governance.

“We move forward by renewing ourselves! We are constantly reborn. We part ways with those who do wrong and those who succumb to their own desires, and we continue on our path stronger than before,” Turkish Justice Minister Akin Gurlek wrote on X after Sayan Kaya’s arrest on Friday.

The investigation has already resulted in more than 100 detentions while Turkey’s Capital Markets Board has ordered the liquidation of 131 investment funds managed by seven portfolio management companies.

According to Reuters, the funds’ assets are worth around 18.8 billion euros, involving about 353,000 investors. A Turkish television channel put the total number of investors at more than 514,000.

Kaya comes from a family with experience of public office. Her brother, Omer Fatih Sayan, a former telecommunications regulator chief and deputy transport minister, was appointed to the Energy Market Regulatory Board in July.

Her sister, Ayse Hilal Sayan Koytak, previously ambassador to Kuwait and Bahrain, was appointed ambassador to Finland in September. Another sister, Nazmiye Sumeyye Sayan, previously served on Istanbul’s municipal council.

World.title: Serbia’s Anti-Terrorism Unit Chief Detained Over Alleged Abuse of Protesters
World.content:
A court in Belgrade on Friday ordered up to 30 days of detention for nine current and former employees of Serbia’s Interior Ministry, including the commander of the Special Anti-Terrorist Unit, Igor Zmiric, over allegations of abusing and torturing students and others inside the government building following protests in August 2025.

According to the court, the nine suspects were remanded in custody over concerns that they could influence witnesses and obstruct criminal proceedings. The court also cited the seriousness of the alleged offence and the public concern it had caused, which could jeopardise the fair conduct of the proceedings.

The suspects are accused of jointly committing the criminal offence of abuse and torture.

According to the prosecution, the suspects used force and threats to inflict pain and suffering on students and other people in the government building’s garage between 10.30 p.m. on August 14 and 1 a.m. the following morning, with the aim of obtaining information, intimidating and unlawfully punishing them.

At the time of the offence, they were working as officers of the JZO, a police unit used to protect high-ranking state officials and major government buildings.

The suspects were arrested earlier this week. Among them is Milan Vukovic, a retired JZO officer who is now acting director of the detention facility where former JZO chief Marko Kricak is being held.

Kricak, who headed the unit at the time of the alleged abuse, has also been arrested, but in connection with a separate investigation into a murder in Belgrade.

During the mass anti-government protests of the past two years, some protesters have accused Kricak of using excessive force. Student Nikolina Sindjelic alleged that Kricak had threatened her with rape while she was detained in the garage beneath the government building in August 2025.

At least 15 people were detained in the garage beneath the government building on the night of August 14, 2025, amid anti-government protests, BIRN reported.

BIRN obtained testimonies given to prosecutors by four detainees and interviewed five others, who described being beaten, threatened with sexual violence and death, and having their personal belongings destroyed. Rights groups Amnesty International and Civil Rights Defenders warned that the alleged treatment could amount to torture and violate international law.

At the time, the Interior Ministry rejected the allegations, insisting that the officers had acted in accordance with the law. Then President Aleksandar Vucic later announced that the ministry’s internal affairs unit would investigate the allegations made by Sindjelic.

At the time of BIRN’s investigation, it was not clear whether the promised internal probe had been carried out.

World.title: Albania’s ‘Coordinator’? The Rapid Rise and Sudden Fall of Ergys Agasi
World.content:
On the afternoon of August 26, as the sun was setting over Durres beach, police in several unmarked vehicles pulled over a black Audi on the southern outskirts of the Albanian port city. Inside the car was Ergys Agasi, a businessman and former official at the environment ministry who had been on the run for the past eight months.

In video released by the police, 39-year-old Agasi is seen in a white T-shirt and shorts, hands cuffed behind his back, head bowed.

Albania’s Special Prosecution Against Corruption and Organised Crime, SPAK, accuses Agasi of leading an organised criminal group that manipulated public tenders linked to the National Agency for Information Society, AKSHI, sometimes through violence.

Less than a month after his arrest, investigators moved against the head of the State Intelligence Service, SHISH, Vlora Hyseni, accusing her of aiding Agasi to evade arrest and providing him with classified information. Hyseni was placed under house arrest and dismissed from SHISH.

World.title: Serbian President’s Controversial Last-Minute Pardons Face Legal Challenges
World.content:
This Friday, a court in Belgrade was supposed to hear the verdict in the case against a man who rammed a car into a 20-year-old female student, Sonja Ponjavic, who was blocking a traffic intersection during an anti-government protest in the Serbian capital in January 2025.

The blockade was one of many rallies organised by students in memory of victims of the November 2024 Novi Sad railway station disaster – an incident that transformed Serbian politics and ultimately led to the ousting of the government led by Aleksandar Vucic’s Serbian Progressive Party at last month’s elections.

However, now the driver might not be punished for hitting the student because Vucic pardoned him in one of his last actions as President before stepping down to run for the premiership in the elections.

World.title: Transnistria’s Separatist Leader Decorated by Moscow, Denounced by Moldova
World.content:
In a ceremony at the Kremlin on Wednesday, Russian President Vladmir Putin formally pinned the Order of Honour award on the lapel of Vadim Krasnoselsky, the leader of Transnistria - a separatist region of Moldova where Moscow has maintained a military presence since the Soviet bloc disintegrated.

Putin said the decoration was awarded to recognise Krasnoselsky’s efforts to "strengthen ties" with Russia and amidst "pressure" from the West. Moldova is seeking to join the EU, but separatist Transnistria remains a potentially disruptive Russian lever of influence that Moscow wants to preserve.

“Despite difficult conditions and attempts at external pressure, the republic [Transnistria], under his leadership, is developing consistently. Its inhabitants, who are of various nationalities, defend their rights and interests together, uphold the historical truth and preserve the Russian language,” Putin explained.

Located on Moldova’s border with Ukraine, and home to 1,600 Russian troops, Transnistria is strategically important for the Russian leader. Speaking in Moscow, Krasnoselsky seemed happy to fall into line.

World.title: Hundreds of bags of red pepper wash up on beach near Bulgaria’s Plovdiv
World.content:
As is traditional, a Remembrance Sunday service was held at the Commonwealth War Graves cemetery in Bulgaria’s city of Plovdiv on November 8.

Remembrance Sunday, held annually on the Sunday closest to Remembrance Day on November 11, commemorates and honours the dead in the wars of the 20th century. The November 11 date arises from the anniversary of the Armistice at the close of the First World War.

In Plovdiv, the service was led by British ambassador Nathaniel Copsey and Father Patrick Irwin, and attended by military veterans from Britain and the Commonwealth, as well as members of the public.

The Lesson was read by Lieutenant Colonel Matthew Walker, and 10-year-old Charles Copsey delivered the Exhortation:

“They shall grow not old, as we that are left grow old,

Age shall not weary them, nor the years condemn.

At the going down of the sun, and in the morning,

We will remember them.”

(Photos: Clive Leviev-Sawyer)

World.title: Hundreds of bags of red pepper wash up on beach near Bulgaria’s Plovdiv
World.content:
Hundreds of bags of red pepper have washed up on the beach near the village of Sinemorets on Bulgaria’s Black Sea coast, Tsarevo municipality’s mayor Marin Kirov said on November 8.

Officials from the Regional Inspectorate for Environment Protection and Water in Bourgas and the Basin Directorate are taking samples of the sea water near Sinemorets to determine if there is any pollution.

According to the Bourgas district administration, the cargo was likely transported in a shipping container that opened at sea and currents carried the sacks to shore.

The incident also follows recent incidents of drones sinking or severely damaging merchant ships off Bulgaria’s coast, in attacks widely blamed on Russia.

The results of the checks on the sea water are expected next week. However, reaching the beach is a serious challenge for the inspectors themselves, as they have to walk nearly two kilometres through difficult terrain.

Kirov, in a post on Facebook, said that although though the beaches are exclusive state property, “we fully recognise the gravity of the situation regarding the hundreds of sacks of red pepper found on an undeveloped beach in Sinemorets”.

He said that the municipality was in constant contact with the district governor, and would assist in the cleanup of the beach.

“Naturally, I would like to make a point: such incidents are likely to become more frequent, and a formal mechanism for cleaning the coastline needs to be established,” Kirov said.

“Should this recur—given that the sea frequently washes various types of cargo onto our beaches and rocky shores—the state must allocate funds to the Bourgas district administration to cover these cleanup operations,” he said.

(Photo via Kirov’s Facebook page)

World.title: Bulgarian Navy team destroys Russian drone found near Shabla
World.content:
A Bulgarian Navy team destroyed on November 6 a drone – identified as a Russian Gerber-2 – that had been found near Shabla on Bulgaria’s northern Black Sea coast, according to a statement by the Defence Ministry.

At 10am, a signal was sent by the operational duty officer of the Ministry of Interior about the presence of a drone in the area of the beach north of the lighthouse on Cape Shabla, the ministry said.

A specialist team from Varna Naval Base established that the aerial drone probably fell into the sea and was subsequently thrown ashore.

According to the Defence Ministry, there were no inscriptions on its hull and it was classified as a Russian Gerber – 2. This contradicts earlier media reports that the drone was marked as a Shahel, a type that is of Iranian manufacture and which is used by Russia.

The drone was destroyed on site, with strict observance of all safety measures. It was established that it did not carry an explosive, the Defence Ministry said.

The incident is the latest of more than 100 in which drones or parts of drones have been found in Bulgarian waters or on beaches since the beginning of 2026, against the backdrop of Russia’s war on Ukraine.

(Photo: Ministry of Defence)

World.title: Two aircraft land at Sofia Airport following latest bomb threats – report
World.content:
Two civilian aircraft that were travelling from London and Brussels landed at Vassil Levski Sofia Airport on November 6 following e-mailed bomb threats, Bulgarian National Television (BNT) said, citing the Transport Ministry.

The aircraft were checked by Border Police teams and no explosive devices were found, BNT said.

The planes landed without any problems.

This is the latest of a succession of disruptions of flights in Europe because of e-mailed bomb threats. On November 5, three aircraft that were the subject of bomb threats landed at Bulgarian airports – two in Sofia and one in Plovdiv.

Director of Air Traffic Management Ivan Dyaksov told Nova Televizia on November 6 that the e-mails were sent by “unknown organisations” whose goal is to sow discord.

There have been at least 24 such cases across Europe in the past week,” Dyaksov said.

National security expert Colonel Assen Peychev told Nova TV: “There are two countries in the world that have an interest in destabilising Europe – Russia and Iran”.

“They aim to both drain resources and test how Nato countries react,” cybersecurity expert Lyubomir Tulev said.

(Photo: Sofia Airport)

World.title: Eurostat: Bulgaria had EU’s third-highest annual increase in retail trade volume in September 2026
World.content:
Dr. Konstantin Trenchev, founder and honorary president of the Podkrepa labour confederation, has died at the age of 71 after a short illness, Podkrepa said on November 6.

“There are individuals whose names remain inextricably linked to a certain historical era,” Podkrepa said.

“For the Bulgarian independent trade union movement and the democratic changes after 1989, this name is Dr. Konstantin Trenchev.”

A doctor by profession, a public figure, a dissident by conviction and a leader by vocation, Trenchev was the man who, in 1989, laid the foundation for the first independent trade union in Bulgaria – Podkrepa, the statement said.

At a time when free association was impossible and the protection of human and labour rights was subordinated to state power, he chose the most difficult path – to oppose the system and give hope that free trade unionism was possible, it said.

The creation of Podkrepa was not simply the establishment of a new organisation, the labour confederation said. “It is an act of civic courage and protection of the dignity of Bulgarian workers”.

Because of this activity, Dr. Trenchev was subjected to repression, was arrested and spent several months as a political prisoner.

“Instead of being crushed, he became one of the symbols of the struggle for democracy, freedom of speech and the right to independent trade union association.”

After the fall of the communist regime, he became one of the founders of the Union of Democratic Forces and participated in the processes of democratic transition in the country, including in the National Round Table between the ruling party and the opposition.

After the democratic changes, Trenchev devoted more than a quarter of a century to building Podkrepa.

Thanks to his efforts, Podkrepa became the first Bulgarian trade union organisation accepted into the international and European trade union family.

He was the first Bulgarian elected as Vice-President of the European Trade Union Confederation, as well as as Vice-President of the International Confederation of Free Trade Unions – “a recognition not only of his personal authority, but also of Bulgaria’s place in the European social dialogue”.

In 2015, after 26 years at the helm of Podkrepa, he handed over the leadership to the next generation of trade union leaders and was elected honorary president of the confederation – recognition for his exceptional contribution to the development of the organization and the Bulgarian trade union movement, Podkrepa said.

(Photos via the Podkrepa website)

World.title: Eurostat: Bulgaria had EU’s third-highest annual increase in retail trade volume in September 2026
World.content:
Bulgaria had the third-highest annual increase in retail trade volume in the European Union in September 2026, according to figures released on November 6 by EU statistics agency Eurostat.

Among EU member states for which data are available, the highest annual increases in the total retail trade volume were recorded in Cyprus (7.6 per cent), Sweden (6.9 per cent) and Bulgaria (5.7 per cent).

The largest decreases were observed in Germany (-2.4 per cent), Romania (-2.3 per cent) and Spain (-1.5 per cent).

In September 2026, compared with September 2025, the calendar adjusted retail sales index increased by 0.4 per cent in the euro area and by 0.9 per cent in the EU, Eurostat said.

(Photo: Ngaulin)

World.title: NSI poll: Consumer confidence in Bulgaria plummets
World.content:
A regular three-monthly poll by the National Statistical Institute (NSI), the results of which were released on November 6, shows that consumer confidence in Bulgaria has dropped by 6.9 percentage points.

The NSI found it to be slightly down in February. This was followed by a downturn in May, then an improvement in the poll reported in August.

In October 2026, there was decreased confidence among both urban and rural dwellers, by 5.3 and 11 percentage points, respectively, the NSI said.

Those polled were more pessimistic in their views of the economic situation in Bulgaria over the past 12 months and the coming 12 months.

Compared to July, their assessments and expectations about the changes in the financial situation of their households were also more negative.

In October, consumers’ assessments about the change of consumer prices over the past 12 months were more unfavourable. However, inflation expectations over the next 12 months were less intense, the NSI said.

While overall expectations were that unemployment in Bulgaria would slightly decrease over the coming 12 months, those living in cities expected that it would increase.

Most consumers saw the current economic situation in Bulgaria as unfavourable for savings.

Their attitude regarding intensions of spending on major purchases of durable goods and home improvements over the next 12 months was also negative, the NSI said.

World.title: Bulgarian sculptor and former Speaker of Parliament Vezhdi Rashidov dies
World.content:
Renowned sculptor and former Speaker of Bulgaria’s National Assembly Vezhdi Rashidov has died at the age of 74, it was confirmed on November 6.

Rashidov was born on December 14 1951 in Dimitrovgrad.

In 1970, he graduated from the Iliya Petrov Art School of Fine Arts in Sofia, and in 1978, he graduated from the Sculpture Department at the National Academy of Arts in Sofia.

From 1978, Rashidov participated in national and international exhibitions, biennials and symposiums.

He presented his works at the International Sculpture Biennale in Ravenna and the World Art Fair in Basel.

Among his solo exhibitions are those at Unesco in Paris in 1989, in Tokyo in 1992 and at the Oscar Wilde Museum in Dublin in 2006. In addition to sculptures, he exhibited drawings and watercolours.

Among his awards are the Vatican’s Dante Alighieri Gold Medal in 1981, the first prize at the International Biennial of Humor and Satire in Gabrovo in 1983, and the Vera grand prize for sculpture at the “Traditions and Modernity” International Festival in Moscow in 2009.

Rashidov was awarded the Order of the Stara Planina with Ribbon and is a Corresponding Member of the Bulgarian Academy of Sciences. He was an honorary citizen of Sofia, Dimitrovgrad, and Kurdzhali, among other cities. His works are held in Bulgarian galleries and in collections abroad, including the Uffizi Gallery in Florence, the Pushkin Museum in Moscow, and the Israel Museum in Jerusalem.

Rashidov was Minister of Culture in the first and second Boiko Borissov governments. He held the post from July 27 2009 to March 13 2013 and from November 7 2014 to January 27 2017.

Rashidov was a member of parliament in seven parliaments. On October 21 2022, he was elected Speaker of the 48th National Assembly and held the position until the end of his term in February 2023.

In the 49th National Assembly, he was an MP from Borissov’s GERB-UDF. On September 1 2023, his resignation was approved by Parliament.

World.title: Zagreb Engineers Turn a Garage Hobby into a Global Tech Business
World.content:
November the 8th, 2026 – Zagreb engineers managed to turn a garage hobby into a truly global tech business, and it all started with hiding cigarettes from inspectors…

In a smaller industrial zone in Rudeš, a Croatian technology company has been working on innovative solutions that are used in the products of large global companies, from Europe to the USA. Paula Hadjur reports for Index that Matija Puškar, one of the founders of Byte Lab, revealed more about exactly what their team is engaged in. Their job is not to create finished products, but to develop technological solutions that make them smarter, simpler and more accessible to customers. For example, after receiving a specific request, their team designed a device that measures performances in motocross, which is then placed on the drivers’ helmets.

“we’re currently working on an electronic nose…”

“The most successful path to a good product is to talk to people who are deep in that niche. We’re exclusively an engineering company that carries out their own ideas. Someone has a problem and from that, a technical solution arises,” he explained.

They are currently busy working on a so-called electronic nose, an idea that arose in their innovations department in which an entire team works on all projects that seem interesting and useful to them for companies that have not yet developed those ideas themselves. “The idea evolved to the level that we went to our standard clients and showed them the technology. Some clients said it wasn’t particularly interesting to them, but there were those to whom it was very interesting. For example, that the nose, just from the smell of the coffee, understands which brand it is and how much it is roasted and on the basis of that automatically adjusts the coffee preparation process,” he says.

cooperation with the rest of europe and even the usa

They cooperate the most with the USA, Puškar explained, but also with European countries such as Switzerland, Germany, the Benelux countries and the United Kingdom. They also work with Middle Eastern countries. “That distribution is quite natural. We are part of the EU so we give the greatest value to clients in Europe. Prototypes that are produced today in our ground floor can already tomorrow at 9 o’clock be delivered to them,” he says. However interesting and abstract the innovations are, perhaps the most valuable thing in this story is the way it arose. In a garage in Špansko two friends, still as kids, started learning about electronics over the summer.

“The whole story started 10 years before the company was founded. Danijel Babić and I were kids from Špansko who were playing around with electronics,” he says. The first more concrete projects Danijel and he carried out still during their studies at the Faculty of Electrical Engineering and Computing (FER), when they developed a system intended for medical diagnostics, such as gait analysis in persons with amputation, because of which they also received the Tesla’s Egg recognition of the VIDI e-novation competition back in 2007. As their desire for innovations did not diminish even with the years, and the projects became larger and larger, both decided to finally open their company, which somewhat later was also joined by their friend and colleague from FER Ivan Dodig.

“In 2011, we came to the situation that the colleague was finishing faculty, I was in the final year. We saw that we already had some revenues and came to the conclusion that we need to formalise so that the whole story would have its head and tail,” he says.

from smart bikes to electric gas meters…

We also went down into Byte Lab’s production plant. Everything starts from an empty board, Puškar explained to us while he was leading us, on which electronic components are placed that are then soldered in ovens, after which additional controls and correctness tests follow, with the help of human hands. That is how some of their most recognisable solutions arose – electric gas meters, smart bicycles and even devices that track performances of motocross races. “If you do motocross, you don’t know how you’re managing to ride, unless you have a friend who times you while you’re passing. We made a device that tracks the complete analytics of entering corners, jump heights, speed tracking,” Puškar says, and subsequently it was interesting for him to hear from clients that that product was later also used among skiers.

“From the standpoint of data, what’s the difference?” Puškar asks himself.

their first product was a cigarette controller

Today, the Byte Lab team, which achieved around 4.5 million in revenue last year alone, still keeps the first product they ever sold as part of the company, in the drawers of the office in which today they close most of their deals with world-famous brands. “We were making cigarette controllers,” Matija laughs. “Advertising of cigarettes was already banned then, and we got the task to make a controller that by pressing a button opens and automatically closes the shutters under which the cigarettes stand, so that traders would reduce the risk of fines.”

Today, they’re a company with around 90 employees, with their own plant, production and a whole series of long-term partners. But, Puškar says, they never thought that the whole story could reach such proportions. “We like to joke that for us the development of new products is like running is for Forrest Gump: you ask yourself where you’re running, you don’t know, but it doesn’t matter. We love creating something new, we strongly nurture that curiosity and it motivates us. The nicest thing is that we work really broadly, from appliances to medical devices. It’s nice to see your products on shelves in shops, in concert halls and at airports,” he concluded.

World.title: Filipinos Overtake Nepalis as Foreign Workers in Croatia
World.content:
November the 8th, 2026 – For the first time, Filipinos have overtaken Nepalis as foreign workers in Croatia, according to the latest data issued by the Interior Ministry (MUP).

It’s important to bear in mind that the mentioned data doesn’t show how many foreigners overall are actually working in Croatia, but how many work permits have been issued to them. Vedran Salvia reports for Index that these statistics are also influenced by legal changes that have enabled the issuance of permits for three years instead of one. Despite that, some trends are quite interesting.

According to MUP data, in the first nine months of 2026, 18,712 residence and work permits were issued to citizens of the Philippines, which is 46.1 percent more than in the same period last year, when 12,809 were issued. At the same time, the number of permits issued to citizens of Nepal fell from 24,948 to 17,386, or by 30.3 percent. An even larger drop was recorded among citizens of India, to whom 7,734 permits were issued, which is 37 percent less than in the same period last year, when 12,274 were issued. Filipinos already last year overtook Indians in the number of permits issued, and this year the difference between them has further increased.

filipinos overtook nepalis, but workers from bosnia and herzegovina and serbia still dominate

Citizens of Bosnia and Herzegovina and Serbia are still at the top in the number of residence and work permits issued in Croatia. In the first nine months of 2026, 22,565 permits were issued to BiH citizens and 19,886 to Serbian citizens. Nevertheless, a drop was recorded in both groups compared to the same period last year, by 12.4 percent for BiH citizens and 4.5 percent for Serbian citizens.

Although workers from neighbouring countries are still the most numerous according to the number of permits issued, in this analysis we particularly focused on changes among citizens of Asian countries, primarily the strong growth in the number of permits for Filipinos and the drop for Nepalis and Indians.

construction declines but hospitality and tourism rises

The largest number of work permits in the first nine months of 2026 was issued in tourism and hospitality – a total of 48,156, which is 5.1 percent more than in the same period last year. In construction 32,701 permits were issued, or 18.5 percent less than last year. The drop is even more pronounced compared to 2024, when 55,507 permits were issued in that activity. In two years their number decreased by 41.1 percent. Industry is also recording a drop, with 15,121 permits issued, as well as transport and communications with 7,853 permits. At the same time the number of permits in trade rose to 7,752, which is 13.5 percent more than last year.

a drop in the number of permits issued doesn’t mean a drop in foreign worker numbers

In Croatia from January to the end of September this year 124,023 residence and work permits were issued, which is 8.9 percent less than last year and 21.9 percent less than in 2024. Particularly pronounced is the drop in the number of permits for new employment, of which 101,841 were issued in 2024, and this year 48,847, or as much as 52 percent less. However, as we mentioned in the introduction to the text, the number of permits issued was primarily influenced by the amendments to the Law on Foreigners that entered into force in March 2025. They enabled the issuance of residence and work permits for a maximum of three years, instead of the previous one year. The amendments to the law enabled foreign workers under certain conditions to change employers without issuing a new work permit, because of which such changes are not recorded in the statistics of permits for new employment.

That a drop in the number of work permits issued does not necessarily mean a reduction in the number of foreign workers is also shown by data from the Croatian Pension Insurance Institute (HZMO). At the end of September 2024, 123,836 insured persons from third countries, i.e. countries that are not members of the European Economic Area or Switzerland, were recorded in Croatia. A year later there were 138,114 of them, and at the end of September 2026 146,307. That is 5.9 percent more than last year and 18.1 percent more than two years ago.

Interesting are also the data according to the countries from which the workers come. At the end of September this year 19,978 insured persons with Philippine travel documents were recorded, as much as 44 percent more than a year earlier. At the same time the number of insured persons with Nepalese travel documents fell by 2.5 percent, to 23,787, and those of India by 4.7 percent, to 10,729.

These data confirm that the number of Filipino workers in Croatia is indeed growing strongly, while the number of Nepalis and Indians is decreasing, but significantly more mildly than could be concluded from the statistics of work permits issued.

Although HZMO data give a different picture of the movement in the number of foreign workers from the statistics of permits issued, the fact is that significant changes are also recorded according to them, especially the strong growth in the number of Filipinos. We spoke with economic analyst Predrag Bejaković about the reasons for these changes. “It’s merely a matter of a reshuffling of the entire European labour migration system. After the pandemic several new destination ‘poles’ emerged, and Croatia is one of them, along with Portugal, Lithuania, Romania and Hungary,” Bejaković explains.

croatia was the top destination for nepalis in 2023

“However, back in 2025 the number of first employment permits issued to those workers in Croatia decreased, while the largest share of those permits was issued in Romania. Thus Nepalese workers are increasingly directing themselves towards Romania, and Indian workers towards Portugal, which in 2025 became their leading destination in the EU. Croatia is thereby competing with other countries for the same workers and is no longer the only ‘new’ destination,” he says.

croatia is the second favourite country in the eu for filipinos

Among the reasons for the changes Bejaković singles out stricter conditions for employing foreign workers, competition from other European countries, and the attitude towards foreigners and the lack of an integration policy in Croatia. With Filipinos, Bejaković explains, a more orderly employment system plays an important role. In 2024 Croatia signed a memorandum of cooperation with the Philippines in the field of the labour market, and Philippine institutions strongly regulate the employment of their citizens abroad. According to the analysis Bejaković is working on, Croatia in 2025 became the second most frequent destination for Filipino workers in the European Union. He emphasises that according to the Eurostat category of first work permits Hungary is in the leading place.

why has the number of permits issued for construction decreased?

To the question of how much these changes are connected with demand in individual activities, he replies that sectoral demand plays an important role, but that the drop in the number of permits issued cannot be directly equated with a drop in the need for workers. “The drop in construction could partially be connected with changes in the intensity of structural reconstruction after the earthquake and the dynamics of the investment cycle financed by EU funds, including funds from the National Recovery and Resilience Plan. Workers on the reconstruction of buildings damaged by the earthquake received permits without a labour market test and without the opinion of the Croatian Employment Service. If the scope of those jobs is decreasing, the need for employment through that special procedure is also decreasing,” he explained.

Bejaković says that in practice differences can be observed in the employment of Filipinos and Nepalis according to activities, but that more precise data are lacking for reliable conclusions. He notes that employment in tourism and hospitality is facilitated for Filipinos by knowledge of English, experience in those activities and developed employment channels. Nepalis, on the other hand, he says, more often came for physically demanding jobs, so a reduction in demand in construction could more strongly affect their employment.

the influence of legal amendments

As for the influence of the amendments to the Law on Foreigners on the statistics of permits issued, Bejaković explains that two waves of legal changes need to be distinguished, from March 2025 and June 2026.

“Part of the drop is statistical, and not real. If a permit lasts three years instead of one, there is no annual extension so fewer permits are issued for the same number of people. The same applies to a change of employer: a worker who is already here changes jobs with a notification and confirmation, and not with a new permit for new employment. The new law additionally facilitates this. A change of employer is no longer tied to the same occupation, and is possible after six months with the first employer instead of after a year. The drop in the number of permits for new employment therefore does not mean that the number of foreign workers has fallen by that much,” he says.

stricter rules for croatian employers themselves

Bejaković emphasises that the second part of the drop in the number of permits issued is real and intentional, that is, a consequence of stricter conditions for employers, including a minimum inflow of money into the account, a prescribed ratio of domestic and foreign workers, and a check of whether they are actually performing the registered activity. Thereby, according to his words, fictitious employers and part of the agencies were removed from the system. “Can that explain the differences between Nepalis and Filipinos? Partially. Stricter conditions most affect the agency model and smaller employers, and they were precisely the main channel for Nepalese workers in construction. The Filipino channel, with the memorandum and more orderly employment, more easily passes the new procedure,” he says.

the future of employing foreign workers in croatia

Speaking about the future of employing foreign workers in Croatia, Bejaković expects a smaller inflow of new workers, but also a more stable structure, with a larger number of those who will stay longer in the country, change employers and gradually integrate. He adds that the need will not disappear because the demographic picture is relentless. “The long-term question is the sustainability of a model based on low-skilled and temporary work. If we want foreign workers to permanently fill the demographic gap, the focus must shift from the speed of issuing permits to integration, language, housing and the protection of workers’ rights,” he concluded.

World.title: Croatian Promotional Video Starring John Malkovich Wins Award
World.content:
November the 8th, 2026 – The now famous Croatian promotional video starring the one and only John Malkovich has won a prestigious award.

The now globally known video “Croatia – I Hear It’s Beautiful” was awarded at the City Nation Place Awards in London. Croatian islands won gold and Dubrovnik also took home silver at the Wanderlust awards ceremony. 24sata reports some excellent news for Croatian tourism is coming from London, where the prestigious City Nation Place Awards ceremony was held, at which the promotional video “CROATIA – I hear it’s beautiful”, starring John Malkovich, won the main award in the Best communication strategy: tourism category.

This is another in a series of awards won by the promotional video of Croatian tourism, and this time it is an award given by City Nation Place (CNP), a global platform and professional organisation dedicated to the branding and marketing of cities, regions and countries.

“This year we’ve made a significant step forward in presenting Croatia on the international scene, and we are particularly proud of the new promotional film that presented the country from a different, fresh and authentic perspective, as well as the entire campaign ‘Croatia I hear it’s beautiful’. At a time when it seems that almost everything has already been seen and presented, it is important to continuously find new, innovative ways of communication and promotion, create different stories and highlight what makes Croatia special,” said Tonči Glavina, Minister of Tourism and Sport.

Croatia’s popularity on a global level is also confirmed by the prestigious Wanderlust Reader Travel Awards, which are awarded by the respected British travel magazine Wanderlust on the basis of votes from its readers. Precisely the travel lovers and readers of this popular magazine declared Croatian islands the most desirable in the European regions category (gold award), while Dubrovnik was declared the second most desirable European city (silver award)

“We are extremely pleased with this international recognition, which confirm that Croatia has a strong and recognisable tourism story. It is particularly valuable that Croatian islands and Dubrovnik were recognised by the readers and travel lovers themselves. More than 250,000 Wanderlust readers took part in the voting and this year broke the record with as many as 8.2 million votes. The success of the promotional video of Croatian tourism shows that creative, authentic and contemporary communication can further strengthen the visibility of our country on international markets. Our goal is to present Croatia as a diverse and high-quality destination throughout the year, highlighting not only its best-known strengths but also the richness of local experiences, culture, local food and way of life,” said Kristjan Staničić, director of the Croatian National Tourist Board.

Gold for the Croatian islands confirms the allure of Croatia’s island diversity, preserved nature and authentic experiences, while the award for Dubrovnik additionally confirms its international recognisability and rich cultural-historical heritage. Let us add that among others the presentation of the Wanderlust awards was also graced by the presence of Prince Harry, Duke of Sussex.

World.title: First Leg Lengthening Procedure Carried Out in Croatia
World.content:
November the 8th, 2026 – The very first leg lengthening procedure carried out in Croatia has been performed at Zagreb’s Clinic for Traumatology.

A medical team from the Clinic for Traumatology in Zagreb has performed the first leg lengthening operation in Croatia using a new method that does not use an external fixator. Index reports that the procedure was carried out on a 28-year-old patient for whom a six-centimetre difference in leg length had been making movement difficult for years.

Kristina Sambolek (28) has had a shorter left leg since birth due to a hip deformity. She has spent her entire life in and out of hospitals, and numerous operations are behind her. Because of the difference in leg length she walks on her toes and wears shoes with soles of different thicknesses. “The first thing they did to me was literally tie my legs so they were hanging in the air and try that way to set the hips back into the socket,” Kristina described.

“The biggest problem was that on the left side I didn’t have a proper socket at all, nor a joint, so for years they tried to fix that with operations. I have the feeling that I spent more of my childhood in hospital than at home,” she recalled.

slovenia has been using this method for around a decade

Over time, she learned to endure the pain and accepted the limitations, but she never gave up hope of a better life. “I’ve been through operations and I know what awaits me, so I’ve come to terms with the fact that I have to go through this so that it will be easier for me. My wish is to be able to put on high heels and be like a real woman,” she said. The operation at the Traumatology Clinic is the result of international cooperation with colleagues from Slovenia. “This is one of the most favourable methods for lengthening long bones. It is much simpler for patients than external fixators,” said Prof. Dr. Sc. Matej Drobnič, specialist in orthopaedic surgery from Ljubljana. He added that in Slovenia this method has been used for about ten years and that five to six such procedures are performed annually without significant complications. The two-hour procedure in Zagreb is the first of its kind in Croatia.

“It’s a type of brand new technology where a nail is implanted into the bone. The leg then grows on its own, one millimetre a day. The patient will lengthen the leg herself with magnetic stimulation and we expect that in 50 days we will get the 50 millimetres we are planning,” explained Assist. Prof. Dr. Sc. Tomislav Čengić, head of the 3rd Department of Geriatric Traumatology and Hip Surgery at the Clinic for Traumatology.

The new method will enable patients with a difference in leg length to be treated in Croatia, without going abroad. “Three to five patients a year could certainly be found in Croatia for this type of operation. This procedure is significant for us, but also for the entire orthopaedic and traumatology profession in Croatia,” emphasised Assoc. Prof. Dr. Sc. Srećko Sabalić, head of the Clinic for Traumatology. Assist. Prof. Čengić emphasised that the success is the result of teamwork. “The entire clinic team took part in the procedure, from anaesthesiologists, scrub nurses, technicians to radiology engineers,” Čengić said. For the patient the operation means a step towards easier walking, and for Croatian orthopaedics the introduction of a modern treatment method.

The operation was performed by Assist. Prof. Tomislav Čengić, Prof. Matej Drobnič, Dr Danijel Jurković and Dr Fabijan Čukelj. Also in the team were anaesthesiologist Dr Ajša Muratović, scrub nurses Martina Stivičević, Tihana Krusha and Barbara Funtak, and radiology engineer Dubravko Kamenar.

World.title: Wanderlust Readers Crown Dubrovnik Second Most Desirable European City
World.content:
November the 7th, 2026 – Wanderlust readers have once again crowned Dubrovnik as the second most desirable European city to visit.

The City of Dubrovnik has once again confirmed its position as one of the most desirable European tourist destinations by winning the Silver Award in the Most Desirable City in Europe category. Dubrovacki Dnevnik reports that the city took home the award at the prestigious Wanderlust Reader Travel Awards 2026, which was held on the 4th of November in London. This recognition continues a series of international successes for Dubrovnik, which in recent years has regularly ranked among the best European city destinations according to readers of the respected British travel magazine Wanderlust.

The awards ceremony was held in the impressive Painted Hall, located in the historic Old Royal Naval College complex in London’s Greenwich. The Silver Award was accepted on behalf of the Dubrovnik Tourist Board by its director Miro Drašković. In this year’s selection Dubrovnik competed against some of the best-known European city destinations, including Copenhagen, Madrid, Lisbon, Istanbul, Bordeaux, Genoa and Tbilisi. This success confirms Dubrovnik’s international recognisability, its rich cultural and historical heritage, unique architecture and exceptional tourist appeal.

Wanderlust is otherwise one of the oldest and most respected British travel magazines, which for more than three decades has been promoting authentic travel, the discovery of new destinations and responsible and sustainable tourism. Its annual Wanderlust Reader Travel Awards, which this year mark their 25th edition, rank among the significant recognition in the international tourism industry. Special value is given to the awards by the fact that the winners are decided by the readers and travel lovers themselves.

Croatian islands were declared the Most Desirable Region in Europe. This recognition for the Croatian National Tourist Board, together with the silver award for Dubrovnik and the Dubrovnik Tourist Board, additionally confirms the strong position of Croatian destinations on the international tourism market.

Dubrovnik has in recent years been repeatedly awarded in Wanderlust’s selection, including winning the gold award in the Most Desirable European City category. At last year’s ceremony it also received a special recognition from Wanderlust editor-in-chief George Kipouros for outstanding achievements in sustainable tourism management. With that recognition Dubrovnik was highlighted as an example of responsible destination development, thanks to the City of Dubrovnik’s “Respect the City” project and measures for managing tourist flows, regulating cruise ship arrivals, and preserving cultural heritage and the quality of life of the local population.

The continuous recognitions from one of the most respected British travel magazines have special importance for Dubrovnik, especially given that the United Kingdom is one of its most important source tourism markets. They represent additional confirmation of Dubrovnik’s international recognisability as a destination that combines exceptional cultural and historical heritage, authentic experiences and a responsible approach to tourism development.

World.title: Croatia Records Strong Cruise Tourism Growth in 2026
World.content:
November the 7th, 2026 – Croatia has recorded some particularly strong cruise tourism growth throughout 2026, with almost a million passengers arrived at Croatian ports on foreign cruise ships.

Over the first nine months of 2026, almost a million passengers arrived at Croatian ports on various foreign cruise ships. Dalmacija Danas reports that the aforementioned figure is as much as 11.7 percent more than in the same period last year. The latest data from the Croatian Bureau of Statistics reveals that Dubrovnik and Split are among the most visited ports in the entire country, while the largest share of cruise voyages took place precisely in two Dalmatian counties.

According to data published by the Croatian Bureau of Statistics (DZS) this week, in the period from January to September 2026, 80 foreign cruise ships entered Croatian seaports and completed a total of 677 cruise voyages. On those massive vessels, there were as many as 958,109 passengers, which is around 100 thousand more than in the same period of 2025, when 858,066 were recorded. The number of cruise voyages rose by 9.9 percent, and the number of passengers by 11.7 percent. At the same time the number of foreign ships decreased slightly, by 1.2 percent.

Foreign cruise ships spent a total of 1,557 days in Croatian territorial waters, which is an increase of 7.7 percent compared to last year.

dubrovnik and split lead the way

The most interesting data concern Dalmatian ports, which continue to play a key role in Croatian cruise tourism. Dubrovnik is by far the most visited Croatian port, with a total of 505 visits by foreign cruise ships in the first nine months of this year. In second place is Split with 284 visits, while third is Zadar with 191 visits. Among the seven most visited ports are also Korčula with 95 visits, Hvar with 89, Rovinj with 84 and Šibenik with 81 visits. This latest data shows exactly how important Dalmatia is for the arrivals of foreign cruise ships, with Dubrovnik and Split particularly standing out.

According to DZS data, of the total of 677 cruise voyages by foreign ships, the largest share was achieved in Dubrovnik-Neretva County – as much as 46.5 percent. Split-Dalmatia County follows with 25.1 percent. This means that in these two counties a total of 71.6 percent of all recorded cruise voyages by foreign ships in Croatia were realised. Further up north in Dalmatia, the expansive and particularly island-strewn Zadar County accounted for 12 percent, and then further up in Istria County the number stood at 7.5 percent, in Šibenik-Knin County 4.9 percent, and finally Primorje-Gorski Kotar County four percent.

the maltese flag reigns

In the first nine months of 2026, Croatian ports were visited by foreign cruise ships sailing under the flags of 15 countries. The most cruise voyages were made by ships under the Maltese flag – a total of 201, which accounts for 29.7 percent of all recorded voyages. They are followed by ships under the flags of the Bahamas with 174 voyages, Norway with 66 and Panama with 52 voyages. Interestingly, ships sailing under the Bahamian flag carried the largest number of passengers – 294,569 – while ships under the Maltese flag carried 265,838 passengers.

184,000 cruise passengers in september alone

In September this year alone, 132 cruise voyages by foreign ships were realised, carrying 184,523 passengers. Compared to September last year this is an increase in the number of voyages of 18.9 percent and in the number of passengers of 11 percent. The highest number of passengers recorded in one single month was recorded in July – 196,389 – while in August, 186,048 passengers were recorded. DZS data thus confirms the continued growth of cruise tourism in Croatia, with Dalmatian ports, led by Dubrovnik and Split, occupying the leading positions.

World.title: Tourism in Central Dalmatia Up in 2026 – Polish Visitors Top the Charts
World.content:
November the 7th, 2026 – Tourism in Central Dalmatia has seen an increase in 2026, with Polish visitors in particular topping the charts as far as visitor numbers go.

“We’re now entering the final stretch of another tourist year, a period in which we’re summing up the results, but at the same time already directing our gaze towards what still awaits us. Although the tourist rhythm is gradually changing, Central Dalmatia continues to do well through all sorts of events and experiences that give people a reason to visit the area outside the main summer months.

The Advent period is on its way, which brings another new opportunity to present Dalmatian cities, places, islands, as well as the Dalmatian hinterland, their traditions, food scene and special festive atmosphere,” stated the director of the Tourist Board of Split-Dalmatia County Ivana Vladović.

18.6 million overnight stays in central dalmatia

Dalmatinski portal also reports that this year’s statistical data also confirms that the effort has well and truly paid off. In the first ten months of this year, Split-Dalmatia County, according to data from the eVisitor system, was visited by 3.9 million guests. They achieved 18.6 million overnight stays in commercial accommodation, which is 1% more arrivals and 0.5% more overnight stays than in the same period last year. The largest number of overnight stays was achieved by guests from all of Europe, including Poland, Germany, elsewhere across Croatia, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Great Britain and the Czech Republic.

“We’re now intensively preparing for 2027, which will be particularly significant for the county because it will carry the title of European Region of Gastronomy. This is fantastic recognition, but also an opportunity to present even more strongly the richness of our gastronomic heritage, local producers, traditional dishes and the people who preserve and pass on the culinary heritage of Central Dalmatia. We’re already working on new promotional campaigns, projects and activities with which we will bring this title closer to domestic and international guests and additionally connect the local food scene with our cultural identity, way of life and year-round tourist offer,” Vladović added.

dalmatia is still aiming to attract visitors throughout november

This November, this region of Dalmatia is also offering an entire series of interesting events that enable visitors to get to know its food, cultural and traditional heritage. In Omiš, the international gastronomic festival Grand Gourmet is being held, in Dugopolje the International Honey Fair Dalmatina, and Kaštela through the manifestation Zinfest – Fešta o’ Crljenka present the rich wine tradition and connection with one of the most famous world varieties.

Lovers of active holidays can participate in or follow the State Championship in rafting on the Cetina and the Hileja Marina Trail, while in Gornji Dolac at the end of the month the popular Christmas Village opens. The Split offer is additionally enriched by Štorije o’ spize, a manifestation dedicated to Dalmatian gastronomy, local producers and traditional flavours, and the Dalmatia Film Festival, which gathers lovers of domestic and international film production.

dalmatia beyond the summer season

Precisely the connection of different experiences and values of the region is one of the directions in which the Tourist Board intends to continue developing and presenting Central Dalmatia. Gastronomy, culture, natural heritage, active holidays, nautical tourism, islands and the Dalmatian hinterland form a diverse offer that goes beyond seasonal frameworks.

“In the period now just behind us, we continued to present Central Dalmatia on important international markets and business events, talk with partners and tourism professionals and monitor the changes that shape global tourist demand. Such meetings are important for strengthening how recognised we are, but also for the timely recognition of new opportunities. I believe that with joint work we will turn the title of European Region of Gastronomy into a strong opportunity for the promotion of Central Dalmatia, its people, tradition and quality offer,” director Vladović said, wishing all stakeholders in tourism a successful end of the year and a lot of creativity and enthusiasm in the preparation for the next tourist year.

World.title: As the European Union Prepares for Crisis, How Prepared is Croatia?
World.content:
November the 7th, 2026 – The European Union is currently preparing itself and its member states for crisis by encouraging the stocking of food and other supplies, but just how prepared is Croatia?

Just how ready is Croatia for more serious crisis situations, such as major power outages, supply disruptions, natural disasters or security threats? Vedran Salvia reports for Index that this specific question is opening up once again after the European Commission published guidelines in which it recommends that people prepare stocks of food, water, medicines and other basic necessities for at least 72 hours of crisis.

The emphasis is placed on three-day self-sufficiency of the general public. The European Commission recommends that households have basic stocks of food, water, medicines and other necessities ready and prepared, as well as a pre-packed bag or backpack with the most necessary things in case of emergency evacuation. In addition, the guidelines cover three more areas: education of children on how to act in crisis situations already from kindergarten age, with an approach adapted to their age, special protection measures for persons with disabilities, and clearer and much more timely information about possible dangers.

All of this is a continuation of the broader Union Preparedness Strategy, which the European Commission presented back in March 2025. The strategy covers 30 measures by which it seeks to strengthen the ability of the EU and its member states to respond to various crisis situations.

the government hasn’t bothered to show much interest in the eu’s recommendations

The new European recommendations have been intensively discussed in the media in recent days, yet the Croatian Government has so far not publicly presented the new guidelines nor explained whether and in what way it plans to implement them whatsoever in Croatia. Although the guidelines are not legally binding for the member states, the absence of official communication is somewhat surprising. The European Commission, namely, expressly states that it wants with them to encourage national authorities to develop their own preparedness measures, adapted to the circumstances and needs of individual countries.

It should be said that Croatia already has its own recommendations for acting in crisis situations. The Directorate of Civil Protection has published on its pages instructions for preparing a survival kit, which includes food, water, medicines, a battery torch, a radio receiver, documents and other necessary necessities. The existing Croatian instructions recommend stocks of food and water for at least two days.

An inquiry was therefore sent to the government in which an answer was requested specifically to the question of whether it plans to present the new European recommendations to the public. The second question was whether or not it plans to issue its own guidelines and, if it plans them, when their publication can be expected. The question of just how ready Croatia genuinely is for more serious crisis situations, what the current state of the shelters is, how many of them are functional and whether there are plans for their renovation was also posed. Information was also requested on the sufficiency of state strategic commodity reserves in the event of a longer-lasting crisis.

there are serious issues with croatia’s shelters

The state of Croatian shelters is called into question by the finding of the State Audit Office from 2024, which warned of numerous omissions in their management and maintenance. The audit established that of the 476 shelters managed by the 14 covered cities, 306 of them were not regularly used, and the cities did not undertake the necessary activities to put them into use. In seven cities only visual inspections of the shelters were carried out, without minutes on their correctness. The auditors also stated that the Directorate of Civil Protection did not have reliable and updated data on the condition and equipment of the shelters, and inspection supervisions did not cover the checking of the public shelters themselves.

City risk assessments did not cover threats such as wars and terrorist attacks. Due to the established deficiencies the State Audit Office issued a total of 158 orders and recommendations, and assessed the management of shelters in seven cities and the Directorate of Civil Protection as partially effective.

there are also massive problems with medicines…

According to the Government report for 2025, state commodity reserves were distributed at a total of 357 locations throughout Croatia. The total value of state commodity reserves at the end of last year amounted to 93 million euros, which is 6.87 percent more than the year earlier. Particularly worrying is the fact that Croatia at the end of 2025 in the strategic commodity reserves did not have recorded medicines, sanitary or consumable medical material, although their holding is provided for by regulations. Namely, the Act on Strategic Commodity Reserves from 2022 expressly includes among strategic products medicines, vaccines, antidotes and medical material, while the state balance determines the concrete products that need to be secured.

In total, it is a matter of 106 types of products for which it is expressly stated in the report itself that they need to be held in state reserves, but they are not in stock. Their procurement has been announced for years, but even at the end of 2025 that part of the strategic reserves was not filled. According to unofficial information from Jutarnji list, the Ministry of Health has for years not amended the regulations necessary for the procurement of medicines into state reserves. The Ministry of Economy confirmed that there are legal obstacles and that the situation has not changed even during 2026.

In the warehouses there were cereals, oil, sugar, cans, tents and other necessities, but certain hygiene products were missing, including soap, incontinence diapers and means for disinfecting water and space. According to the Annual Report of the Ministry of Economy for 2025, the total filling of the planned balance of strategic commodity reserves amounted to only 51.39 percent. The filling of food reserves amounted to 72.4 percent, and of non-food 81.75 percent. This is the realisation of the state stock plan.

risks already faced by croatia

As we have already written, the European Commission warns of a series of threats, from geopolitical tensions and possible military conflicts to cyber attacks, sabotage of critical infrastructure, natural disasters and disruptions in supply. It is clear that such risks do not bypass Croatia either, especially when it comes to cyber attacks, possible supply disruptions and other disruptions that can spread across national borders. However, there are also dangers that the Croatian institutions themselves warn about. According to official data of the Directorate of Civil Protection, among the significant risks for Croatia are earthquakes, floods, open space fires, landslides, extreme temperatures, strong winds and epidemics. Croatia has in recent years already experienced the consequences of devastating earthquakes in Zagreb and in Banovina, large fires and floods.

Such natural disasters can cause longer-lasting interruptions in the supply of electricity and water, damage transport infrastructure and hinder the work of emergency services.

the great power outage of 2024 – a stark warning

How possible such disruptions are is also shown by the example of the 21st of June 2024, when due to a major failure in the electricity system across a lot of southeastern Europe, a large part of Dalmatia was left without electricity, as were large parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Montenegro and Albania. The power outage caused problems in traffic, communications and the everyday functioning of people and almost all infrastructure.

According to the report of the Croatian Energy Regulatory Agency for 2024, the supply interruption in Croatia affected almost 200 thousand network users, and individual users were without electricity for almost four hours. The incident showed how quickly a disruption in interconnected electricity systems can spread across state borders. Therefore the question of preparedness is not related only to possible war and security threats, but also to the dangers that Croatia has already faced. The question remains how ready the civil protection system, shelters and state commodity reserves are today to respond to a new major crisis.

World.title: Migrant boat sinks off Senegal, 34 killed: authorities
World.content:
DAKAR: A small boat carrying migrants sank off northwestern Senegal, killing 34 people in the latest tragedy along the dangerous Atlantic Ocean route from Africa to Europe, the authorities said Sunday.

It was the latest disaster on a route where thousands have died in recent years trying to reach Spain’s Canary Islands from west Africa.

An initial statement from the Senegalese interior ministry said 21 bodies and only one survivor had been recovered following the sinking, but that those numbers were provisional as the search continued.

Later Sunday, however, the Senegalese Press Agency (APS) said the toll now stood at 34 at least, a figure confirmed by Action for Human Rights and Friendship (ADHA) in a statement to AFP.

An “indeterminate number” of people were reported missing, APS added.

Media reports said the pirogue-type flat-bottom boat capsized on Saturday off the Loumpoul dunes in Kebemer department, between Dakar and the northern city of Saint-Louis.

However, Saliou Diouf, founder of Senegal’s main migrant aid association Boza Fii, told AFP that “the sinking occurred on Friday.”

The nationalities of all the victims had not been confirmed “as the search is ongoing,” he said.

“But the bodies recovered yesterday (Saturday) are Senegalese,” he added.

Senegal’s President Bassirou Diomaye Faye wrote on Facebook on Sunday: “All state authorities and resources have been mobilized to locate those who have gone missing, provide care for the survivors and support families.”

Thousands of people from West Africa try each year to reach Europe on the perilous Atlantic route.

Senegalese authorities also said they had intercepted 142 migrants on Friday who were on a similar small boat aiming to reach Spain.

The group included 23 women, two babies and two other children, and were from Senegal, Gambia, Guinea-Bissau, Guinea and Nigeria, according to police.

Senegal’s interior ministry stressed “its determination to combat people smuggling networks, notably through strengthened cooperation with neighboring countries” in a statement Sunday.

The country’s interior minister would visit the region where the accident happened to meet families of the victims and express condolences on behalf of the state, it added.

Spanish authorities on the Canary Island of El Hierro declared an emergency on Saturday after a surge in migrant boat arrivals.

Since the start of November, El Hierro authorities said more than 3,300 people had arrived aboard around 30 boats.

Senegal, Mauritania and Morocco have stepped up maritime patrols around departure points for small boats, forcing them to head further south toward the coasts of Gambia, Guinea-Bissau, and Guinea, which prolongs the duration of the already hazardous crossing.

World.title: Saudi foreign minister arrives in Paris for G7 talks
World.content:
RIYADH: Saudi Foreign Minister Prince Faisal bin Farhan arrived in Paris on Sunday to attend a meeting of Group of Seven foreign ministers focused on international crises, security and humanitarian challenges, the Saudi Foreign Ministry said.

France is hosting the talks Nov. 9-10. Prince Faisal is attending at the invitation of the French G7 presidency.

The agenda includes efforts to resolve conflicts, strengthen maritime and port security, combat smuggling and improve humanitarian responses.

Ministers will also discuss food security, nutrition and artificial intelligence security.

The ministry said Saudi Arabia’s participation reflects its commitment to coordinating with international partners to address regional and global challenges.

World.title: Trump says resumption of war with Iran ‘highly unlikely’
World.content:
WASHINGTON: US President Donald Trump on Sunday cast doubt on renewed fighting with Iran, telling CNN that it was “highly unlikely” so long as talks progressed.

“The answer is highly unlikely it’s going to be necessary... I would if necessary, but we hit them really hard,” Trump said, while warning that any decision to resume hostilities “depends on whether or not they sign a very strong agreement.”

World.title: US asks Iraq to shut most Iran border crossings, Iraqi foreign minister says
World.content:
The US Treasury has asked Iraq to close all border crossings with Iran except for two as part of Washington’s policy of ‌increasing economic ‌pressure on Tehran, Iraqi ‌Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein said in an interview with Al-Jazeera.

One of the exceptions is in the Kurdistan region.

“There are many official ‌and ‌unofficial border crossings with Iran, ‌and closing all ‌of them would be difficult and would affect our economy. The Americans ‌are still demanding the closure of the crossings, and we are currently in discussions with them,” Hussein said.

Last month, Iraq closed the busy Sheeb border crossing with Iran to review security and install detection equipment to stop smuggling.

Iraq has also reached ​understandings with the US to allow Iraqi ‌oil ‌exports ​through ‌the ⁠Strait of ​Hormuz via ⁠a shipping lane near Oman, Hussein ‌​told Al-Jazeera.

He said ‌Iraq's losses from the Iran ⁠war ⁠and disruptions to oil exports had reached $60 billion.

World.title: Nigeria’s president courts key state in oil-rich south
World.content:
PORT HARCOURT: Nigeria’s President Bola Tinubu has taken his campaign for reelection to the city of Port Harcourt, seeking to secure another victory in the key state of Rivers in the oil-rich Niger Delta

Tinubu and his All Progressives Congress, won Rivers at the last vote in 2023, but opposition candidate Peter Obi — then of the Labour Party and now a candidate for the Nigeria Democratic Congress — polled strongly.

A slew of defections to the All Progressives Congress in the six states that make up the south-south geopolitical zone since then has put the president in a strong position.

“Thank you for the last election. 2022, 2023. I looked very hopeless. But you trooped out to support me, gave me the mandate,” said Tinubu, who appeared alongside his ally Nyesom Wike, nominally a member of the Peoples Democratic Party but who has backed the president as minister of Federal Capital Territory.

Wike, a former Rivers governor, still holds sway in the state, which has the fifth-largest number of registered voters. His Rainbow Coalition, a group of opposition figures, is working for Tinubu’s victory.

Rivers has more than 3 million registered voters, according to the Independent National Electoral Commission, making it one of the most electorally significant states in southern Nigeria, behind Tinubu’s home state of Lagos.

“Rivers state has already concluded, already agreed that come Jan. 16, they will vote for you,” Wike said in front of tens of thousands of supporters at a packed stadium.

Still, the state is shaping up to be a key battleground, with Atiku Abubakar of the African Democratic Congress also in the race, alongside his running mate, Rotimi Amaechi, a Rivers state native.

Although analysts say Tinubu is the favorite to win the Jan. 16 election, a string of grueling economic reforms he introduced after coming to power in 2023 has had drastic effects.

Investors have praised the reforms as long overdue but ordinary Nigerians have felt the pinch from soaring inflation as fuel and other costs have skyrocketed.

World.title: US midterms and the emerging paradoxes
World.content:
Nothing lasts forever. Last week, the US held highly consequential midterm elections — part of the cycle of elections held every two years in which all members of the House of Representatives, a third of the Senate and a number of state governors are elected.

Important as it is, the election remains an ordinary exercise of democracy and experience has taught us that every election has its circumstances and its heroes, just as it has its issues and its casualties.

In my estimation, President Donald Trump had not been expecting these results. Indeed, I would almost swear that many Democrats, politicians and supporters alike, did not dare take such an optimistic view of what their candidates actually achieved across the length and breadth of the country. The Democrats were not content with changing the balance of power in Congress by seizing the majority in both the House and the Senate; they also won striking victories among state governors, including surprising political and cultural breakthroughs.

In the House, at the time of writing, the Democrats had won a landslide: 252 of 435 seats, against 162 for the Republicans.

There had been signs before polling day that they would take the House but the margin exceeded expectations. So did the Senate result, as Democrats now control 54 of 100 seats, against 44 for the Republicans, with the official results from Mississippi and Alaska still to come.

The shift in Congress was mirrored in the governors’ races, where the surprise was arguably bigger and more painful for the Republicans. They lost the governorship of Texas, their greatest stronghold of all and the apple of the right-wing trillionaire Elon Musk’s eye.

In Texas, a state with a long history of hostility toward its neighbor, Mexico, the right-wing Republican Gov. Greg Abbott — one of the heroes of Trump’s campaign and of the “Make America Great Again” movement against illegal immigration from Latin America — lost to his Democratic challenger, the Latina progressive Gina Hinojosa.

The Democrats won the popular vote by nearly 13 points, the largest margin for either party since 1976. Yet their real test begins now. Eyad Abu Shakra

Texas, the second most-populous state after California, also gave a national platform to James Talarico, who won one of its two Senate seats.

To appreciate what Hinojosa and Talarico achieved, consider that Musk had come to see Texas as a safe haven for the investments of the tech oligarchs who were fleeing California’s taxes, as the last time a Democrat won a Texas Senate seat was in 1970. That year, Lloyd Bentsen, a future Cabinet minister, defeated George H.W. Bush, who nonetheless ultimately went on to win the presidency, as did his son George W. Bush, a former governor of the state.

Trump’s plan for a separation wall along the Mexican border has also suffered a painful setback: the Democrats now control all four border states — Texas, New Mexico, Arizona and California.

As for the broader picture, which may or may not shape the 2028 presidential race, women had a large and influential showing. Among the winners was the physician Annie Andrews in South Carolina, who took the seat of the late Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham, while Native American Democrats won a Senate seat in Minnesota and the governorship of New Mexico.

The Democrats now hold 28 governorships to the Republicans’ 20, including most of the largest states — Pennsylvania, Ohio, Michigan and Georgia, alongside Texas, as well as their impregnable strongholds of California, New York and Illinois.

A clear majority of Latino/Hispanic voters also turned against the Republicans this time, reversing the pattern of the presidential election two years ago. And a cohort of young Democratic leaders has emerged, some of them so-called radical progressives from ethnic and religious minorities, led by Georgia’s new governor, Keisha Lance Bottoms, the first African American woman to govern the state.

Overall, the Democrats won the popular vote by nearly 13 points, the largest margin for either party since 1976. Yet some argue that their real test begins now.

In politics, where there are no certainties but plenty of paradoxes, the Democrats will soon face two real problems, both rooted in the divide between their young radicals and the old guard led by Chuck Schumer in the Senate and Hakeem Jeffries in the House.

The first is that Schumer and Jeffries are men of compromise and of lobbies, the pro-Israeli lobby foremost among them, which will make it easier for the Republicans to exploit their differences with the new generation.

The second is that Trump has chosen to stand up to this Democratic hurricane rather than bow before it, appointing Stephen Miller, the closest of his hard-line advisers, as White House chief of staff.

The days ahead will bring a great deal, whether in peace or in war.

Eyad Abu Shakra is managing editor of Asharq Al-Awsat, where this article was originally published.
