World.title: Traditional owners and uni students work together to unearth history
World.content:
Deep within Ityamaiitpinna Yarta Glenthorne National Park, in Adelaide's southern suburbs, tools tinker against the earth beneath silver-striped gumtrees.

Eleven traditional owners from across Australia work alongside a group of Flinders University archaeology students to unearth history.

There is no shortage of colonial history at the park, which was formerly Glenthorne Farm — a warhorse training ground, a colonial house, and research station.

In the few days the traditional owners and students have been on site, they have found colonial era bottles, a medicine bottle, part of a glass pane and a window frame.

The traditional owners and students are at the site as part of a new five-day course designed by the Australian Resources Sector, Flinders University and traditional owner groups.

The federal government-funded program teaches students and traditional owners the theoretical and practical skills involved in excavation, archaeological surveying and ground-imaging.

Ashley Wedding-Corbett says he hopes to use his experience to do field work on Country. (ABC News: Stephen Opie)

Western Australian traditional owner Aunty Lorna Corbett, a member of the Palyku-Jartayi Aboriginal Corporation, said she valued being able to participate in something she believed "should have happened many years ago".

"I think it's very important to have Aboriginal people right across Australia to be called upon in the initial stages of anything to do with Country," she said.

"Creating this workshop, allows us to go out there … and be involved in what decisions they make on Country."

Palyku and Noongar man Ashley Wedding-Corbett, who is also a Palyku-Jartayi member, said he hoped to use his experience to do field work on Country.

"It'd be awesome to do that where I live … to try and get into that kind of environment and be out there actually doing it," he said.

Course a two-way learning experience

While the program does not give participating traditional owners formal qualifications in archaeology, they do receive a certificate equivalent to one graduate level topic in archaeology.

Ian Moffat says traditional owners have been "doing as much teaching" as they have done learning. (ABC News: Stephen Opie)

Professor of Archaeological Science at Flinders University Ian Moffat said the training added to the traditional owners' cultural knowledge.

"Sadly, archaeology in Australia has done a terrible job at bringing First Nations people to universities and providing practical training," he said.

"Our traditional owner partners are the people that are on Country, managing heritage."

Mr Moffatt said the traditional owners "have been doing as much teaching … as they have doing learning", by sharing their cultural knowledge with the students.

"We really appreciate them coming, sharing their cultural knowledge, sharing their perspectives and the best way to manage heritage in Australia," he said.

Aunty Lorna said she had enjoyed sharing her cultural knowledge with the Flinders students.

"It's just like a two-way learning … whether it's here in the classroom or in the field," she said.

Hopes the course will continue

The university has secured funding to run the program over the next five years.

Traditional owners hope the program will become a mainstay, saying it is a crucial step to help preserve and pass down cultural knowledge to the next generation.

"It's very important for our culture to keep those histories," Ms Corbett said.

"That's why oral history is very important.

"We are here today because of our ancestors."

World.title: Firms using telemarketers to spruik super switches could lose licences
World.content:
Over 17 months, unqualified and unlicensed telemarketers urged Australians to switch about $678 million of their investments — mostly their superannuation savings — into riskier schemes.

That is among the findings the corporate regulator, the Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC), unveiled today in a review focusing on 15 Australian financial services licensees operating between January 2025 and June 2026.

The report looked at the practice of telemarketers, also known as lead generators, using social media advertising and telephone calls to identify consumers and introduce them to licensed financial advisers.

These advisors would then switch their superannuation out of APRA-regulated funds in a practice known as lead-generation.

Earlier this year, ASIC announced it would be looking into the firms that allow these lead generators to operate.

Crackdown on super ads Unlicensed telemarketers who cold call and make unsolicited approaches to consumers to convince them to switch their super will be banned under long-awaited reforms.

The regulator found that the licensees obtained about 7,639 new clients through lead generation services over the period, which represented about 35 per cent of total new clients for these licensees.

This resulted in more than $678 million being switched or invested, with about 90 per cent coming from superannuation savings.

Licensees deducted $9.8 million in up-front advice fees from clients and clients agreed to a further $4.5 million in annual ongoing fees.

ASIC says the high-profile collapses of Shield and First Guardian — which left almost 12,000 investors losing over $1 billion of their retirement savings — illustrate the potential impact when financial services providers do not act in the best interests of Australian investors.

Earlier this year, Assistant Treasurer Daniel Mulino announced that unlicensed telemarketers who cold call and make unsolicited approaches to convince people to switch their super will be banned.

Lead generators going beyond referrals

Under the law, only a licensed financial adviser can give a consumer advice about their investments.

Deep flaws in Australia's $4.3 trillion system exposed The collapses of the First Guardian and Shield schemes have exposed deep flaws in the regulation of Australia's $4.3 trillion superannuation sector.

But ASIC's review found the 15 licensees used unlicensed lead generators to lure Australians into investment schemes.

The regulator said these lead generators took activities beyond simple referral, including lead qualification, appointment setting, fact-finding, product research and discussing investment performance or Statements of Advice (SOA) recommendations.

In one case, a lead generator had assisted with advice implementation.

ASIC also said some lead generators had used potentially misleading statements, fear-based claims, and non-like-for-like performance comparisons to persuade investors to switch their super.

"Many Australians invested in the funds because their financial adviser failed to act in their best interests and many of these people were advised to make these investments after being approached by a lead generator," ASIC said in its review.

It found involving lead generation in financial advice was likely to be "inconsistent with the obligations that apply to financial advisers" and their authorising licensees.

This included the obligation to act in the best interests of the clients and to only provide personal advice if appropriately authorised.

" Consequently, such activities put advisers and licence holders at risk of breaking the law. "

Licensees had inadequate controls

ASIC said some licensees were failing to supervise or understand what was happening within their networks.

Five of them did not have controls or standards in place that prohibited, or were likely to identify, high-risk superannuation switching by their authorised representatives.

A further four licensees were operating businesses that had some features of "high-risk superannuation switching", the review said.

Alan Kirkland says consumers should be wary of lead generators.

ASIC commissioner Alan Kirkland said lead generators use "slick sales tactics to convince people to switch their super" and that this "can expose Australians to serious financial harm".

"Far too often, we have seen how harmful lead generation practices can steer people towards investment choices that leave them worse off," Mr Kirkland said.

"Our message to advice licensees is clear: we will continue to take enforcement action under current laws where we find evidence of serious consumer harm."

Super Consumers Australia chief executive Xavier O'Halloran said ASIC's findings exposed "the greed driving high-risk super switching schemes".

"Good advisers don't need to cold call people to get clients," he said.

Xavier O'Halloran says good financial advisers do not cold call prospective clients. (ABC News: Daniel Irvine)

World.title: Aged care bed crisis hits boiling point for families waiting years
World.content:
Horrendous, horrible and sleepless nights.

This was how 74-year-old Betty Cameron described the past two years trying to find her husband a residential aged care bed in South Australia.

Darryl Cameron has late-stage dementia, and is living in NDIS-funded supported independent living care.

With his health declining, Ms Cameron was told her husband's funding is likely to cease in three weeks, with Mr Cameron now facing hospitalisation if an aged care bed is not secured.

"If he was a right [frame] of mind, he would want to be dead now," Ms Cameron said.

"He always said he hoped his heart would give out before he got to this point."

Betty Cameron says the aged care bed crisis is taking a physical and mental toll. (ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters)

Mr Cameron's NDIS provider, Hola Support, said his funding was being reviewed through an NDIS tribunal process.

The couple live three hours away from Adelaide in the state's Riverland, a drive Ms Cameron said is unfeasible to do each day if her husband were relocated.

Some days Darryl Cameron smiles, and other days he cannot get out of bed. (Supplied: Betty Cameron)

She was left to look interstate in Mildura, about 150 kilometres away, for a suitable facility she could visit daily due to unavailability in the Riverland.

"I want to be there every day with him. I want to have fun and just interact with him until he does pass away," she said.

" I don't want to be somewhere else, and then they ring and say I'm sorry he's passed away. "

Darryl Cameron (centre) was a die-hard Adelaide Crows supporter. (ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters)

Ms Cameron said the process has taken a significant mental toll on her and she has felt unseen by a system meant to help.

"Some days I feel like punching everyone out, and other days I'm alright," she said.

"I get more days of wanting to punch people out than I do good days.

"When this is all sorted, I'll be right. But until then, nah, I'm a mess some days."

Stuck in bed and waiting

The aged care crisis is a national issue, with all states and territories seeking ways to find solutions.

South Australia is the oldest mainland state and has the longest wait times in the country for residential aged care beds.

There are also about 500 people in hospital waiting for a residential aged care bed in the state. Four years ago, it was only 60.

Lisa Turton believes incentives should be handed out to attract more aged care staff to the sector. (ABC Riverland: Amelia Walters)

NDIS support coordinator Lisa Turton said aged care bed shortages have been an issue for more than a decade.

She said some families are having to make life-altering choices because of the delays.

"I've been involved with participants who have had to make choices over their life expectancy over accommodation previously. It's inhumane," she said.

The number of those in hospital who are waiting for an aged car bed has increased by 830 per cent in the past four years. (ABC News: Keane Bourke)

Ms Turton believed infrastructure across the state needed to be fast-tracked, with regional areas prioritised.

"They should at least quadruple accommodation and facilities in regional areas, as there is the room to build," she said.

"[There should be] a focus on getting more staff to the area that are passionate about this field, or offering incentives and supporting people to find their passion in supporting others."

Federal-state stalemate

Conducting a roundtable with stakeholders last week, South Australia's Minister for Health and Wellbeing, Blair Boyer, said the state government would leave "no stone unturned" to address the aged care crisis.

"[The statistics] will continue to grow and potentially be much higher next year if we don't get some action and support from the federal government, who are responsible for aged care in this nation," he said.

Blair Boyer says the federal government needs to step up. (ABC News: Daniel Taylor)

The minister hoped to generate 650 new beds from a recent no-interest loan scheme for developers, as well as create 600 beds inside part of the old Women's and Children's Hospital.

"We need at least 10,600 additional federal residential aged care places nationally each year over the next two decades," Minister Boyer said.

"Last year, just 800 beds were added to the system."

A spokesperson for the federal Minister for Aged Care and Seniors said delayed discharge is a nationwide challenge and it invested $600 million in 27 state and territory initiatives to reduce delayed discharge.

"We're supporting the construction of around 5,000 additional residential aged care beds [nationally] each year," the spokesperson said.

The spokesperson said 268 beds were slated across five Adelaide sites as part of the 5,000-bed plan.

Darryl deserves dignity

Ensuring her husband has dignity is front of mind for Ms Cameron.

She said securing an aged care bed is the only way he would receive the consideration and care he deserves.

"Just think about these people who have put in years looking after this country. Giving something back to them, that's what they need to do," she said.

" [Darryl] deserves to be looked after and well thought of because he's been a good person and, you know, he never did anything wrong. "

Betty Cameron says her husband, Darryl, has a wicked sense of humour. (Supplied: Betty Cameron )

Ms Cameron will continue to try to savour the special moments with her husband where she can until a bed is secured.

"He is just beautiful. I love it when he remembers my nickname, Betty Spaghetti," she said.

"If he comes out with that or if he just looks at me and says, 'I love you darling,' it makes my day."

World.title: Trump's war in Iran driving shift from fossil fuels
World.content:
During the 1979 Iranian oil crisis, US president Jimmy Carter gave a speech that would likely resonate today.

"Solar energy will not pollute our air or water. We will not run short of it. No one can ever embargo the Sun or interrupt its delivery to us," he said.

Rising fuel prices were crippling the world, and energy sovereignty was front of the president's mind. Behind him as he spoke was a new solar hot water system he had installed at the White House.

President Jimmy Carter inspects solar panels on the roof of the White House's West Wing in 1979. (Supplied: Harvey Georges)

But while Carter's solar prophecy took decades to realise, experts say Donald Trump's decision this year to start a war with Iran has accelerated global electrification efforts and may be considered a tipping point in the shift from fossil fuels.

Renewables continued to grow in the US under Trump even before the war — despite his opposition. Solar generation is up 20 per cent, coal is down, and a record 86 gigawatt hours (GWh) of renewable projects are planned.

And now that voters have stripped Republican control of Congress, the economic momentum behind renewables may be even harder to derail.

Soaring oil prices during the 1970s drove a shift toward fuel-efficient cars and accelerated research in new energy sources, such as solar. (Supplied: US National Archives)

A rocket under EVs

Unlike the oil shocks of the past, this time, consumers have real electric alternatives, and the cost of installed solar and batteries has fallen 90 per cent since 2010. But the biggest story of the war has been the unprecedented rise of electric vehicles (EVs).

Since the US and Israel began bombing Iran in February, both the fuel price and the sale of EVs have risen sharply around the world.

"I think Donald Trump is the best salesperson for electric vehicles the world has ever seen," said Gabrielle Kuiper, an energy expert affiliated with the CSIRO and the ANU.

"Everywhere is recognising that why would you be reliant on liquid imported fossil fuels when you can generate your own electricity with sunshine or with wind and then you can drive an electric vehicle."

In Australia, EVs now make up close to a quarter of all new car sales, lining up with the global average, and in September and October 2026, battery electric cars outsold petrol cars.

Asia leads EV boom

Global EV sales were already rising before the Iran conflict, but growth has surged in emerging markets and places dependent on liquid fuel imports.

Euan Graham, an analyst with global think tank Ember Energy, said a massive EV boom is taking place in South-East Asia.

"Vietnam, Singapore, Thailand, now as well as Indonesia [are] all really picking up in their rate of EV sales and it's more than just the actual sales of cars themselves," he said.

"The best-selling car in Vietnam is a VinFast car, which is a domestic manufacturer that already completely dominates the Vietnamese market and is now expanding overseas."

Based in Vietnam, VinFast is now a leading manufacturer of EVs in South-East Asia. (Reuters: Nguyen Ha Minh)

While the Australian government's efforts to secure fuel supplies have minimised shortages domestically, other countries have been hit hard.

Three-quarters of the world imports fossil fuels, and about 75 per cent of the world's oil supply is traded by sea.

Countries are taking direct action to reduce dependence on imported fuel.

In May, Laos suspended the import of internal combustion engine (ICE) vehicles, following Ethiopia's 2024 decision to ban the imports.

"I don't think people would necessarily have expected a few years ago that it would be emerging markets taking those steps," Graham said.

In Europe, despite concerns about the impact of imported Chinese cars, EV sales have reached record levels, including in auto-manufacturing powerhouse Germany, where sales hit 37 per cent in October.

The US is the only country where EV sales have fallen as US automakers pivoted back to ICE cars in the aftermath of the 2024 Trump victory.

It is a bitter irony for a country that has just delivered a verdict on high gas prices.

Avoided costs and emissions

EVs might be the headline-grabbing story of 2026, but electrification more broadly continues to grow.

"Around the world last year, about three quarters of the growth in electricity demand came from solar alone. And in some countries, solar was providing all of the growth already," Graham said.

Australia's booming battery fleet, and the threat of a gas tax, have seen electricity prices drop since the start of the war, but overseas they have shot up as the conflict disrupted the supply of gas exports from Qatar.

In response, heavy fossil fuel users like South Korea are investing hundreds of billions in renewables.

In Vietnam, plans to build the country's biggest gas-fired power station have been scrapped to shore up energy sovereignty.

Wind turbines along the Sinchang Windmill Coastal Road on Jeju Island, South Korea. (Supplied: Слава Ли/Pexels)

Anna Freeman from the Energy Efficiency Council said the soaring cost of fossil fuels has made the economics of renewables more compelling.

"Prior to this crisis, we were on track to spend $US4 trillion a year on oil and gas globally," said Anna Freeman, from the Energy Efficiency Council.

Freeman also leads the Electrify Now coalition, which published research this week forecasting this year's total oil and gas bill could be over $US5 trillion.

"We will be spending an additional $1.2 trillion, not for any additional products, just that is the price premium associated with this fossil fuel crisis," Freeman said.

"By contrast, we can deliver the net zero energy transition for $3.5 trillion per year," Freeman said.

"And that gets us so much more because it builds us a more efficient and a more affordable and a more secure energy system."

A recent report from Ember found that the global electric car fleet has helped save about $20 billion in crude oil costs in the six months since the US-Israel war with Iran.

Dawn of the age of electricity?

But there are some hard numbers that grind against the electrification narrative. EVs may now make up about a quarter of new car sales, but make up only five per cent of cars on the road.

Coal, oil and gas still supply about 60 per cent of the world's final energy. And record growth in renewables in 2025 of 887 terawatt hours (TWh) did outpace electricity demand of 849TWh, but not by much.

A planet-wide solar boom is beating expectations Satellite imagery reveals the staggering rise of solar farms around the world in recent years.

Electrification will be a key focus of the UN's annual climate summit, the Conference of Parties — or COP31 — this week.

In June, the UN set a goal of 35 per cent electrification by 2035.

"The world is entering the age of electricity. At COP31, we will flick the switch," wrote COP31 president-designate Murat Kurum, in a special report on electrification by the IEA last month.

It is welcome news for Kylie Turner, the sustainable economies lead at Monash University's Climateworks Centre, who describes electrification as "the unloved child of the energy transition."

"At COP28 in Dubai, the world signed up to a global pledge to triple renewables and double energy efficiency, and the piece of the puzzle that's missing is actually electrification."

Almost 50 years after Jimmy Carter declared solar "feasible and cost-effective," Ember Energy analyst Euan Graham says the economics of electrification have moved beyond politics.

"I'm most optimistic about transforming the power sector because it's gone far beyond climate targets," he said.

"In terms of economics and the speed at which they can be built, clean technologies — especially wind, solar and batteries — are just winning."

World.title: Left without wages or answers, workers break silence on Bathla collapse
World.content:
After working for nine years at one of Sydney's biggest property developers, Jagdeep Singh has estimated he is owed $80,000 in unpaid wages and entitlements.

But more than two months after the company was labelled insolvent, the former stormwater engineer does not know whether he will recover the money.

He is among hundreds of workers affected when the developer entered voluntary administration in August owing at least $3.4 billion.

Former Bathla personnel want answers about unpaid wages and uncertain futures. (ABC News: Fletcher Yeung)

Now, former employees are speaking publicly for the first time about their fight to recover unpaid wages, missing pay slips and the personal toll of the collapse.

Dozens of former Bathla personnel have told the ABC they have struggled to find full-time work after losing their jobs.

Some have been forced to dip into their savings or borrow from friends and family to make do during challenging economic times.

Others face an even more uncertain future, with the loss of their jobs potentially jeopardising their right to remain in Australia.

"We are not asking the administrators to pay from its own funds," Mr Singh said.

" What we are asking is for them to give us clear, transparent answers in a timely manner, we need full details of our entitlements. "

Former Bathla staff are protesting over unpaid wages and entitlements after the collapse. (ABC News: Fletcher Yeung)

Former workers left chasing millions

Mr Singh is part of a group of about 200 former Bathla personnel who have joined forces in recent weeks to demand answers from the company's administrators, Teneo.

In a September affidavit filed in the NSW Supreme Court, Teneo's senior managing director Andrew Scott put employee-related creditor claims at around $6 million, covering wages, superannuation and leave entitlements only.

More than a dozen former employees told the ABC they had experienced irregular wage payments and missing pay slips in the months leading up to the company entering administration.

The ABC has seen emails exchanged between the workers and Teneo.

In one response last month, the administrators acknowledged a "significant delay" in calculating employee entitlements, citing hard-copy employment contracts and an "outdated" payroll system which required "manual adjustments and additional review processes".

Former Bathla employees say they are struggling with financial uncertainty following the company's collapse. (ABC News: Fletcher Yeung)

'I'm not sure what my future will be'

For some former employees on temporary employer-sponsored visas, losing their jobs has also put their futures in Australia at risk.

Former Bathla employee, Arjun, who asked not to be identified by his real name, told the ABC he was worried he would be required to leave the country after his job was terminated.

The draftsperson, who was recruited from overseas three years ago on a subclass 482 visa, said he was owed an estimated $10,000 in outstanding entitlements and had struggled to find another employer willing to sponsor him.

The ABC has sighted his termination letter and visa documentation.

"We have worked hard for this company, and we deserve to receive our outstanding entitlements," he said.

"I'm not sure what my future will be.

" If we leave the country, how are we suppose to follow up and recover our money? "

Temporary visa holders are not eligible for the federal government's Fair Entitlements Guarantee, a safety net designed to help employees recover certain unpaid entitlements when their employer collapses.

For these workers, recovering their money will depend on the outcome of Bathla's insolvency proceedings.

Do you know more? If you have more information about this article or any other tips, you can securely contact reporter Lin Lin at linreporting@proton.me

Uncertain over staying in Australia

Former Bathla architectural drafter Kelly worries she may have to leave Australia. (ABC News: Fletcher Yeung)

Another former employee, Kelly, who also asked not to be identified by her real name, faces a similar predicament.

She is on a subclass 482 visa, while awaiting a decision on an employer-sponsored permanent residency application.

With the company's collapse, she faces uncertainty over the future of that application and her ability to remain in the country.

The graduate architect worked at Bathla for almost two and a half years and estimates she is owed about seven weeks of wages, outstanding superannuation and other entitlements.

"Everything that I built, my career, my experience, my knowledge is here," she said.

Bathla's messy next chapter Bathla has bought itself time, but not a rescue. Its future is increasingly being decided project by project.

"It's been a hard time, and we are near the end of the year, so there aren't many openings."

Kelly is among several former employees interviewed by the ABC who used Brothers Migration & Education Services, a migration agency co-owned by Rajinder Mohan, who is also a co-founder of Bathla.

The agency's listed business address is at the same location as Bathla's headquarters.

The agency is not among the Bathla companies in administration.

Administrators say the complexity of Bathla's employee and payroll records means reconciling the situation will take longer than usual. (ABC News: Fletcher Yeung)

Workers face an uncertain wait

Bathla Group entered voluntary administration on August 25, triggering one of Australia's largest and most complex property insolvencies.

In a statement to the ABC, Teneo said it understood employees' concerns and was treating their entitlements as a priority.

The administrators said the "nature and complexity" of Bathla's employee and payroll records meant reconciling outstanding wages and entitlements was "taking longer than usual".

Teneo said the Bathla Group did not have sufficient funds to pay outstanding entitlements for at least six to 12 months.

Workers can generally access the government's Fair Entitlements Guarantee (FEG) scheme only when the employer enters liquidation, but not while it remains in administration.

Box Hill and other suburbs in Sydney's north-west were a major focus of Bathla Group's residential projects. (ABC News: Berge Breiland)

However, Teneo said it was working with the federal government to secure early access to the scheme.

"The Administrators are hopeful that early access to FEG will be approved by the beginning of December."

Bathla did not respond to a request for comment.

University of Sydney law professor and insolvency expert Jason Harris said employees had rights to employment records and payroll information, even when a company was in administration.

"If it's taking a long time, I suspect it's because they don't have the money, or they don't have the information, or both," Professor Harris said.

He said workers could raise concerns about missing employment records and pay slips with the Fair Work Ombudsman.

Under insolvency laws, employees have priority over ordinary unsecured creditors for certain unpaid entitlements, but recovering their money depends on the funds available.

Loading...

The NSW Supreme Court has extended the deadline for Bathla's second creditors' meeting until September 2027.

"We cannot sit and just wait for one year, and then afterwards hear that we are not getting anything," said Mr Singh.

With Christmas approaching, the uncertainty is taking its toll.

"In and around Christmas time, people plan for holidays," another former worker said.

"All we are planning is how we will get our money back."

World.title: Man charged with murder after delivery driver dies near Queen Victoria Market
World.content:
Breaking NationalVictoriaCrime Man charged with murder after delivery driver dies near Queen Victoria Market Roy Ward November 9, 2026 — 6:32am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. A Footscray man has been charged with murder over the alleged stabbing attack of two food delivery drivers in central Melbourne on Friday night. The man, 51, was charged with one count of murder and one of intentionally cause serious injury. He will face Melbourne Magistrates’ Court on Monday. Feng Jianming with his wife Xu and children Yawei and Changhui from several years ago. Feng Jianming, 47, was working for food delivery platform HungryPanda on Friday night near Queen Victoria Market when he and another delivery driver confronted a man who was allegedly tampering with their bikes. Police were called to Chongqing Chicken Pot City restaurant in Frederick Way soon after 8pm where they found a critically injured Feng. Another driver, 34, was allegedly found nearby with stab wounds.



Paramedics performed CPR on Feng but he was declared dead at the scene. The 34-year-old man was taken to hospital with serious injuries. The Footscray man allegedly left the scene and was arrested in Footscray on Saturday morning. Jianming Feng Feng’s death has sparked anger in Melbourne’s Asian community over public safety in the CBD while the safety and work conditions of delivery drivers has also come under scrutiny. Hundreds of people joined an emotional rally at the State Library on Saturday night to honour Feng.



His wife, Xi, and adult children daughter Yawei and son Changhui expressed their heartbreak from their home in China. Xi told this masthead that Feng worked tirelessly to send money back to China to support his family, including his elderly parents. Feng Jianming with his son Changhui. Few family photos exist due to Feng’s many years spent away from China supporting them. She said he had not returned home for nine years to save on airfares. “He wanted to save the money and continue working,” she told this masthead through a translator.



“But he promised that when our son got married, he would definitely return. That was the plan. He would come home for our son’s wedding, and then we could finally be together as a family. We thought we only had to wait another year or two.” Melbourne Lord Mayor Nick Reece, who attended the vigil on Saturday evening, told this masthead he had spoken with HungryPanda management and offered to hold a roundtable to discuss safety conditions for delivery riders in the city. A second vigil held outside the State Library for delivery rider Feng Jianming on Saturday evening. Alexander Darling “Delivery riders have to be some of the most underappreciated people in our city,” Reece said. “They deliver our meals, our packages, rain, hail or shine seven days a week and are often not well paid… and, as we have seen, their jobs are very risky as well, not just from other vehicles on the road but from horrible attacks like the one we saw last night.”



With Alexander Darling Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Woeful Wallabies smashed by England in record rout
World.content:
Breaking SportRugby UnionAustralian rugby Woeful Wallabies smashed by England in record rout Iain Payten Updated November 9, 2026 — 6:15am ,first published 4:32am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Shattered Wallabies skipper Harry Wilson conceded his team “didn’t fire a shot” after being smashed by a rampant England in a record 45-22 defeat at Twickenham. There was to be no repeat of the Wallabies’ 2024 heroics at the famous venue on a woeful afternoon from the Australia side, who were dominated in all facets of play by England. Jack van Poortvliet scores his team’s fourth try against the Wallabies. Getty Images The hosts repeatedly picked apart Australia’s shoddy defence, both wide and narrow, and scored seven tries to three. Two consolation tries to the Wallabies in the last quarter appeared to have saved the Wallabies from the embarrassment of a record margin of defeat (24 points), but a late intercept try to Ben Spencer saw England secure some history in a different way, with their biggest ever score against the Wallabies. Despite a lacklustre opening 40 minutes, Australia were still in the contest at halftime after Max Jorgensen scored an intercept to make the score 19-10.



But any hope of a further fightback in the second half was dashed when they gave up another simple try soon after the break, and when flashy back-rower Henry Pollock - who was deployed as a winger - scored two tries in three minutes midway through the second half, the contest was over. Ollie Chessum scores for England. Getty Images Late tries to Filipo Daugunu and Jeremy Williams in the last quarter bolstered the Wallabies’ score but it was far too little, and far too late. The Wallabies’ attack wasn’t any better than their defence, and their game long struggle to exit their half gave England ample opportunity to build pressure and score. Most of the Wallabies promising opportunities in attack were ruined by a steady stream of errors or penalties. The decision to start powerhouse back-rower Rob Valetini was exposed as a never-to-be-repeated mistake by the Wallabies’ inability to make any headway against a strong England defence.



In one of a number of telling stats, Australia didn’t enter England’s quarter until the 37th minute of the game. England missed just two of 81 tackles in the opening half, and the only line break conceded was Jorgensen’s intercept. Australia’s other main carrier, Angus Bell, was sin-binned for a hip-drop tackle before halftime. “We struggled to get our game going, England put us under the pump in the first half and we didn’t get too many a-zone entries,” Wallabies captain Harry Wilson said in an on-field interview. “England were the better side. They fronted up physically. Our defence wasn’t physical enough, and we didn’t slow the ball down. Credit to England.” Ollie Chessum of England wins the ball during a line-out in Sunday’s match. Getty Images



Speaking later at the media conference, Wilson said the Wallabies had been thoroughly outplayed by a strong England but couldn’t put his finger on why. “It is really disappointing,” he said. “We didn’t really fire a shot, in that first half and I guess we were really excited to go out there and try and fire some shots and really back our game. “England put us in tough field position. It felt like we’re always trying to exit, get out of our end. “I am really disappointed because I expect better from us, and we’ve got to take those learnings next week into Scotland because we know when we’re at our best and we’re backing our game and we’re really putting teams under threat.” Wallabies coach Les Kiss said: “England pinned us well. They controlled that field position, and put pressure on us at different times. We just didn’t get going, particularly in the first half.



“I give a lot of credit to England, the way they imposed their plan on us and didn’t give us a chance to impose what we would like to have done with the ball”. “Our training all week was really about making sure we found those opportunities that we believed was in the defence line of England. We just didn’t really fire a shot to get to those spaces.“ The Wallabies trailed 19-10 at halftime after a sloppy opening 40 minutes in which they were lucky to not concede more than three tries. England were immediately on the attack and had a second try scratched for an earlier forward pass. But after an obstruction penalty, England kicked to the corner and rolled in a try to hooker Jamie George in the 8th minute. Max Jorgensen runs with the ball to score Australia’s first try. Getty Images



Ryan Lonergan banged over a penalty in the 10th minute but Australia’s exits continued to be poor, and though Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii was doing well catching contestable kicks, the Wallabies attack run by Declan Meredith was tentative and disorganised. It seemed a matter of time that England would reap more dividend from their territory dominance, and that came via an Ollie Chessum try in the 25th minute in the left corner. It came from more defensive spacing problems that left an extra man on the end for England after sustained phases. The Wallabies’ problems got worse when Bell was sin-binned in the 32nd minute for a hip-drop tackle, which have just been outlawed in rugby. It was not upgraded to red but Australia paid a price anyway, with England again kicking to the corner and rolling in another try to prop Joe Heyes. Jorgensen’s try helped the Wallabies enter the sheds with some confidence, but it quickly faded after oranges when more gaps in the defence saw England halfback Jack Van Poortvliet score in the 42nd minute. Pollock’s two tries in the 54th and 57th minute ended the contest.



The entry of Daugunu and Ben Donaldson in the last 25 minutes saw the Wallabies attack begin to throw better punches, and the Reds winger scored. Jeremy Williams also crossed after a long-range attack. But Daugunu gave away a try to England in the dying stages by trying to pop an offload that was intercepted by Ben Spencer. World.title: Proof that life only gets better with every decade
World.content:
Sponsored LifestyleLife & relationshipsBolton Clarke Proof that life only gets better with every decade Sponsored by Bolton Clarke November 9, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Finding new firsts: stories of positive ageing We eagerly await childhood firsts: the first word, the first step, the first day at school. But when we think about older age, the joy of new opportunities and experiences is not the first thing that springs to mind. Research has found the sense of purpose that comes with learning new things is an important part of ageing well. So, too, is seeing and hearing about how other people are making the most of life at every age. Positive ageing is contagious. By sharing the lived experiences of older Australians, this series aims to change the conversation around ageing, for the positive.



For Bolton Clarke retirement living resident Maria, 70, an innate curiosity drove her to leave her career as a banker to start over in catering. And in retirement, it has meant always being on the lookout for a new adventure, big or small. Proving that life only gets better, Maria says she still feels 21 and firmly believes that every decade can be the best decade of your life. Bolton Clarke “I’ve always had the motto that you do the best that you can do, and if there’s something else that you want to try, have a go at it. Embrace opportunities even if you doubt yourself,” she says. “I left school and went into the bank as a postage clerk. At 40 I was in a very demanding middle management job, and I was working very long hours and felt that work was taking over my being.



“I thought, ‘there’s more to life than coming home at 10 o’clock at night and not sleeping well.’ Then I saw an ad in the local paper for a certificate of commercial cookery at the local TAFE school and thought, ‘Oh, that sounds interesting.’ “So I threw in my banking career, went back to school and did a three-month full-time cooking course, and then went into hospitality for 13 years. “I managed to get a start on the bottom rung as a kitchen hand and worked for a big catering company, then I worked my way up to management.” Maria loves to travel. Along the way, Maria found one of the great loves of her life: travel.



“I’d been working for two years, and I saved my annual leave and all my money, and Mum and I headed off to Italy, where we met Dad’s family for the first time.” That first trip was the beginning of an obsession that continues today. “I’ve got an inquisitive mind. I love learning about things.” “Embrace opportunities even if you doubt yourself.” - Maria In 2018, Maria moved into her Bolton Clarke retirement village and found a community and a posse of regular travel companions.



“We have four married couples and three single women in my street who I travel and socialise with,” she says. “We’re all of the opinion that we’re living our best lives. “My friend Joyce uses the words culture and adventure: to go somewhere where you’ve never been before or do something that’s out of your comfort zone and make the most of it. “The village is a community, it’s happiness. There are some sad moments, but we’re all there for each other. “I have enjoyed getting older because I’m now doing things that I want to do. I still feel 21, although I don’t know that I’d go back to being 21! I think each decade that you’re in, you can say is the best decade of your life.” Bolton Clarke is Australia’s largest independent, not-for-profit aged care provider, shaping the future of positive ageing. Bolton Clarke supports people to live independently at home and across 42 retirement living communities and 87 residential aged care homes. To hear more and join the positive ageing conversation, visit boltonclarke.com.au/positive-ageing.

World.title: There are no traffic lights in my suburb, and the biggest motoring hazard is ducks crossing the road
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

As we drove towards the property, an enormous avocado tree sprawling across the front lawn came into view. That was all it took. “Sold!” I declared before even stepping inside. My daughters thought I’d lost my mind. They may have had a point. Most people inspect the kitchen or check the plumbing, but I saw an ancient avocado tree and decided the rest was paperwork. Having grown up in Brisbane, I thought I knew my own backyard. Yet, somehow, the islands just across Moreton Bay had remained a mystery to me. While working in Italy, I began dreaming of a new chapter. One night, scrolling through the real estate sites, I spotted a property on Russell Island. Intrigued, I flew back to Australia, and arranged to meet the agent, who collected me from the ferry. A slow-moving convoy refusing to give way. Cindy Jensen The island’s best-kept secret comes with bubbles. Cindy Jensen Commute envy starts here. Cindy Jensen



More than 20 years living in beautiful parts of the Gold and Sunshine coasts hadn’t prepared me for Russell Island. I hadn’t anticipated a place where I’d sleep better than anywhere else, become deeply involved in the community, and treat the mainland as somewhere I occasionally visit rather than somewhere I need to be. Life here moves at a different pace. It’s like living in 1989, before everyone became permanently attached to screens and schedules. It takes just over 10 minutes to drive from one end of the island to the other, yet a quick errand can stretch into an hour after chatting with neighbours and collecting enough local gossip to fill a newspaper column. There are no traffic lights, and the biggest road hazard is a family of ducks crossing as though they own the place. Curlews patrol the neighbourhood like disgruntled security guards, delivering their mournful night-time soundtrack. Strangely, I find their calls more calming than any sleeping app. Some permanent inhabitants of our nearest neighbouring island, Karragarra. Sculpture by Michael van Dam. Cindy Jensen Island wildlife carers go the extra mile - sometimes that means a pram ride and a ferry crossing! Cindy Jensen David Hogan makes Native American-style flutes. Cindy Jensen Cockatoos, kookaburras and plovers are also regular visitors. I’ve become a wildlife caterer, sharing my little patch of the world with feathered guests who seem to consider my property part of their real estate portfolio.



The houses are just as characterful: quirky cottages, colourful gardens and creative renovations accumulated over decades. I love that individuality, although identical new builds are beginning to appear. At the Russell Island Bowls Club, two vodka sodas cost less than $15. You can sit outside, watch the afternoon unfold and enjoy a proper conversation without competing with televisions the size of garage doors. And despite what some mainlanders might imagine, there’s always something happening. Markets, performances, creative gatherings and community events fill the calendar. Through my writing for The Friendly Bay Islander magazine and organising local events, I’ve become part of a community that continually surprises me. Our greatest attraction isn’t a beach or a view; it’s the people. I’ve met an artist whose home is covered in artwork, a retired police officer who makes Native American-style flutes, and a 93-year-old woman who donated land to council for a public park. The bathroom of local artist Kinga Rypinska. Cindy Jensen The view from the office isn’t half bad. At the studio of artist Beth J. Leach. Cindy Jensen



Making a difference: The Blue Tree Project. Cindy Jensen There’s the couple who painted a massive tree blue in memory of their son, hoping to encourage conversations about suicide and asking others if they’re OK. Volunteers Robert and Shane, meanwhile, sit on the back of a ute at the IGA, helping elderly residents, caring for animals and children, and tackling mechanical problems. They’re reminders that some of the most valuable people in a community are simply those who turn up when someone needs a hand. My most adventurous encounter involved a boat, a surfing dog and its owner. I wondered whether I’d accidentally sailed into a surreal pirate movie. You couldn’t make this stuff up. Colourful local Ben Siely and his kelpie Chasse, waterskiing. Cindy Jensen Chasse has had years of practice and still loves every tow. Cindy Jensen Lucy Gallant performing at Russell Island event Somewhere Else #3. Cindy Jensen I also started The Mooring, a Facebook media page, because online descriptions of Russell Island seemed so far removed from the place I was discovering. There was plenty about crime and undesirable characters, but little about the generosity, creativity and humour I experienced firsthand.



I’m not suggesting the islands are perfect. Ferry travel requires planning; infrastructure is under pressure; tradespeople can be difficult to pin down; and healthcare access is a genuine consideration. I’ve also noticed an influx of new residents over the past year. Growth brings difficult conversations about development, parking and protecting the bushland that makes these islands so special. Loving a place also means caring about its future. Still, the everyday pleasures keep winning me over. I can swim and picnic at Karragarra Beach, enjoy what I consider the best gelato at 8th Sense Kitchen on Macleay Island, and watch extraordinary sunsets from the Macleay Island Bowls Club. The passenger ferry between the islands is free, making it easy to explore our watery neighbourhood. Related Article Opinion

Life in the ’burbs No one has heard of my Brisbane suburb, but it was good enough for Elvis Gillian Wills Contributor My daughters thought I’d lost my mind buying a house on an island I’d never visited and where I knew nobody. Instead, I’ve found a community, work I love, stories to chase, and a front yard that doubles as a wildlife viewing platform. Sometimes, overthinking stops us from finding the very things that make us happiest. There’s a lot to be said for trusting your instincts and seeing where they lead. In my case, it led to Russell Island, a community I adore, and a collection of stories I’m privileged to tell. Not a bad return on one impulsive decision. And if the avocado harvest comes good, the investment might even pay dividends.

World.title: Brisbane’s grey line: The surprising suburb where over-65s outnumber those under 20
World.content:
NationalQueenslandAgeing Brisbane’s grey line: The surprising suburb where over-65s outnumber those under 20 Marissa Calligeros and Matt Wade November 9, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The share of Brisbane suburbs where over-65s outnumber those aged under 20 has increased fourfold in the past two decades as the city’s population ages and the cost of housing locks young families out of many neighbourhoods. The population of those aged over 65 outstripped children and teenagers in 28 Brisbane suburbs in 2025. That compares with only seven suburbs in 2001. A quiet retirement by the water is highly attractive to many Brisbanites, which has made a cluster of the city’s bayside suburbs – arguably Brisbane’s grey line – a magnet for those over the age of 65. Bribie Island – with its numerous retirement villages and over-50s communities – has the highest population balance in favour of seniors.



The island, 80 kilometres north of Brisbane and separated from the mainland by the calm, shallow waters of Pumicestone Passage, has nearly 8000 more people aged over 65 than those under 20. Other seaside suburbs dominated by seniors include Cleveland (2096 more people aged over 65), Redcliffe (1790 more), Victoria Point (1371 more), Scarborough-Newport (1346 more) and Margate-Woody Point (1022 more). People cool off in the calm waters of Pumicestone Passage on Bribie Island. Glenn Campbell However, one affluent inner-city suburb is also proving popular with seniors. The riverside neighbourhood of Newstead – known for its trendy bars, artisan bakeries, pilates studios and high-end fashion stores – has 791 more people aged over 65 than those under 20.



Terry Rawnsley, a KPMG economist who analysed the latest area population figures, said property prices played a role, as well as the prevalence of new apartment developments in Newstead. Some residential towers, such as Aveo’s Newstead Residences and Ozcare’s Rendu Towers, are offered specifically as retirement living. Upmarket bakery and cafe, Baker D. Chirico, in Newstead. Tammy Law “Some inner-city locations such as Newstead-Bowen Hills may be attracting older residents who have cashed in on higher housing values and downsized to apartments,” he said. “They are seeking lower-maintenance properties while retaining easy access to the cafes, restaurants and amenities of the inner city. At the same time, higher property prices in these areas may be making it more difficult for families with young children to live there.”



The same factors and the development of bespoke, luxury riverside apartments may be influencing the population in Kangaroo Point, where there are 609 more seniors than people under 20. The traditional blue-chip suburbs of Ascot and Hamilton also have more over-65s than children and teenagers, as does the southside suburb of Robertson, where an early wave of Chinese migrants settled. The bayside lifestyle is a magnet for retirees. Dan Peled Areas with older age profiles also tend to have more women than men, reflecting females’ longer life expectancy. Brisbane’s population has been ageing more slowly than Sydney and Melbourne’s because – until recently – it was more affordable for young families to buy a detached house with a backyard.



But it is still ageing. In the mid-1970s, about one in 12 Australians was aged over 65, but that has now climbed to one in six. The share of over 65s is forecast to reach one in four by the 2060s. Related Article Population Where have the kids gone? Brisbane’s shrinking suburbs revealed Fewer births have also been a factor. Brisbane’s fertility rate, which measures expected births per woman, has fallen by 19 per cent in the past decade to a historic low of 1.44. It has been a different story in a swath of suburbs on Greater Brisbane’s urban fringe, where sprawling housing developments offer young families affordable house and land packages. The population balance in favour of under-20s is greatest in the Ipswich suburbs of Springfield Lakes (8218 more under-20s than over-65s), Redbank Plains (7528 more people under the age of 20) and Ripley (6762 more).



Rawnsley said the character of many suburbs will shift as the share of older residents increases. School enrolments fall, parks will be used differently, there will be fewer childcare centres, yet there will be a greater demand for aged care. “Demographics shape the personality of a suburb. As the population ages, you often see a shift from shops and services focused on school-aged children towards health services and lifestyle amenities. The suburb doesn’t necessarily slow down, but it does begin to cater to a different stage of life,” he said. “We’ve seen this play out in parts of Sydney and Melbourne, where decades of strong house price growth have gradually priced younger households out of some suburbs. As a result, those areas have become older over time. “If housing remains unaffordable for many young families in Brisbane, a similar trend could emerge, but demographic change of that nature typically takes many years.” Start the morning with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: The Wallabies have the talent. But something is going badly wrong
World.content:
SportRugby UnionWallabies Opinion The Wallabies have the talent. But something is going badly wrong Peter FitzSimons Columnist and author November 9, 2026 — 5:51am

November 9, 2026 — 5:51am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Things were grim, and on the rim. Of the abyss. At 19-3 down to England, with a minute to go in the first half and England pressing the Wallabies’ line, there was every chance the visiting team in gold at Twickenham would go to the break broken, and down 26-3. Henry Pollock makes a break. Getty Images At this point a 50-point drubbing seemed in the offing. And now it happens.



Defending out on the right wing, Max Jorgensen took his chances and the England back-line ball all in one, snatching the looping pass from the skies to run away 70 metres for the intercept try and bring it back to 19-10. At this point we knew Australia was saved ... and we were wrong. Ollie Chessum scores for England. Getty Images For when England scored again in the first two minutes of the second half, to go to a 26-10 lead, it was time to assess just what was going wrong. But as this is a column, not a novel, we’ll have to go to the lowlights only. The England forward pack made ground with every charge, with our own blokes struggling to shut them down.



The English back line was slick, and in the ebb and flow between them and our own three-quarter line surging against each other, the men in white seemed to habitually move the advantage line at least two metres forward with every surge, which all added up. Related Article Breaking

Australian rugby Woeful Wallabies smashed by England in record rout On our side, balls were perpetually spilled in crucial positions. Penalties were less being conceded than given freely – at one point five of them in a row. Wallaby prop Angus Bell, who was as good as ever in breaking the line, became the first international player to spend 10 minutes in the bin for a hip-drop tackle under the new rules forbidding them. England scored two tries in his absence. Every time the Wallabies got close to the England line in the first 50 minutes – by which I mean, twice – basic errors were made. Balls not being put in straight into the lineout at this level is as unforgivable as throwing awry passes just when the English line was at last starting to crack. Against that, the home side were ruthlessly professional, giving the visitors next to nothing. In front of a sold-out 80,000-plus crowd, they just kept piling on the pressure and when they went to a 38-10 lead courtesy of the blonde light-houser English back-rower Henry Pollock – rushed on in the second half as an emergency winger – scoring two successive tries, it was starting to look like a complete humiliation was in the offing again.



Yes, Australia jagged two tries back through Jeremy Williams and Filipo Daugunu to close to 38-22, which showed some fight, but it was all a little beside the point as the game was long gone already, and a final English try to finish at 45-22 was a fair reflection of the match. Max Jorgensen scores. Getty Images Just what happened to the magnificent Wallaby side that beat South Africa in Perth two months ago is not obvious. This loss to England after two successive drubbings at the hands of the All Blacks is more than disappointing after our team had gone six matches without a loss over August and September. On the upside of a down match, Wallaby skipper Harry Wilson got through a mountain of work, as did Fraser McReight and Josh Canham. Meanwhile, in the centres, Len Ikitau was useful and Jorgensen was dangerous when he got the ball, which was, alas, not enough. Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii was good in the air and twice pulled it out of the skies on a Wallaby kick to put Australia on the attack. “His-name-is-Su” might have done it another three times, bar for the fact our kick-offs were so often just too long. Why on earth – when Suaalii is dangerous in the air at 25 metres from a standing start – would we just about always kick it 30 metres? Give the bloke a chance! It is such a basic, endlessly repeated error, it takes my breath away. It was at this very ground two years ago that Suaalii demonstrated that he is all but unstoppable from short kick-offs, and yet we’ve barely seen him given those opportunities since.



All up, it was a very disappointing start to the Spring Tour, but at least not the absolute drubbing it might have been – just an average drubbing, which is little enough to hold onto. Filipo Daugunu breaks clear from Ben Earl. Getty Images From here, the Wallabies head north to take on Scotland at Murrayfield. Coach Les Kiss will have to add Rob Valetini to the starting line-up. The penetrating back-rower made an immediate impact when he came off the bench in the second half, and it is a mystery why he was not there from the first. The other one who must be added is Carter Gordon, who right now is in his usual position – coming back from injury. Despite Gordon’s seeming fragility at five-eighth, our team needs a joker in the deck, if not the pack, and he’s it. In those times he has played for the Wallabies, he’s always been able to unleash the backline, and that is what we desperately need right now – someone who can act as a catalyst to liberate the talent that’s there. We are a year out from a home World Cup. We know we have some excellent pieces to put together into the jigsaw puzzle of the team that will contest it, but right now, the picture is so messy it’s more Picasso than Tom Roberts. I still think there’s a masterpiece in there somewhere – for we really have seen glimpses of it this season – but we’re a long way from it right now. World.title: Australia needs to fix its ailing batting order. These 12 players are vying for the job
World.content:
SportCricketAustralian cricket Australia needs to fix its ailing batting order. These 12 players are vying for the job Jon Pierik November 9, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The batting line-up of Australia’s men’s Test team is in a state of flux heading into the four-match series against New Zealand, beginning next month. Marnus Labuschagne is likely to be axed from No.3 after a disappointing series in South Africa, while the No.6 or No.7 slot – depending on where Alex Carey bats – is also up for grabs. Peter Handscomb, Kurtis Patterson, Marnus Labuschagne, Josh Inglis and Sam Konstas are among those competing for spots in the Australian test batting line-up this summer. Stephen Kiprillis Matt Renshaw was elevated into the opening role for the final Test in South Africa, but does he remain there for the home campaign or return to the middle-order where had great success? Travis Head and Cameron Green are expected to retain their spots, but what of Josh Inglis, who delivered a swashbuckling first-innings ton at Newlands after being a late replacement for Steve Smith?



While Smith is expected to be fit after dealing with a neck issue, he is resting at his base in New York, and still needs to prove his fitness. Clearly, there is much riding on the next round of Sheffield Shield matches, beginning Wednesday, and through the three-match ODI series against England, beginning on Friday in Perth, for the selectors are also turning their attention to the heavy-duty Test tour of India from January. In total, the Australian Test team has 10 matches scheduled over a period of little more than three months. From the start of the Perth Test against the Kiwis, that would amount to 50 days of cricket in the space of 96 days if all matches were to go the distance. Here are the leading batting contenders who must deliver if they are to fill the vacant roles in the team ahead of that gruelling program.



Sam Konstas (NSW) Will play Test cricket again, but close Shield observers say a return this summer to partner Travis Head at the top of the order may be too soon for the 21-year-old. Sam Konstas celebrates his century against Western Australia, and is keen for a Test recall. Getty Images Has begun the new campaign like a runaway bull, thumping 67, 71, 151 not out and 149 for Australia A and NSW, but returned to earth with a thud, scoring just 5 and 2 against Tasmania. Regardless, former Test captain Mark Taylor says Konstas is near the “top of my list” for a recall. Having failed with an overly aggressive approach in his first stint in the Test side, Konstas now has a more composed temperament, while simplifying his game. Will put pressure on the selectors if he goes big against the Redbacks.



Nathan McSweeney (South Australia) Is facing the old England conundrum of being regarded as a future Test captain, but has yet to prove he can forge a spot as a blue-chip batsman. Nathan McSweeney is regarded as a leader of the future, but sometimes that expectation can be a burden. Getty Images Was let down by the selectors when told to open against India in his sole series, an unfamiliar role he failed in, and is seen as a No.3 or middle-order batter. Has a one-day century and two Shield half-centuries this summer, but is only averaging 33 since the start of the 2024-25 season. Needs to slap down a major score.



Jack Clayton (Queensland) Has been publicly endorsed by Usman Khawaja as a strong Test candidate in a summer when he is second on the Shield run-scoring list with 303 runs at 75.75. Building a case: Qieensland left-hander Jack Clayton has been backed by Test great Usman Khawaja. Getty Images The classy left-hander, who typically bats at No.4, has a century against Victoria (the seventh of his first-class career) and scores of 66 and 37 not out against South Australia, and an 88 against WA. Since the start of the 2024-25 season, Clayton has 1,408 runs at 46.93. At 27, is in the prime of his career. Can also bowl left-arm spin.



Beau Webster (Tasmania) The 200cm all-rounder may have played the last of his 12 Tests, having struggled to have an impact with either bat or ball in his two Tests in South Africa before he was dropped ahead of the Cape Town clash. Has done some nice things since his shock Test debut against India in 2025, but will find it tougher to return should Cameron Green resume bowling. Kurtis Patterson (NSW) At 33, age may count against the NSW left-hander, who has a Test century to his credit, and has averaged more than 45 since the start of the 2024-25 season. In another world, would have played more than the two Tests he managed in 2019. Has a century against WA this summer, but cannot afford to fail against the Redbacks.



Peter Handscomb (Victoria) Has failed to pass 39 in six first-class innings this summer, and is a long-shot to win a Test recall, having played the last of his 20 Tests in 2023. Peter Handscomb’s skill on turning wickets will weigh on the selectors’ minds when they come to pick their squad for the fiveTest tour of India. AP India, however, appears a better option. At 35, age is also against the Victorian, but the fact Travis Head recently name-checked him when declaring strong Test teams deserved to have senior players as replacements ensured he was added to this list. “It’s great that we’ve got a strong Test team. It’s great that that means that we know that our next guys in are hardened first-class cricketers. If you look at the guys that you guys talk about, it’s the Kurtis Pattersons of the world, the Peter Handscombs. I’m going to miss people, but guys that have played a lot of first-class cricket,” Head said.



Marnus Labuschagne (Queensland) Related Article Exclusive

Australian cricket As Marnus Labuschagne faces the axe, his batting coach won’t answer two key questions Even the Test veteran’s batting coach concedes the incumbent Test No.3 will be axed, but a strong showing at the Gabba – should he play – may give the selectors pause to at least rethink. However, three years without a Test ton means he has run out of credits. Needs to work out which stump is best to take strike on. Sam Harper (Victoria) The wicket-keeper-batsman was a surprise squad call-up for South Africa, despite being Victoria’s Shield player of the year last summer. Would have liked more runs against Queensland last week in his newish role as an opener, and can ensure he remains in the Test conversation against WA.



Related Article Opinion

Test cricket Selectors’ disdain for Sheffield Shield is sabotaging the Test team Geoff Lawson Cricket columnist And don’t forget this quartet in the Australian ODI squad facing England next week: Josh Inglis (Western Australia) Returned to the Test side in a blaze of glory with a dashing first-innings century at Newlands after Smith was a late scratching. Big scores in the ODI series could make it extremely difficult for selectors to drop him.



Cooper Connolly (Western Australia) Returned to the Test side at Newlands where he made 29 and 0 at No.7 and took a wicket with his left-arm finger spin. Has been chosen in Australia’s white-ball squad to face England, so the left-hander will miss the next Shield round. Cooper Connolly played his second Test in the series against South Africa. Getty Images The selectors clearly see the 23-year-old as a key plank of the future, but it’s worth noting he has yet to post a first-class century, averaging 39.4 in 14 first-class games. Would relish playing in front of family and friends in the series opener against the Black Caps at Optus Stadium.



Ollie Peake (Victoria) Related Article Australian cricket Khawaja’s explosive confession puts Australian bowlers in the firing line The slick left-hander is on the rise and firmly in the selectors’ thoughts, becoming part of the white-ball set-up. But the 20-year-old hasn’t done much for Victoria this summer, with just the one half-century and a pair of 30s. Unlikely to win Test selection yet, but could be in the mix if he slaps down three figures against England. Jack Edwards (NSW) The tall 26-year-old doesn’t attract the headlines, but the selectors have loved his progress, and he could fill the No.7 slot if it’s felt Beau Webster or Cooper Connolly are not worthy. Claimed 5-67 against the Proteas in an ODI in Johannesburg in September, and has a century against Tasmania and a four-wicket haul against WA this summer. A Footscray man has been charged with murder over the alleged stabbing attack of two food delivery drivers in central Melbourne on Friday night. The man, 51, was charged with one count of murder and one of intentionally cause serious injury. He will face Melbourne Magistrates’ Court on Monday. Feng Jianming with his wife Xu and children Yawei and Changhui from several years ago. Feng Jianming, 47, was working for food delivery platform HungryPanda on Friday night near Queen Victoria Market when he and another delivery driver confronted a man who was allegedly tampering with their bikes. Police were called to Chongqing Chicken Pot City restaurant in Frederick Way soon after 8pm where they found a critically injured Feng. Another driver, 34, was allegedly found nearby with stab wounds.



Paramedics performed CPR on Feng but he was declared dead at the scene. The 34-year-old man was taken to hospital with serious injuries. The Footscray man allegedly left the scene and was arrested in Footscray on Saturday morning. Jianming Feng Feng’s death has sparked anger in Melbourne’s Asian community over public safety in the CBD while the safety and work conditions of delivery drivers has also come under scrutiny. Hundreds of people joined an emotional rally at the State Library on Saturday night to honour Feng.



His wife, Xi, and adult children daughter Yawei and son Changhui expressed their heartbreak from their home in China. Xi told this masthead that Feng worked tirelessly to send money back to China to support his family, including his elderly parents. Feng Jianming with his son Changhui. Few family photos exist due to Feng’s many years spent away from China supporting them. She said he had not returned home for nine years to save on airfares. “He wanted to save the money and continue working,” she told this masthead through a translator.



“But he promised that when our son got married, he would definitely return. That was the plan. He would come home for our son’s wedding, and then we could finally be together as a family. We thought we only had to wait another year or two.” Melbourne Lord Mayor Nick Reece, who attended the vigil on Saturday evening, told this masthead he had spoken with HungryPanda management and offered to hold a roundtable to discuss safety conditions for delivery riders in the city. A second vigil held outside the State Library for delivery rider Feng Jianming on Saturday evening. Alexander Darling “Delivery riders have to be some of the most underappreciated people in our city,” Reece said. “They deliver our meals, our packages, rain, hail or shine seven days a week and are often not well paid… and, as we have seen, their jobs are very risky as well, not just from other vehicles on the road but from horrible attacks like the one we saw last night.”
