World.title: ‘I am hungry’: Pesutto tipped for frontbench return
World.content:
Last week, we heard from voters in Sydenham, a once safe Labor seat that formed part of the ‘red wall’ of outer-suburban Melbourne electorates.

After years leaning left, voters told investigative reporter Liam Mannix they feel increasingly ignored by the government, with infrastructure, roads and hospital wait times proving to be major issues.

In Ringwood, another seat currently held by Labor, the attack from the Liberals and a number of minor party and independent candidates is well and truly under way.

Reporter Bridget McArthur last week took us inside a lively candidate’s forum where the Family First candidate for the seat was sidelined by a colleague who insisted he speak on her behalf. We also heard from locals that some of the main concerns going into this election are potholes, affordable housing and crime.

World.title: What an uncertain election result means for households' finances
World.content:
New Zealand's election has delivered a less-than-decisive result, but what does it all mean for household finances?

With the election result still uncertain until the final count at the end of the month, economists say much depends on how those numbers fall and how coalition agreements are struck.

Massey University economist Matt Roskruge said, if National was able to form a coalition, as many pundits say it is likely to, it would probably mean more restrained government spending, particularly if ACT was to take the finance portfolio.

"That could mean continued pressure on public sector jobs and services, particularly in Wellington, with knock-on effects for local businesses. It could also help contain inflation and interest rates, although that depends on the overall package, including any tax cuts."

He said, if Labour had the numbers, there would be more support for public services and household incomes, which could help employment and those in urban areas.

"There could be a trade-offs with inflation and interest rates, if it adds substantially to demand, but that isn't automatic. It depends on how spending is funded and how much room the economy has to grow."

He said global conditions would matter enormously, no matter who was in charge.

"Strong farm returns are helping support some regions, while many urban households are still facing a difficult job market. AI looks a lot like a bubble, and between political uncertainty and conflicts around the globe, there is only so much our government can do.

"Businesses might hold off on hiring or investment, until the policy direction becomes clearer. A narrow majority could make it harder to advance an agenda, although it doesn't necessarily mean an unstable government.

"Longer term, I think the bigger differences for households will be access to healthcare, privatisation and how much they have to pay themselves, investment in infrastructure and whether we make meaningful progress on housing."

Otago University economist Murat Ungor agreed some of the most important things to households were out of government control.

"I'd be cautious about expecting big near-term changes to household budgets either way. The things that matter most to most households right now, such as mortgage rates, rents, council rates, insurance and food prices, are driven largely by the Reserve Bank's interest rate path, global conditions and the labour market.

"The real policy differences, such as Labour's proposed capital gains tax and cost-of-living relief versus continuity under the current coalition, would take time to legislate and implement. Any multi-party arrangement tends to dilute headline promises, so I'd expect incremental change, rather than a sharp turn.

"In the coming weeks, I'd watch three things - the shape of the coalition or support agreement, any early signals on fiscal settings, and whether cost-of-living help is targeted at those who need it most or spread broadly. The first full Budget in May will be the real test of how far any promises survive."

Infometrics chief forecaster Gareth Kiernan said, based on the current numbers, major changes for households seemed unlikely.

"If you get a switch to Labour somehow and they manage to cobble things together, the policy direction starts to become a bit different. You have questions around what kind of additional tax may come in and then if there is any specific relief around the cost of living as well.

"It's the sort of thing that's not really going to start to have an impact until 12 months down the track.

"It's been clear from both major parties' points of view that they do recognise the tightness of the fiscal position that they're working with. I don't see government policy particularly adding to inflation depending on who gets in."

Westpac chief economist Kelly Eckhold said the result meant that whichever side was able to form a government would not have a very strong mandate to make big changes.

He said a left-wing coalition could have had an impact on interest rates, if it changed the Reserve Bank mandate to require it to take employment into account in rate-setting decisions. Unemployment lifted in the most recent update, but business confidence was likely to be buoyed by a National-led coalition.

There could also be an impact simply due to the uncertainty of the result.

"Markets don't like uncertainty, particularly in the foreign exchange market. Given the New Zealand dollar is already starting on the back foot, we went through the low point Friday night... which is, aside from perhaps a couple of very short-lived episodes in the last 10-15 years, the lowest since the global financial crisis.

"We are in an environment here where you've already probably had a few factors leaning heavily against the New Zealand dollar and this uncertainty, I think, probably will add to those. That's one of things that makes it a bit tougher for the Reserve Bank, because you've got the potential of a bit more imported inflation filtering into the outlook, if you're going to be building in a weaker exchange rate outlook."

World.title: Severe thunderstorm warnings, watches for upper North Island
World.content:
Several thunderstorm watches are in place for the upper North Island.

It follows storms in Auckland and Canterbury on Friday and Saturday.

MetService issued a severe thunderstorm warning for the Far North before 7am on Monday - but has since lapsed.

Meanwhile, severe thunderstorm watches are in place for Northland, Auckland and Great Barrier Island.

Northland's watch is in place until 9pm while the watch for Auckland and Great Barrier is in place from 11am until 9pm on Monday.

"There is a moderate risk of severe thunderstorms with localised downpours (25 to 40 mm per hour) over Auckland and Great Barrier Island from late morning until this evening," MetService said.

"Rainfall of this intensity can cause surface and/or flash flooding, especially about low-lying areas such as streams, rivers or narrow valleys, and may also lead to slips.

World.title: Election results: Was the overhang artificially caused?
World.content:
Audio player for " Harry Mowbray discusses vote splitting campaign " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/politics_election-2026/2448753%2Felection-results-was-the-overhang-artificially-caused

Harry Mowbray discusses vote splitting campaign Morning Report Download MP3 4m

A constitutional law expert is not convinced a billionaire's vote-splitting campaign is behind National's historic election seat overhang.

On the preliminary results, the typical 120-seat Parliament is looking to swell by 11 MPs, with both National and Te Pāti Māori winning more electorate seats than their party vote entitles them to.

National has an extra seven "overhang" MPs, while Te Pāti Māori has an extra four after campaigning on an overhang strategy, asking supporters for their candidate vote, but to vote Green or Labour for the party.

Businessman Harry Mowbray also told National supporters to give their electorate vote to National but their party vote to ACT or NZ First.

But lawyer Graeme Edgeler is questioning what has happened and said there was a reasonable chance the overhang came about organically.

"Was this something that was artificially caused? Or was it just because, well, both National and Labour were very unpopular going into this election?

"And because of that, when major parties are highly unpopular, this is a risk. This is something that can happen."

He said the Electoral Commission's split-vote analysis would shed more light on what happened and why, but speculated that if the two main parties turned around slumping support, the extent of the overhang could be a one-off.

"Three or six years' time, if the major parties sort of pick up some support from their smaller parties, it might not happen or might not happen to the same extent in the future."

He said the result was not "a mockery of a MMP", but said it should prompt another review of the MMP electoral system if a repeat looked likely.

"If it looks like it might actually affect the result of who can govern, then there are going to be incentives in play to other parties to try things like this."

Edgeler said countries had dealt with the overhang problem in different ways, such as only giving one vote, which elects the local MP, but is also the party vote.

Germany "balanced" the overhang by giving parties extra MPs for years until it became too unwieldly, he said, and now give MPs seats in parliament based on the party vote.

"You've got party votes for two MPs. You're getting two MPs, even though you won five electorates. And that's perhaps an extreme thing."

The way parliament operated could also change, Edgeler said, such as limiting voting rights on bills to the party vote, rather than giving a vote to each MP.

Under that scenario, and based on current results, National would get 35 votes rather than 42, while Te Pāti Māori would have one vote as opposed to five.

Edgeler said any rule changes would have to signalled well in advance.

"We voted under this election with the rules we have. And so for the next three years, that'll be what we're looking at.

"But beyond that, [it's] certainly something we should review."

World.title: How 399,000 votes could cost Christopher Luxon his majority
World.content:
Audio player for " Lauren Crimp wraps up election results " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v0.KrRTFtoPsaA8nSDloPZ4KejQJr59ANQpD9ULgGwzaM0/politics_election-2026/2448587%2Fhow-399-000-votes-could-cost-christopher-luxon-his-majority

Lauren Crimp wraps up election results Morning Report Download MP3 5m

Analysis - National's Christopher Luxon has called it an "MMP special", but a shambles might be more appropriate.

On the preliminary results, New Zealand is looking at a near-farcical 131-seat Parliament, thanks to a record 11-seat overhang.

National's party vote entitles it to 35 MPs, but its lead in 42 electorates gives it an extra seven "overhang" MPs.

Likewise, Te Pāti Māori has won five electorates, despite a party vote worth only one MP, adding another four seats to Parliament.

That overhang has made all the difference - on a strictly proportional basis, Parliament would be deadlocked at 60 seats apiece.

Instead, the existing coalition holds 67 of 131, just one more than the 66 needed to govern.

Labour, the Greens, Te Pāti Māori and Opportunity have 64 among them.

There is a reason, though, that no-one is celebrating just yet, with an estimated 399,000 special votes still to be counted, roughly one vote in seven.

Historically, those votes have tended to favour the left and several knife-edge electorate races remain in play, but there's a catch - the final count could also alter the size of Parliament itself.

Here are five ways the numbers could shift when the official results are released on 27 November. Any combination of them could happen at once.

Scenario one: National loses electorates to Labour

Two National MPs face particularly nervous waits.

In Wairarapa, Mike Butterick leads Labour's Kieran McAnulty by just 139 votes.

In Hamilton East, Ryan Hamilton is 456 ahead of Labour's Georgie Dansey.

Either seat could yet change hands, although the margins alone tell us little about how the remaining voters have cast their ballots.

Because National has more electorate MPs than its party vote affords it, every electorate it loses also reduces the size of Parliament, while Labour's count remains unchanged.

Labour's Kieran McAnulty trails National's Mike Butterick by just 139 votes in Wairarapa. SAMUEL RILLSTONE / RNZ

If National loses Wairarapa alone, the coalition falls to 66 MPs in a 130-seat Parliament, still a majority.

If Hamilton East flips too, the coalition drops to 65 in a 129-seat Parliament. Again, just enough.

Scenario two: National takes electorates from Labour

The reverse could also happen, strengthening Luxon's hand.

Labour's Michael Wood leads National's Carlos Cheung by just 262 votes in Mt Roskill.

In Hutt South, Labour's Ginny Andersen is 889 ahead of National's Chris Bishop.

If National overturns either result, its overhang grows, pushing up the size of Parliament.

Labour would lose an electorate MP, but bring in another from its list, leaving its total unchanged.

National's Carlos Cheung. Liu Chen

For National, every additional electorate victory is effectively a bonus seat.

Scenario three: Greens win a Māori electorate

In one of the stranger twists, a Green Party victory would actually hurt the left's chances.

In Te Tai Tokerau, Te Pāti Māori's Aperahama Edwards leads the Greens' Hūhana Lyndon by 436 votes.

If Lyndon wins, she'll take a seat already included in the Greens' proportional allocation, but Te Pāti Māori would lose one of its four overhang seats, shrinking Parliament to 130.

All else unchanged, the coalition would keep its 67 seats, while the other parties would fall to 63.

In other words, a victory for the Greens would make Luxon's majority safer.

Greens' Hūhana Lyndon RNZ / Peter de Graaf

Scenario four: Some of National's party vote shifts to the left

Here's another peculiarity - National could lose party-vote support without losing a single MP.

If its vote share drops enough to entitle it to just 34 MPs, it still keeps all 42 of its electorate MPS and its overhang simply grows from seven to eight.

That would free up an extra proportional seat for another party, potentially Labour, the Greens or Opportunity.

Parliament would grow to 132 seats, but the coalition would still hold 67, against the opposition's 65.

Scenario five: Some of ACT or New Zealand First's party vote shifts to the left

This is one of most dangerous possibilities for Luxon. Unlike National, neither ACT nor NZ First has an overhang protecting its numbers.

If either loses a list MP to Labour, the Greens or Opportunity, the coalition's total falls without Parliament shrinking along with it.

One lost seat would leave the coalition on 66 out of 131, just enough, but two would leave it on 65, with the other four parties holding 66 between them.

In one scenario Opportunity would be kingmaker, in a position to deliver a majority to either side. RNZ

Opportunity would be kingmaker, in a position to deliver a majority to either side.

Of course, any gains for the Greens or Opportunity could come at Labour's expense instead, leaving the overall balance unchanged.

The 27 November tangle

Remember, any combination of these scenarios could happen at once.

Imagine National loses Wairarapa, while NZ First loses a list seat to the Greens.

That would leave National with 41 MPs, Labour 36, the Greens 17, ACT 13, New Zealand First 11, Opportunity seven and Te Pāti Māori five.

The coalition would hold 65 seats in a 130-seat Parliament. One short of a majority.

Now imagine National's party vote also falls enough to increase its overhang, with Opportunity picking up an extra list MP.

All of a sudden, we're back to a 131-seat Parliament - but Luxon's side would have only 65 MPs.

Labour, the Greens, Te Pāti Māori and Opportunity would have 66 between them.

World.title: Car crashes through Auckland restaurant while people inside
World.content:
A local says the street where a car came off the road and tore through an Auckland restaurant is a hot spot for street racers.

The car reportedly lost control at a roundabout on Great South Road, colliding with Burger Fuel Takanini.

Emergency services were called to the crash just after 10:15pm on Sunday night. Fire and Emergency said there were people in the building, and a few people in the car, and reports of one person trapped.

Nick, a local delivery driver, said the stretch of Great South Road sees a lot of street racing.

The building in Takanini after a car crashed into it. Felix Walton/RNZ

"They always have races down here all the time, down the straight, it was just a matter of time before someone was going to go through that," he said.

He said the car must've been doing about 180 to 200 kilometres per hour in a 50km per hour zone to do that much damage.

Tire marks on the side of the road show the car's path, which ran over a grassy verge, smashed through a fence and into the building's window.

Marks left by a car that drive into a South Auckland building. Felix Walton/RNZ

"This business here is going to be shut down for quite a long time... it will be devastating for them, " he said.

Nick told RNZ, there needed to be more precautions.

RNZ / Nick Monro

"They need to put a big barrier up, it may slow people down... it's up to the council to do something and if they don't get on top of the route cause of what is happening", he said.

An RNZ reporter at the scene said the restaurant's interior has been scattered, tables and chairs thrown across the room.

RNZ / Nick Monro

Police confirmed they attended the crash in Takanini on Sunday night.

They said the road was closed while emergency services worked at the scene but had since reopened.

Part of the car's bumper near the crash scene. Felix Walton/RNZ

World.title: Who are the 31 new MPs headed to Wellington?
World.content:
The election night result points to 31 new MPs entering a 131-seat Parliament.

That includes several new electorate MPs for National - which also lost high-performing frontbenchers Nicola Willis, Chris Bishop, Paul Goldsmith and outgoing Speaker Gerry Brownlee.

It also includes a whole new party in Opportunity, a couple of new faces in the Māori seats and a bunch of new list MPs for the other minor parties.

Some results are still close and could yet change after the final count expected on 27 November.

National

For the first time, National secured more electorate seats than its share of the party vote, giving it a six-seat overhang.

Those electorate wins included several new faces, ranked according to their list placing.

Mahesh Muralidhar (Tāmaki): He has made history by becoming National's first Indian MP to win an electorate seat, defeating Labour's Max Harris and ACT's James Christmas.

He is the chief executive of venture firm Phase One Ventures, which funds and supports start-ups. He was born in Kerala, India, and spent part of his childhood in Singapore, before moving to New Zealand in the '90s to attend high school.

Katie Milne (West Coast-Tasman): A dairy farmer who previously served as Federated Farmers president. In 2015, she was named Fonterra's Dairy Woman of the Year and won the Women of Influence rural award.

Milne won West Coast-Tasman, which had been vacated by the departure of National's Maureen Pugh, defeating Labour's Rory Paterson and former Buller Mayor Jamie Cleine of NZ First.

Mahesh Muralidhar becomes National's first Indian MP to win an eloctorate seat. RNZ / Blessen Tom

Blair Cameron (Nelson): After narrowly losing Nelson to Labour's Rachel Boyack by just 26 votes after special votes and recounts at the last election, Cameron will feel more secure with a 1210-vote majority in 2026, despite Labour winning more party votes there.

Now 35, he won scholarships to the United World College of Hong Kong and Brown University in Rhode Island, and has worked at Princeton University, the World Bank, the International Monetary Fund and the Asian Development Bank.

Emma Chatterton (Papakura): After serving as senior advisor to Erica Stanford in this term of Parliament, Chatterton was selected for the safe National seat vacated by party veteran Judith Collins' retirement.

She has worked at former party leader Sir Bill English's ImpactLab analytics and charity support company, and is a skilled pianist.

Matthew Paul (Port Waikato): After National incumbent Andrew Bayly chose not to return, the party selected this environmental consultant for the safe Port Waikato seat.

Offered a chance to buy the tree-trimming business he was working for at age 23, Paul ran the business for eight years, before consulting on roading projects and tree protection.

Jessica Rowe (Kaipara ki Mahurangi electorate): A former Newshub journalist, Rowe was selected to contest this north-of-Auckland electorate, after incumbent Chris Penk was demoted following the attempted leadership spill against leader Christopher Luxon in August and quite Parliament.

She is also engaged to the head of the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet Ben King - the couple have agreed not to discuss confidential information.

Opportunity

The Opportunity Party is headed to Parliament as the first to secure a place in the House without either a former MP among its ranks or an electorate win that would negate the need to surpass the 5 percent threshold.

Qiulae Wong: The leader who took Opportunity to Parliament - 10 years and three days after the party was founded - Wong has carefully maintained a clear purpose for the party to work with either the left or right bloc in the hopes of achieving more consensus.

Jessica Hammond has run for Opportunity at every election it has contested. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

The first Asian leader of a party in Parliament, she was born in Fiji, and studied law and politics, before working as a sustainable business consultant for brands like Vivienne Westwood and Stella McCartney, Kiwibank and Sharesies, and at consulting firm KPMG.

Deputy leader Daniel Eb is joined by others on the list, including Jessica Hammond, who has run for Opportunity in every election it has contested, Kayla Kingdon-Bebb, Eden Skipper, Jodie Kuntzsch and Sarah Lucas.

Labour

Labour gained two more seats compared to the last election and also saw some movement in the electorates.

Craig Renney (Wellington Bays): Ranked low on the list, Renney - previously Council of Trade Unions chief economist and policy director, and before that, a staffer who worked in Grant Robertson's office - will closely watch the special votes, with the Wellington Bays race coming down to just 140 votes on election night.

George Hampton (Christchurch Central): The nephew of former Labour MP for Mana Dame Winnie Laban, Harvard and Columbia-educated Hampton took over from Chris Hipkins as a political advisor to Helen Clark in 2008 and was later a diplomat, becoming deputy ambassador to Austria.

After spending summers selling raspberries from the boot of his car in his youth, he later worked for the United Nations on renewable energy policy, before moving back to New Zealand.

Dominik Yanzick (Wigram): With Labour incumbent Megan Woods running as a list-only candidate this time around, technology consultant Yanzick - who previously campaigned for her - fended off a fierce campaign by National's Tracey Summerfield with a nearly 2000-vote margin.

He's into hunting, diving and mountain biking, has an International Relations Masters degree, and has travelled to both Ukraine and the West Bank.

Mananui Ramsden (Te Tai Tonga): Running for the electorate only, Mananui Ramsden (Kāi Tahu, Kāti Mamoe, Waitaha, Rangitāne, Raukawa, Tainui) reclaimed the largest electorate in the country from Te Pāti Māori-turned-independent MP Tākuta Ferris.

Michael Wood (Mt Roskill): A former minister in Jacinda Ardern's government, Wood leads the incumbent - National's Carlos Cheung - by just 262 votes.

He resigned from Cabinet under Chris Hipkins' leadership before the 2023 election, after failing to declare and manage conflicts of interest over shares held in a family trust, despite being reminded to do so 16 times by the Cabinet Office.

Greens

Despite losing one electorate - Wellington Bays - to Labour, the Greens held onto Auckland Central and Wellington North, and their higher party vote upped their total number of seats to 16 on the night, bringing three new faces in from the list.

New MPs include high-profile lawyer Tania Waikato, environmental scientist and former Canterbury Regional Councillor Craig Pauling, and organiser/advocate Rohan O'Neill-Stevens, who became Nelson's youngest ever city councillor in 2019 and went on to become deputy mayor.

ACT

ACT also upped its party vote and walks away with 13 seats total, despite losing the Tāmaki seat to National.

New Zealanders are already familiar with former broadcaster Paul Henry.

He will be joined by public law specialist and former National candidate James Christmas, who was defeated by Muralidhar in Tāmaki, but comes in on the list, Hornby High principal and former Air Force leading airman Iain Murray, and intellectual property lawyer and computer scientist Antonia Modkova.

New Zealand First

New Zealand First won no electorates, but secured a party-vote increase and will have 12 MPs in Parliament, with 9.8 percent of the vote - several of them returning to Parliament, after previous terms with National.

Former All Blacks captain Taine Randell has found fresh challenge. © Photosport Ltd 2002 www.photosport.nz

These include former Pacific Peoples Minister Alfred Ngaro, who went on to lead the socially conservative Christian party NewZeal for the 2023 election, broadcaster and former National MP Michael Laws - who may not last long in Parliament, after leader Winston Peters denounced his comments about women in the Opportunity Party - and Harete Hipango-Brownlie, who has also been controversial in the past.

Former Financial Markets Authority chair Craig Stobo will enter Parliament for the first time, along with former All Blacks captain Taine Randell.

Te Pāti Māori

Aperahama Edwards (Te Tai Tokerau): Te Pāti Māori was the big winner in the Māori seats, walking away with five electorates - its four sitting MPs and one new one.

World.title: Advocacy group warns proposed US Census changes could deepen inequalities in Pacific territories
World.content:
Proposed changes to the United States Census could worsen longstanding data inequalities in Guam, the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands (CNMI), and American Samoa, raising concerns about access to federal resources, disaster recovery funding, and political representation.

The non-profit organisation Right to Democracy has urged the US Census Bureau to withdraw the proposals, warning they could further marginalise communities in American territories that already face significant gaps in federal data collection.

The proposed regulations, announced on 10 September, would remove questions about race and ethnicity from the decennial census, introduce new residency criteria based partly on tax records, and exclude certain non-citizen residents from population counts used to determine congressional representation.

Right to Democracy co-director Adi Martínez-Román said the proposals failed to address their potential impact on the territories.

"These sweeping rule changes don't even mention the US territories or explain how they will impact people that live here," Martínez-Román said.

"Our jurisdictions already face data challenges related to Census counting, and these changes create even more dangerous uncertainty that will lead to the further invisibilization of our communities."

The organisation said the proposed removal of racial and ethnic questions would be particularly damaging to Guam, American Samoa, the Northern Mariana Islands, and the US Virgin Islands because they are excluded from the American Community Survey, which provides more detailed demographic information between censuses.

Although those questions would remain in the survey, territorial communities would not benefit from that continued data collection.

The group also raised concerns about proposed residency rules that would rely partly on federal tax records.

Many residents of US territories file income tax returns with their local governments rather than the Internal Revenue Service, and the proposed rules do not explain how those records would be treated.

The proposed 3 January to 1 April reference period also raises questions about how the Census Bureau would account for residents temporarily displaced by natural disasters or those moving between the territories and the US mainland.

Another concern involves US nationals from American Samoa living in the states, whose status the organisation said should be explicitly addressed to avoid confusion over citizenship and immigration classifications.

Saipan, CNMI RNZ Pacific / Mark Rabago

Closing data gaps

Right to Democracy co-director Neil Weare said the federal government should instead be addressing existing shortcomings in census coverage.

"Rather than taking steps to further exclude people from US territories, the Census should be taking steps to close the data gaps that have long harmed our communities," Weare said.

"Federal rules that overlook these communities can deepen inequities that already exist. People in the territories deserve accurate data that reflect their lives and needs."

CHamoru legal scholar Marlee Sonico, a member of the organisation's Cross-Territorial Coalition, said the consequences could extend beyond population statistics.

"Public services, disaster recovery, and community investment all rely on accurate census data," Sonico said.

She warned that losing detailed demographic information would make it harder to identify racial disparities, enforce civil rights protections, and demonstrate unmet community needs.

Sonico said the territories' exclusion from congressional apportionment did not diminish their need for accurate census information.

'Data equity is fundamental'

Public health researcher Lianeris Estremera Rodriguez, another coalition member, said changes to the 2030 census could further undermine the political visibility of territorial communities.

"Structural and political erasure begins with data erasure. Data equity is a fundamental civil right," she said.

Right to Democracy submitted its objections ahead of the 2 November public comment deadline and called on the Census Bureau to work directly with territorial communities before implementing any changes.

World.title: From 15-minute drones to instant kill chains: What does NZ's future army look like?
World.content:
Analysis: What does NZ's army of the future look like?

A new report shows a potential combination of electronics and warfare in ways only dreamed about a decade ago.

The NZDF's new 50-page 'Future Fighting Concept' report - like its 2017 cousin called 'Future Land Operating Concept 2035' - dealt in the Army General Staff's forecasts.

The former indulged in some pretty vague imaginings, while the latter deals with the emerging reality of weapons tech inflicting terrible damage in Ukraine and changing terribly fast in tests around the Pacific.

In 2017, the drones example was how Russia put 13 fixed-wing drones and one type of quadcopter over Donbas, following its annexation of Crimea.

One drone linked to a rocket launcher "in particular... could deliver fire-missions within 15 minutes of the drone identifying a target".

Now, militaries have what the Pentagon calls the 'kill chain' down to seconds and the drones themselves can be the rockets, bearing down on Kyiv at up to 1000km/h.

The 2017 report mentioned drones a handful of times, although it foresaw counter-drone systems would become vital.

Nine years ago, AI was not even a thing. In July 2026, artificial intelligence drove Human-Machine Integration as Australian and New Zealand troops tested ground drones in the Mojave desert.

This week, the United States delivered more than a billion dollars of drones to its Central Command that covers the Middle East - 1300 kamikazes, more than 100 unmanned surface and underwater drones, and more than 24,000 counter-drones.

The speed of turning military dreams into reality is still hitting bureaucratic bottlenecks, thinktank studies overseas show.

However, it looks laser-fast compared with international efforts to rein in increasingly autonomous lethal weapons. A few weeks ago, for instance, 128 countries at the UN agreed on a text "defining" lethal autonomous weapon systems.

That is a record number - NZ was among them - but this was described as "a first step" towards talks on a possible international treaty to regulate them

In 2017, the electronics to enable machines to talk to humans and each other, and across different militaries, and doing this by lasers between satellites, were the stuff of computer modelling.

Last month, they were tested in the toughest environment - the sea, where the physics of brine are difficult to surmount - in exercise Keen Sword.

It linked sensors to shooters - a Japanese underwater drone linked to an Australian 'Rock Lobster' surface drone, using US communications systems. New Zealand took part, a little, off the bench.

Embedded content removed for printing https://twitter.com/DefenceAust/status/2117527198298996977

Keen Sword tapped into what a US commander called "a massive framework of integration on the US side that we have very rapidly rolled out to our partners during these recent exercises and persistently now".

The NZDF is also part of a so-called Coalition Information Environment project, so militaries can see a battlefield the same way.

The Future Fighting Concept focuses on the army, sayingz; "The NZ Army must prioritise investment in advanced capabilities that enhance agility, lethality, and responsiveness.

"Key focus areas include AI, Machine Teaming, Predictive Analysis, Distributed Decision-making, Network-Centric Warfare, Automation and Rapid Targeting, Cyber and Electromagnetic Spectrum Operations."

Dominance in this last - electronagnetics - would be decisive, it said. However, NZDF has denied expanding into electromagnetic spectrum operations at a satellite-monitoring hub set up by the US in Auckland, although other US hubs are expanding this way.

Where do people fit in among all these capitalised electronics?

"One of the primary changes introduced by modern technologies is the increased speed of decision-making, lethality and precision in military operations," said the new report.

"The concept of 'human-in-the-loop' systems, where operators retain ultimate control over critical decisions, is being complemented by increasingly autonomous systems capable of understanding complex operations independently.

"High automation will accelerate human-in-the-loop targeting through autonomous systems that identify, classify and engage threats."

The future is about being more lethal and joining hands to do it.

"Our next-generation weapons systems will utilise NATO and ABCANZ partner forces systems."

ABCANZ is a five-nation army interoperability agency of the US, UK, Canadian, Australian and New Zealand armies.

The report gets to ethics.

"Human-machine integration raises ethical concerns in warfare about accountability, and the moral implications of delegating life-or-death decisions to machines, marking a significant shift in the philosophical understanding of warfare.

"'This also prompts a re-evaluation of international norms and regulatory frameworks governing warfare... [and] the need for comprehensive dialogue among nations regarding the ethical and legal implications of deploying such technologies."

The report also briefly mentions the politics of this.

"A future-focused NZ Army must train MDO [for multiple domains], and promote a change in policy to government for the rapid acquisition of new and rapidly evolving technology platforms."

Rapid acquisition reflects the underlying theme of the need for speed.

There is also the need for money. On the election campaign trail, Labour raised the question of how New Zealand would pay to futureproof the military.

It said, if elected, it would take another look at that.

The path ahead is at least partially underwritten by a Pentagon budget line showing $60m spent on its main project for integrating allies (called C5) in past years and another $110m for that out to 2031.

It is also underwritten politically by the White House, that says: "The United States will leverage S&T [science and tech] capabilities of international allies and partners as a force multiplier to advance national security objectives and outcompete adversaries.

"The Trump Administration is expanding cooperation in... areas including AI, nuclear energy, quantum, advanced communications, PNT [positioning, navigation, timing], and space."

The NZ army's future concept of weapons of war is not the only one. Armies around the world are thinking about this too.

World.title: Live: New world champion in a spin as Norris survives wet-dry-wet F1 Brazil GP
World.content:
Lando Norris, one week after the crown of world champion was taken off him, survived a wet-dry-wet race in São Paulo to claim his third F1 grand prix win this season.

Max Verstappen finished second after starting from 21st on the grid, while his Red Bull teammate Isack Hadjar was third.

McLaren teammate Oscar Piastri bounced back from a disappointing qualifying to place sixth.

Mercedes became constructors' world champions for a ninth time, and first since 2021, with George Russell finishing fourth and Kimi Antonelli fifth after both suffered spins in the tough conditions.

Follow all the action of the Formula 1 São Paulo Grand Prix on the live blog below.

World.title: England hammer Wallabies with record-breaking, seven-try spectacular
World.content:
The Wallabies have been handed another brutal reality check, subject to a seven-try hammering by England at Twickenham.

England started fast and never let up, subduing a woefully off colour Wallabies team 45-22, their biggest ever total against the Wallabies, to retain the Ella-Mobbs trophy.

"England put us under the pump," Harry Wilson said after the match.

"We weren't physical enough, we didn't slow their ball down, we were just playing from behind."

England have now beaten the Wallabies in 12 of their last 14 meetings.

The defeat is the Wallabies' third in a row, and means they are mathematically eliminated from final contention in the Nations Championship.

England thought they had scored inside the opening two minutes, cutting through a painfully porous Wallabies defence only for the TMO to rule it out for a clear forward pass.

That didn't hold them up for long though, as Jamie George powered over from a rolling maul to open the scoring.

Ryan Lonergan kicked a penalty to keep Australia in touch, but the Wallabies were stung twice in the 15 minutes before half time, Ollie Chessum finishing a move on the left and Joe Heyes powering over from another catch and drive.

Ollie Chessum scored to help underline England's dominance. (Getty Images: RFU/Alex Davidson )

The Wallabies by that stage had been reduced to 14 men, when Angus Bell was sin binned for a hip drop tackle on the lively Immanuel Feyi-Waboso.

But against the run of play, the Wallabies managed to score before the break, Max Jorgensen with an intercept score that reduced the gap to just nine.

The more optimistic Wallabies supporters may have felt that slice of fortune could have been the turning point.

How wrong they were.

Max Jorgensen scored a superb try at the end of the first half to keep the Wallabies in touch. (Getty Images: David Rogers)

Jack van Poortvliet scythed through to score just two minutes after the restart, before Henry Pollock, the firebrand flanker, scored two quick tries after coming on as a winger.

Some quick hands from the Wallabies saw replacement flyhalf Ben Donaldson assist in sending Filipo Daugunu over in a rare passage of pleasing play from the Wallabies.

Then, Jeremy Williams dived on a Maro Itoje drop to further reduce the deficit.

But as the Wallabies pushed for a bonus point try, Ben Spencer intercepted a Daugunu offload to race away and seal a spectacular seven-try performance from England.

The Wallabies head to Murrayfield next week, searching for answers from another desperate performance.

"We've got seven days to just take some feedback from this game and make sure we're a lot better," Wilson said.

"Scotland are a really good team, we've got to be ready for it and take these harsh lessons."

Look back on how all the action unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: Against Samoa, Australia's old power conquered the new world
World.content:
They say you can't fight city hall, but sometimes against Australia, it feels like you're flat out breaking a few windows.

The Kangaroos cruised into the World Cup final by turning Samoa's dream into a recurring nightmare via their 44-12 win in Sydney on Sunday night.

As New Zealand did the night before, Australia won this on the finer margins.

Spirit filled the night through the anthems, where tears again flowed freely, and the Siva Tau, which ended with Brian To'o and Tino Fa'asuamaleaui sharing a moment more powerful than words can say.

Moments like that are the big things, the reason these matches matter in the first place. And it's what makes them feel like more than a game but through the blinding emotion there is still a game to be won.

To do it when it really matters, you need to do all the little things and Australia proved it's the little things that make up life right from the start as, not for the first time, its science defeated Samoa's magic on the big stage.

Against any other team, it might not matter that Francis Manuleleua and Jazz Tevaga, two middle forwards, found themselves defend together off a scrum. It's not the done thing, but you can get away with it.

But the Kangaroo punished Samoa for that lapse when Tom Dearden took them and threw a dummy everyone knows is coming but nobody seems to know how to stop for the first try of the night.

Like the hardest teachers, Australia stressed the same lesson over and over again and Samoa's inability to change the course meant frustration took hold, which only made things worse.

Three times in the first half alone, Samoa conceded a penalty, a set restart and a try in quick sequence. For the final 19 minutes of the half, they got to their kick just twice.

Give Australia that much ball and field position and you're asking for punishment.

The Kangaroos ran up the tries and carried a 26-2 lead into the break that killed off the game as a contest and robbed the blue wave in the stands of their power.

Samoa's army of fans were silenced by Australia. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer )

The harder the Samoans tried and the more venom they played with, the more it turned to a choking bile in their throats.

Spencer Leniu dropped the ball with his first touch, got sin-binned for dissent, then dropped the ball with his first touch on return.

They did what they could to the end, and twice had tries chalked off by the barest of margins. But in the end Australia were too clinical, too clever, too willing and able to exploit every little edge on offer until it all added up to a comfortable win.

Samoa's poor discipline — Adam Gee pinged them for a combined 12 restarts and penalties in the end — and errors would have been much to overcome against most sides and most sides aren't packing Australia's heat.

RLWC live The Kangaroos will face New Zealand in the final of the Rugby League World Cup after overwhelming Samoa 44-12 at Sydney Football Stadium. Follow live.

Reece Walsh, raced in a brilliant hat-trick to continue his dazzling tournament and put himself right in the frame to be awarded the Golden Boot on Thursday as the best international player of the year.

The Broncos firecracker was the explosion and the fuse was lit by Cameron Munster and Harry Grant, who were in total control of every aspect of the match throughout.

Pat Carrigan and Tino Fa'asuamaleaui were both strong in the middle in a performance that should help restore a little of the Australian forwards battered reputation.

The win would have been a personal triumph for Fa'asuamaleaui given the Samoa international copped plenty from the crowd.

The Pacific nations have given this World Cup so much and they feel like the future of Test football. But this game was a reminder of the power of old money and that the most dangerous creatures in these waters are still Kangaroos.

There is a reason, for all the improvement Samoa and Tonga have made in recent years, they only have one win over Australia from a combined 10 attempts.

It's the same reason Australia has only lost one game from 18 starts in the set restart era, which is the same reason they haven't lost a game on home soil in 11 years.

Samoa's frustration was palpable as the game slipped away. (Getty Images: Spencer)

To climb the green and gold mountain, you need to be as close as perfect as reality can allow because need a way to douse their firepower and blunt their smarts while getting just about everything right yourself.

New Zealand have the team to do it, to the point they should be favourites for the final. But it's no guarantee they will because team as fierce and skilled as Samoa, for all their might and power, couldn't really get themselves in the fight.

After all their growth, it is the last step they need to take but perhaps the longest of all.

The Kangaroos are as ruthless as they are well-drilled, as fast as they are merciless.

That is why, even as the Davids have gotten bigger, Goliath still reigns.

World.title: Wounded Jillaroos into World Cup final after Fiji smackdown
World.content:
Facing the Jillaroos at this Rugby League World Cup has been like heading straight into the eye of the storm.

Those who have dared to venture there have emerged either gallant in an ultimately big defeat, like Fetu Samoa, or humbled into merciless submission, like England and Wales.

But the Fiji Bulikula storm chasers stared the beast down in the semi-finals, and rattled them. Not besting them this time, but firing a warning shot that their time is coming.

This will be sold as a Jillaroos' scare or wake-up call, but this was more like much-needed proof of life for the international women's game.

Fiji's time is coming

Most fans and experts predicted another Jillaroos' trouncing.

The three-time defending champions steamrolled their opposition in their three pool games, with a combined score of 242-6.

SYDNEY, AUSTRALIA - NOVEMBER 08: Isabelle Kelly of Australia is tackled during the 2026 Women's Rugby League World Cup Semi Final match between Australia Jillaroos and Fiji at Allianz Stadium on November 08, 2026 in Sydney, Australia. (Photo by Mark Metcalfe/Getty Images) (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

They have lost only one game in a decade, and that was to their long-time nearest (and truthfully only) rival, New Zealand.

The two-horse race in the women's game has been holding it back, and this tournament has had some ugly scorelines, showing much more investment is needed.

But Fiji, in its first World Cup appearance, could be the one that can finally break the Australia-New Zealand duopoly.

Where no other side has made the slightest dent in the Jillaroos' machine, the Bulikula turned it into a write-off in the first half.

The Fijians brought incredible defensive intensity; they crunched the Australians in tackles with perfect technique as they forced countless uncharacteristic errors.

The Australians' completion rate was around 40 per cent, a figure unheard of for the best side in the world, as the visitors executed to perfection.

Their long kicking game in particular was on point. They consistently pinned the Australians back, then regained possession deep into their opposition's half.

Un-Jillaroos-like things were happening. Tamika Upton failed to collect bombs. Jocelyn Kelleher dropped the ball unchallenged. Abbi Church was stopped dead in her tracks, sprinting towards the tryline.

This was Fiji's first appearance at the women's World Cup. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

Five-eighth Luisa Yaranamua, destined for the NRLW sooner rather than later, played the game of her life, as she orchestrated an 8-0 lead.

But the Australians did not have to be perfect to come back and win this one.

They started to wipe out the unforced errors, the completion rate improved, and when they entered the red zone, they scored.

Church was the stand-out with four tries, including one where she steamed into the in-goal to collect a kick which almost any other player surely would have dropped.

But the gritty win took its toll; Jamie Chapman left the game early with cramp, and the Australians will come away with bruised bodies, if not slightly bruised egos. All for the greater good of the game.

Fiji players perform the hymn Noqu Masu before the game. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

The Fijians tired in the second half, unable to hold back the Australian wave, but they kept turning up till the end, and were rewarded by a late try.

Their contributions extended to the pre-game too, as they performed their moving hymn, the Noqu Masu.

Another reminder of the power of the Pasifika nations in this World Cup, where culture, faith, and footy collide.

The Jillaroos' juggernaut may have stuttered for the first time in what feels like an age, but it ultimately remains on track for its final destination.

A final against the Kiwi Ferns in Brisbane next Sunday, and a fourth straight World Cup trophy beckoning.

World.title: Jillaroos avoid all-time upset to progress to World Cup final
World.content:
The Jillaroos have qualified for the Rugby League World Cup final, but only after surviving an almighty scare against tournament debutant Fiji at Sydney Football Stadium.

The world champions conceded first and were level at half-time, but surged clear after the break to triumph 30-14 and avoid one of the sport's all-time upsets.

Winger Abbi Church scored four tries as the Jillaroos booked a date with old foe New Zealand in next Sunday's final in Brisbane.

Speaking on Channel 7 at full-time, Fiji captain Sereana Naitokatoka was bristling with pride for her team, which provided one of the World Cup's great storylines in its run to the semifinals.

"I'm so proud of all my lewas [girls], they put in the hard work from the first minute of the game to the very end, and I'm very proud of them," Naitokatoka said.

Luisa Yaranamua gave Fiji a shock early lead. (Getty Images: Mark Metcalfe)

After cruising through the group stage with an aggregate scoreline of 242-6, the Australians were challenged for the first time in the competition, caught off guard by a disciplined, aggressive Bulikula outfit.

A penalty goal from five-eighth Luisa Yaranamua earned Fiji a shock 11th minute lead, before the same player dummied and then slid over to provide one of the most sensational scorelines in international rugby league history.

8-0 down after 16 minutes, the Jillaroos were far from their best and clearly rattled, with their hopes of a fifth-straight World Cup final seemingly under threat.

Two unconverted tries, courtesy of Church and Tamika Upton, ensured scores were level at half-time, but the hosts reached the break having completed just 12 of their 19 sets.

Do you have a story idea about women in sport? Email us abcsport5050@your.abc.net.au

An improved second-half showing saw the Jillaroos hit the front and then find some breathing space, Church striking three times in the second 35, including one spectacular aerial effort.

Player of the match Church was full of praise for Fiji, saying it was a much needed test ahead of her side's clash with the Kiwi Ferns, who qualified for their seventh straight decider with victory over Samoa on Saturday.

"Fiji did exactly what we thought they were going to do," Church said on Channel 7.

"They came out hard and gave us a real fight and a real arm wrestle.

"I think it was an incredible game, we really needed that going into next week and they really tested us."

A cause for concern was the absence of star winger Jaime Chapman, who crossed early in the second period but spent much of the half off the field, struggling with what was reported as cramp.

Fiji was able to conjure a second try, but Maria Paseka's late four-pointer, scored after a neat short-side play, was quickly cancelled out by Church's fourth effort of the day.

World.title: Kangaroos cruise into World Cup final with victory over Samoa
World.content:
The Kangaroos will face New Zealand in the Rugby League World Cup final after overwhelming Samoa 44-12 at Sydney Football Stadium.

Fullback Reece Walsh crossed for a hat-trick and five-eighth Cameron Munster was influential with three try assists as Australia produced by far its most convincing performance of the tournament.

It sets up a rematch of the tournament opener, when the Kangaroos snuck past the Kiwis 24-22 four weeks ago, but Sunday night's win over a poor Samoa side was a comfortably better performance for Kevin Walters's side.

The fireworks started before the game when the teams came face to face during a dynamic siva tau, with winger Brian To'o touching foreheads with Kangaroos prop Tino Fa'asuamaleaui, who is eligible to play for Toa Samoa.

It was one of the moments of the World Cup and ignited the atmosphere at the Sydney Football Stadium, sold out and dominated by Samoa fans.

Samoa drew first blood with a penalty goal, but the next time the crowd favourites troubled the scorers early in the second half they had conceded five tries and were down to 12 men courtesy of prop Spencer Leniu's dissent to referee Adam Gee.

The Kangaroos, who had looked so clunky for the first three matches of their campaign, clicked almost every time they were given chances by an error-riddled and ill-disciplined Samoa.

Jarome Luai and Samoa fell afoul of the officials. (Getty Images: Spencer)

Tom Dearden's opener, using Walsh as a distraction to allow the halfback to scythe through off a scrumbase play, set up the onslaught as Samoa seemed powerless to stop the surging Australians.

Munster and Walsh wreaked havoc with their footwork and ball playing to lead Australia to a 26-2 advantage at half-time.

Samoa crossed twice in the second half, through Stephen Crichton and Izack Tago, but the comeback attempt never really got off the launchpad as Walsh completed his hat-trick and Jack Bostock dove in late while the game devolved into messy footy and occasional spot fires.

Earlier, the Jillaroos were caught cold early by a red-hot Fijian outfit and trailed 8-0, but ultimately hold off the Bulikula to win 30-14 and set up a fifth straight World Cup final against New Zealand.

The women's and men's finals will be played at Brisbane's Lang Park next Sunday at 4:10pm and 7:35pm AEDT respectively.

Look back at all the semifinal action in our live blog below.

World.title: Swans, Hawks prevail in AFLW elimination finals
World.content:
AFLW superstar Chloe Molloy has once again lifted Sydney to victory, with the Swans defeating the Western Bulldogs by 29 points in an elimination final.

League-leading goalkicker Molloy pulled off a surprise cameo down back to help the Swans claim a 7.4 (46) to 2.5 (17) win at a wet and windy Henson Park on Sunday.

Sydney will next play Geelong in an away semi-final. The Bulldogs' season is over.

Molloy's leadership in a wet-weather scrap proved the difference for the Swans, with the former Swans co-skipper finishing with one goal, 12 intercepts, and 14 contested possessions.

Tanya Kennedy was just as crucial for the Swans, locking down Bulldogs co-captain and gun midfielder Isabelle Pritchard.

Pritchard, on return from a knee injury, was kept to just 14 disposals and three clearances as Kennedy laid 17 tackles.

Fellow Bulldogs midfielder Ellie Blackburn, also returning after being rested in last week's loss to the Cats, led the visitors with 29 touches and a goal.

Swans captain Lucy McEvoy needed just 20 seconds to score the opener with a long bomb from outside the 50-metre arc thanks to the strong breeze.

A rushed behind gave the Bulldogs their sole score of the first quarter, as the hosts made the most of conditions to fire off their four unanswered goals and build a 24-point lead.

The Bulldogs could only manage one point with the breeze in the second, with Molloy helping limit the damage with five contested possessions and four intercepts as a defender.

Molloy's stint in defence forced Bulldogs coach Tam Hyett to bring defender Vaomua Laloifi into the forward line, and the pair's battle continued well into the second half.

Sunday's final turned into a slog after torrential rain came in the third quarter, with the Swans doing just enough to maintain a 25-point lead en route to victory in front of 4,325 dedicated fans.

Hawks break through for finals win over Suns

Hawthorn has broken through for their its AFLW finals victory in an 18-point defeat of Gold Coast.

A commanding third quarter paved the path for the Hawks to prevail 8.9 (57) to 6.3 (39) at People First Stadium on Sunday.

Hawthorn, who bombed out of the finals in straight sets in 2024 and 2025, will face Carlton in the first semi-final next Saturday night at Princes Park.

Eliza West (29 disposals, one goal) and Laura Stone (21, two) were outstanding for the Hawks, while Casey Sherriff, Hayley McLaughlin and Jasmine Fleming all picked up 20 touches.

Jenna Richardson was a wall in defence, with a game-high 11 marks while completely blanketing Suns forward Dekota Brown.

The Davies sisters — Darcie and Georja — impressed for Gold Coast, who were also chasing their maiden AFLW final success.

Charlie Rowbottom battled hard for her 20 disposals (18 of them handballs), a figure matched by Niamh McLoughlin and Daisy D'Arcy.

Adding injury to insult for the Suns, young gun Ava Usher suffered a serious-looking injury to her right knee in a heavy collision with teammate Maddy Brancatisano in the dying stages.

Hawthorn kicked two goals in the last 77 seconds of a high-octane opening term — through Poppy Stockwell and Jacqueline Dupuy — to lead by six points.

The Suns responded to take a three-point half-time lead, but Hawthorn raised its pressure in the third quarter and Gold Coast couldn't go with it.

The Hawks' backline repelled 11 consecutive entries from the Suns, while their midfield trampled Gold Coast at clearance and on the outside.

Hawthorn had 33 more disposals for the term, 13 more tackles and pulled ahead by 15 points at three-quarter time.

Mikayla Nurse goaled early in the fourth quarter to give Gold Coast a sniff, but the Hawks continued to pile on the pressure and exorcise their own demons.

AAP

World.title: Meet the surgeon saving the careers of cricket's best fast bowlers
World.content:
Fast, fearsome, and fragile were words often associated with former New Zealand fast bowler Shane Bond, whose promising cricket career was drastically curtailed by injury.

He debuted as a 26-year-old against Australia in Hobart in 2001, but it was in his next series, against Bangladesh, where he truly announced himself.

He took 11 wickets in two Tests at an average of 13, and it looked like the beginning of a long and lucrative career.

But Bond's back had other ideas. A stress fracture kept him out the game for almost two years from 2003.

Shane Bond is considered "patient zero" after his successful back surgery allowed him to continue his international career. (Phil Walter: Getty Images)

A meeting with back surgeon Grahame Inglis offered him hope he could overcome his injury by undergoing a little-known surgery that is now commonplace in the fast bowling fraternity.

"If I can't fix this, then the career is potentially over," Bond said of his decision to undergo pars stabilisation surgery in 2004.

"He [Inglis] talked about a procedure that he had done, one on a New Zealand high jumper and one other athlete.

" He thought that the chances I came back and bowled fast were slim, but ... I was prepared to give it a go. "

While other injuries limited Bond to just 14 more Tests before he retired in 2009, his back didn't trouble him again.

Last surgeon standing

Renowned New Zealand spinal surgeon Rowan Schouten was working with Dr Inglis at the time and said Bond was "patient zero in this whole story."

Bond took 147 ODI wickets, including a stunning hat-trick against Australia at Bellerive Oval in 2007. (AAP Image/Andrew Cornaga)

The success of that surgery laid the groundwork for a procedure that Schouten and his team have now performed on around 30 professional cricketers.

When surgeons in the UK stopped performing the procedure and Dr Inglis retired, Dr Schouten became the world's leading authority on repairing spinal stress fractures in fast bowlers.

Rowan Schouten says pars stabilisation surgery isn't a new procedure, but has recently become popular with cricketers. (Supplied: rowanschouten.co.nz)

"We were kind of left as the last man standing with experience on international fast bowlers and since then it's taken off essentially," he said.

"We're dealing with calls and connections from all around the world, from the UK, India, South Africa, Europe, Bangladesh, everywhere."

Bond still helps fast bowlers who have struggled with back issues and is often approached for advice.

He's coached Jofra Archer, Jason Behrendorff and James Pattinson, who all had the surgery and returned to play at the top level.

What is pars stabilisation surgery?

When a fast bowler is considering spinal surgery, like Australia's Lance 'Wild Thing' Morris did in 2025, it sounds like a drastic step.

Loading Instagram content

But Dr Schouten said the surgery was straightforward and "not that extreme".

It involves grafting the spine to stimulate repair, before putting screws and wires around the injured portion to provide stability.

WA quick Lance 'Wild Thing' Morris hopes to be even faster after surgery After years of back issues, Lance Morris is finally fit and firing, and the West Australian is keen to put his name in the frame for a Test call up once again.

"We've got a few little added components to it that we believe are important ... but it's a pretty standard technique," he said.

The injury, often referred to as a stress fracture, is common across sport and very prevalent in cricket.

Dr Schouten stressed the surgery is not a fusion, and most stress fractures do not need it.

"You need to preserve all that spinal motion that these guys need to be able to bowl full pace," he said.

Cameron Green opted for surgery in 2024, following several stress fractures during his career. (Getty Images: Darrian Traynor)

If a player did opt to go under the knife, the recovery involves a six-to-nine month rehab program.

"Some stress fractures in some players become a recurring theme," Dr Schouten said.

"And then if you do that, if you have that two or three times in a row over multiple seasons, it can really disrupt a career."

Tech.title: Elvis and Eminem rights holders are suing Suno
Tech.content:
is the Verge’s weekend editor. He’s covered the tech industry for over 18 years and knows a thing or two about synths.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Suno is facing yet another pair of lawsuits. A group of rights holders of Elvis Presley’s music and the publisher of some of Eminem‘s biggest records are suing the AI music company, claiming it illegally generates music and lyrics that mimic those artists. The lawyers in the Presley suit claim that Suno has violated Tennessee’s Ensuring Likeness Voice and Image Security (ELVIS) Act, which makes it illegal for an AI company to clone a singer’s voice.

In the suit, lawyers representing Presley’s rights holders argue that “Suno has mechanically encoded itself with artists’ identities, hard-work, creativity, and time, and harnessed them all for a consistent conveyor belt of

cold hard cash.“ These suits closely mirror one filed by Jason Isbell and others in September, which claimed Suno created imitations of the plaintiffs but did not claim copyright infringement directly.

Later in the complaint, the lawyers write that “Suno’s ravenous race to the bottom aims to make human creativity obsolete, coldly replicating without a license in seconds what takes years to learn, struggle with, maintain, and endlessly attempt to make better and perfect.”

Suno spokesperson Cat McCormack told The Verge that, “Suno exists to help people create new, original music, not to trade on anyone’s name or likeness, and we prohibit any unauthorized use of an artist’s work. To protect against this, we do not allow prompts for specific artists’ names and songs and work with third-party providers to screen uploaded audio files and lyrics for potential misuse. We are always working to strengthen our guardrails and we will continue to add new safeguards that protect artists and our users.”

This adds to the pile of lawsuits Suno is currently facing from Sony, UMG, Isbell, Reservoir Media, and more.

Tech.title: Apple’s M5 MacBook Air is down to its lowest price since July
Tech.content:
is an editor covering deals and gaming hardware. He joined in 2018, and after a two-year stint at Polygon, he rejoined The Verge in May 2025.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The latest 13-inch MacBook Air is currently available for $1,099.99, marking the second time we’ve seen this $200 discount following the company’s hefty price increases over the summer. Although the base model — which features Apple’s M5 processor, 16GB of RAM, and 512GB of storage — often sold for around $950 to $1,000 shortly after it launched in May, savings have been rare since July, making the current deal worth flagging. Amazon, Best Buy, and B&H Photo are all honoring the price across all color options.

If you’d prefer something with a larger screen, a six-speaker array instead of four, and slightly more power (with two additional GPU cores in the M5), Apple’s 15-inch MacBook Air is also on sale for $200 off. Amazon, Best Buy, and B&H Photo are each selling the 16GB RAM / 512GB SSD configuration in most colors for $1,299.99.

Although it’s pricier than the newer MacBook Neo, the Air offers better value in numerous ways. It’s an ideal choice if you want faster performance, as it offers double the RAM and a speedier CPU with more cores. You also get twice as much storage, better speakers, a backlit keyboard, and a larger, higher-resolution screen. Given said differences, it’s easy to see how the Air’s improvements might make it worth the extra cost for some people.

If you’re still on the fence, though, I’d recommend reading my colleague Antonio G. Di Benedetto’s reviews, both of which were published before the summer price increases.

Read our full MacBook Neo and M5 MacBook Air reviews.

Code in the iOS 27.3 beta suggests that Apple could add support for chatbots to its smart home hub. There’s a flag listed for a “Conversational Apps” category.
